issues.title: Here are our favorite deals from REI’s giant Holiday Sale
issues.summary: Black Friday has become a shopping season of its own, with retailers once again offering discounts well ahead of the actual shopping holiday. We’ve already rounded up some of the best early Black Friday deals we’ve come across, but if you’re looking to save on outdoor gear or pick up something for an upcoming trip, […]
issues.author: Sheena Vasani
issues.content_html:
Black Friday has become a shopping season of its own, with retailers once again offering discounts well ahead of the actual shopping holiday. We’ve already rounded up some of the best early Black Friday deals we’ve come across, but if you’re looking to save on outdoor gear or pick up something for an upcoming trip, REI’s annual Holiday Sale, which runs through November 23rd, is worth checking out.

As usual, the outdoor retailer is offering discounts on everything from smartwatches to camping equipment. In some cases, we’re seeing some of the lowest prices we’ve seen on our favorite wearables, including Garmin’s Forerunner 570, while gadgets like the InReach Mini 3 are also receiving sizable discounts. REI members can also use promo code HOLIDAY2026 to save 20 percent on one full-price item, plus an additional 20 percent on one REI Outlet item.

To save you time, we’ve sifted through the deluge of discounts to find an assortment of deals we recommend here at The Verge. We’ve also noted when competing retailers are offering lower prices on the same items, so you can be sure you’re getting the best deal possible.

Smartwatches and fitness tech

Garmin Forerunner 570

Garmin’s Forerunner 570 features a bright OLED display, skin temperature sensors, and a built-in speaker and microphone for taking calls. It also offers multiband GPS, personalized training plans, and up to 11 days of battery life.

Where to Buy:

  • $549.99 $449.99 at Amazon
  • $549.99 $449.99 at Best Buy
  • $550 $449.99 at REI

Garmin Venu 4

Garmin’s Venu 4 is geared toward the average athlete, offering heart rate alerts, detailed sleep insights, guided meditation, and a wheelchair mode. It also introduces caffeine and alcohol tracking, along with Garmin Coach, which tailors workouts to your fitness history, sleep, and recovery.

Where to Buy:

  • $549.93 at Amazon
  • $549.99 at Best Buy
  • $550 $449.99 at REI
  • REI, Amazon, and Best Buy are also selling the Garmin Lily 2 Active for $249.99 ($50 off), which is its lowest price to date. The stylish smartwatch is a great budget-friendly Garmin, especially for people with smaller wrists. Like the standard Lily 2, it offers basic fitness tracking, notifications, and up to five days of battery life; however, the so-called “Active” model adds a physical button, built-in GPS, and support for more sports tracking. Read our Lily 2 review.
  • The Garmin Vivoactive 6 has returned to its all-time low of $249.99 ($50 off) at Amazon, Walmart, and REI. The fitness watch offers up to 11 days of battery life and tracks a range of workouts, including walking, running, cycling, HIIT, golf, and more. It also provides extensive health monitoring, including wrist-based heart rate detection, menstrual cycle and pregnancy tracking, and a customizable morning report that summarizes helpful health-related info. However, it lacks ECG compatibility, though it does have a slightly slimmer profile than its predecessor.

Garmin Fenix 8

The Garmin Fenix 8 is a premium multisport watch that features a speaker, mic, and on-device assistant for calls, timers, and voice commands. It also offers elite battery life, dual-frequency GPS, and robust sensors. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

  • $999.99 $749.99 at Amazon (43mm)
  • $1099.99 $749.99 at Walmart (47mm)
  • $1099.99 $849.99 at REI (47mm)
  • The Wahoo Kickr V6 Smart Trainer is on sale at REI for $679.99 ($170 off). Like the more affordable Kickr Core 2 we covered in July, the Kickr V6 turns your existing bike into an indoor exercise bike, with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity for pairing with apps like Zwift. However, the higher-end trainer offers up to 2,200W of resistance and can replicate inclines of up to 20 percent, compared to the Core 2’s 1,800W and 16 percent. It also provides more accurate power measurements and is designed so that indoor rides feel more natural.

Phone accessories and entertainment

EcoFlow Rapid Magnetic Power Bank

EcoFlow’s Rapid Magnetic Power Bank is a 10,000mAh Qi2 battery that can snap to the back of your device if you’re using a newer iPhone or select Android devices, thus supplying it with up to 15W of power. It also includes a built-in USB-C cable that can provide up to 65W of power to larger devices, including a 13-inch MacBook Air.

Where to Buy:

  • $90 $66.93 at REI
  • If you own an older iPhone with a Lightning port, you can grab InfinityLab’s InstantGo 10,000 Power Bank for $41.93 (about $28 off) at REI. The portable battery features a 10,000mAh capacity and a built-in Lightning cable, making it a solid all-in-one option for days when you won’t be near an outlet. It also supports passthrough charging, so you can charge your phone and the power bank at the same time.
  • DJI’s Osmo Mobile 8 is on sale for around $128.99 ($21 off) at REI, Amazon, and Best Buy, which is $10 shy of its best price to date. The smartphone gimbal supports 360-degree horizontal rotation and Apple’s DockKit, which allows the gimbal to track and follow pets and people across a wider range of camera apps. This discounted Advanced Tracking Combo also includes a multifunctional module for tracking people and pets, as well as a built-in tripod and extension rod that make it easier to film yourself without someone behind the camera.

Soundcore Liberty 5

The Soundcore Liberty 5 feature adaptive noise cancellation and support for Dolby Audio, along with six swappable tips so you can find the right fit. They also sport an IP55 rating for water and dust resistance and can last up to 48 hours with the included charging case.

Where to Buy:

  • $129.99 $89.99 at Amazon
  • $129.99 $89.99 at Walmart
  • $130 $89.99 at REI
  • You can buy Soundcore’s AeroFit 2 for $79.99 ($20 off) at REI, Amazon, and Best Buy, which is $2 shy of their lowest price to date. Their open-ear design lets you listen to music while staying vigilant in your surroundings; they also feature adjustable ear hooks for a secure fit, IP55 water and dust resistance, and up to 42 hours of battery life with the included charging case.

Anker Nebula P1 projector

Anker’s Nebula P1 is a portable 1080p projector with built-in Google TV and two detachable Bluetooth speakers that deliver better sound than many all-in-one portable projectors. It offers 650 ANSI lumens of brightness and can project images up to 180 inches, while the speakers last up to 20 hours on a charge.

Where to Buy:

  • $799 $599.99 at Amazon
  • $799 $599 at Soundcore
  • $799 $699.99 at REI

Communication and safety gear

Garmin InReach Mini 3 Plus

The Mini 3 Plus is identical to the standard model in that it allows you to stay connected while off the grid; however, it also features an audible siren and the ability to send photos and voice messages, in addition to standard texts.

Where to Buy:

  • $499.99 $399.99 at Amazon
  • $499.99 $399.99 at REI
  • $499.99 $399.99 at Garmin
  • Garmin’s base InReach Mini 3 is available from REI, Amazon, and Garmin for around $349 ($100 off), nearly matching its lowest price to date. Like the Mini 2, the rugged, palm-sized satellite communicator lets you send texts, share your location, check the weather, and trigger SOS alerts when you’re off the grid, all while offering battery life that can outlast your average smartphone. Unlike the prior version, though, it features a color touchscreen, which makes it easier to navigate menus and bang out messages.
  • Garmin’s InReach Messenger Plus is also on sale at REI, Amazon, and direct from Garmin for $299.99 ($100 off), matching its best price to date. The subscription-based Plus model provides satellite connectivity and access to emergency services like the aforementioned InReach Mini 3, except it can also send photos and audio clips in addition to standard text messages.
  • The Chapter MIPS Bike Helmet is on sale starting at around $112.39 ($41 off) at REI, which nearly matches its best price to date. The lightweight helmet features a hidden PopLock for securing it with a U-lock or chain. It also has a sleek visor and a Micro-USB taillight with 30 lumens of brightness, one that automatically turns on when magnetically attached to the helmet.
  • Garmin’s Varia RTL515 Radar Taillight is on sale at REI and Amazon for $149.99 ($50 off), which is about $10 less than its all-time low. The headlight combines a bright LED light with a rearview radar that, when paired with a compatible device, warns you of cars approaching from behind from up to 153 yards away.

BCA Tracker 3 Plus Avalanche Transceiver

The Tracker 3 Plus is a pocketable, lightweight avalanche beacon designed to help locate people buried in snow. It features a real-time display, lights to guide searchers, and tools for finding multiple people. It also comes with a harness and batteries.

Where to Buy:

  • $349.95 $279.89 at REI

Camping and travel gear

Exped MegaMat Duo

The MegaMat Duo is a four-inch, self-inflating mattress that’s become one of our favorites thanks to its extra-wide design. It uses a combination of open-cell polyurethane foam and generous padding for comfort, which helps keep you warm when temperatures dip. It also makes for a stellar air mattress for guests.

Where to Buy:

  • $399.95 $299.89 at REI (medium)
  • $549.95 $412.39 at REI (queen)
  • $449.95 $337.39 at REI (long wide)
  • A small chair is nice to have for lounging by the campfire, and REI’s Flexlite Camp Chair is a great option now that it’s down to around $67.39 (about $22 off) in multiple colors at REI. It features an aluminum frame, a stable four-leg design, and a ripstop polyester seat with water and stain resistance. When you’re done, it also folds down quickly into a drawstring bag, so you can throw it in your car.

Kelty Low Loveseat

The Kelty Low Loveseat is a sturdy, low-profile camp chair built for two. It features a steel frame, a padded seat, and extra-large cup holders for your drinks or gear. It also includes a padded roll-tote storage bag, making it easy to transport when it’s folded down.

Where to Buy:

  • $149.95 $112.39 at REI
  • $149.95 $119.96 at Backcountry
  • REI is currently selling its Magma 30 Sleeping Bag in a variety of sizes starting at $243.93 ($105 off). The bag uses 850-fill-power, water-resistant down for warmth and weighs under 20 ounces, depending on the size, making it a great budget pick if you’re looking to get into ultralight backpacking. It also includes a hood to help retain heat, extra room around the feet, and a terrific zipper design that’s less likely to snag when you’re crawling in or out.

REI Siesta Hooded 20 Sleeping Bag

The Siesta prioritizes comfort with a roomy rectangular shape that gives you space to stretch out. The synthetic sleeping bag features an insulated hood — one that’s spacious enough to accommodate a real pillow — along with multiple zipper configurations so you can vent your feet or fully unzip it into a quilt-like blanket.

Where to Buy:

  • $149 $111.69 at REI (medium)
  • $159 $119.19 at REI (long)

Rumpl Original Puffy Blanket

Rumpl’s classic lightweight blanket features synthetic insulation for warmth, a weather-resistant outer shell, and a stuff sack. It also comes in an array of attractive designs and pairs with Rumpl’s Cape Clip, so you can wear it hands-free.

Where to Buy:

  • $99.95 $74.89 at REI (one-person)
  • $99.95 $74.96 at Rumpl (one-person)
  • $199.95 $149.89 at REI (two-person)
  • Osprey’s Atmos AG 65 Pack is on sale in several colors and size configurations for around $258.93 ($112 off) at REI, which is one of the lowest prices we’ve seen. The 65-liter pack — which remains a go-to option for The Verge’s own Brandon Widder — is loaded with all sorts of bells and whistles, including an integrated rain cover, a floating top lid, and plenty of compression straps. The hallmark, though, is the ventilation system, which leverages a 3D-suspended mesh for comfort and breathability, making it a great pick for multi-day trips.
  • REI’s Ruckpack Waist Pack is on sale for $33.69 ($12 off) at REI, which is one of the best prices we’ve seen as of late. Made from a water-repellent material, this small adjustable bag can be worn around your waist or across your body and features three interior pockets for keeping your essentials organized.

Sea to Summit Hanging Toiletry Bag

Sea to Summit’s small toiletry bag lets you keep all of your essentials close at hand for weekend getaways. It features a water–resistant fabric and a convenient hanging hook, along with internal mesh pockets so you can quickly find whatever it is you need.

Where to Buy:

  • $49.95 $37.39 at REI
  • The JetBoil Stash Cooking System is a compact, lightweight cooking system that’s currently down to $123.69 (about $41 off) atREI, which is one of the lowest prices we’ve seen all year. It features a standalone stove with a titanium burner and a 0.8-liter cooking pot, allowing you to boil water or heat food at your campsite. The pot comes with a lid and a pour handle, too, and everything can be stowed inside the pot when you’re finished, making it exceptionally easy to pack up.

Sea to Summit Aeros Premium Pillow

Sea to Summit’s lightweight, inflatable camping pillow features a soft memory foam layer, adjustable firmness, and a curved design that cradles your head. It’s also quick to inflate and includes patches to keep it from sliding while you sleep.

Where to Buy:

  • $54.95 $41.19 at REI (Regular)
  • $59.95 $44.89 at REI (Large)
  • $69.95 $52.39 at REI (XL)
  • You can buy the ultralight Nemo Tensor in multiple sizes starting at REI for $131.93 (about $88 off). Designed for backpacking, the four-season sleeping pad offers 3.5 inches of cushioning and insulation to keep you warm in colder conditions, with a 5.4 R-value. The nylon construction is also relatively quiet, which, frankly, isn’t the case with many of the camping pads we’ve used over the years.
  • Nemo’s Stargaze Evo-X is on sale for $99.99 ($80 off) at REI, which is a great price for the surprisingly portable camping chair. The plush, versatile chair automatically reclines when you lean back, making it ideal for relaxing around the campsite (and stargazing). It also features a padded headrest, two cupholders, and a folding frame. And did we mention it swings? Because it swings.
  • REI’s Wonderland Cot is down to $187.39 ($62 off) at REI. The foldable cot — which is designed more for car camping than anything else — features a spacious, padded sleeping surface, an adjustable backrest, and a sturdy aluminum and steel frame that supports up to 300 pounds. The new version also comes with a webbing carrying strap, making it easier to lug around than prior models.

Headlamps and lighting

Mpowerd Luci Solar String Lights: Color

Mpowerd’s solar-powered string lights are perfect for camping or a backyard shindig. The 18-foot string can display six colors and last up to 15 hours on a single charge; the case also doubles as a charger, allowing you to top off your phone in a pinch.

Where to Buy:

  • $54.95 $19.83 at REI
  • Black Diamond’s Spot, the newer version of the Spot 400 headlamp, is on sale for $47.89 ($12 off) at REI. It offers up to 450 lumens of adjustable brightness, up from 400, along with red night vision and an IPX7 water-resistance rating. You can also choose to power it with standard AAA batteries or Black Diamond’s rechargeable battery.
  • The Petzl Tikka is on sale at REI for $18.77 (about $16 off). The basic headlamp is a great option that features a max output of 350 lumens, tilt functionality, and an IPX4 rating, making it safe to use in light rain. It also features a lock function that prevents it from accidentally turning on when packed.

Black Diamond Moji Plus Lantern

The Moji Plus offers 200 lumens of warm, dimmable light and adjustable brightness, along with an IPX4 rating for water resistance. It also features a double-hook design and the same dual-fuel tech as the Spot 400 Headlamp, meaning you can use it with standard AAAs or Black Diamond’s rechargeable BD 1500 Li-ion battery.

Where to Buy:

issues.title: Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he’d lost coverage
issues.summary: The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.
issues.author: Rachana Pradhan, KFF Health News
issues.content_html:
Eli McCreary of Omaha, Nebraska, said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn’t insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.

McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.

“You’re required to do work to stay on,” McCreary said a representative told him. “And you haven’t fulfilled your work requirement.”

For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

“I don’t understand what job I can get,” McCreary said. “I can’t walk. I can hardly breathe. I can’t move around. What job am I going to get?”

McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation’s largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. “I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month,” he said.

Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary’s experience. In an emailed statement she said that “CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources.”

Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states will do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear whether they will be successful, because Trump could veto the measure.

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen said in December that state officials “certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform.” Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.

“We’re excited to be able to be the first to make it happen,” the Republican governor said.

Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn’t respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska’s Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout “has been very successful.” He pointed to state data showing 86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.

Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.

About 70,000 adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they’re working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.

To deploy the law’s Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska’s health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.

Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states, which outsource the work to companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska’s health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.

The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.

One of the companies has praised Nebraska’s implementation of work requirements. A post on Public Consulting Group’s website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux. “I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement,” Michaux said, crediting the firm’s “incredible relationship” with the state.

Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department “uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets.”

Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don’t know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have received inaccurate information. In December, Pillen said the state “won’t be adding workforce” to implement the work requirements, a decision those advocates have criticized. Pillen in July also instituted a government-wide hiring freeze.

Nebraska listed at least half a dozen contractors costing more than $250,000 each, including one person whose compensation exceeds $1.8 million, the documents show. Nebraska submitted the records to federal Medicaid regulators as part of a routine process to secure federal money. Powell said the funding requests “may not reflect actual expenditures.”

Sarah Maresh, a program director with the social justice advocacy nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed, said the amounts were “shocking.”

“When you put in complicated policies like this, there are large corporations making money behind the scenes,” Maresh said. “This just further confirms that it’s happening in Nebraska quietly.”

Confusion and Longer Wait Times

The Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other changes shepherded by Republicans will curtail insurance gains that came from the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. The GOP tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade, adds reporting requirements and restrictions making it harder for people to stay enrolled.

As of early July, most denials related to the work requirements among Nebraska adults applying for Medicaid were due to unsubmitted paperwork, according to internal documents from Nebraska’s health department that KFF Health News obtained through a public records request. The state wrote this was “expected.”

State data shows that average wait times at a Nebraska health department call center nearly doubled between May and July, going from about 13 minutes to 26 minutes, before declining in August. In interviews, advocates for Medicaid enrollees said they’ve encountered people who have waited on the phone for hours.

Nebraska received more than 101,000 calls in August, a 66% jump from May.

“If people are working, they just don’t have time to be sitting on the phone to go through all of this stuff,” said Kenny McMorris, CEO of the Charles Drew Health Center, a federally qualified health center in North Omaha. He said roughly half of Charles Drew’s 13,385 patients are on Medicaid, and of those, 42% are in the population subject to the work requirements.

“You can leverage the technology, but you still got to have people there to help,” McMorris said.

Then there are experiences the official data may not catch, like what happened to McCreary — saddled with figuring out what happened with his Medicaid benefits amid a health crisis, and whether it was even true that he had to work to keep them.

McCreary had heard about the Medicaid work requirements but didn’t know they might apply to him. Powell confirmed McCreary was eligible for Medicaid because of the ACA — putting him in the population subject to work requirements.

His ordeal underscores the fallout from being caught in confusing government systems and silos that aren’t obvious to the public.

“This cancer ain’t going to stop just because I ain’t got insurance,” he said. “It’s going to keep working on me.”

When he received the call from the hospital about his coverage, “I was really in despair,” McCreary said. Eventually, he said, he called for help.

Nebraska’s health department runs AccessNebraska, a call center for help with safety net benefits such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps. But the number McCreary recalls dialing ended up not being AccessNebraska — it was for a different call center, one for SNAP accounts that Nebraska outsources to a private company. Powell said the state has no record of McCreary calling the health department.

McCreary said the worker didn’t have a good explanation for why the Medicaid work requirements would apply to him. Before his health deteriorated, McCreary worked as a driver for an asphalt services company. He said he worked “until I couldn’t do the job anymore.”

“I really had hoped to work longer,” he said. “I kind of enjoyed that job.”

Attorneys and policy professionals who work with people on Medicaid and other public benefit programs said that McCreary’s substance use treatment, lasting four months starting in November 2025, and other health conditions should have exempted him.

The federal law outlines categories of exemptions, such as being too sick to work. People who are considered too ill include those who have a serious medical condition or a substance use disorder.

Nebraska’s health department said it sent tens of thousands of letters, text messages, and emails to inform enrollees about the new requirements. According to state documents, Nebraska said it would “implement enhancements” to its computer system and online portal, including allowing people to submit documents online and having “clear, plain-language” enrollee notices. McCreary, however, doesn’t have an account on Nebraska Medicaid’s online portal, preferring to handle things over the phone or in person.

He also said it’s possible he missed letters from Nebraska Medicaid about his coverage.

“I don’t know if it’s my fault or not,” McCreary said.

The Cornhusker State’s experience could be a harbinger of things to come. Next year, work requirements will apply to millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.

‘We Definitely Had Fun’

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s Medicaid changes are the most complicated in years — changes that government benefit experts say will strain and exacerbate long-standing problems with state technology systems for health benefits.

“It’s already a shaky system, and now you’ve added more burdens on top of that,” said Gelila Selassie, director of health advocacy for the nonprofit Justice in Aging.

Nebraska and federal officials, as well as consultants advising the state, detailed the difficulties and successes with the state’s May 1 launch during an August panel discussion at a national conference in Oregon.

“They said, ‘We’re going to go live May 1.’ To which CMS said, ‘Oh, my God!’” Brent Weaver, an official who specializes in Medicaid IT at the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said about Nebraska.

Nebraska officials knew “they weren’t as agile as they probably would have liked to have been,” Weaver said, “but they didn’t let that stop them.”

“If they fail, we looked at it as a failure,” he added in comments that broadly praised the state’s approach.

CMS did not answer questions from KFF Health News about Nebraska’s rollout and Weaver’s remarks.

In Nebraska, a group of 60 people held hours-long meetings three days a week that were “very exhausting,” Michaux, of Public Consulting Group, said during a different session at the conference.

“Our calendars were cleared, and that was the focus,” Michaux said.

Because CMS had not yet issued regulations outlining key details such as how people could get exemptions — it would do so June 1 — Nebraska officials said they had to rely on the law’s broad language to make initial decisions.

“We had to get comfortable being uncomfortable,” Jacob Kawamoto, a deputy director at Nebraska’s Medicaid division, said at the conference.

Public Consulting Group said it worked with the state to develop new guidance and “process guides” — materials for Nebraska eligibility workers with instructions on how to process Medicaid applications or renewals. Training materials for Nebraska caseworkers reviewed by KFF Health News refer to those guides.

“The training was very robust, and the process guides were very robust,” Michaux said.

Maresh disagreed with that characterization. “There are gaps” in the state’s training materials, she said, and caseworkers “are confused” about work requirements.

Public Consulting Group also helped the state institute changes to Nebraska’s Medicaid IT system, according to the company. “We are preparing for future updates and enhancements,” Michaux said.

In response to questions, Public Consulting Group spokesperson Alyssa Brown said the company “has supported Nebraska Medicaid via a broad range of consulting services since 2019, including work on federal and state compliance initiatives.” She said Michaux “discussed” the process guides at the conference but Nebraska developed them. Similarly, Brown said the company did not develop training.

Federal taxpayers will largely bear the costs of implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s Medicaid policies in Nebraska and elsewhere. Congress allocated $200 million in one-time funding to states. Under federal regulations, the U.S. government picks up most of the tab for state IT system changes, paying as much as 90% of the cost.

“Even though it was not so easy,” Michaux said at the conference, “we definitely had fun standing up the Medicaid work requirement program.”

Public Consulting Group’s employees, Brown told KFF Health News, are “passionate about public service and helping our clients improve the lives of the people they serve.”

Dropping Medicaid Enrollment

As of August, roughly 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied benefits because of Medicaid work requirements. Most denials were because people did not respond to requests for information.

Nebraska’s total Medicaid enrollment has declined by roughly 4,600 people since May, a drop of 1.4%, according to an August report.

As for McCreary, the Nebraska health department’s Powell maintained he experienced “no lapses in coverage” and said he was disenrolled from Medicaid after turning 65. Despite what McCreary said he was told, Powell said, Medicaid work requirements weren’t the reason: He aged out of Medicaid and into Medicare before they could be applied to him.

Selassie, of Justice in Aging, said McCreary’s care shouldn’t have been disrupted.

McCreary is now enrolled in Medicare, and Medicaid covers some of his health costs. He was able to reschedule his canceled appointments.

“The cancer has grown so much,” he said.

He had surgery in early November to remove his right kidney.

KFF Health News correspondent Samantha Liss contributed to this report.

issues.title: Brazil’s fertilizer gap is a global food risk
issues.summary: Brazil feeds 800 million people on imported fertilizer.
issues.author: Lorenzo Rosa
issues.content_html:
Brazilian agriculture feeds roughly 800 million people, about 10% of the world’s population. In 2024, according to World Trade Organization data, Brazil exported US$144.4 billion in agricultural products while importing just US$15.4 billion — a net surplus of roughly US$129 billion, more than four times Argentina’s, the next-largest net agricultural exporter. Brazil is the world’s largest exporter of soybeans, beef, poultry, coffee, sugar and orange juice, and a top-three producer and exporter of corn. Brazil alone supplies more than half of global soybean trade. The world’s food supply increasingly depends on Brazil, and Brazil’s harvests depend on fertilizer it barely produces.

That is the paradox: the country that feeds so much of the world cannot feed its own fields without imports from a handful of foreign suppliers. Its farms run on three nutrients — nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium — and, according to the latest UN Food and Agriculture Organization data, in 2024, Brazil imports roughly 90% of the fertilizer it used.

Brazilian farms use more than a tenth of the world’s fertilizer, but the country produces barely 1% of it, despite meaningful domestic capability, and imports nearly a fifth of all fertilizer traded internationally. By nutrient, the same data puts nitrogen import dependence at about 99%; Brazil runs the largest nitrogen-fertilizer trade deficit of any country in the world, at US$4.3 billion in 2024, with most supply coming from China, Russia, Nigeria and Oman. Even phosphate, which Brazil partly mines at home, is about 70% imported, mostly from Morocco and Russia. Even more concerning is potash, given its production is highly concentrated: Brazil imports about 98% of its potash, almost all from Canada, Russia and Belarus. A country that uses nearly a quarter of the world’s potash relies on just three suppliers for almost all of it. Global potash output is concentrated in just four countries, Canada, Russia, Belarus, and China, and potassium has no substitute as a plant nutrient.

Since Brazil is the world’s largest net food exporter, fertilizer concentration is what turns import dependence into a food-security risk. And because nitrogen fertilizer is made mostly from natural gas, it also turns every energy crisis into a farm crisis. When global prices spike, sanctions bite or shipping lanes close, the cost lands directly on Brazilian farms. Farmers who cannot afford or obtain fertilizer apply less, and yields fall. A fertilizer shock does not stay an industrial problem; it becomes a systemic risk to the global food supply, reaching every country that buys Brazilian soy, corn or meat. Energy security, fertilizer security and food security are, in practice, links in the same chain.

That risk is no longer being ignored. The shocks of recent years, from the price spike that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine to this year’s disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, have moved fertilizer from a niche commodity concern onto the agendas of governments and development banks.

In the United States, the Trump administration has committed more than US$1.3 billion across eight projects to expand domestic fertilizer manufacturing, and multilateral development banks issued a joint statement in August 2026pledging to shore up fertilizer supply chains worldwide. Brazil is moving, too: its National Fertilizer Plan sets targets to raise domestic potash fertilizer production to 6.3 million metric tons by 2030 and 14.6 million metric tons a year by 2050, measured as potassium oxide (K₂O), part of a broader goal to cut imports to about 45% of the fertilizer Brazil uses by 2050. The Profert law, signed in September 2026, goes further, authorizing up to R$10 billion (about US$2 billion) in tax credits and incentives for domestic fertilizer plants. Together, these moves signal that fertilizer is finally being treated as a matter of food security — and, increasingly, of national security.

Building resilience means producing more of these nutrients at home, and there are two complementary ways to do it. The first is large-scale and centralized: mines and industrial complexes built on Brazil’s own mineral and energy resources. Brazil holds substantial, largely undeveloped potash reserves, including deposits in Amazonas state that companies such as Brazil Potash are seeking to develop. Meanwhile, Petrobras has signaled plans to restart two idled ammonia and urea plants and build two new ones, aiming to cut Brazil’s reliance on imported potash and nitrogen. Brazil Potash, which funded this research, is developing one of those deposits in Amazonas. Such projects take years and millions of dollars to build, but once running, they deliver the volume and low cost per metric ton that only scale can provide, the backbone any serious strategy needs.

The second is small-scale and decentralized: modular units, above all for nitrogen, that run on renewable power or agricultural waste and sit close to the farms they serve. They can be built faster and added step by step, spreading risk across many sites instead of concentrating it in a few, and shortening the long haul from port to field. The same logic extends to potassium: recovery systems that capture it from manure, crop residues and food-processing wastecan create a regional supply alongside mined potash.

Brazil does not have to choose between the two. Potash and phosphate are geological: they depend on mineable reserves, which favors large, centralized operations where those reserves exist. Nitrogen is an energy problem, so it can draw on both: large plants for volume, and decentralized, renewable-powered production built on Brazil’s abundant hydropower.

Making both models work will take coordinated leadership from policymakers, industry and investors. The policy tools now exist; what matters is whether they turn into projects that get built. International finance is lining up too: the six development banks behind the August statement, including the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, are preparing a joint roadmap to finance fertilizer production, storage and transport, an effort the G20 has welcomed. Brazil should be first in line to use it. It can become more self-sufficient in fertilizer while remaining open to the world. The more secure Brazil’s agricultural engine is, the more reliably it can keep sharing its surplus with everyone else who depends on it.

The next disruption to potash or nitrogen supply, and there will be one, will not ask Brazil’s farmers for a grace period. The time to build resilience is before the shock, not after it. Brazil has shown it can feed the world. The next test is whether it can secure what it needs to keep doing so, because when Brazil’s fields falter, the whole world’s food supply feels it.
