issues.title: Nvidia had no succession plan when Jensen Huang quit. Former Fortune 500 CEOs call it ‘preposterous’
issues.summary: Jensen Huang had 60 direct reports and no clear heir. Ex-CEOs weigh in on how that could have been allowed to happen.
issues.author: Shawn Tully
issues.content_html:
Nvidia’s total lack of the settled succession plan that’s a cornerstone of all well-run companies exposed a shocking weakness in its corporate governance. That’s the view of three former Fortune500 CEOs, and a leading consultant, whom Fortune interviewed on arguably the most consequential leadership earthquake ever to rock the business world. Each of the former CEOs serves on prominent corporate boards.

On November 12, the Nvidia board issued a press release announcing Jensen Huang’s resignation shortly after reports of the CEO’s second affair emerged. Nvidia stated that longtime CFO Colette Kress will immediately start serving as “interim CEO” while the directors conduct a “search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.”

Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft, before joining Nvidia in 2013. According to her resume posted on the Nvidia website, Kress’s past jobs don’t include any positions where she’s run a business or been responsible for a P&L. Hence, it’s highly probable that she’s a temporary pick, not a candidate to replace Huang.

It’s not clear if Nvidia had an emergency succession plan in place where Kress would temporarily take the top job in a crisis, or whether it had no plan at all and just improvised. In the opinion of one of the retired CEOs Fortune interviewed, it’s the latter. (They’re identified here as ex-CEOs 1, 2, and 3.) “It seems like a knee-jerk, panic reaction where the board’s saying, ‘We’ve got to name someone!'” says ex-CEO 3. “You’ve got to ask why a tech company would go with a financial person.”

It astounds these sources that the world’s second-most-valuable company, in business 33 years and public for 27, didn’t have a seasoned leader long groomed for the role ready to step in—especially given that Huang will turn 64 in February, and is already the oldest CEO by far in the Mag Seven. For these observers, that failure is the ultimate sign of poor corporate governance, and a shocking disappointment for an enterprise that until now, seemed to be doing just about everything right.

The sources identified four red flags warning that if its co-founder and America’s most celebrated tech CEO suddenly exited, Nvidia would face a stunning vacuum of leadership.

First: The success problem

Huang’s feat of hiking Nvidia’s valuation by well over $5 trillion in just four years to a peak of $5.8 trillion in early October—the highest summit ever reached—has never been equaled. But that record so intoxicated investors that they didn’t install the safeguards that should have protected Nvidia should this ultimate “key man” depart in a crisis.

“No one peeled back the layers on how Nvidia was run because they were so successful,” says ex-CEO 1. “No one looked behind the curtain. Their success lulled people into a false sense of security.” This person notes that Huang’s obsession with occupying center stage, with casting himself as the leather-jacketed face of AI, and his otherwise slick salesmanship should have stirred doubts. “This is preposterous,” says this interviewee. “When you have a celebrity CEO, that person merits a closer look, especially when you have a leader who’s always putting on a show.”

Second: The lax board issue

Unlike Elon Musk at SpaceX, Sergey Brin and Larry Page at Alphabet, and Mark Zuckerberg at Meta Platforms, Huang does not own a special class of supermajority stock that gives him control over the board. On the contrary, Nvidia has a single category of Class A shares that each carry one vote. In terms of percentages, its ownership resembles the profile at many Fortune 500 members: Nvidia’s largest shareholders are the big institutions; Blackstone leads at 8.1%, followed by Vanguard (6.5%), State Street (4.2%), Fidelity (3.9%), and a combination of Morgan Stanley, T. Rowe Price and J.P. Morgan at around 5%. Huang holds “just” 3.5%.

Despite this highly diverse, non-concentrated ownership, it appears that Huang totally controlled the board. “In any company that runs well over time,” says ex-CEO 2, “you’ll find the board has lots of current or retired CEOs, and credible outside senior executives. When you see a board that looks like a lot of old friends and people who’ve been there for decades, it flashes danger.”

Of the seven directors excluding Huang, none has served as CEO of a Fortune 500 company, and four are mainstays of between 13 and 29 years. “The board wasn’t paying attention to how the company was run,” says ex-CEO 2. “When you have a CEO leave and everybody is asking what is the succession plan, the directors aren’t doing their job.” Ex-CEO 2 avows that indeed, the board’s first responsibility is preparing a successor: “It’s the most important thing the board does by a mile. The ground has to be plowed for succession. The board likes to talk about M&A and all these exotic things but they pale beside succession. The directors should be meeting regularly on the succession subject and talking about the best prospects at the next level, and level below that. They should be making sure those candidates get the best roles to prepare them.”

Ex-CEO 1 states that in the first year or two of a relatively young CEO’s reign, the board may not yet have anointed their permanent replacement. But, the ex-CEO adds, “you’re moving people through different settings to see if they can grow, moving towards choosing the heir.” Hence, after a short interim period, a highly qualified candidate will ascend from a super-strong bench. Far more often, a permanent replacement stands in the wings, ready to take charge in the event the current CEO suddenly departs.

Echoing ex-CEO 1, ex-CEO 3 intones that “Boards have all kinds of governance rules but just two major responsibilities. First, don’t do a deal that kills you, and second, have the right person running the place and a backup plan to replace them. Nvidia’s board failed on one of the two big items.”

The leading consultant highlights the dangers of the Nvidia predicament. “The lesson from Nvidia is that emergencies happen more often than you think and it’s a big mistake to have a structure and mindset that assumes they won’t happen to you,” notes this person. “That Nvidia has no obvious successor imposes a real cost.”

Third: The “too many reports” pitfall

Huang talked proudly about overseeing around 60 “direct reports,” extolling the supposed virtues of a “flat” organization. What appears to be an extreme division of responsibility may account for the lack of a leader ready to lift the mantle from the legend. “It’s highly possible that none of those lieutenants had enough responsibility to have actually been tested,” notes ex-CEO 3. Adds ex-CEO 1, “In big companies, the optimal number of direct reports is 8 to 12. The presence of 60 direct reports that Huang was making a big deal about tells you the board wasn’t doing its job.”

The issue also struck the consultant as a major negative. “The downside of having a very high number of direct reports is that none have been exposed to top roles in a deep and meaningful way. So it’s hard to imagine anyone internally who is ready to take over.”

Fourth: The “what do we do now?” issue

The consultant reckons that training an insider would prove a big challenge. “They’d have to telescope the training to get the candidates up to speed in a hurry since it appears they haven’t been doing that and need to catch up,” says this person. Or, Nvidia could look outside. Ex-CEO 3 believes they’d go not for a veteran in, say, their early 60s, but a young tiger in their 40s or early 50s. “They’d want someone who is, say, 50 and wants to show the world something,” says this observer.

Ex-CEO 2 concludes that the board was so excessively lax that, “If Nvidia hadn’t been performing well, it would have been exhibit A for an activist attack.” The fall of Jensen Huang unleashed another kind of broadside that exposed a big need for reform, and hopefully, it will have the same legacy as a raid from outsiders: A new era where this exceptional performer masters what it’s sorely lacking, and what most of the Fortune 500 already does far better: strong corporate governance.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: $970 million Pacsun CEO says Gen Alpha and Gen Z are ‘greatly misunderstood’—so she made a board of 13- to 22-year-olds to give her advice
issues.summary: Brieane Olson, the CEO of Pacsun, says leaders will get a “get a much better return” if they listen to Gen Z and Gen Alpha instead of writing them off.
issues.author: Emma Burleigh
issues.content_html:
Bosses and senior staffers often moan about how young professionals are disengaged and lack initiative. But Brieane Olson, the CEO of Pacsun, warns against overlooking Gen Z and Gen Alpha—and she’s even ensuring they get a seat at the table of the fashion giant that hit $970 million in sales last year.

“I definitely felt, having spent so much time on the front-line with young consumers, that Gen Z and Gen Alpha were greatly misunderstood,” Olson tells Fortune. “And so, what could we do as a brand that caters to young people to really give them a seat at the table and to build something meaningful and really put community first?”

Once every year, Pacsun’s Youth Advisory Council gathers with company executives to discuss big business concerns.

The mini board of directors—comprised of 15 Gen Alpha and Gen Zers aged 13 to 22 who are rotated in each year—weigh in on pressing industry needs, what Pacsun should do differently, and the best paths moving forward.

The country’s youngest minds bring critical feedback directly to Olson and other company executives, touching upon everything from the customer experience to the way stores operate.

“I think one of the things that has taught me personally about working with this council over the last two years, is really that working with these younger generations requires sometimes giving additional context. And so it’s really important to bring them along for the journey and to answer the whys before they become a why,” the CEO says. “The most important thing is to truly listen—allow to have a dialogue, be a part of the reasoning, the why, the discussions—and you get a much better return.”

Pacsun taps 300 Gen Z and Gen Alpha ambassadors to help shape the company

Pacsun’s youth council quickly gained popularity among young generations wanting their voices to be heard.

The company hand-selected participants in its first year spanning between 2024 and 2025, but when it opened the floodgates to young people across the country, almost 1,000 people applied to the 2026 to 2027 cohort. The surge of interest ended up fueling an entirely new ambassador program, giving even more young people an opportunity to influence the brand.

The company now works with about 300 13- to 22-year-olds who weigh in on business areas they’re most passionate about—including design, styling, visual arts, and emerging trends. Olson says Pacsun’s young advisors have helped with everything from redesigning how store flows should work, to analyzing and contrasting what retail competitors are up to. While some employers scrutinize young generations for being disengaged or unwilling to contribute, Pacsun’s CEO recognizes how motivated they are to have an impact, and is giving them the floor.

“They really do have a true seat at the table,” Olson says. “They have a direct line of communication with myself and all of the other leaders…”

“In return, they’re also getting great mentorship, and they’re getting opportunity and access and the ability to help co-create the future of the brand. And I think there’s a lot of shared benefit to bringing young people in, and helping also to fight the stereotypes that these younger generations are facing.”

It’s just one of several youth initiatives Olson has introduced since taking the reins as CEO in 2023

Pacsun has also been hosting a Purpose Summit for the past two years, bringing brand partners together with the company’s youth council.

Olson says tech partners from Snapchat, Pinterest, and TikTok have all attended, as well as philanthropic collaborators like Selena Gomez’s Rare Impact Fund. Executives, creators, cultural leaders, brand partners, and young voices exchange ideas, discuss industry hurdles, and strategize how to lead a business with purpose at the day-long event.

Additionally, Pacsun releases a youth report every year that captures a snapshot of the attitudes, behaviors, spending habits, and cultural interests of thousands of Gen Z and Gen Alpha survey participants.

“Creating moments and opportunities for us to pause and really think about how we’re leading and what we need to do differently is important,” Olson says, adding that Pacsun’s youth research helps the company do a “better job to collectively create a future that is a better place for the youth.”

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: What 50 years in business has taught Springetts about building brands that thrive
issues.summary: As it celebrates its half-century, the agency that named The Happy Egg Co., Nuii and Frubes shares the wisdom it's acquired along the way. Most UK businesses don't make it to their fifth birthday; acc...
issues.author: Tom May
issues.content_html:
As it celebrates its half-century, the agency that named The Happy Egg Co., Nuii and Frubes shares the wisdom it's acquired along the way.

Most UK businesses don't make it to their fifth birthday; according to the ONS, fewer than four in 10 do. Getting to 50, to many, can seem like an impossible dream. So when a studio spends five decades successfully serving food and drink brands through recessions, retail revolutions and the rise of social media, it's worth hearing what it has to say.

I'm talking here about Springetts, which today describes itself as a "brand life-stage agency". Founded in 1976 by Rod Springetts, its list of clients reads like the contents of my kitchen cupboard right now: Weetabix, Walkers, Ryvita, Kettle Chips, McVitie's, Nestlé Fab, Linda McCartney and Rubicon among them.

It's also created a fair few brands of its own, coining Frubes, Frijj, The Happy Egg Co., Walkers Salt & Lineker and, more recently, the premium ice cream brand Nuii. (Anyone else feeling peckish yet?) Along the way, it's picked up 24 Pentawards and 19 Design Effectiveness Awards.

After 50 years of this kind of success, you might expect the agency to be feeling pretty smug about itself. But rather than resting on its laurels, it's marking its anniversary with a burst of fresh energy, relaunching with new positioning and a refreshed identity.

And here's where Creative Boom readers can benefit directly: it's also launched a field guide to help others learn from its success.

What you can learn

Titled How Brands Live Forever, the guide distils half a century of experience into a framework the agency calls Forever Brands. So what's it all about, exactly?

The central idea of the guide is simple but often overlooked: design for longevity rather than novelty. That involves, according to the agency, a level of restraint.

As creatives, we of course are constantly chasing the new. But designing for 'forever' isn't about that. Instead, it's about tying fresh ideas to what's already familiar and protecting what existing customers love. It's about going deeper into what a brand already has, rather than tearing it up every few years because someone fancies a change.

"A great brand story isn't just told. It's retold again and again," stresses CEO Paul Williams. "Food and drink brands are never purely functional. The job is understanding the emotional role they play, and the story people want to be part of. That's how you make brands loved for generations to come."

In practice, that means thinking beyond individual packs and products, and building systems of recognition that flex across every channel and keep the story going.

The four life stages of a brand

At the centre of this approach is the notion that brands pass through four distinct life stages, each with its own job to do:

  • Launch: make an entrance, create attraction and ignite the spark.
  • Grow: build momentum, grow desire and make people want more.
  • Extend: gain new ground, deepen attachment and give people more to love.
  • Renew: reclaim relevance, reignite interest and make people fall in love again.

Starting with the Launch stage, the guide says: "Every new brand enters a crowded room. When 85% of new brands fail, the challenge is not simply to exist; it's to be instantly understood, emotionally felt and easy to remember."

It then breaks this stage into four principles: start with a point of view, build memory blocks, bend category codes and design for becoming, not just being. (The point of that last one is that a launch identity needs room to grow, into channels, products and audiences that don't exist yet.)

At the other end of the life cycle, the Renew stage is about rescuing brands that have faded into the background. "The danger for legacy brands is not age, it's invisibility," says design director Sophie Broderick. "Renewal gives a brand back its presence, its point of view and its reason to be chosen now."

The importance of culture

Another thing Springetts says has contributed to its 50-year success is its culture. The company has always been fiercely designer-led, and says it does so without the usual layers of account management.

That means designers own the client relationships and lead the strategic conversations about business challenges and opportunities, which means the thinking and the doing are blended together: what it calls the 'designer brain'.

To learn more about all of this, you're best off reading the guide itself. But I'd say the main lesson is that the brands that last don't get complacent; they adapt. Fifty years on, with a new look and a philosophy written down clearly, Springetts seems to be taking its own advice.

issues.title: Tanmay Saxena on leaving a banking job to make surreal photographs about life's stranger moments
issues.summary: From superheroes experiencing creative slumps to braids that trace generations of womanhood, the London-based artist draws on memories and the unexpected things he encounters while wandering. Even sup...
issues.author: Ayla Angelos
issues.content_html:
From superheroes experiencing creative slumps to braids that trace generations of womanhood, the London-based artist draws on memories and the unexpected things he encounters while wandering.

Even superheroes need a day off sometimes. For London-based photographer and artist Tanmay Saxena, this rather amusing thought became the starting point for Superhero Downtime, a photograph made earlier this year during a period when his own creative powers weren't quite firing on all cylinders. As anyone who's experienced a creative block will know, it's an uncomfortable feeling, particularly when making things is such a big part of who you are. So, naturally, Tanmay decided to make something out of it.

"It's very personal to me," he says. "I shot it earlier this year while going through a minor creative drought. It is a self-assuring and reflective piece about the lulls that come without warning but have the potency to make one feel very lost and confused." He also appreciates the irony of creating something from a momentary lack of creativity, which feels rather fitting for an artist whose work frequently finds humour and meaning in life's peculiarities.

Originally from India, Tanmay moved to London around 18 years ago and spent a decade working as a business analyst at a bank in the City. It was a career that, despite its longevity, never quite felt right. "That was not what I was naturally meant to do, and so a sadness became part of my daily life," he recalls. "It was only after I gave that life up and took up art that I began my second life."

That second life has since seen him explore photography, moving image fabric and painting, creating curious, often surreal scenes that draw on everything from personal memories and nostalgia to the lives of people he's encountered. His work has also appeared in exhibitions at London's National Portrait Gallery, Helm Gallery and HBH Gallery, among others.

Spend some time looking through his photographs, and there's a dreamlike quality to them, as though something familiar has been plucked from everyday life and given a slightly uncanny feeling. His subjects are often solitary, caught in moments of contemplation, while the ideas behind them can be deeply personal or wonderfully strange.

As for where these ideas come from, Tanmay isn't entirely sure himself. "I have a very open membrane to catch ideas first. In fact, they just come to me rather than me looking for them," he explains. "I wander around a lot, aimlessly and quite literally. And subconsciously things get registered that at a later moment turn into executable ideas."

Sometimes he'll eventually trace a finished piece back to something he saw or experienced months earlier. Other times, the connection remains a mystery. "Sometimes I do not know why I made what I made," he admits.

One work that took a little more planning is The Tree of She, a piece he'd been hoping to create for almost a year before everything finally fell into place. Drawing on his childhood in India's small towns and villages, it explores the different stages of womanhood through the image of a braid, which becomes a way of thinking about roots, family histories and the passing of time. "I wanted to trace the journey of womanhood as seen by me while growing up in small towns and villages of India," he explains. "The everyday life of a woman through the different phases and ages depicted through her braid/roots and how the world around her flows through it for generations after generations."

This willingness to follow an idea wherever it leads also shapes how Tanmay works behind the camera. He estimates that around 70 per cent of any finished piece comes from his own decisions, while the remaining 30 per cent is down to circumstances beyond his control. He's quite happy with that arrangement, allowing the location, people and unexpected happenings of a shoot to have their say. "When it comes to photographing people, I can catch a glimpse of their mood and energy and let the narration be guided by it rather than being hard-handed about it," he says.

It's perhaps why his work can feel so open to interpretation, with enough familiar details to draw us in and enough unanswered questions to keep us looking. Tanmay is keen to preserve that freedom for his audience, too. Rather than spelling out what each photograph should mean, he prefers to "keep it open-ended and set the viewer on a path that can go anywhere I may not have envisioned".

Next up, he's working on a couple more surreal projects spanning photography and moving image, alongside a solo exhibition bringing the two mediums together. And if Superhero Downtime is anything to go by, even the quieter, less productive moments might end up fighting their way into the work. After all, you never quite know when an idea might arrive.

issues.title: This identity for a women's sports community swaps cheerleading for real talk
issues.summary: New Zealand studio Essential Viewing crafted an identity for Woven that turns triathlon's three disciplines into a braided symbol. The word Ironman might make you think of superhero movies. But it's a...
issues.author: Tom May
issues.content_html:
New Zealand studio Essential Viewing crafted an identity for Woven that turns triathlon's three disciplines into a braided symbol.

The word Ironman might make you think of superhero movies. But it's actually the name for a type of long-distance triathlon, in which competitors swim 3.8km, cycle 180 km, and then run a full 42.2km marathon, all in a single day.

The first Ironman race took place in Hawaii in 1978. Since then, the Ironman Group has grown it into a global series of hundreds of events.

But for all the global reach of the sport, not enough women are signing up. The organisation wanted to change that. It already had a women's community, Women For Tri, which launched in 2014. But it wanted to think bigger, to get closer to its stated goal of having an equal number of male and female participants. So it approached Essential Viewing, a women-owned, New Zealand-based brand studio.

Essential Viewing handled the naming, brand strategy, identity, tone of voice, merch design and launch campaign. The new brand, titled Woven, was unveiled at the Ironman World Championship in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, in October, and has since rolled out across 45 territories.

Brand concept

The name might not seem obvious at first, but it makes perfect sense once you think about it. Triathlon is, after all, made of three disciplines woven together. Woven, then, sets out to weave together women from all kinds of backgrounds, while avoiding the usual sporting clichés.

That concept is reflected clearly in the symbol. It's made from three interlocking chevrons, representing swim, bike and run, which stack and overlap to form a subtle 'W'. Essential Viewing calls it a "braid of resilience"," and it's anchored by the tagline 'Strength in every thread'.

In practice, it's a simple, flexible mark that works well in all the places it needs to live. Repeated down the spine of a black jacket, it becomes a bold orange pattern. As a brushed metal charm threaded through laces, it feels like jewellery. As a temporary tattoo, it looks like a badge of honour.

Tone of voice

For me, what really sets Woven apart, though, is its tone of voice, which is mercifully free of the trite "You go, girl!" messaging that can quickly become grating. Instead, Essential Viewing aimed for an authenticity that "validates the truths and ambition of our audience", as an antidote to imposter syndrome. The guiding insight here is that the only requirement for entry is the will to try.

That comes through most clearly in the campaign line 'I Am Not One Thing'. On billboards, it's paired with 'Neither Is My Sport', alongside images of a woman in deep concentration, a swimmer gasping for breath and a mother kissing her child.

On another execution, rows of small type list the roles that make up a life: mother, friend and sister; runner, cyclist and swimmer; accountant and nurse.

The message is clear: you don't have to be a full-time athlete to belong here. The photography, meanwhile, is all close-ups on freckled, sunburnt faces, motion-blurred swimmers churning through water and grainy textures of bubbles and tarmac. It's as far from airbrushed as you can get. Instead, it looks exactly how triathlon feels: gritty, tough and messy.

Garage gradients

Unusually for a sports brand, the identity was inspired by "the raw heart-on-the-sleeve essence of 90s UK garage music culture", according to the studio. And you can see that in the hazy, grainy gradients of orange, pink, lilac and blue, which feel more like a club flyer than a sports brand.

Those gradients map to moods, by the way: cool blues for support and care, hot oranges for power and energy, and pinks for the excitement of race day. They sit alongside a wide, confident sans-serif for headlines like 'Progress Over Perfection' and 'Born For This, Made For This', with small monospaced type running across images like a ticker: 'We Are Woven. Together In Triathlon.'

That club-culture influence carries into the merch, which blurs the lines between athletics and streetwear in a good way. It makes triathlon feel like something women would want to be part of, rather than just something to endure.

Essential Viewing also wrote, directed and produced the campaign's hero film, Not One Thing, which acts as the centrepiece of a 12-month rollout across digital, social, Strava, events and merchandise.

The studio says that Woven has been "fiercely embraced by the global triathlon community". Given how much warmer and more authentic it feels than typical sports branding, that's not hard to believe.

issues.title: Koto points Giffgaff towards its next chapter with a signpost-led rebrand
issues.summary: The global agency gives the challenger telecoms brand a bolder, greener identity built around a simple signpost. Giffgaff is a UK-based mobile operator that has gradually grown into a broadband provid...
issues.author: Tom May
issues.content_html:
The global agency gives the challenger telecoms brand a bolder, greener identity built around a simple signpost.

Giffgaff is a UK-based mobile operator that has gradually grown into a broadband provider, with more than 4 million members. Although it's been part of Virgin Media O2 since the two big brands merged in 2021, it still sees itself as a challenger brand.

So what's so different about it? Its main selling point is flexibility. While it does offer longer contracts on phones and broadband, most of its SIM plans are monthly rolling or pay-as-you-go, meaning you can switch plans month to month without huge fees.

Giffgaff also doesn't do mid-contract price rises, lets members switch plans up or down if their circumstances change, and even tells them if a cheaper plan would suit them better. EU roaming of up to 5GB is included on plans, too.

The company is a certified B Corporation and emphasises sustainability in the way it operates. For instance, it sells refurbished phones alongside new ones.

Rebranding a challenger brand, though, is always a bit of a, well, challenge. Change things too much, and you lose the quirky personality that attracted people to sign up in the first place. Change things too little, and… what's the point?

That's the balancing act global creative agency Koto faced. With new entrants crowding into an already competitive market, Giffgaff asked it to set the brand up for its next chapter while holding on to what makes it different. It delivered exactly that, with a fresh identity centred around the concept of a signpost.

Logo design

That signpost is in the new wordmark, although you might not spot it if you're not looking carefully. The final 'f' now ends in a pointed tip, turning it into a little arrow. That shape is also peppered throughout the whole identity, directing the eye to prices, pointing to offers and generally helping users work out where to go and what to do next.

"Giffgaff has always had a strong personality," says Joe Ling, creative director at Koto. "The challenge was to give it room to evolve without losing the energy and attitude that makes it unmistakable. We took the idea of helping members decide what's next, and expressed it through a simple signpost.

"Built into the logo and carried through the wider system, it gives the identity a clear organising idea that feels distinctive to Giffgaff while playing a practical role in all its communications." The device, by the way, works just as well off screen. For example, green packing tape printed with a "Your Next Move" slogan is slapped across brown cardboard parcels. It's just the kind of little, well-thought-out touch that makes an identity feel lived-in.

Colours, type and photography

As for the colour scheme, the familiar black-and-white palette is now joined by a feisty dose of acid green. This gives the brand renewed confidence and helps it stand out in a market that's typically characterised by blues, reds and purples.

Koto has also created a custom font, Giffsans: a tall, condensed and punchy sans that gives snappy slogans like "Great tech. No traps." the impact they need to land. A distinctive 'gg' ligature, meanwhile, connects back to the original logo in a way that feels natural.

In terms of photography, Koto has avoided the trap of glossy stock shots and gone for a candid, flash-lit, TikTok feel instead. We're talking friends with arms around each other, a couple laughing on a night out, two sunburnt older men in swim shorts by the sea. None of it looks professionally shot; instead, it feels like it was created by normal people in the moment, which suits a brand that leans heavily into community.

Digital system

As for the all-important website and app, Koto has also delivered a system that's simple to follow and use, without losing the quirky personality, which is a tough tightrope to walk. Importantly, it's built on Giffgaff's existing design tokens and ready for development from day one, so it can be rolled out rather than sitting in a deck. An app promo asks you to take "Control without the faff", which is exactly the sort of Giffgaff language users will expect.

"Our over 4 million members have always been at the heart of Giffgaff, and this next chapter is no different," says Georgina Bramall, chief marketing officer at Giffgaff. "We've earned their trust by looking after them, and we want to keep earning it as their lives change. The category can feel needlessly complicated, so this new look and feel takes what people already love about us and makes it even simpler, bolder and relevant, delivering value you can see straight away."

"A good deal gives people a reason to look," says James Greenfield, founder and CEO of Koto. "With Giffgaff we wanted to bring their character to life, brand and offer reinforcing each other. It's about remembering what unmistakably Giffgaff feels like."

The refresh is rolling out across Giffgaff's website, app and email campaigns, and its upcoming Black Friday campaign will be a big test of the system in action. It's all part of a longer-term partnership between the two companies, with Koto continuing to develop Giffgaff's brand strategy and identity as the business evolves.

issues.title: The Peralta D Supercar Is Literally Sculpted From Copper
issues.summary: Designed by Fabrizio Giugiaro, the one-off grand tourer pairs hand-hammered copper bodywork with a sculptural silhouette
issues.author: Will Sabel Courtney
issues.content_html:
For the last century or so, ever since wood fell out of style, the bodies of most automobiles have been made from a few tried-and-true materials: carbon fiber, fiberglass, aluminum, and steel, with the metals proving most popular. The choices are a balancing act, forcing carmakers to weigh price, safety, convenience, and appearance to determine which substance makes the most sense for the masses.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

But what if you didn’t have to worry about such concerns? What if cost was no object, practicality a formality, and there was no need to cater to the wants of more than one owner? Well, that was the lucky circumstance designer Fabrizio Giugiaro, founder and CEO of GFG Style, found himself in when creating the Peralta D, a gran turismo with a body made of hand-hammered copper.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

“It was a proposal I made to the client, Carlos Peralta,” Giugiaro says. The duo had worked together before on the design house’s first one-off automobile, the spitshine-polished 1980s-esque Peralta S. For the follow-up, Giugiaro wanted to draw a deeper connection to the owner. As an industrialist, Peralta has business interests involving copper, so Giugiaro suggested it as the material.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

Giugiaro’s name is well known in the automotive world. His father, Giorgetto Giugiaro , is a master of clean-line designs—he penned the DeLorean DMC-12, the BMW M1, the original Lotus Esprit, and the first Volkswagen Golf. The senior Giugiaro’s career has included work for Ferrari, Lamborghini, Bugatti, and many more of the world’s most notable automotive brands. The father-and-son duo founded GFG Style together over a decade ago, but it’s only been in recent years that they’ve been dedicating their talents to bespoke coachbuilt cars for individual collectors, as with the Peralta D.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

And while using copper for a car’s bodywork may be unorthodox, the designer says it wasn’t as difficult as it may seem. “It really surprised us that copper proved to be much more malleable than the aluminum we had worked with previously; it is also considerably easier to weld and polish,” Fabrizio says. “Of course, it does come with the disadvantage of greater weight, but since it was combined with a supporting structure made entirely of carbon fiber, the overall balance between the materials ultimately worked out well.”

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

Beneath all that copper lies the chassis of a 2025 Maserati GranTurismo Trofeo—itself a stylish design, but one far removed from the almost brutalist simplicity of the Peralta D’s angles. Instead of traditional doors, the car features a dramatic opening system inspired by the Peralta S’s single-motion dome, with independently opening side windows and gullwing-style openings at the rear to access the back seats.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

Inside, copper-colored leather adorns most surfaces, broken up (almost) only by the infotainment and dashboard screens, which offer some of the few hints of its Maserati roots. Meant to showcase the bond between its owner and his daughters, the car comes with a few (perhaps stereotypically) female-oriented features, such as a passenger-side makeup station with an illuminated mirror and dedicated cosmetic storage. And while the rear seats are tight, a retractable refrigerator designed to hold a bottle of champagne and four copper glasses means occupants can easily distract themselves.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

While the Peralta D might seem to push the boundaries—or at least the materials—of road-going automobile design to their limits, Fabrizio suggests even wilder builds may follow in its tire tracks.

“I have another alternative material in mind, one that has only ever been used once before,” he says, “so it will be another surprise…”

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

issues.title: Friday Five With Shaina Tabak: Art, Architecture, and the Spaces Between
issues.summary: The Brooklyn-based artist shares the exhibitions, architectural theories, and artworks that inspired her curatorial debut at '260 Madison'
issues.author: Danine Alati
issues.content_html:
Though she’s still pursuing her MFA in Visual Arts at Columbia University, artist Shaina Tabak is hardly a newcomer to the art world. The RISD graduate, who earned her BFA in furniture design, already has more than 20 exhibitions under her belt. Now she’s adding curator to her résumé with 260 Madison, an artist-run exhibition bringing together more than 50 artists across a former Duane Reade storefront and a 23,000-square-foot office floor above it in Midtown Manhattan.

Tabak’s own work is equally expansive. Drawing on history, technology, and materiality, she explores the relationship between the digital and physical worlds, often starting with digitally modeled forms that she translates into sculptures through hands-on processes such as cutting, perforation, lamination, and extrusion.

‘On Certainties (streetlight)’ (2026) by Anthony Discenza and ‘Arbor Armor’ (2015–2026) by Yasue Maetake on display at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

But her interest in materials extends beyond their physical properties. She also sees them as records of labor, manufacturing, extraction, and use. Her work examines contemporary material culture through a historical lens, imagining how the things made and valued today might be understood generations from now. As she puts it, her sculptures are “less concerned with imagining the future than with creating historical distance from the present.”

That perspective comes through in her recent work, which examines the increasingly blurred line between looking and shopping. In her Brooklyn studio, the Queens-born artist has been embedding collected industrial objects in three-ply cardboard, referencing the packaging and shipping systems that support consumer culture. She’s also exploring the influence of visual search and algorithmic commerce, where objects spotted in an image can lead to an endless stream of purchasable alternatives. It’s a commentary on a culture in which images don’t just inspire desire; they generate transactions.

‘First Water (deer)’ and ‘First Water (banner)’ (2026) by Dexter Barker-Glenn on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

For today’s Friday Five,we spent five minutes with Shaina Tabak to explore the ideas behind her curatorial debut at 260 Madison and the influences shaping her own work in the exhibition.

‘Ghosts’ (2025) by Alisa Berger and ‘Big Red Piece’ (2026) by Kari Cholnoky on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

The Project: ‘260 Madison’

For her curatorial debut, Tabak drew on Columbia University’s MFA community and her own network of artists, bringing together emerging talents and established names. Co-curated by artistic duo Dayana Matasheva and Edson Niebla Rodríguez of Demon Lovers, Inc., 260 Madison includes artists such as Simon Denny, Jon Kessler, and Eva and Franco Mattes. The exhibition was organized in collaboration with the building’s owner, AmTrustRE, which gave the curators full creative control.

‘Longcat’ (2026) by Eva & Franco Mattes on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

On view through Nov. 22, 2026, the expansive exhibition brings together familiar materials, objects, and technologies that are dismantled, reconstructed, or made strange. Exposed HVAC, ripped-out toilets, and corporate-logo wallpaper create the backdrop for works spanning sculpture, new media, and video. Tabak’s goal for 260 Madison is to “examine the systems organizing contemporary life—from control, surveillance, AI, and extraction to the material and architectural structures that shape how we work, move, and live.”

Below, in her own words, Tabak shares the influences that shaped her approach to 260 Madison, from artist-run exhibitions that challenged traditional institutions to architectural theories and sculptures that informed her own work.

Shaina Tabak’s works ‘Localized Collapse / Frozen Zone’ (2026) and ‘Sweep Towards Skylight’ (2026) on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of the artist.

What Inspired 260 Madison?

2 Exhibitions That Set a Precedent

“The first one, Damien Hirst’s Freeze (1988), was suggested to me by my professor Jon Kessler. Freeze was particularly compelling because it took place amid the redevelopment of London’s Docklands and was itself supported by real-estate developers, revealing the uneasy relationship between artistic independence and the production of urban capital. That history made me particularly conscious of a contradiction in our own project: While 260 Madison temporarily interrupts the building’s commercial function, the exhibition also generates cultural value for a property undergoing modernization.”

“A more recent exhibition, Christopher Wool’s See Stop Run (2024), took place in New York City’s Financial District and demonstrated how artists could operate outside established institutions by appropriating vacant commercial spaces. Wool’s exhibition was also installed on a gutted office floor and offered a more immediate architectural reference, allowing the building’s exposed infrastructure and traces of demolition to enter into dialogue with the work. With 260 Madison, we wanted to push these precedents even further, treating the vacant corporate office as a material record of changing relationships between labor, capital, and the built environment.”

Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak

The Writing of Rem Koolhaas

“Rem Koolhaas’ book Delirious New York and his essay “Junkspace” were really helpful in connecting the architecture of the space to the exhibition. My partner has worked on the 17th floor of 260 Madison for the past three years—a complete coincidence—and his 9-to-5 job as a paralegal brought to mind Koolhaas’ concepts of the vertical schism, architectural lobotomy, and definitive instability as I considered the exhibition’s function.”

“All three of Koolhaas’ concepts, in their own ways, describe the Manhattan skyscraper as a structure in which the exterior remains independent of the interior, allowing different floors to accommodate radically different and constantly changing activities without altering the building’s outward appearance.”

Rachel Whiteread’s ‘House’ (1993)

“I was thinking about House, a temporary public sculpture by Rachel Whiteread, when creating my sculpture Swept Towards Skylight (2026) for 260 Madison. I embedded an earlier work in insulation foam and coated it with cement to give the illusion that the negative space around it had been cast solid. Whiteread’s work transformed the interior of a house slated for demolition into a concrete monument to its former inhabitants and the lives that had occupied it.”

“I kept returning to this idea while curating 260 Madison, where the vacant office floor still bears physical traces of the labor and routines that once animated it. I wanted the building to function not simply as a container for artworks, but as an artifact in its own right, with its exposed infrastructure and signs of abandonment becoming part of the exhibition. What interests me about House, and what I hoped to capture at 260 Madison, was how architecture outlives its function and becomes a monument to the systems that once gave it meaning.”

260 Madison is on view through Nov. 22, 2026, at 260 Madison Avenue in New York City.

issues.title: Cold Plunges Are Finding a New Place in Residential Design
issues.summary: As homeowners increasingly prioritize wellness, new hydrotherapy systems allow cold plunging to be incorporated into homes without separate equipment
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
Once relegated to backyards and home gyms, cold plunges are finding a new place in residential design. As the wellness practice grows in popularity, homeowners are increasingly looking to incorporate cold therapy directly into their bathrooms, transforming what was once a standalone piece of fitness equipment into an integrated feature of the home.

The interest goes beyond athletic recovery. Cold-water immersion has been associated with potential benefits ranging from reduced muscle soreness to improved sleep and stress management, although research into its broader health effects remains limited. Still, the appeal is evident. According to Houzz’s 2024 Summer Trends Report, searches for “cold plunge” increased 74% year over year, while searches for “indoor sauna” rose 69%.

In the Heber, Utah, residence by Berg Design Studio, Hydro Systems’ Marquis bathtub demonstrates how traditional freestanding tubs can accommodate emerging wellness technologies, including cold plunging. Photography by Steve C. Wilson.

That interest reflects a larger shift toward wellness-focused residential spaces. The company’s 2026 report found that searches for “wellness room” had increased 164%, suggesting that homeowners are thinking more intentionally about how their environments can support relaxation and well-being.

For interior designers, these changing priorities are introducing new considerations into residential projects. Arizona-based designer Stephanie Larsen, who incorporates cold plunges, infrared saunas, and integrated aromatherapy systems into her work, has seen clients place greater emphasis on these features. “Today’s clients are craving homes that heal and inspire,” she told Luxe Interiors + Design. “They want spaces infused with wellness technology.”

Accommodating those requests means thinking beyond individual fixtures to how different wellness experiences function together. Cold plunges, for instance, are often paired with saunas for contrast therapy, which alternates between hot and cold exposure. Bringing both into a residential setting requires careful consideration of available space, plumbing, and the relationship between the different elements. Manufacturers, meanwhile, are developing more integrated systems that offer greater flexibility.

Hydro Systems integrates cold-plunge technology into freestanding bathtubs, bringing cold therapy into residential bathrooms without the need for separate equipment. Photography courtesy of Hydro Systems.

“We’re seeing wellness become a more intentional part of residential design, with dedicated spaces that bring together multiple hydrotherapy experiences in a single tub, from cold plunging and whirlpool to oxygenated microbubble therapy,” says Ashley Steinhardt, VP of Sales at Hydro Systems.

The California-based bath manufacturer has developed its Hydro Chill technology to incorporate cold plunging into customizable bathtubs, eliminating the need for a separate fixture. Its latest iteration also introduces smart-home functionality, allowing users to adjust water temperatures and schedule plunges remotely.

Hydro Systems is also exploring how multiple hydrotherapy experiences can share the same footprint. Its new Hydro Chill Ultra delivers both hot and cold water through a self-contained system that generates its own hot water. Because it doesn’t require a traditional hot-water connection, the technology offers additional flexibility for installations in pool houses and dedicated wellness rooms.

Featured in an Atlanta Homes Showhouse, Hydro Systems’ Slate bathtub features a custom color and polished finish, with integrated Hydro Chill cold-plunge technology. Paired with a wood-paneled sauna, the tub demonstrates how cold therapy can become part of a thoughtfully designed residential wellness space. Photography courtesy of Hydro Systems.

While expansive home spas provide room for separate saunas, plunge tubs, and other amenities, integrating hydrotherapy into an existing bathroom requires a different approach. Multifunctional fixtures can help reduce the space needed for these experiences, making them easier to accommodate within conventional residential layouts.

“Wellness doesn’t have to be confined to a dedicated room,” Steinhardt says. “Hydrotherapy can also be incorporated into smaller bathroom footprints, bringing wellness into everyday routines.”

Hydro Systems’ Hydro Chill cold-plunge system is incorporated into a home gym alongside weight-training equipment, bringing cold-water immersion into a dedicated fitness and recovery space. Photography courtesy of Hydro Systems.

Cold plunges may still be a relatively niche residential amenity, but their growing visibility is prompting designers to reconsider what a bathroom can accommodate. As more wellness features make their way into the home, the challenge will be integrating them without compromising the functionality, comfort, and aesthetics of the spaces around them.

Editorial Transparency: This article was developed with the assistance of AI tools, which may have been used for research, outlining, editing, or copy refinement. Reporting, fact-checking, and editorial decisions were made by the Design Milk editorial team.

issues.title: ROOM’s Designers on Design Series Returns with A Story of Hospitality and Human Connection
issues.summary: In the latest episode, industry icon Anda Andrei and award-winning designer Matthew Goodrich discuss the ups and downs of hospitality design, creative inspirations, and more
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
Who understands the struggles and successes of a designer better than another designer? That’s the core concept behind ROOM’s Designers on Design video series, which pairs leading designers together for open conversation on the future of architecture, design, and human connection.

“When we launched ROOM’s Designers on Design series, the idea was simple: create a space for designers to have the kinds of conversations that don’t always happen in the day-to-day,” says Elyse Heckman, SVP, Brand & Communications at ROOM. “No interviewer, no moderator, no prescribed talking points. Just two creative minds coming together to exchange ideas, challenge perspectives, and explore what moves the industry forward.”

Hospitality legend Anda Andrei of Anda Andrei Design and award-winning designer Matthew Goodrich of Goodrich design studio sit down for a discussion in the most recent installation. Unlike earlier episodes of this series, Andrei and Goodrich know each other outside of the studio—and have for years. Goodrich attributes his love of hospitality design to Andrei’s hotels, while Andrei has had a front-row seat to the evolution of Goodrich’s career. (Plus, their work shares a certain symbiosis: Andrei’s recent renovation of the Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris aligns with Goodrich’s past in museum exhibition design.)

“For this episode, we wanted to take a slightly different approach to our previous pairings,” says Heckman. “Rather than bringing together designers who may be meeting for the first time, we were drawn to the idea of connecting two individuals who already share a history and familiarity with each other’s work. We loved the opportunity to explore how those relationships shape our perspectives, influence our creative instincts and ultimately help us grow as designers.”

Photography by Eric Vitale, courtesy of ROOM.

Tapping into the spirit of authentic exchange that ROOM set out to foster, the duo’s conversation begins with their first (almost) meeting. In 2003, Goodrich was helping his partner, Barnes Foundation Executive Director Thomas Collins, open Zaha Hadid’s Contemporary Arts Center in Cincinnati when he heard that Andrei would be there in 20 minutes. “I looked to Thom, and I said, ‘You’ve got to go home, take a shower, and put on a suit. This is a big deal,’” Goodrich shares.

However, the pair didn’t officially meet until years later—after Andrei had left the Ian Schrager Company, starting her own firm at 59 years old. “You came very highly recommended, and I wanted to hire you,” she says. “But then I asked you a crucial question: ‘Have you ever opened a hotel before?’” “And I had to say no,” Goodrich adds.

Designing a hotel is no easy feat, which Goodrich learned when opening his first hotel, Arlo SoHo, in 2016. He shared how the final month before opening was chaos. With nearly 40 years shaping hospitality projects, Andrei knows this reality well—but emphasizes that it’s even more painful when operations start changing after the design is finished. Like living organisms, hospitality projects evolve with the staff, users, and guests over the years.

Still, the pair agree that all these issues and pain points provide valuable lessons. “Understanding how operations affect the success of restaurants and of hotels is foundational for making great designs,” Goodrich says.

Photography by Eric Vitale, courtesy of ROOM.

On the topic of design inspiration, Andrei believe the best hotels have a story. Much like an elevator pitch, she believes projects should have a one-sentence design concept. For example, at the Delano Miami Beach Hotel, which she created in collaboration with Philippe Starck, the one-liner was: “a Greek fisherman that finds a diamond in the sea.” Goodrich agrees with the sentiment of this design tool: “If you have that short phrase, if you can go back to the essence of what your concept is, things fall into place.”

Throughout the episode, there is a sense of mutual respect and deep appreciation for the other’s work. Goodrich calls Andrei a superhero collaborator, while Andrei compliments Goodrich’s work (and name). Both value collaboration, imagination, and challenging work. Heckman sees the pair’s connection as proof of the series’ larger purpose: “It’s a wonderful example of how seemingly different creative paths can intersect, and how the work we encounter early in our careers can continue to influence us in unexpected ways.”

“When you started your company, we had some empty desks in my office and we shared offices. And who knew that nine and a half years later, we would be sitting here and talking about how amazing you did,” Andrei says with a laugh.

This is what ROOM’s Designers on Design series does so well: It brings design to the human level. From the ideas and experiences that shape the work to the friends, colleagues, and mentors who leave a lasting impact, each episode looks at the people behind the portfolio.

“What makes this episode especially compelling is that the conversation extends beyond design itself,” shares Heckman. “It gets to the heart of how we become the designers we are — the people who influence us, the experiences that shape our creative instincts, and the ways inspiration gets passed from one generation to the next. In that sense, it embodies exactly what we hoped the series would become: a platform for authentic exchange, unexpected perspectives and the stories behind the work.”

And who knows? The series might even inspire new work of its own. “I want to do a project together,” Andrei says. Goodrich answers: “I know, me too. That’s my dream.”

Watch the episode at room.com

issues.title: Reims 502 uses pink palette for "non-referential" commercial building in Mexico
issues.summary: A stepped facade fronts this pink commercial building in Mexico called Rosadoce, designed by local studio Reims 502 to suit various tenants over its lifespan. The post Reims 502 uses pink palette for "non-referential" commercial building in Mexico appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Lizzie Crook
issues.content_html:
A stepped facade fronts this pink commercial building in Mexico called Rosadoce, designed by local studio Reims 502 to suit various tenants over its lifespan.

Rosadoce is located in a low-density residential neighbourhood near the historic centre of Querétaro, a state in north-central Mexico, which is redeveloping into a mixed-use area.

Drawings and photographs

    Drawings and photographs

    The studio said the 840-square-metre building was "conceived as an adaptable urban asset" that can function as a single unit, four independent commercial spaces or sixteen smaller modules, ensuring its longevity and usability well into the future.

    "Rosadoce by Reims 502 is a flexible commercial building in Querétaro, Mexico, designed as an adaptable urban platform for work, commerce and public life," said the studio.

    "Designed during the pandemic, it rethinks commercial architecture in response to changing patterns of work, consumption and urban life."

    Local planning constraints determined the building's scale, while its "non-referential form" evolved from various design strategies, the studio said.

    It reaches seven metres in height – the maximum height allowed above street level – which led the studio to carve out a semi-basement level to increase usable area.

    Above ground are two open-plan levels, organised around a central stair and punctured by vertical voids that naturally light and ventilate the building.

    Meanwhile, the basement currently contains service spaces including parking and plant rooms. However, similarly to the rest of the building, it has an open-plan layout to support future commercial activity.

    Crowning Rosadoce is a usable rooftop filled with planters that provide thermal insulation.

    Rosadoce's distinct front elevation is formed from a series of staggered openings, described by the studio as evoking an "inverted stair". This allows in light and ventilation while maintaining privacy.

    "The inverted-stair facade creates horizontal openings for daylight and views while regulating visual permeability from the street," said the studio.

    "Because the building’s future uses remain open-ended, the facade avoids excessive transparency and provides a controlled threshold between public exposure and interior flexibility."

    The pink render that colours the building's exterior, provided by lime-based products manufacturer Nanocal, was chosen as a nod to the rose-colored quarry stone that defines Querétaro’s historic centre.

    This same colour was used throughout the project, with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone, creating a warm feel for the interior.

    According to the studio, the building's future flexibility is achieved through the combination of open plans as well as "exposed construction, passive environmental strategies and an active rooftop".

    Read:

    Duggan Morris builds office with millennial-pink exterior in London's King's Cross

    "This allows it to respond to different economic scenarios, tenant profiles, subletting arrangements and future programmes without major structural alterations," said Reims 502.

    The project is on the eight-strong shortlist for the small workplace interior category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

    Other pink buildings in Mexico include a co-living apartment block with a series of arched forms by Estudio Zero and a minimalist house sandwiched between two buildings by César Béjar Studio.

issues.title: Mecanoo transforms former gold vault into "city’s living room" in renovation of De Nederlandsche Bank in Amsterdam
issues.summary: Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands' central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault. The post Mecanoo transforms former gold vault into "city’s living room" in renovation of De Nederlandsche Bank in Amsterdam appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Amy Frearson
issues.content_html:
Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands' central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.

The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation's ugliest building.

Located in the heart of Amsterdam, this huge concrete-slab building is in complete contrast to the city's historic canal houses.

Photographs

    Photographs

    The original architect, Marius Frans Duintjer, had hoped to emulate the modernist works of Mies van der Rohe, but security requirements had resulted in "a fortress with fences, large boulders and armed military police," according to Mecanoo.

    The building was further complicated by later extensions, which included an extra storey above the low-rise main building and a cylindrical 14-storey tower built alongside the original central tower.

    Mecanoo's transformation was enabled by the relocation of gold reserves and banknote operations to a location in Zeist.

    This allowed the architects to give the building a sense of transparency and openness that was envisioned from the outset, but had never been possible before now.

    The project is an exemplar for sustainable renovation, as proven by its nomination for Dezeen Awards 2026.

    Removing the cylindrical tower was pivotal, as it allowed space for a new public garden at the heart of the scheme.

    This tower was carefully dismantled, allowing many materials to be reused.

    Salvaged concrete was used to build a new quay beside the canal, while the rest was donated to social housing projects in the city.

    Plans and sections

      Plans and sections

      The removal enabled a reorganisation of the ground floor.

      The entrance was relocated to Frederiksplein, while floorplates were cut away to reveal the 61-metre-long former vault, which has been transformed into an exhibition gallery.

      "The most secretive part of the bank is now its most public," said Mecanoo.

      "Inside the vault, visitors can immerse themselves in exhibitions and interactive games that tell the story of gold, money, the economy and DNB's core activities."

      The retained structures were newly clad in red ceramic bricks. These incorporate the brown tiles that clad the building previously, with the old tiles crushed for use as pigment.

      These combine with new glazing, a Kastenfenster system of ventilated double-glazing with integrated sun shading, which has helped to reduce the building's day-to-day energy requirements by an estimated 80 per cent.

      Inside, the space linking the vault with the courtyard was designed as an indoor street, with seating areas along the edges and auditoriums (one formal, the other informal) at each end.

      "Francine Houben's inspiration came from the vibrant 'street' of the central hall in the former Faculty of Architecture building at TU Delft, which was destroyed by fire," said Mecanoo.

      The rest of the building is organised into zones with varying levels of security.

      A five-storey atrium organises the semi-public area, which includes a meeting centre and a restaurant overlooking the Singelgracht, while the more secure employee zones are located in both the courtyard building and the tower.

      The meeting centre occupies what was previously a double-height cash hall, with distinctive tree-like columns.

      The original spiral staircase still stands, alongside a second added by Mecanoo, while custom-designed tables feature integrated lamps.

      Timber was used for many of the new surfaces, including a slatted ceiling made from locally felled poplar trees.

      Shades of red, blue and orange extend across other surfaces and interior elements, including walls covered in recycled-plastic felt, carpets and furniture.

      Read:

      Mecanoo completes rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi

      "The colour scheme is inspired by the vibrant paper currency from the last period of the Dutch guilder," said Mecanoo.

      The interiors are completed by DNB's collection of artwork, energy-efficient lighting systems and circular planting boxes.

      "The renovation transforms De Nederlandsche Bank from a closed fortress into a transparent circular landmark, repurposing the former gold vault as the city's living room for the public," concluded Mecanoo.

      Other recent projects by the firm include the rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, the tile-clad Villa BW and the book-inspired Macau Central Library.

      Project credits:

      Client: De Nederlandsche Bank
      Architecture, restoration, interior and landscape: Mecanoo
      Construction: Pieters Bouwtechniek
      M&E engineer: Valstar Simonis
      Building physics and fire safety: DGMR
      Lighting design: Frans van Hooijdonk
      Project management: Stevens Van Dijck Bouwmanagers en Adviseurs
      Cost consultant: IGG Bouweconomie
      Main contractor: SPIE
      Exhibition design: Platvorm, Duinzand, IJsfontein, Redrum Bureau
      Wayfinding: Mijksenaar

      The post Mecanoo transforms former gold vault into "city’s living room" in renovation of De Nederlandsche Bank in Amsterdam appeared first on Dezeen.

issues.title: Kohler's gut-health tracker clips onto the toilet bowl
issues.summary: American bathroom brand Kohler has created Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet, through its spin-off venture, Kohler Health. The post Kohler's gut-health tracker clips onto the toilet bowl appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Rima Sabina Aouf
issues.content_html:
American bathroom brand Kohler has created Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet, through its spin-off venture, Kohler Health.

Dekoda is designed to be discreet and intuitive, clipping to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

In the emerging toilet-based health tracker market, it is the first device capable of blood detection, which it does through sensors developed at Kohler Health that identify haemoglobin.

Photographs

    Photographs

    The company said the device is particularly useful for older individuals or those with chronic gut illnesses, who need to track their symptoms as part of their disease management programmes.

    “When we developed Dekoda, our goal was to give people the tools to listen to their bodies, track meaningful results over time, and take charge of their own wellness journey," said Kohler Health managing director Nora Tophof.

    "It’s important to realise that the human eye is only capable of seeing so much – and trace amounts of blood or other issues are not always apparent," she continued. "Subtle biological markers, such as microscopic blood or early signs of dehydration, often go unnoticed."

    "Dekoda works quietly behind the scenes to capture those crucial clues, giving people clear, objective data they can use to help shape behaviours or share with their doctor," Tophof said.

    People with dementia often forget to drink or lose the feeling of thirst, while people with gut diseases such as Crohn's usually need to track their daily bowel symptoms.

    A secondary target market is competitive athletes and fitness enthusiasts, who Kohler says can use the hydration data to make training adjustments.

    Dekoda is compatible with most toilets. It has a simple flattened capsule shape in gleaming white polycarbonate and attaches to the outside of the rim with an adjustable clamp.

    On the other side of the clamp, a camera and advanced optical sensors point down into the bowl, using spectroscopy to detect the quantity, colour and consistency of urine and stool.

    Read:

    Urify is a toilet-cleaning tablet that helps diagnose kidney disease

    Most of the electronics are contained on the capsule side, along with a magnetic battery that can be removed for charging outside the bathroom. An accompanying fingerprint scanner is designed to be wall-mounted near the toilet so that users can log in and begin their session.

    To withstand the bathroom environment, the exterior of the device is made of a polycarbonate that is antibacterial and chemical-resistant, while the mechanical components are made of stainless steel.

    A specially trained algorithm analyses the collected data and insights are viewed in the accompanying Kohler Health app. It automatically tracks bathroom routines and identifies trends, while users can also add information about their meals, medications and exercise to add context, and share insights directly with their doctor when they desire.

    Users' data is encrypted as it travels between their devices and Kohler's systems but decrypted and processed to provide the service.

    Kohler Health said Dekoda, which was released in October 2025, is helping destigmatise the collection of gut health-related metrics, which individuals could previously only monitor through test strips or stool samples.

    It is part of a small wave of new devices focused on analysing the body's fluids, from spit to menstrual blood, as wellness technology expands beyond watch-style heart rate monitors and activity trackers.

    The post Kohler's gut-health tracker clips onto the toilet bowl appeared first on Dezeen.

issues.title: Arudeko transforms discarded wool into paper-like material
issues.summary: Mexican studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material from colourful waste wool, which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers. The post Arudeko transforms discarded wool into paper-like material appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Anna Skrebels
issues.content_html:
Mexican design studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool, which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Photographs

    Photographs

    The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper.

    Skilled local artisans initially wove the discarded dyed wool onto a pedal loom, then, using cotton threads, wove strips of recycled paper crafted by local papermakers into the material.

    The result is a translucent, flexible textile that can be crafted into diverse objects, from lampshades to decorative headboard panels, room dividers and wall art.

    "Through exploring the material's qualities, we discovered its potential, particularly the way light revealed colours that had been hidden within the paper, almost like a secret waiting to be uncovered," Arudeko co-founder and CEO Denisse Arnaiz told Dezeen.

    "Once the paper was woven, I began observing how it behaved as a textile," added Arnaiz.

    "Its translucency was what ultimately inspired us to explore its use in lighting. However, the material has many other possible applications."

    With Bianni, Arudeko aimed to uncover the hidden value of discarded wool whilst reimagining the ancient material's ancestral history and "cultural memory".

    "Bianni was born from the idea of giving new life to the leftover wool from our rug and cushion production in Oaxaca," said Arnaiz. "This wool carries within it the knowledge of the artisans who work with it, as well as the colours of the earth embedded in its fibres."

    Arnaiz explained that the material is made purely from natural materials, with no additives.

    "No additives, just natural materials – why mix these fibres?" she said. "Not only for an aesthetic purpose, as wool brings fire resistance to the paper."

    Throughout the process, the studio aimed to minimise water consumption and carbon dioxide production as much as possible. Bianni's production was also kept local to reduce transport needs whilst supporting the local community.

    Read:

    Harvard University transforms waste wool into cladding for retrofits

    By working with artisans from rural communities and blending traditional craft knowledge with contemporary design practice, Bianni aims to champion historic crafts whilst fostering long-term community development and economic inclusion.

    Other wool projects recently featured on Dezeen include waste-wool cladding designed for retrofits and a collection of rugs with architectural designs.

issues.title: Alibris has made a deal to sell used books on Temu.
issues.summary: As Sam Spratford reports in Publisher’s Weekly, Alibris has inked a deal to make over a million books available on Temu’s massive digital marketplace. It’s not too shocking, as Alibris seems to be chasing a model of breadth and speed;
issues.author: James Folta
issues.content_html:
As Sam Spratford reports in Publisher’s Weekly, Alibris has inked a deal to make over a million books available on Temu’s massive digital marketplace. It’s not too shocking, as Alibris seems to be chasing a model of breadth and speed; the company partnered with fast fashion brand Shein last year.

Temu already sell books, though they’re mostly craft and hobby titles, many coming from overseas. The deal with Alibris is part of Temu’s Local Seller program, meaning the listings won’t affect the supply chain: books will be sourced, stored, and shipped locally in the US.

Temu (originally a play on “Team Up, Price Down”) has become a shorthand for crappy quality and weird knock-offs. It’s also been dogged by accusations of breaching data privacy and intellectual property, not to mention other bad practices; among other things, a congressional study found a high risk of forced labor in their supply line.

We’ll have to see how it works out, but it seems like expansion to a larger online footprint through consolidation or partnership is the preferred business plan for digital retailers these days. With Goliaths like Amazon out there, I get the logic, but it’s always a little dispiriting to see everything, including used books, getting funneled into the same few buckets.

issues.title: Put off Bolaño’s 2666 for too long? In 2027, tackle it with the Equator book club.
issues.summary: The Equator reading group is back by popular demand. After a successful summer outing with Mike Davis’s Late Victorian Holocausts, the globally minded magazine is sponsoring another book club. This time, the subject is a literary doorstop—Roberto Bolaño’s 2666. Why
issues.author: Brittany Allen
issues.content_html:
The Equator reading group is back by popular demand.

After a successful summer outing with Mike Davis’s Late Victorian Holocausts, the globally minded magazine is sponsoring another book club. This time, the subject is a literary doorstop—Roberto Bolaño’s 2666.

Why read 2666 in a flock? Bolaño’s final novel, published posthumously, is famous for exasperating as often as it rewards. Appropriately, this reading group has a questing name: “Into the Abyss.”

As Sam Anderson noted in a review for New York, in 2666 the late Chilean maestro “follows his restless talent down every available rabbit hole of improvisation, no matter how dark and unpromising.” Over the novel’s near thousand pages, “single sentences stretch on…obsessively sifting the most minor gradations.”

The sum total is “indisputably brilliant,” but also “crowded, brutal, dense.”

A novel like this rewards accountability mechanisms, and deserves plenty of conversation. (That’s the bet Equator has made, anyway.) Readers who’ve been ISO buddies to sift through all the brilliance can now sign up for five discussion sessions that break the book up into 150 page chunks.

Periodic club meetings will be moderated by scholars, fans, and special guests. And I do mean special. Rachel Kushner, Karl Ove Knausgård, Benjamin Kunkel, Pankaj Mishra, and Bolaño translator Natasha Wimmer anchor a starry slate of speakers.

But perhaps most exciting is the discussion framework. Over its five sessions, “Into the Abyss” will consider the novel through its many thematic lenses.

Violence, literary obsession, borderlands and “the wreckage of the twentieth century” are all on the menu. So if you love structuring chaos, consider joining the fray.

As with Davis Summer, Bolaño January is open to all Equator subscribers, runs on pay-what-you-can contributions. It also takes place fully online.

No more excuses! Stay warm this January with a good group and a big book.
