issues.title: The Most Read Books on Goodreads This Week
issues.summary: The most read books on Goodreads this week include romantasy books, a dystopian novel, and a witchy thriller.
issues.author: Community
issues.content_html:
There’s no question what the most read book of the moment is: the title that took the #1 spot this time has almost triple the readers of the book in the #2 spot. We do have one change-up in the top five since last week. Can you guess the 2025 novel that’s risen in popularity recently? Here’s a hint: the movie adaptation comes out later this month.

Two New Books Out This Week You Should Know About

Unfortunately, the most read books on Goodreads tend not to be diverse by any definition of the word. So, here are a couple of new books out this week that deserve wider readership.

Take My Word for It: A Memoir by LeVar Burton, Tracey Michae’l Lewis-Giggetts

Very few actors have been front and center in so many culturally historic moments as LeVar Burton. From playing Kunta Kinte on Roots to Geordi La Forge on Star Trek, and being the host on Reading Rainbow—one might even say that Burton has embodied and portrayed many aspects of America’s past, present, and its (hopeful) future. Here, he traces his life, first as a child experiencing the Civil Rights Movement, then his acting career, and later his advocacy for literacy. He fills in the moments in between his major roles to show the struggle and resilience it has taken to lead such a remarkable life. —Erica Ezeifedi

Bones of Jade, Flesh Like Ice by Gracie Marsden

You don’t often come across historical fantasy inspired by Taiwanese mythology and the enthusiasm around this debut novel is big. Yu’er’s story unfolds in the Eleventh century in a small village. First sold off for marriage in her youth at the advice of a jing, then estranged from the husband she’s come to love, Yu’er takes matters into her own hands. She strikes a bargain with a jing that sets her on a path to riches and agency but away from her humanity. —S. Zainab Williams

The Most Read Books on Goodreads This Week

#5:

Sunrise on the Reaping by Suzanne Collins

This prequel novel in the Hunger Games series was published in 2025, but it’s getting new interest ahead of the movie adaptation, which is out November 20th. It follows Haymitch’s Hunger Games, 24 years before the events of the first novel. It was read by almost 17,000 users this week and has a 4.5 average rating.

#4:

Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke

Still in the top five is Yesteryear, which came out in April. It’s one of several buzzy tradwife novels out this year. In this one, a tradwife influencer wakes up one day in the time period she’s been romanticizing, and real-life homesteading turns out to be much more difficult—and dangerous—than it looks on Instagram. Yesteryear was read by 21,000 users this week and has a 3.8 average rating.

#3:

Threshing Day by Rebecca Yarros

The fourth book in the Empyrean series still doesn’t have a release date, so fans likely have a long time to wait. In the meantime, they can revisit the world in this new novella, which follows 13 characters on their Threshing Days, when they endure a deadly trial in attempts to bond with a dragon. It was read by almost 32,000 users this week and has a 4.4 average rating.

#2:

The Witch by Freida McFadden

The reigning queen of thrillers is back, this time with an October-appropriate story. After losing her job, Julia moves in with her elderly grandmother in their family’s 17th-century estate in Massachusetts. Soon, she begins to suspect the house is haunted by a woman executed for witchcraft in 1692. It was read by 40,000 users this week and has a 4.0 average rating.

#1:

A Court of Splintered Harmony (A Court of Thorns and Roses #6) by Sarah J. Maas

With more than triple the readership of the #2 book on this list, the latest A Court of Thorns and Roses book is by far the most popular book of the moment. It’s the first in the Valkyrie Cycle, following the Night Court as they face off against the return of Koschei the Deathless. The next book in the Valkyrie Cycle comes out in January. This one was read by 119,000 users this week and has a 3.9 average rating.

If you’re looking for more buzzy books, check out The Bestselling Books of the Week, According to All the Lists.

issues.title: The Most Beautifully Illustrated Manga
issues.summary: If you're an art lover, don't miss the stunning beauty that is manga.
issues.author: Carolina Ciucci
issues.content_html:
If you’re an art lover, you probably frequent museums and galleries. Likely, you also have a penchant for browsing through biographies about the masters. Mayhaps you’re even a fan of picture books, coffee table books, or any sort of book where art plays a large role. But do you know what art form you may be missing? Manga.

Most of this Japanese genre conforms to a very specific art style developed in the late nineteenth century, so even if you’re not a reader, you can spot manga when you see it. According to Denise Tempone, it consists of expressive eyes, slender silhouettes, and cartoonish characters in realistic settings, among other traits. Combined, these characteristics have made manga an extremely recognizable genre worldwide — and for good reason. Before I even knew what manga was, I, a child in Argentina, could always pinpoint what I then called “Sailor Moon-like art”.

Still, not all manga are created equal. The four titles I gathered here are all distinctive: they take these traits and make them theirs. From astounding brushwork to coziness incarnate, these manga will make you want to hang them on your walls just to stare at them in wonder.

If you do decide to give manga a try (assuming you haven’t already, and I’ve been preaching to the choir this whole time!), then not only will you be treated to some truly stunning art, but you’ll also get a thrilling story to go with it. That’s a win-win if I ever saw one.

Vagabond by Takehiko Inoue

Based on the life of real-life Japanese swordsman Miyamoto Musashi, this historical manga stuns thanks to its incredibly realistic depictions of, well, everything, really. If there’s a tree, I promise you’ll feel the leaves against your fingertips.

What’s it about, you ask? It follows Takezō Shinmen and Matahachi Hon’ide, who barely survive the Battle of Sekigahara and take two very different paths…until they unknowingly reunite.

Witch Hat Atelier by Kamome Shirahama

Reminiscent of Studio Ghibli, Witch Hat Atelier’s style screams cozy. Warm colors and whimsical details form the core of this adorable manga.

Oh wait, maybe you want to hear about the plot too. My bad. Coco is a teenage girl who accidentally turned her mother into stone (as one does), and is seeking to become a witch’s apprentice in order to turn her back. I’m sure I don’t need to tell you that shenanigans ensue.

Mushishi by Yuki Urushibara

The composition of this manga is so good it drives me a little mad. The way it alternates between soft muted colors and vibrant saturated hues to evoke different moods sets an ambiance better than any words ever could.

Ginko is capable of seeing Mushi, ubiquitous ethereal creatures with (most likely) supernatural powers whom humans typically can’t see. Under such circumstances, it is only to be expected that he declare himself Mushi Master and devote himself to protecting people from them.

The Guy She Was Interested In Wasn’t a Guy at All by Sumiko Arai

This is known as the Green Yuri, which I really think ought to render any explanations unnecessary. But if you insist on other reasons to read it, I’ll point you to the gorgeous artwork, complete with incredibly vivid expressions (which, yeah, is a characteristic of manga as a whole, but still) and vibrant colors that capture the kaleidoscope of falling in love for the first time.

Because oh yeah, this is a love story. Aya Osawa develops a crush on the mysterious clerk at her favorite record store…only, the clerk in question is her classmate, Mitsuki Koga. The two girls form a friendship that then blossoms into love.

If you prefer your manga fantastical, make sure to check out these cozy fantasy manga for your TBR. And if you’re in the market for a new activity, start a new hobby with these manga drawing books.

issues.title: Broken People Don’t Break the System. Broken Systems Break the People
issues.summary: “America, The Never Event,” an excerpt from The Fleeing Season by Jamie D Brooks “We needed to move quickly because of the severe pelvic fracture and damage to the left kidney. It was the bleed, we had to stop the bleed. . . . Somehow, the repair to the kidney didn’t, wasn’t somehow, we . […] The post Broken People Don’t Break the System. Broken Systems Break the People appeared first on Electric
issues.author: Jamie D Brooks
issues.content_html:
“America, The Never Event,” an excerpt from The Fleeing Season by Jamie D Brooks

“We needed to move quickly because of the severe pelvic fracture and damage to the left kidney. It was the bleed, we had to stop the bleed. . . . Somehow, the repair to the kidney didn’t, wasn’t somehow, we . . . I . . . it was the wrong side—the wrong kidney we were trying to work on.”

I am no doctor, but I could tell that the physician’s voice was stripped raw, the way voices sandpapered by anguish often are. I understood that his 20-plus years practicing as an orthopedic trauma surgeon could weather his soul, but I detected much more than the strain of accumulated sorrow in Dr Gordon’s voice coming through my phone. Before I could ask my follow-up questions—there were so many—the fresh river of pain coursing through him gave way, breaching the composure he’d fortified through decades of delivering devastatingly bad news to the hopeful. His tears brought me right to his pain. If I wasn’t careful, I could have been swept along with him in his surging current of hurt. For the empathetic, other people’s pain can be a contagion. I resisted my reflexive urge to comfort with, “It’s okay.” It wasn’t. Dr Gordon had just described a wrong-side surgery: a medical Never Event.

In theory, as the wording suggests, Never Events should never happen. In reality, they do—a lot, or at least a lot more than we’d like to think they do. Hospitals are miraculous institutions of healing, aided by the hands of dedicated practitioners. They also can be profoundly dangerous places, their risks obscured in part by whether, and how, Never Events are reported, and by nondisclosure provisions in medical malpractice settlements. Legal barriers are used to shield the public from the grim reality that iatrogenic death—death caused by medical activity—is the third leading cause of death in the United States. 1 I was in my first year of law school in 2001 when physician Ken Kizer coined the term “Never Event,” and the medical community soon coalesced around a general definition: serious, preventable errors that often result in serious harm or death to the patient. 2 To be clear, not all iatrogenic deaths are Never Events. Never Events are a tiny subset of those. They are the most egregious ones, signifying a complete system failure. They are often what valid medical malpractice claims are made of.

A Never Event wasn’t new to me. I’d had a front-row seat to the devastating reality of Never Events, but my conversation with Dr Gordon took place during the life-halting early days of the first COVID-19 lockdown, and the concept took on a new meaning for me in those scary, uncertain times in early 2020. What was the United States in this moment if not a Never Event itself, a failing system riddled with preventable errors, resulting in serious harm and death to so many of her people? My people, especially as of late. My conversation with Dr Gordon that morning was pivotal. As something was breaking within him, so too it was within me. That day, I made a decision—a drastic one that would change the course of my life, and my family’s, forever. A year later, cradling the roots of our family trees, I tenderly gathered my husband and three children and planted us into unfamiliar soil an ocean away—away from America, the Never Event.

When Dr Gordon called me, in late spring 2020, hospital intensive care units across the country were at capacity, morgues were overflowing, masks and other lifesaving personal protective equipment were in short supply, and health care officials were racing to understand the speed and extent of COVID-19’s contagion.

I took his confession hard, and sitting down at my bed-desk. Seven weeks into the COVID-19 lockdown, and this was the best I’d managed to pull together.

I was running the department of risk management and insurance for a group of 700 clinicians and residents at a major teaching hospital in the Washington, DC area. Perched atop my duvet, my pandemic work life was contorted by the demands of homeschooling and parenting my three kids, who were two, four, and six years old at the time. “America, the Never Event” became the new framing that I couldn’t unsee. “It’s this damn COVID. We are all just too fucking strained,” Dr Gordon sobbed into the phone that morning. Teary-eyed, I nodded my head, agreeing. Even though Dr Gordon couldn’t see me, his words resonated deeply. COVID-19 was breaking us.

Eventually Dr. Gordon’s cries exhausted themselves into self-soothing exhales through what sounded like pursed lips. I held space for him—and my tongue. It’s something a dear friend, Jocelyne, had modeled for me years before when we worked together at one of the biggest health care providers in the United States. She was one of the best health care ombudsman mediators, and I was shadowing her for the day in my role as one of the organization’s national leaders in patient safety and risk management. During our first appointment, Jocelyne and I sat face-to-face with a doctor wearing a starched white lab coat. The doctor was emotionally destroyed because of her involvement in a medical Never Event. Jocelyne showed me how you compassionately bear witness to pain. You don’t talk at it; you listen. I’ve never forgotten it. So once Dr Gordon quieted, I began. “You are in a safe space, Dr Gordon. Let’s take our time and start from the beginning,” was my offering—“while I pretend that two of the most important things in my life aren’t clinging desperately to me at this very moment” was my omission.

Dr Gordon started over. I sat typing notes on my laptop. Meanwhile, my four-year-old, Sinclair, stood behind me on the bed “making my hair,” raking her tiny fingers through my curls. She’d taken on this task, unrequested and strongly discouraged, for nearly a month, “to help Mama get ready for work.” It is one of the myriad ways her old soul has always attempted to care for mine when she senses my distress—never mind that I, as her parent, should have been doing all I could to take care of her in those early days of the lockdown. As she frizzed me from the top, her two-year-old sister, Yves, sat straddling my ankles, on the verge of soiling her teal-and-yellow polka dot tankini bottoms, and, to my horror, the bits of my feet beneath her. Her ever-smiling eyes rimmed with tears as she whisper-pleaded for a diaper. Whisper-pleas were the compromise we’d reached because the pandemic lockdown had repeatedly shown us the venom I could spew when she or her sisters repeatedly interrupted my work meetings. The interruptions happened frequently, given that my children were still too young to exhibit restraint or patience.

Since the lockdown, Yves had decided that she would only pass a bowel movement in a diaper, and only if I watched her squat behind the glider rocking chair where I’d weaned her six months before. Yves is not my first child; I fully understood that a potty-trained two-year-old is not a given. But Yves had been, just prior to lockdown. Selfishly, during the lockdown, I still needed her to be, because with this regression she was serving up, she might as well have been Satan. I rebuked it. Five years on, I think I now know what was happening. She regressed because of the drastic shift in her routine. I wasn’t the safe space that I had been. I was often mentally or emotionally unavailable even though she could—and did—reach out and grab me. I understand now that her regression was playing out behind what was to her one of the safest spaces inside our home: the rocking chair. It was the place where we’d convened every single day of her life in the waning light so I could sing, and where for many nights she could suckle. That was the spot she could count on to be cocooned in a swaying blanket of love every night before bed, just as her two older sisters had been before her, in a seat my husband had assembled by hand.

At that moment, however, all I could think was, Where the fuck is my husband? I needed him to be protecting my work time in that moment, but he was protecting his own, and the unpredictable demands on both of us during work hours with three young children at home had turned us into people we hardly recognized. To say that my husband and I were busy doesn’t even begin to cover it. During the first seven months of the lockdown, we were lucky if either of us managed a shower every four or five days. Still, I felt entitled to more leeway with my job because I was serving people on the front lines, and he was not.

I’d learn directly after that call, and a terse discussion between us, that my husband hadn’t even been tending to our six-year-old, Lee. She knew how to fend for herself by that time and had busied herself by reading a book. My husband was, of course, also working. He is a journalist and was out walking the neighborhood, taking a work call with a source that necessitated privacy and confidentiality. He had so many of those calls. Eventually I convinced myself that some of them simply had to be made up so he could escape our home. They weren’t.

I am embarrassed now by how utterly unempathetic I was toward my own daughters then, while at the same time holding the deepest empathy for Dr Gordon. He was a man I had heard of but had just met for the first time on that call. I didn’t even know what he looked like until I looked him up on the internet afterward. My instinct, of course, was to be there for both my family and Dr Gordon, but in a world layered with intersectional injustices, one thing I know to be true: It’s nearly impossible to multitask empathy. But that’s what pandemic parenting was all about: splintering oneself to tend to the ruins about you, not recognizing that your efforts would leave you in ruins just the same.

I half-assed my mothering duties and gambled on Yves’s ability to hold her bowels for a few more minutes, betting my clean ankles and my adored linen duvet. These were the stressful concessions that moms working full time from home while providing care for their young children were making all over the country—even those who had a willing and able-bodied partner at home to help, like I did. My husband was present, even helpful. But I had what I thought were substantive signposts that I was doing far too much more. For example, I made breakfast, lunch, and dinner appear on the table every single day for five people during lockdown. If I didn’t, mealtimes would come and go without any food on the table. That meant I was on the hook for 105 servings of food on the table every week—in addition to my job.

I chalked up everything I was handling to small potatoes. I was speaking with Dr Gordon, one of my hospital’s most highly regarded trauma surgeons. Working in trauma is status-quo stress. Imagine performing emergency surgeries on critically ill or injured patients where the only predictable part of your workday is that nearly every decision you make could have life-or-death consequences for your patients. Further, those decisions must be hurried. My job, by comparison, didn’t seem nearly as stressful, but even before a global pandemic, it was stretching me to my limits—and I had an only-on-the-job eye twitch to prove it.

As the hospital’s director of enterprise health care risk management and insurance, I had a hand in all the operational, financial, strategic, and legal matters of the hospital. In addition, I oversaw our various insurances: medical malpractice, professional liability, indemnity, cyber, and excess. Those were the nuts and bolts of the work—aspects aptly covered by the job description. But there was so much more, like my work with the director of member services, Anise, who was so good at her job that she ran circles around some of those in the C-suite. We frequently partnered to manage dissatisfied patients and help ensure that their issues were meaningfully addressed and did not escalate and become litigious later.

Each day was unpredictable. We might have a patient threatening to beat up a gentle, elderly receptionist we’d employed for over 20 years; or the fertility clinic might be seeking guidance on how to respond to disgruntled, now-divorced former clients who were each claiming exclusive rights to embryos they had created together with donated gametes; or a patient might be threatening to leap from the roof. Or we could have all these things happen on the same day—as that particular trifecta did.

On one rare occasion, I had to manage a physician who consistently wasn’t meeting the standard required in the medical care he delivered, but who insisted he was. Sometimes the messy romances between our staff members made their way across my desk. Even insurance, the tamer bit of my work, could catch me off guard—like the day I received a request to check whether our insurance would cover a group of our surgeons who had been approached by veterinarians to assist them with a particularly complicated surgery on a gorilla from the local zoo. It was work I coveted. Despite the pace and breadth of the demands, it wasn’t the frontline work of hospitalists like Dr Gordon. Instead, I was on the back end—clean-up duty, tending to messes after they happened. This is why I felt compelled to give Dr Gordon all the leeway and time he needed that morning. This is why I decided my youngest baby’s bowel movement would simply have to wait.

Dr Gordon went on to explain: “The patient was a John Doe who arrived at our hospital via ambulance with no identification, only an incomplete witness report. He sustained his injuries when he either jumped or fell from a 16-foot overpass to the concrete below.” I winced, envisioning the crush of bone and flesh on hot pavement. Sinclair paused doing my hair and instinctually moved her four-year-old hand to my shoulder. I wanted to know which one it was—a jump or a fall? Was this something John Doe made happen, or was it something that happened to him? I’d turn it over for weeks afterward. In that moment, however, I was concerned that we caused John Doe further harm by trying to help him, and that he was all alone in our facility. It meant there was no next of kin notified when Dr Gordon and his team tried to put John Doe back together. There was no one to tell that John Doe’s life would likely forever be changed. There was no one to pray for him. So I did, silently, then dropped in a deftly timed, unmuted “hmmm, mmm” so Dr Gordon knew I was tracking before muting my phone again. I had to ensure that he didn’t hear Sinclair, two glitter-covered barrettes in hand, letting me know she was spraying my hair with water to prepare me for my second look of the day.

I thought I was such a clever clogs: I was balancing the impossible.

But I couldn’t see just around the bend. By year’s end, I’d realize that I hadn’t balanced a damn thing. In between, I was the nastiest version of myself I had ever been to my children. I’d had the biggest fight I’d ever had with my husband. I’d compromised the mental and emotional well-being of the people I loved most—my husband and children—not to mention my own. When I came to terms with what I’d lost later that year, and who I had become, I sat in the guilt-ridden shadows of those cold winter mornings, whispering affirmations that I’d be able to piece my family back together again, praying it would work. But on the day that I got the phone call from Dr Gordon about John Doe, I was still trying my hardest to both support my family and keep my hospital open and staffed to treat the sickest COVID-19 patients in our city, all in a country that didn’t seem to truly be supporting any of us.

I was about to conclude my conversation to rush Yves to a diaper near her rocking chair when Dr Gordon seemed to crumple again. “This one is entirely on me, it’s my fault. I was the trauma lead.” I assured him of something he likely already knew but couldn’t access in the moment: “Never Events rarely come down to one person, Dr Gordon. They often arise due to a series of small errors and oversights by numerous individuals that align to create catastrophic failures. They’re system failures. When we conduct our root-cause analysis, I suspect this will be the case in this instance too.” It was akin to my insistence to friends gathered at dinner parties, before the pandemic, often griping about the demagogue “destroying America” and angrily tweeting at us from the White House: “When things go really wrong, rarely does it come down to one person,” I’d quip. “Broken people don’t break the system; it’s almost always the other way around.”

That night, after putting the children to bed, on the day of Dr Gordon’s Never Event, I noodled on the message I had left him with: Broken people don’t break the system; broken systems break the people. I could see America, the Never Event, for what it was: a broken system. With the pandemic layered on top, the long-standing cracks in the country’s approaches to health care, childcare, and education, not to mention ensuring the protection and safety of its citizens, immediately erupted into view. I saw how those conditions worked together to drive me to break alignment with my core values, with what I knew to be most true in this world: I am here to protect the sacred lives I ushered into being. And that meant protecting them not just from COVID-19 but also from my own poor, strained, and overextended parenting decisions. At that moment, when everything in our world had come to a stop—something their young minds couldn’t comprehend—I may have been physically present, but I was ghosting them, right in their faces.

With Dr Gordon still on my mind and John Doe still in my heart, I declared to my husband, as we got ready for bed, that I had finally had enough. “There is no safe or viable life for us here in the United States. It’s an entirely broken system. Our best and only option would be to leave. We’ve got to leave,” I pleaded. My husband looked at me, and I could see he recognized what I felt. This was not a drill.

  1. Michael Saks and Stephan Landsman, Closing Death’s Door: Legal Innovations to End the Epidemic of Healthcare Harm (Oxford University Press 2021). ︎
  2. UC Davis PSNet Editorial Team, “Never Events” Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, September 15, 2024, https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/never-events ︎

issues.content_html:
In a Hollow at the Metaverse

Click to enlarge

Special Relativity

Like others in search, I chased
rainbows, twinkles, fantasies.
Not brambles, not cathedrals,

nor hummingbirds. No time for
the bark of a sea lion,
the fragrance of fresh lemon.

I revisited Plato’s Allegory
of the Cave. Tried to improve
upon War and Peace.

Your good tentacle is waving
goodbye, Grandpa.
Forgive me—I was busy

filming a Venus flytrap
in time lapse. I lied when
I said I had no time.

Is it too late to turn the tide on machine writing? T he romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt dra
issues.author: Sophie McBain
issues.content_html:
With authors losing lucrative deals and writers removed from prize shortlists, accusations of AI use are sending shock waves through the publishing industry. Is it too late to turn the tide on machine writing?

The romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time.

Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself “high six figures”.

issues.title: This Cursed Beautiful Land by Evan Gershkovich review – jailed in Putin’s Russia
issues.summary: The US reporter wrongly imprisoned for espionage writes compellingly about his ordeal Evan Gershkovich is the Wall Street Journal reporter who, in the early phase of Putin’s war in Ukraine, was snatched up by the Russian authorities on bogus espionage charges and spent a year and a half in Russian jails (first Lefortovo and then Yekaterinburg) before being released in a prisoner exchange in 2024.
issues.author: Sam Leith
issues.content_html:
The US reporter wrongly imprisoned for espionage writes compellingly about his ordeal

Evan Gershkovich is the Wall Street Journal reporter who, in the early phase of Putin’s war in Ukraine, was snatched up by the Russian authorities on bogus espionage charges and spent a year and a half in Russian jails (first Lefortovo and then Yekaterinburg) before being released in a prisoner exchange in 2024.

The opening section of his book about the experienceis gripping and rather moving. He recounts his arrest in a sting operation, after meeting a contact who promised to supply him with information about Russia’s military-industrial preparations. Born to Russian Jewish immigrant parents in the US, Gershkovich grew up in suburban New Jersey on a diet of Soviet cartoons and “Krylov’s fables rather than Aesop’s”; he was betwixt and between. When he found his way into journalism in his early 20s – first working nights as an editorial assistant at the New York Times, then getting started properly as a reporter at the Moscow Times– he gravitated to Russia and fell in love with it.

issues.title: Transcription by Ben Lerner audiobook review – a meditation on memory for the smartphone era
issues.summary: Actor Seth Numrich vividly captures the neurotic tendencies of a middle-aged man with a digital dependency, in an intense multilayered tale of family and storytelling We meet the unnamed narrator of Transcription on a train to Providence, Rhode Island. He is going to interview his one-time mentor Thomas, a celebrated German writer and film-maker, who is 90 and who, owing to his age, probably won’t
issues.author: Fiona Sturges
issues.content_html:
Actor Seth Numrich vividly captures the neurotic tendencies of a middle-aged man with a digital dependency, in an intense multilayered tale of family and storytelling

We meet the unnamed narrator of Transcription on a train to Providence, Rhode Island. He is going to interview his one-time mentor Thomas, a celebrated German writer and film-maker, who is 90 and who, owing to his age, probably won’t be interviewed again. The narrator confesses to his young daughter, Eva, that he is nervous about the meeting. Those nerves are replaced by panic when he gets to his hotel and drops his iPhone into a sink of water, rendering it useless. Not only does he have no means of recording the interview, he won’t be able to FaceTime Eva at bedtime.

Ben Lerner’s novella is a thoughtful meditation on memory, storytelling and lives lived through technology. The middle-aged narrator’s anxiety over his phone falls away as he engages with the world around him and with his past. He is pleased at being “able to convert the sense of being screenless into a kind of super­sensitivity” though later, in Thomas’s house, he finds himself “glitching, craving my cellular phone on a cellular level, shamefully unresponsive to the old media that surrounded me”. For the interview, he pretends to record the conversation on his dead phone and tries to commit Thomas’s words to memory.

issues.title: Tout selling £1million of U2 tickets has raised questions about clampdown on bot use for bulk-buying
issues.summary: More than 2,000 tickets for the band's upcoming London shows were listed by a single seller on StubHub, with some priced at over four times their face value The post Tout selling £1million of U2 tickets has raised questions about clampdown on bot use for bulk-buying appeared first on NME .
issues.author: Max Pilley
issues.content_html:
A ticket tout has advertised more than £1million worth of tickets for U2‘s upcoming London shows, raising fresh questions about the use of automated bots to bulk-buy tickets and sell them on at inflated prices.

  • READ MORE: As live music returns, let’s build back fairer – by wiping out unscrupulous touts

The Irish band’s four nights at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in June 2027, part of their ‘The Greatest Show On Earth’ world tour, sold out shortly after tickets went on sale last week.

However, a new investigation by The Guardian has revealed that one seller listed more than 2,000 tickets for the concerts on resale site StubHub, despite strict limits on the number that any individual buyer can purchase.

The seller, identified as Vladyslav Skrypka and claiming to be based in Harlow, Essex, advertised over 1,800 tickets for one night alone, some at more than four times their original price. If all of the tickets were sold at their advertised prices, they would generate more than £1million in sales.

The findings have raised concerns about how such large quantities of tickets can be obtained, given that the use of automated software to bypass ticket-buying limits has been outlawed in the UK since 2018.

Adam Webb of the music industry campaign group FanFair Alliance suggested that the listings could indicate either the use of bots or ‘speculative selling’ – where touts advertise tickets they do not yet possess, hoping to acquire them after a buyer has paid.

View this post on Instagram

Webb questioned whether StubHub had verified the seller’s tickets, asking: “Have they seen evidence of Vladyslav’s receipts?”

There is no confirmation that either practice was used to obtain the tickets in question.

StubHub International has said it does not permit speculative selling and requires sellers to confirm that they own, or have the right to sell, the tickets they advertise.

“We are firmly against the use of bots,” the company said, arguing that stronger enforcement is needed at the original point of sale.

Ticketmaster disputed the suggestion that primary ticketing companies were responsible for the problem, saying it blocks 20 billion bots every month and that secondary marketplaces create the incentive for their use.

The controversy comes amid continued pressure on the UK government to introduce its long-promised ban on reselling tickets for profit.

In November 2025, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy confirmed plans to prohibit reselling tickets above face value, telling NME: “We promised when we were elected that it would be time up for ticket touts. It’s a good day.”

She also explained that the proposed legislation would give the Competition and Markets Authority powers to fine resale platforms up to 10 per cent of their annual turnover for breaches.

However, the plans have yet to become law. In May this year, the music industry expressed widespread disappointment when the government included only a draft Ticket Tout Ban Bill in the King’s Speech.

The decision raised fears that further consultations and parliamentary scrutiny could delay the introduction of tougher protections for fans.

At the time, Webb told NME: “Why take the long road when you could protect music fans today?”

The issue has affected several other major artists in recent weeks. In October, RAYE revealed that her Royal Albert Hall ticket registration system had been overwhelmed by scalpers using AI bots, after receiving 1.8 million sign-ups for just 5,000 seats.

Later that month, Sam Fender was forced to delay the pre-sale for his Newcastle stadium shows following what he described as a “sophisticated bot attack” on ticketing website Gigantic.

U2’s 2027 stadium tour will see Wolf Alice support them across the UK and Europe, following the release of their new album ‘Carnaval De Luz’ on Friday (November 13).

issues.title: Philippines crowned first Eurovision Asia winners as Carmelle triumphs with ‘Sobra-Sobra’
issues.summary: The 19-year-old singer topped both the jury and public votes at the inaugural contest in Bangkok The post Philippines crowned first Eurovision Asia winners as Carmelle triumphs with ‘Sobra-Sobra’ appeared first on NME .
issues.author: Max Pilley
issues.content_html:
The Philippines has been crowned the first-ever winner of Eurovision Asia, with 19-year-old singer Carmelle taking victory with her song ‘Sobra-Sobra’ – watch her performance below.

The long-awaited spin-off of Eurovision held its inaugural final at the One Bangkok Forum in Thailand yesterday (November 14), with 11 countries competing for the title.

Carmelle, whose full name is Carmelle Collado, finished with 211 points, receiving 93 from the national juries and 118 from the public vote. She topped both categories to finish 41 points ahead of the host country’s representatives, MANG x DAOU, whose song ‘Aroma’ received 170 points.

Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên finished third with ‘EM TIÊN’ on 164 points, while Malaysia and Laos completed the top five.

Carmelle’s winning song ‘Sobra-Sobra’, meaning ‘Too Much’, is a women’s empowerment anthem that combines dance-pop and rap with traditional Filipino instruments, including the kubing and kulintang.

Watch the winning performance below:

Speaking after her victory, Carmelle described the song as “a tribute to all Filipino women”.

“I made history, since this was the first time,” she told the Associated Press. “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.”

The singer, who grew up in the Bicol region of the Philippines, previously found success on televised singing competitions, finishing as runner-up on The Voice Kids and winning Tawag ng Tanghalan. She also appeared on Pinoy Big Brother.

View this post on Instagram

The contest brought together performers from the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Laos, Bhutan, South Korea, Mongolia, Nepal, Cambodia and Bangladesh.

Other notable performances included Thailand’s MANG x DAOU, whose emotional duet ‘Aroma’ received a huge reception from the home crowd, and Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, who performed entirely a cappella, using beatboxing to recreate drums and basslines.

The full final standings were:

  1. Philippines – Carmelle – 211 points
  2. Thailand – MANG x DAOU – 170 points
  3. Vietnam – Tóc Tiên – 164 points
  4. Malaysia – Aina Abdul – 152 points
  5. Laos – Thinla – 139 points
  6. Bhutan – Nyendra – 126 points
  7. South Korea – JUNHEE – 113 points
  8. Mongolia – Beck – 94 points
  9. Nepal – Pratik Himal Rai – 69 points
  10. Cambodia – Monetrey – 61 points
  11. Bangladesh – Beatmosphere – 35 points

View this post on Instagram

The evening also featured guest performances from Thai singer Jeff Satur and Bulgaria’s Dara, who won the main Eurovision Song Contest earlier this year with ‘Bangaranga’.

Dara performed her winning song alongside her new single ‘Bad Idea’, before presenting Carmelle with the trophy.

The Asian edition had been discussed for years, with several previous attempts to launch a regional version of Eurovision having failed to materialise.

Martin Green, director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said: “Congratulations to CARMELLE and the Philippines on becoming the first-ever winners of Eurovision Song Contest Asia. What an historic achievement!”

Carmelle will now perform at Eurovision 2027 in Burgas, Bulgaria, although she will not be competing in the European contest.

issues.title: Watch Noel Gallagher join Goldie and Skunk Anansie’s Skin on stage for first performance since Oasis reunion tour
issues.summary: The trio shared the stage at the London Jazz Festival, backed by a live band, choir and orchestra The post Watch Noel Gallagher join Goldie and Skunk Anansie’s Skin on stage for first performance since Oasis reunion tour appeared first on NME .
issues.author: Max Pilley
issues.content_html:
Noel Gallagher has made his first live appearance since Oasis‘ reunion tour, joining Goldie and Skunk Anansie‘s Skin on stage at the London Jazz Festival – check out footage below.

  • READ MORE: ‘Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger’ review: an emotional, irreverent reliving of rock’s unlikeliest reunion

The guitarist appeared at the Royal Festival Hall in London last night (November 14), as part of Goldie’s two special ‘Dare To Dream’ performances at the EFG London Jazz Festival.

The shows saw the drum and bass pioneer joined by the Elysian Collective orchestra, a choir and his live band, alongside a range of special guests.

Gallagher played guitar during Goldie’s set, with Skin also appearing on stage. One audience member shared footage of the collaboration on Instagram, writing: “My mind’s blown… Goldie, Skin from Skunk Anansie & Noel Gallagher!!!! With a live orchestra!!! My life is complete!!!”

Watch footage from the show here:

View this post on Instagram

View this post on Instagram

Noel Gallagher playing guitar on stage with Goldie at London Jazz Festival tonight pic.twitter.com/O3rtTXze1Z

— Oasis Planet (@OasisPlanet_) November 14, 2026

The performances had been announced earlier this month, marking Gallagher’s first appearance outside Oasis since their hugely successful ‘Live ’25’ reunion tour.

Goldie and Gallagher have been friends for decades, having previously collaborated on the 1998 track ‘Temper Temper’, from Goldie’s album ‘Saturnz Return’.

Announcing Gallagher’s appearance, Goldie had said: “Me and Noel Gallagher do it again. 30 years, that’s what we’ve got between us. We’re here, going to Royal Festival Hall to do it all over again.”

Speaking to NME ahead of the shows, he added: “They said this music would only last five years, 35 years later I’m still here ready to do another iconic show ‘Dare To Dream’ at the Royal Festival Hall.

“This time I have Noel Gallagher, Skin, Anaiis, Yussef Dayes and many more incredible guests plus my live band and an orchestra. New and classic material, it’s a very very special show. Two shows, One Dream.”

In October 2024, Goldie visited Gallagher’s Lone Star Studio in London, where the musician showed him the guitar equipment he was planning to use on Oasis’ reunion tour.

The ‘Dare To Dream’ performances formed part of the 34th EFG London Jazz Festival, which runs from November 13 to 22 across more than 70 venues in the capital.

Meanwhile, Oasis are preparing to return to the road for their sold-out ‘Live ’27’ world tour, following their long-awaited reunion in 2025. The run will include 42 shows across the UK, Europe and North America, including 11 nights at Manchester’s Etihad Stadium and six at Knebworth.

Gallagher has already promised that the new concerts will be “so much better” than the 2025 shows.

The band were also inducted into the Rock And Roll Hall Of Fame this weekend, although neither Noel nor Liam attended the ceremony in Los Angeles.

In other news, Gallagher has been working on new music, although it remains unclear whether the material is intended for Oasis, the High Flying Birds or another project. His most recent solo album was 2023’s ‘Council Skies’.

issues.title: Six Short Stories That Play with Time
issues.summary: Stories of memory, loss, and the passage of time, by Grace Paley, Alice Munro, Anjali Sachdeva, Edward P. Jones, William Trevor, and Jamaica Kincaid. The post Six Short Stories That Play with Time appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: The Editors
issues.content_html:
Memory, the passage of time, and the inextricable hold that the past has on the present are all essential elements of narrative art. Fiction, unlike other artistic media, can seamlessly manipulate time—whether keeping the reader firmly in the grasp of the present, enfolding different time periods into one scene, or leaping forward twenty years with a single paragraph break. These stories demonstrate how language can transport us through time. As always, all are free to download.

“Wants” by Gracey Paley

A woman meets her ex-husband on the steps of a library and remembers the life she shared with him. Paley turns a single scene into a container for decades of regret and tenderness, her sentences conveying the breathless passage of years: “First, my father was sick that Friday, then the children were born, then I had those Tuesday-night meetings, then the war began.”

“What Do You Want to Know For?” by Alice Munro

The Nobel Prize winner is famous for her obsession with the past and how it shapes us. In Munro’s story, a woman, who discovers a lump in her breast, avoids her health anxieties by fixating on a crypt in the countryside and learning about the history of southern Ontario. Her own mortality seems insignificant against the languorous pace of geologic time. Look for Munro’s use of section breaks to move the reader seamlessly forward in time—skipping ten days, two weeks, a year.

“The World by Night” by Anjali Sachdeva

Anjali Sachdeva’s story opens with sixteen-year-old Sadie helping the gravedigger bury her parents. The story then jumps forward to Sadie at twenty, married, but with her husband gone indefinitely on a long trip. Missing her husband, she becomes obsessed with exploring a cave on the outskirts of her homestead. The story’s shifts in time are seamless and elegant, and the central image of the cave becomes a haunting metaphor for grief.

“First Day” by Edward P. Jones

We meet Daisy on her first day of school. Here, instead of folding one moment into the next, Jones gives us the slow, sensuous experience of a day that becomes forever preserved in a child’s memory—her mother plaiting her hair extra carefully, the smell of her new pencils, and the click of her mother’s shoes as she leaves Daisy at school. When Daisy encounters disappointments she can’t yet comprehend, we know her adult self will one day grasp their significance.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

“Miss Smith” by William Trevor

William Trevor’s short story recounts the course of a strange relationship—between a bully and her victim, a teacher named Miss Smith and her student, James. James is obsessed: why is Miss Smith so intent on mocking him at every turn, even after she retires from teaching to marry and have a child? The third-person narration gives us the answer, tied as it is to our fears about enduring the passage of time: “Miss Smith recognised in [her son] some trait she disliked and knew that she would be obliged to watch it develop, powerless to intervene.” In time, James gets his revenge.

“Ovando” by Jamaica Kincaid

In Kincaid’s surreal parable, a strange skeleton of a man named Ovando comes to the door, and the narrator allows him into her house. We feel immediate tension from his presence, and the narration repeatedly jumps forward in time, revealing the narrator’s regrets about having let this humanoid creature inside. Their relationship evolves over immense swaths of time—enough for Ovando to colonize the narrator’s world entirely. Of all the selected stories, “Ovando” is the strangest and most abstract in its manipulation of time.

issues.title: Beyond the Plantation House
issues.summary: Historic photographs and maps reveal the changing landscape of a Texas plantation and the overlooked history of those who labored there. The post Beyond the Plantation House appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: The Editors
issues.content_html:
The history of plantations across the southern United States is inseparable from one of the darkest chapters of American history—slavery. These sprawling estates, often characterized by grand plantation houses and agricultural buildings, typically produced crops like tobacco or cotton, and depended on enslaved labor until the Civil War.

Rice University’s Archaeology Project at the Varner-Hogg Plantation in Brazoria County, Texas, brings a community-oriented approach to studying and documenting this dark period of history. Conducted in cooperation with the Texas Historical Society, the project focuses on the lives of the enslaved and incarcerated people who labored at the plantation in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Local residents were invited to observe the excavation, ask questions, share their knowledge, and engage with archaeologists and their students during the work.

Community archaeology like this aims to make archaeological knowledge accessible beyond the researchers working in the field. By engaging local communities, it encourages dialogue and a broader understanding of the past. As archaeologist Yvonne Marshall emphasizes, community archaeology “is the only way that indigenous people, descendant communities and other local interest groups will be able to own the pasts archaeologists are employed to create.”

Prior to Rice University’s archaeological work, the history of the Varner-Hogg Plantation was largely told through the restoration and development of the property as a historic site in the 1950s and 1960s, under the direction of Ima Hogg. Hogg was the daughter of former Texas governor James Stephen Hogg, who purchased the property in 1901, believing that the land held large amounts of oil. He was correct, although oil wasn’t found until nearly fifteen years after his death in 1906. Following the conventions of the time, Ima restored the home with each room decorated to celebrate a different period of Texas history.

The history of the Varner-Hogg Plantation begins in 1824 when Martin Varner settled the property through one of the land grants offered by Stephen F. Austin between 1823 and 1825. Varner sold the property ten years later to Columbus R. Patton. Known as the Patton Place for the rest of the nineteenth century, the plantation expanded significantly under the Patton family through the labor of enslaved people. At its peak, over 100 enslaved people were forced to work at the site. They built numerous buildings, including the plantation house and their own living quarters, as well as structures such as a smokehouse and sugar mill.

The Patton family sold the plantation in 1869. The new owners soon began to use incarcerated labor to operate the plantation, but that arrangement ended in 1875 when state investigators documented the “particular cruelty” with which incarcerated laborers were treated at the site. It would not be the only time inmates were used as a labor source on the plantation. The property changed hands several times over the rest of the century until former governor Hogg purchased it in 1901.

In the late 1950s, Ima Hogg donated the plantation to the State of Texas as a historic site. But her restoration largely overlooked the history of the enslaved people forced to labor there. While her notes from the time included research questions about slavery at the plantation, Hogg chose to exclude that history from the restoration project. Historian Lonn Taylor explains that “Hogg believed that African Americans were not interested in the history of slavery and that any mention of the subject was an embarrassment to them. As a result, slavery was omitted from her original interpretive plans at Varner Plantation.” At the time, plantation histories commonly centered on white owners and their experiences, leaving the lives of enslaved people largely untold.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

In their analysis of community archaeological projects focusing on the African diaspora, scholars V. Camille Westmont and Elizabeth Clay note that the shift toward community archaeology did not happen by chance. They write that “[w]hile archaeologists studying plantations made an early shift in focus away from elite whites and towards enslaved African populations, it was not until the growth of critical archaeology and the passage of the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA)—both in the 1990s—that calls to bring community stakeholders into research projects became commonplace.”

Rice University’s Archaeology Project encourages local communities and tourists to engage with this dark chapter of history in a more open and thoughtful way. Reflecting a broader shift toward community engagement in archaeology, the project seeks to deepen public understanding of the legacy of historic sites like the Varner-Hogg Plantation.

issues.title: In Defense of the Humanities
issues.summary: Why studying literature and philosophy remains essential in a world increasingly focused on career-ready skills. The post In Defense of the Humanities appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Jonathan Aprea
issues.content_html:
Loss and literature

Often, the shortest stories are the most resonant. In 2020, I lost my maternal grandmother. “Maternal,” in her case, was more than a qualifier—she quite literally played the role of “mother” in my life. My first words, my first steps, and the most formative milestones of my childhood and adolescence happened in her care. She bore the brunt of my insufferable teenage angst, offering a consoling embrace when life seemed to get ahead of me. When I lost her, a chapter of my life ended.

To lose such a constant in one’s early twenties is to lose a tether to one’s reality. The years after my grandmother’s death have been fraught with uncertainty. How could I possibly recover from such a loss? How are my accomplishments meaningful if she is not present to witness them? And, perhaps most disconcerting: who will I be by the time my own life begins to wane?

Everyone copes with and experiences loss differently. For me, it was acutely alienating. My relationship with my grandmother was singular, making my perspective on loss unique. I operated for what felt like ages on the assumption that no matter how much support I had, I could not possibly be seen.

The connection I achieved through literature highlights the critical importance of the humanities.

That is, until I picked up A Very Easy Death. This brief, 112-page memoir by Simone de Beauvoir details her mother’s final days from an honest, compassionate perspective. Laden with recollections of a mother-daughter relationship and personal confrontations with mortality, it resonated with me in a way that no other text had. The acts of death and grief are explored in her memoir as though de Beauvoir were sitting across from me at a bistro recounting the experience. For the first time since my own experience and despite preceding me by thirty-six years, someone had finally seen me.

The humanities: Studies of the human condition

The connection I achieved through literature highlights the critical importance of the humanities. Encompassing history, literature, philosophy, art, and more, the humanities provide a lens through which one can view one’s personal experiences—making the universal personal and the personal universal.

The humanities and humanism have evolved significantly over centuries. In Western society, humanism traces back to Greece in the fourth and fifth centuries BCE. Sophists saw humanism as a cultural-educational program, aiming for the development of human faculties and excellence, as noted in Perez Zagorin’s “On Humanism Past & Present.”

In Rome, the concept evolved into “an ideal expressed in the concept of humanities … [which] designated a number of studies—philosophy, history, literature, rhetoric, and training in the oratory.” Most influential, though, was the humanism that emerged from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries that was “centered increasingly upon human interests and moral concerns rather than religion.” Its purpose was to cultivate a population of Christian men who were well-spoken, literate, and capable of integrating with high society.

Growing more secular over time, humanist values began to compete with the physical and biological sciences, the social sciences, and other modern subjects which comprised nineteenth-century liberal education. Zagorin suggests that scientific and empirical research approaches overtook human-centered perspectives, particularly after the massive loss of life in World War I and the disillusionment that followed.

Scholarly perspectives on the importance of the humanities

Scholars argue that the humanities are essential for comprehending complex social dynamics and ethical questions. In “The Power of the Humanities and a Challenge to Humanists,” Richard J. Franke argues that humanistic interpretation “contributes to a tradition of interpretation.” Franke posits that human emotions and values are at the core of humanistic study, offering the ability to explore domains that “animate the human experience.” This is precisely how my engagement with Simone de Beauvoir’s memoir, A Very Easy Death, provided a foundation for evaluating broader human concerns.

Through de Beauvoir’s philosophical inquiries into life and death, I was able to confront and process my own grief more profoundly. Her reflections on mortality and the mother-daughter relationship resonated deeply with me, helping me to navigate my personal loss while also offering insights into the universal human condition. This connection underscores the humanities’ power to transform personal experiences into a deeper understanding of shared human emotions and values.

Moreover, Franke postulates that subjects under the humanities all lend themselves to critical thinking, which he defines as “that Socratic habit of articulating questions and gathering relevant information in order to make reasonable judgements.” Through the humanities, one can approach topics from varied vantage points to develop a holistic understanding of them.

In a study published in 2018 by the Journal of General Internal Medicine, medical students across institutions suggested that exposure to the humanities had an appreciable influence on their “tolerance of ambiguity, empathy, and wisdom.” The study’s discussion section further indicates that both the performance and observance of drama increase empathy, and that “even good literature prompts better detection of emotions.” These findings highlight that studying the humanities cultivates essential skills and attributes that have practical applications in real-world settings.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

Scholarship, then, suggests that the humanities teach us to be human, whether through the ability to form nuanced questions or to feel empathy. I experienced this firsthand while reading Simone de Beauvoir’s A Very Easy Death. Her detailed account of her mother’s final days helped me navigate my own grief. It also gave me a deeper understanding of the emotional complexities involved in facing mortality as a concept. These characteristics—developed through engagement with the humanities—can improve interpersonal relationships and foster a more empathetic and accepting society.

The impact of the humanities extends beyond personal growth; it influences professional practices and societal outcomes. The empathy and wisdom nurtured by humanities education can enhance the quality of patient care in the medical field, as evidenced by the medical students’ testimonies. Similarly, professionals in law, education, and public policy benefit from the critical thinking and ethical reasoning stimulated by humanities education. By emphasizing these real-world applications, we can better advocate for the continued support and integration of the humanities in various sectors of society.

Challenges affecting the humanities: Economic pressures and academic isolation

Even in light of their demonstrated value, the humanities face significant challenges that threaten their vitality and relevance. In “The Decline of the Humanities and the Decline of Society,” Ibanga B. Ikpe describes how today’s labor market increasingly demands qualifications for specific sectors. Courses in the humanities that are not tailored to particular career paths put them at a disadvantage in universities.

Ikpe also attributes the decline in humanities education to the fact that “economic rather than academic motivations have become the primary basis for decision making in universities.” He raises the notion that the humanities and similar disciplines cannot be elucidated into digestible pieces of information, which makes them more difficult to sell. The more defined the subject, the more profitable. Thus, funding for humanities programs at educational institutions has declined significantly. This has both limited resources for teaching and research and signaled a devaluation of the humanities as a whole.

More to Explore

Frankenstein, The Vampyre, and the Spirit of the Humanities

Maria Papadouris October 20, 2026 How one ghost story competition continues to haunt the humanities—just in time for Halloween.

Finally, Ikpe presents the argument that humanities scholars are partially to blame for the current state of the humanities. He raises the accusation that humanities scholars have become withdrawn from greater society, sequestering themselves in academia. The niche views and dialogues they produce in this environment may sever their connection with a broader audience.

Sustaining the humanities today

The future implied by the above rings grim, but there are still significant opportunities to advocate for the humanities by highlighting their interdisciplinary relevance to contemporary issues. For example, the study of ethics in philosophy can provide crucial insights into debates on artificial intelligence and biotechnology. Similarly, understanding historical contexts can help policymakers make informed decisions about current social and political challenges.

By leveraging the support of organizations like JSTOR and embracing technological advancements, we can turn the tide in favor of the humanities. Advocating for their interdisciplinary relevance and addressing contemporary social issues will ensure that these vital disciplines thrive. The humanities are not relics of the past—they are essential to navigating the complexities of the present and shaping the future.

This is an installment of a series that first appeared on the JSTOR Blog about the enduring importance of the humanities. Stay tuned for more insights on why the humanities still matter.

issues.title: Iron Age frog mass grave explained
issues.summary: Scientists at Bournemouth University and Museum of London Archaeology have discovered the reason 8,000 frog and toad bones were found buried in a 45-foot-long trench at an Iron Age settlement near Cambridge in the UK. The bones were unearthed during highway improvement works between 2016 and 2018. The trench was located near a Late Iron … Read the full post → "Iron Age frog mass grave explained"
issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
Scientists at Bournemouth University and Museum of London Archaeology have discovered the reason 8,000 frog and toad bones were found buried in a 45-foot-long trench at an Iron Age settlement near Cambridge in the UK.

The bones were unearthed during highway improvement works between 2016 and 2018. The trench was located near a Late Iron Age (400 B.C. – 43 A.D.) roundhouse, so the frogs were thought to have been buried between that range. It was a perplexing find. Frog bones had been found before in archaeological contexts, but only as an individuals. Mass burials of animal remains had been found before in archaeological contexts, usually from ceremonial feasting, but they were the usual food animals – livestock like cattle and sheep or chickens – not hundreds of tiny amphibians.

Archaeologists eliminated the possibility that they had been cooked in a feast because there were no cut marks or evidence of heating. Grain found nearby indicates the settlement grew crops that would attract amphibians, but it would take a Moses-level pestilence to explain the numbers. Another possibility was migrating frogs becoming trapped in the ditch on their way to breeding waters, or freezing to death in a sudden temperature drop while seeking shelter in the mud.

Well, it turns out all of those ideas were wrong. The frogs were eaten, but not by humans, and hundreds of years after the roundhouse was built.

After comparing the damage to the frog bones to previous studies, Dr Clarkson found they had been eaten by birds of prey, with short-eared owls and hen harriers being the most likely suspects.

But the story didn’t end there. Onsite archaeological evidence shows the ditch filled within a single year and therefore this still left the question of how so many bones appeared in such a short period of time. So, the Bournemouth team investigated further.

By measuring the size of the frog humeri (arm bones) – a pioneering new method of analysis – they discovered most of the frogs died young, having been eaten in the winter of their first year of life. Radiocarbon dating by the University of Vienna also showed the remains dated back 1700 years to Roman period.

The Fen waters were retreating in this valley in the Roman period, creating ideal conditions for the frogs to breed in – leaving an abundance for the birds to eat.

Humans were the owls’ accomplices in the mass slaughter. The area had previously been wooded, but in the Late Iron Age, people gradually felled the trees to make more land available for grazing their livestock. Short-eared owls hunt on grasslands, so the frogs were much more exposed with fewer trees to shelter them.

“We don’t often get an owl’s eye view of what it was like in the past from archaeological sites,” said Dr Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth University who led the study.

“The mystery of these frogs has been solved – a feast of frogs that were eaten and their bones left behind by a group of owls. These bones not only tell us about life for people living near the Roman Fens, but they also give insights into the natural world – what wild animals were getting up to in the past, and what life was like for them,” he added.

issues.title: Rare artifacts from Viking double burial found on Isle of Man
issues.summary: A remarkable combination of rare and unique artifacts likely from a Viking double burial has been discovered on the Isle of Man. More than 1,100 years old, the objects attest to the lives and deaths of some of Man’s earliest Viking settlers. The artifacts were discovered by a metal detectorist. They consist of three bronze … Read the full post → "Rare artifacts from Viking double burial found on I
issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A remarkable combination of rare and unique artifacts likely from a Viking double burial has been discovered on the Isle of Man. More than 1,100 years old, the objects attest to the lives and deaths of some of Man’s earliest Viking settlers.

The artifacts were discovered by a metal detectorist. They consist of three bronze brooches, a sword, a bronze ladle, an axe head and a set of trading weights and scales. While no human remains were found, the type of artifacts, particularly the jewelry and weapons, are characteristic of male and female burials from the Viking Age.

The brooches are beautifully decorated. Two of them are a matched pair of concave oval brooches decorated with interlocking animal motifs. Known as skålspænder (scoop brooches), this type of brooch was used to fasten apron dresses at the shoulder. They were found in women’s graves. Only one other pair has ever been found on the Isle of Man, and the newly-discovered pair is about 50 years older, so it’s evidence of the earliest Viking women’s grave on the island.

The third brooch is unique on the archaeological record of the Isle. It is round with a wide outer border, an inner band decorated with spirals and a central boss of colored glass. It was originally gilded, although only traces remains.

The sword found in the assemblage is also elaborately decorated. It is broken, likely deliberately as part of the funerary ritual, and about two thirds of it survives. The surviving hilt is decorated with silver inlay and twisted silver wire. Out of the 13 Viking swords found on the Isle of Man, only two others are so richly decorated.

The discovery also provides further evidence of trade and cultural connections across the Irish Sea. Decorated lead weights and fragments of bronze balance scales would have been used to weigh precious metals and coins during trading. The weights are the first of their type found on the Isle of Man.

One weight features a decorative bronze fitting, possibly reused from a small chest or religious object, with an artwork style typical of Britain and Ireland at the time. It offers a fascinating example of how Viking settlers adopted and reused objects from other cultures.

A bronze ladle, possibly used for feasting or ceremonies, is another type of object not previously recorded on the Island. […]

With several objects being the first of their kind found on the Island, the collection offers an important opportunity to learn more about Viking settlement, burial traditions and everyday life.

issues.summary: Two rare stone casting molds for a sword and a jewelry pendant from the Bronze Age Urnfield culture (1300-800 B.C.) have been discovered in Großeibstadt, Lower Franconia, Bavaria. The intact half of a mold for a tanged sword is unique on Bavaria’s archaeological record. The second is a mold for a pendant. The objects are … Read the full post → "Bronze Age casting moulds, hoard found in Bavaria"
issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
Two rare stone casting molds for a sword and a jewelry pendant from the Bronze Age Urnfield culture (1300-800 B.C.) have been discovered in Großeibstadt, Lower Franconia, Bavaria. The intact half of a mold for a tanged sword is unique on Bavaria’s archaeological record. The second is a mold for a pendant. The objects are evidence that a bronze caster worked his trade at the site around 3,000 years ago.

The casting molds are among the most significant finds reported since the amended Bavarian Monument Protection Act went into effect on July 1, 2023. Before then, any archaeological artifact found in Bavaria was subject to “Hadrianic division,” meaning objects belonged 50/50 to the finder and the landowner. Protection of Bavaria’s cultural heritage had no role in this arrangement.

Under the new law, all archaeological artifacts belong to the state. Finders and landowners are entitled to a reward if the market value exceeds 1000 euros and the object was recovered in keeping with the law. Regional institutions are given the opportunity to apply for transfer of the items based on predetermined criteria.

A second major discovery begun in October 2024 also attests to the success of the new law. A metal detectorist found several bronze objects in a field near Grabenstätt in the Chiemgau region of Upper Bavaria. He followed the law, documenting each find in detail and then reporting them to the Bavarian State Office for Monument Preservation (BLfD).

The objects were part of a late Urnfield period (ca. 880–800 B.C.) hoard that was likely scattered by later agricultural work. Throughout 2025 and 2026, the finder, coordinated by the BLfD, surveyed the site, discovering more pieces. The final tally was 52 solid arm and leg rings, two flanged axes, fragments of a sheet-bronze arm ring, parts of at least one bronze cup, and a plate-sized cast ingot (a “cake” of raw metal) were recovered. It was one of the largest and most varied hoard of the period found in southern Bavaria.

Taken together, the casting molds and the hoard attest to the skills of Bronze Age metalworkers in the production of weapons and adornments in Bavaria during the Urnfield period.

issues.title: Vandal warrior grave weapons given to museum in Poland

issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
The Father Stanisław Staszic Museum in Hrubieszów, Poland, has received an complete set of Vandal weapons, likely from a cremation burial, that is one of the richest Vandal warrior burials ever found in the region. The assemblage includes a sword, spearpoints, shield fittings, spurs and a bronze fibula.

Buried approximately 2,000 years ago, the group consists of an iron sword deliberately broken into three parts, plus pieces of its scabbard, two spear points, one intact made of iron and the other broken, a shield boss with a sharp protrusion, a shield handle, a helmet with a collar, a dagger, two spurs, a belt buckle, a bronze fibula for closing a cloak. All of these elements, especially the presence of the rare scabbard and spurs, indicate that the deceased was a high-ranking cavalry warrior.

The origin of the find is murky. The collection was delivered anonymously, and the only thing museum officials know is that the artifacts emerged on farmland in a few years ago in the municipality of Werbkowice. They were not recovered at that time, and since then the contents were exposed to damage.

The objects are in poor condition, heavily corroded, and in need of urgent intervention to prevent further deterioration. Specialists have been engaged to conserve the pieces. The process is expected to take months.

The museum plans to verify the location with an excavation next year. For now, researchers believe the objects came from a single grave. There may be others at the site, which would shed light on the assemblage that has been removed from its context.

issues.title: Why did thousands of Spaniards risk their lives to fight for Hitler?
issues.summary: Still recovering from the Spanish Civil War, tens of thousands of men joined the Nazis so that they could rid the world of communism
issues.author: Jonny Wilkes
issues.content_html:
During the Second World War, Spain maintained an official policy of neutrality, or at least ‘non-belligerence’, but that did not stop the nascent regime of dictator Francisco Franco from finding ways to side with the Axis Powers of Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.

One way for Franco to show support and keep Hitler happy without committing the country to all-out war was the Blue Division.

Spanish versus Soviet

In June 1941, the Nazis launched Operation Barbarossa, the invasion of the Soviet Union. In Spain, this was seen as an opportunity for the diehard fascists to wage their ongoing crusade against communism, as well as get revenge on the Soviets for their role in supporting the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War. Germany and Italy had given significant support to Franco’s nationalists.

Just days after the invasion got underway, Franco offered assistance to Hitler in the form of a special unit for the Eastern Front. When the call went out, recruiting offices were inundated with more than 18,000 volunteers, the majority being serving military personnel or civil war veterans, or members of the fascist party, the Falangists. A large number of ideological university students would also enlist.

Under the command of Agustin Munoz Grandes, they formed the 250th Infantry Division within the German army, but became known as the Blue Division on account of the blue shirts of their symbolic uniform. Spanish pilots, meanwhile, formed the Blue Squadron.

Resilience and courage

The Blue Division was sent to Bavaria for training, which would be fast-tracked to ensure that they got to the action before all the fighting was over. (They had no reason to think, of course, that the Eastern Front would drag on for years and ultimately seal the Nazi defeat.)

Although criticised by their German comrades for a lack of discipline, the Spanish soldiers quickly earned a reputation for unyielding resilience. Indeed, their deployment involved a march of 500-plus miles from Poland to Russia, where they endured the freezing conditions, disease and shortages, the latter exacerbated by constant communication issues with the Germans supplying them.

  • Read more | “Weimar's citizens cheered on Hitler”: why the home of German democracy was easy prey for the Nazis

Then once in battle, as part of the Siege of Leningrad, they demonstrated a fearless courage. For months, they held the line against the Red Army even though it cost many lives. Around this time, command of the Blue Division was given to General Emilio Esteban-Infantes Martin after Grandes was recalled to Spain, having been decorated with one of the highest military honours in Nazi Germany, the Knight’s Cross of the Iron Cross.

At the battle of Krasny Bor in early 1943, a 5,000-strong detachment of the Blue Division held off a force outnumbering them sixfold, and equipped with tanks and artillery. They suffered horrific casualties yet successfully halted the Soviet offensive in the region. Hitler himself remarked: “One can’t imagine more fearless fellows. They scarcely take cover. They flout death.”

In 1944, the entire division would be granted a unique honour, the Commemorative Medal for Spanish Volunteers in the Struggle Against Bolshevism.

Legacy of the Blue Division

By then, however, Franco had been pressed by the Allies to reaffirm his country’s neutrality and disbanded the Blue Division. While most of the men returned to Spain, several thousand refused and continued to fight, either under the new name of the Blue Legion or assimilated into other units of the Wehrmacht. The last remnants of the Blue Division fought right up until the fall of Berlin in 1945.

Around 47,000 men served on the Eastern Front in total, with 5,000 never returning. Thousands more were injured or taken prisoner, some of whom were not released by the Soviets until 1954.

The Blue Division has a complicated legacy in Spain, remembered by some as anti-communist heroes or Nazi collaborators by others. While they never took part in the worst atrocities committed by the Nazis – in fact, they drew ire from the Germans for their fair treatment of the Jewish people they encountered – the Francoist regime looked to downplay their role quickly in the aftermath of the war.
