issues.title: Unwavering cooperators make group efforts easier to start but harder to sustain
issues.summary: Every group effort seems to benefit from a few people who always pitch in. A new mathematical model suggests those reliable contributors make collective action easier to start, but can also give everyone else an excuse to coast.
issues.author: Eric W. Dolan
issues.content_html:
A small band of unconditionally cooperative individuals can make it much easier for a group to get a shared effort off the ground, yet their reliability may also encourage others to slack off over the long run. According to a new mathematical modeling study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, unwavering cooperators act as a double-edged sword in group tasks that require a minimum number of contributors to succeed. The findings suggest that committed minorities can help spark collective action while simultaneously reducing overall participation once coordination takes hold.

Cooperation allows living things, from bacteria building protective films to humans funding public infrastructure, to achieve together what no single individual could manage alone. Yet pitching in carries a personal cost in time, energy, or resources, leaving contributors vulnerable to free-riders who enjoy the shared benefits without doing any of the work.

To study when helpful behavior survives or dies out under these pressures, scientists often turn to evolutionary game theory, a mathematical framework that tracks how competing strategies spread or shrink in a population depending on the payoffs they earn. Even in anonymous, one-time encounters where people cannot reward helpers or punish slackers, outcomes can shift in the presence of what game theorists call zealots: committed individuals who always cooperate and never change their strategy, regardless of what others do.

Earlier research suggested that a small fraction of these steadfast contributors could nudge an entire group toward helpfulness. For example, a 2012 mathematical modeling study indicated that ordinary players often copy unwavering cooperators and tip an entire population into cooperating, provided individuals do not base their choices strictly on maximizing payoffs. Committed minorities can similarly reshape group consensus in real human interactions, as demonstrated by a 2018 behavioral experiment in which planted group members who consistently promoted an alternative name overturned an established naming convention once they made up roughly 25 percent of the group.

Newer work indicates that unconditional generosity does not always boost group participation, especially when individuals strongly favor whichever behavior yields the highest personal return. When researchers simulated spatial group resource games in networked populations in a 2023 modeling study, a moderate share of zealous cooperators actually lowered overall cooperation by giving nearby free-riders easy rewards and blocking local clusters of ordinary cooperators from expanding. Still, most prior research on zealots focused on classic social dilemmas such as the prisoner’s dilemma, where acting selfishly always pays better for an individual and universal defection is typically the sole stable outcome.

Many real-world collective challenges, such as pack hunting in animals or international climate negotiations, instead operate as multiplayer coordination dilemmas. Often modeled as a multiplayer stag-hunt game, these situations generate shared rewards only if at least a minimum critical number of group members contribute; if participation falls short of that threshold, the effort fails and contributors lose what they put in. To see how committed minorities affect these threshold-based challenges, Yuting Dong and Lei Shi of Yunnan University of Finance and Economics in China, working with Chen Shen of Kyushu University in Japan and a colleague, modeled multiplayer stag-hunt games containing a minority of zealots.

Rather than recruiting human participants, the researchers relied on mathematical equations and computer simulations, posting the code for their numerical calculations publicly on Zenodo. They examined anonymous, single-round interactions in a well-mixed population, meaning every player had an equal chance of being randomly grouped with anyone else.

“We wanted to understand how a minority of committed cooperators influences collective cooperation in social dilemmas,” study co-author Chen Shen, a research associate professor in the Faculty of Engineering Sciences at Kyushu University in Japan, told PsyPost. “Previous studies have shown that such individuals, known as ‘zealots,’ can promote cooperation in two-player social dilemma games in well-mixed populations. However, much less was known about their influence in multiplayer settings, where success requires a minimum number of individuals to cooperate. We therefore asked whether zealots are equally beneficial in these settings.”

In each round, a fixed number of players formed a group and chose either to cooperate by contributing one unit to a shared pool or to defect by contributing nothing. Once the number of contributors met or exceeded the required threshold, the pooled contributions were multiplied by a productivity factor and divided equally among all group members, free-riders included; otherwise, no public reward was produced and contributors lost their investment. Alongside adaptable players who could switch strategies over time, the population included a minority of zealots who always contributed and never changed strategies.

In their first analysis, the authors modeled an idealized, infinitely large population to map out the game’s long-term equilibrium states, which are the stable outcomes a population naturally settles into over time. Using an evolutionary formula called replicator dynamics, they tracked how the share of cooperators among adaptable players grew or shrank under strong payoff sensitivity, where whichever strategy earned a higher average return steadily spread. Ordinary players could not tell zealots apart from other cooperators, so zealots shaped the dynamics only by changing the mix of contributors in each group.

Without zealots, once collective returns are high enough to make teamwork worthwhile, the game typically features an unstable tipping point known as a coordination barrier: if initial participation falls below that mark, cooperation collapses to zero. Starting above that mark, by contrast, leads adaptable players into either full cooperation or a stable coexistence mix of cooperators and free-riders.

Keeping zealots capped at no more than half of the total population, the researchers found that adding a small share of them, such as 0.2 zealots per adaptable player (about 17 percent of the total population) in a 15-person game requiring at least 5 contributors, pushed that barrier downward so fewer adaptable cooperators were needed to get collective action started. Under moderate collective returns, however, that same downward shift also lowered the stable coexistence point, meaning a smaller proportion of adaptable players cooperated in the long run than in a population with no zealots.

“Our main finding is that zealots can have two opposing effects: they can make it easier for cooperation to emerge, but they may also discourage others from cooperating in the long run,” Shen explained. “In other words, having individuals who always cooperate does not necessarily encourage others to do the same.”

Increasing the proportion of zealots past specific mathematical thresholds reshaped the menu of stable outcomes altogether, creating standalone endpoints that do not appear in the standard stag-hunt game. At a ratio of 0.5 zealots per adaptable player (one-third of the total population) in the same 15-person setup, the starting coordination barrier vanished completely. That shift ensured adaptable players reached stable coexistence under moderate returns or 100 percent cooperation under high returns, regardless of where participation began. Raising the ratio further to 0.9 zealots per adaptable player (roughly 47 percent of the total population) wiped out the coexistence state across part of the moderate-return range, leaving all adaptable players to defect.

The team also tested the two extreme versions of the threshold rule. When just one contributor was enough to generate a group reward, turning the scenario into a standard public goods game with no coordination hurdle, zealots did not change the stable outcomes at all. At the other extreme, when every single member of a group had to pitch in for the effort to succeed, zealots lowered and at higher densities eliminated the coordination barrier, provided each person’s payoff from group success exceeded their contribution cost.

Because real groups draw from finite populations where random chance affects who ends up together, the researchers ran a second analysis in populations of limited size. In this probabilistic model, adaptable players compared payoffs step by step under strong payoff sensitivity and tended to adopt higher-earning strategies, paired with a 0.1 percent chance of randomly switching strategies at each step to reflect occasional exploration. Using a probability method called a Markov chain, the scientists calculated the long-run share of time the population spent at each level of cooperation.

Simulating 10-person groups that required at least 5 contributors, with zealots accounting for 30 percent of the total population, showed that total population size shapes what committed cooperators achieve. In a tiny population of 10 players, where everyone landed in the same group, free-riding prevailed among adaptable players and zealots had almost no effect. At intermediate population sizes of 20 and 50 under moderate returns, populations without zealots spent nearly all their time near low cooperation, whereas adding 30 percent zealots helped overcome the coordination hurdle and shifted adaptable players into sustained coexistence.

As the finite population grew larger, the trade-off seen in the infinite model resurfaced. In a population of 500 players under moderate collective returns, having 30 percent zealots lowered the long-run share of adaptable cooperators compared with a 500-player population without zealots, a dual pattern that held up in additional checks across smaller zealot fractions and varied group sizes and thresholds.

That downside ran counter to initial intuition. “I initially expected zealots to promote cooperation because their consistent contributions bring groups closer to the minimum number of cooperators needed for success,” Shen noted. “What surprised me was that these same contributions could also weaken others’ incentives to cooperate.”

In the authors’ reading, this dual influence stems from how a guaranteed baseline of contributions alters incentives for everyone else. Zealots initially make it likelier that a group will pass its participation threshold, reassuring adaptable players that their contributions will not be wasted, yet once cooperation takes hold, that same cushion lets groups meet the target with fewer ordinary contributors and gives free-riders wider room to coast. The researchers propose that similar trade-offs could arise in other threshold challenges, from climate mitigation to the spread of group social norms, where dedicated advocates may ease initial coordination while inadvertently dampening broader participation.

“The effects of zealots depend on factors such as their proportion, coordination requirements, population size, and the benefits of collective cooperation,” Shen said. “These findings have potential implications for collective action challenges requiring coordinated efforts, ranging from addressing climate change to developing artificial intelligence. They suggest that relying on committed cooperators alone may not be sufficient for successful collective action.”

There are a few caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The work is based entirely on mathematical equations and computer models rather than experiments with people or animals. As a result, it boils behavior down to payoff-driven rules and leaves out real-world factors such as moral norms, leadership, and unequal wealth.

The models also assume that strangers are grouped at random for single, anonymous rounds, meaning individuals cannot recognize who the unconditional cooperators are, discuss plans beforehand, or build reputations over repeated encounters. Just as important, the equilibrium curves track cooperation among adaptable players alone, while overall participation in the population also includes the guaranteed contributions of the zealots themselves.

“Our findings should not be interpreted as suggesting that zealots are generally harmful to collective cooperation,” Shen cautioned. “Reduced cooperation among other individuals does not necessarily mean that overall cooperation declines. Moreover, our study is theoretical, and further research is needed to understand how these effects operate in real-world settings.”

Future studies could examine whether this dual effect persists in structured social networks, where people interact repeatedly with the same neighbors, coworkers, or friends. Incorporating pre-game communication, reputation systems, and behavioral experiments with human participants could help scientists determine when committed minorities sustain real-world teamwork and when they invite others to free-ride.

“Our long-term goal is to understand how committed individuals influence participation in real-world collective efforts, such as environmental campaigns and voluntary charitable initiatives,” Shen added. “We hope to investigate how social network structures shape these effects and explore the underlying behavioral mechanisms through experiments involving human participants or AI agents.”

The study, “Zealots lower coordination barriers but undermine cooperation in multiplayer games,” was authored by Yuting Dong, Hao Guo, Chen Shen, and Lei Shi.

issues.title: Popular cannabis supplement shows inconsistent anti-inflammatory effects in brain cells
issues.summary: Cannabigerol, a non-intoxicating cannabis compound sold as a supplement, is often promoted as anti-inflammatory. A new laboratory study found its effects on brain immune cells were inconsistent, and that most doses broke isolated DNA strands.
issues.author: Eric W. Dolan
issues.content_html:
Cannabigerol, a non-intoxicating compound from the cannabis plant, has gained popularity as a dietary supplement for its purported anti-inflammatory and brain-protecting properties. However, new laboratory research published in Toxicology suggests that its effects on brain immune cells are inconsistent and heavily dependent on concentration. Low doses left cells intact, yet all but the smallest broke isolated DNA in a cell-free test. The highest concentration killed cells and triggered severe chemical stress, and lower doses failed to reliably calm an induced inflammatory response.

Cannabigerol is a naturally occurring chemical belonging to a class of molecules called phytocannabinoids, which are produced by the Cannabis sativa plant. Unlike tetrahydrocannabinol, the primary compound responsible for the cannabis “high,” cannabigerol does not cause intoxication or impair coordination, making it an attractive candidate for everyday supplements and potential therapies. Early human research has added to that interest, including a placebo-controlled trial in adults that found taking 20 milligrams of hemp-derived cannabigerol reduced feelings of anxiety and stress and modestly improved verbal memory recall compared to a placebo.

Beyond mood and memory, scientists have investigated whether cannabigerol can protect the nervous system from neuroinflammation, a persistent immune response inside the brain and spinal cord that contributes to neurodegenerative illnesses. Brain immunity is managed primarily by microglia, specialized immune cells residing in neural tissue that sweep up cellular debris and defend against microbes. When microglia stay overactivated for too long, they release reactive chemicals and inflammatory proteins that harm neighboring nerve cells.

Initial laboratory experiments suggested that cannabigerol could help protect brain cells from immune-related damage, with a 2018 cell-culture study indicating that pre-treating mouse motor neurons with the compound helped shield them from inflammatory proteins and cell death. Similar anti-inflammatory signs appeared in microglia themselves when a 2023 laboratory and mouse study found that modest doses of cannabigerol reduced the release of inflammatory chemicals in the same mouse microglial line used in the new study after exposure to bacterial toxins.

As consumption of cannabis-derived supplements has expanded, toxicologists have begun testing whether concentrated doses of minor cannabinoids carry hidden cellular or genetic risks. High concentrations of cannabigerol, for instance, disrupted normal cell division and produced chromosomal fragments in a 2024 toxicity study on human immune cells, although those effects occurred at levels roughly a thousand times higher than typical blood concentrations measured in human consumers.

Scientists also lacked experimental data on how cannabigerol interacts with one of the primary molecular engines of chronic brain inflammation: an intracellular multiprotein sensor complex called an inflammasome. Inside microglia, this sensor complex assembles in a two-step process when exposed to danger signals. That switches on an enzyme called Caspase-1, which releases potent inflammatory molecules and cuts a protein that punches pores in the cell membrane, killing the cell.

Led by Júlia Maiara dos Santos of the University of São Paulo in Brazil, the research team designed a dish-based study to test cannabigerol’s safety across a wide span of doses and evaluate whether non-toxic concentrations could quiet this two-step inflammasome response without harming DNA.

To evaluate basic cellular safety, the researchers cultured mouse microglial cells from an established laboratory cell line at a density of 100,000 cells per well. After overnight stabilization, the cells were exposed for 24 hours to purified cannabigerol at five concentrations (0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 micromolar, a unit measuring micromoles per liter), alongside untreated controls and a solvent control containing 0.1 percent dimethyl sulfoxide. Assays were run in triplicate, with results drawn from at least three independent experiments, and study data are available from the authors upon request.

Following the 24-hour exposure, the team measured cell survival using a dye metabolized by mitochondrial enzymes in living cells, and photographed the cells under a microscope to see whether they retracted their normal branched projections into a rounded, activated shape. They also tracked two chemical stress markers: reactive oxygen species, which are unstable oxygen-containing molecules that damage cell components when overproduced, and nitric oxide, a signaling gas that becomes inflammatory when it accumulates.

To check for genetic toxicity, the scientists paired a cell-free screening test with a whole-cell test. First, purified double-stranded DNA in a liquid solution was directly exposed to cannabigerol across the full concentration range for 30 minutes to measure the compound’s raw chemical ability to break DNA strands. Second, intact human white blood cells were treated with cannabigerol (0.01 to 10 micromolar) for 24 hours and placed on electrified gel slides in an alkaline comet assay, where broken single-stranded DNA trails behind the cell nucleus like a comet tail. Two blinded analysts scored 100 cells per sample.

Next, the authors triggered the two-step inflammasome pathway in mouse microglial cells by priming them for three hours with bacterial lipopolysaccharide (1 microgram per milliliter). They then treated the cells for two hours with cannabigerol at 0.01 to 10 micromolar and activated the complex for one hour with nigericin (10 micromolar), a bacterial antibiotic routinely used in the lab to switch the complex on. A comparison group received a selective inflammasome-blocking compound (100 nanomolar) instead of cannabigerol, after which the researchers re-evaluated cell survival, reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, and messenger RNA levels for the Caspase-1 enzyme.

In the 24-hour safety screening, concentrations of cannabigerol up to 10 micromolar appeared well tolerated, causing no measurable cell loss. Every non-toxic dose also modestly lowered nitric oxide in unstimulated cells, to about 80 percent of untreated levels. At 100 micromolar, however, cannabigerol cut cell survival to about a fifth of untreated levels.

That highest concentration also triggered severe chemical stress, raising nitric oxide to about four times untreated levels and reactive oxygen species to roughly ten times, while microglial cells appeared to lose their branched resting structure and adopt a rounded, activated shape. Cells treated with the lower doses looked like untreated controls.

The two genetic safety tests yielded contrasting outcomes. When purified double-stranded DNA was exposed directly to cannabigerol in a cell-free solution, every concentration above 0.01 micromolar caused measurable strand breakage, with the 10- and 100-micromolar doses producing damage indices roughly two to three times the control level. Based on the combined cell-killing and DNA breakage results, the researchers excluded the 100-micromolar dose from the subsequent neuroinflammation experiments.

When intact human white blood cells were exposed to cannabigerol at concentrations up to 10 micromolar in the comet assay, however, differences in DNA damage compared to untreated cells were not statistically significant. The authors suggest this discrepancy indicates that while cannabigerol has an intrinsic chemical capacity to break bare DNA strands, living cells may shield their genetic material through built-in antioxidant defenses, metabolic breakdown, and DNA repair enzymes.

In the two-step inflammasome challenge, inducing inflammation modestly reduced microglial survival, and cannabigerol doses up to 10 micromolar helped partially restore survival to a degree matching the selective inflammasome blocker. Despite preserving cell survival, no concentration of cannabigerol attenuated the surge in reactive oxygen species triggered by the inflammatory protocol, and some doses pushed levels higher still, though these changes did not affect cell survival.

Effects on nitric oxide during the inflammatory challenge varied by dose, although the bacterial triggers alone did not produce a statistically significant rise in nitric oxide in this setup. Adding 1 micromolar of cannabigerol elevated nitric oxide production, whereas 10 micromolar lowered it compared with the inflamed group.

Meanwhile, when the team measured Caspase-1 gene expression at the 0.01-micromolar concentration (selected because it was the sole dose free of bare-DNA breakage), cannabigerol increased Caspase-1 messenger RNA to roughly 375 percent of untreated levels rather than suppressing the gene. The selective inflammasome blocker, by contrast, reduced Caspase-1 expression under the same conditions.

In the authors’ reading, these paradoxical results indicate that cannabigerol does not behave as a straightforward anti-inflammatory agent in microglia. They propose that moderate concentrations might activate protective nuclear receptors that curb nitric oxide production, whereas trace amounts might prime Caspase-1 gene transcription and very high doses may disrupt mitochondrial membranes and amplify oxidative stress.

Daniele Piomelli, a distinguished professor of anatomy and neurobiology and director of the Center for the Study of Cannabis at the University of California, Irvine, who was not involved in the research, offered a measured assessment. “This intriguing in vitro study, conducted in a single cell line, encourages us to consider cannabigerol as a potential player in the neuroinflammation space, though the modest effect sizes and narrow therapeutic window suggest that considerable work remains before any translational conclusions can be drawn,” Piomelli told PsyPost.

In pharmacology, a narrow therapeutic window means there is only a small margin between a concentration that produces beneficial effects and one that causes toxicity, making it difficult to apply dish-based results directly to human treatments. The study’s own numbers show that tight margin: 10 micromolar was the only dose that lowered nitric oxide during the inflammation challenge, and that same dose broke bare DNA in the cell-free assay.

There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The authors note that the immortalized mouse cell line used here differs from primary microglia taken from living tissue, and that they chose it for consistency and low cost rather than for biological fidelity. Experiments in plastic wells also cannot capture how cannabigerol behaves inside a living body, where digestive enzymes, liver metabolism, blood proteins, and the blood-brain barrier limit how much of an ingested cannabinoid ever reaches brain microglia.

Some aspects of the laboratory measurements also call for caution, as the survival assay tracks mitochondrial enzyme activity rather than directly counting dead cells. Caspase-1 was also evaluated only through messenger RNA, at a single low concentration, rather than by measuring active protein across doses. The researchers note that future work using primary brain cell cultures, three-dimensional tissue models, animal studies, and specialized mutation tests will be needed to determine whether these cellular shifts translate into real-world health risks or therapeutic benefits.

The study, “Could cannabigerol protect against neuroinflammation? Insights from an in vitro microglial study,” was authored by Júlia Maiara dos Santos, Amanda Kolinski Machado, Djenifer Leticia Ulrich Bick, Michele Rorato Sagrillo, Elaine Aparecida Del Bel, Alencar Kolinski Machado, and Antonio Cardozo dos Santos.

issues.title: People who feel humiliated tend to be less happy, and rumination may partly explain why
issues.summary: Humiliation can leave memories that are hard to shake. A new study suggests that people who have felt humiliated tend to be less happy, and that repetitive negative thinking may be part of the reason.
issues.author: Vladimir Hedrih
issues.content_html:
An online survey conducted in Poland found that people who reported more humiliation, including both past humiliating experiences and fear of being humiliated in the future, tended to be less happy and more prone to rumination. Statistical analyses suggested that rumination partly accounted for the link between humiliation and lower happiness. The paper was published in Current Issues in Personality Psychology.

Humiliation is a distressing experience that can leave vivid, lasting memories and negatively affect how people see themselves and their relationships with others. It has been linked to lower self-esteem, impaired concentration, disrupted relationships, emotional distress, and depression, and dwelling on humiliating experiences may even motivate aggressive behavior.

A related psychological phenomenon is rumination, which involves repetitive negative thinking about distressing experiences, personal concerns, and fears. Rumination can prolong and intensify negative emotions, interfere with cognitive functioning, and make it more difficult to recover from upsetting experiences.

Both humiliation and rumination may reduce a person’s happiness, understood here as overall well-being and satisfaction with one’s life. Humiliation and rumination may also interfere with posttraumatic growth, a process through which individuals experience positive psychological changes following adversity.

Study authors Natalia Cichecka and Sonia Antosz of SWPS University in Katowice and Aleksandra Żenda of the University of Silesia examined the relationships between humiliation, rumination, and happiness. They also investigated whether rumination might help explain the link between humiliation and happiness.

The researchers conducted an online survey distributed through social media. Participants were 323 adults from Poland, including 212 women, 107 men, and four people who identified as another gender. Their ages ranged from 18 to 79, with an average age of 26, and about half (49%) had a higher education.

Participants completed assessments of happiness (the Oxford Happiness Questionnaire), rumination (the Perseverative Thinking Questionnaire), and humiliation (the Humiliation Inventory). The Humiliation Inventory measures two aspects of humiliation: past experiences of being humiliated and fear of future humiliation. The rumination questionnaire assessed a general tendency toward repetitive negative thinking rather than rumination about humiliating events specifically.

Results showed that participants who reported more humiliation tended to be less happy and more prone to rumination. Fear of future humiliation was slightly more strongly linked to lower happiness than past experiences of humiliation. People more prone to rumination also tended to be less happy, especially those who viewed their repetitive thinking as unproductive.

Statistical analyses indicated that rumination partially mediated the relationship between humiliation and happiness. In other words, people who reported more humiliation tended to ruminate more, and greater rumination was in turn associated with lower happiness. However, this pathway through rumination accounted for only part of the association, and humiliation remained strongly linked to lower happiness even after rumination was taken into account.

“The results suggest that feelings of humiliation may have a devastating effect on stated happiness through rumination about difficult experiences and fear of future humiliation. Knowledge of the role of rumination and humiliation in perceived happiness may help in diagnosis and treatment, especially of anxiety and affective disorders,” the study authors concluded.

The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the links between humiliation and happiness. However, it should be noted that the design of this study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results, and because all measures were collected at a single time point, the analyses cannot establish that humiliation led to rumination, which then reduced happiness. Additionally, all the data were collected using self-reports, leaving room for reporting bias to have affected the results. The sample was also recruited through social media and was mostly young and female, so the findings may not generalize to the broader population.

The paper, “I can’t stop thinking about it: The mediating role of rumination in the relationship between humiliation and happiness,” was authored by Natalia Cichecka, Sonia Antosz, and Aleksandra Żenda.

What do you think?

What are your perspectives on the debate? Has the i-frame vs. s-frame debate influenced your work? Where do you agree, and where do you disagree? What related questions are you grappling with? Where do you think the applied behavioral science goes next?

Share your perspective via our “letter to the editor” form.

Five questions to consider

In advance of the event, I asked each of our five guests to prepare a question for the group. We didn't get to all of them during the discussion, so I thought it might be valuable to share them with everyone. The questions can serve as leaping off points to advance your own thinking and for your discussions with colleagues.

Here they are:

1. Systems-level change (from Nick): How can behavioral science most effectively help with system-level (s-frame) change?

2. Inadvertent harm of the i-frame vs. s-frame argument (from Michael): From where you sit, do you think the i-frame vs. s-frame argument could inadvertently diminish interest in applying behavioral science to public policy?

3. Equity (from Crystal): How does an equity focus complicate (or settle?) the i-frame/s-frame question?

4. The case of gambling (from George): Considerable research suggests that online gambling is causing extensive harm, particularly to poor and young people. How can behavioral insights inform interventions at both the individual level and the system level? And which level do you expect to be more effective?

5. The next generation of behavioral scientists (from Chiara): How does this debate translate into action, such as the training and mentoring of the next generation of behavioral scientists?

issues.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
issues.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinct
issues.author: Evan Nesterak
issues.content_html:
Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen?

Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work they’re asked to do, as well as the work they’d like to do?

These are all questions that applied behavioral scientists are grappling with as they try to realize the promise of the field—to leverage the scientific understanding of psychology, behavior, society, and culture to help one another live happier, healthier, and more peaceful lives.

On October 14, join Editor-in-Chief Evan Nesterak and five leading behavioral scientists—Nick Chater, George Loewestein, Crystal Hall, Michael Hallsworth, and Chiara Varazzani—for a roundtable discussion about these questions and more. The leaping off point will be the i-frame vs. s-frame debate initiated by Chater and Loewenstein, first in an academic article and now in their new book, It’s on You. (Further background on the debate below.)

The guests of the roundtable don’t all agree on how to answer the questions above. In fact, in many cases they sharply disagree. But they all have extensive experience working in both academic and applied settings, especially in public policy, so we have the opportunity for an interesting and constructive conversation. The goal isn’t to settle the debate but to explore areas of agreement and disagreement, open a dialogue about how applied behavioral scientists approach their work, and surface the questions that can move the debate forward.

The event will take place online and is free to attend. You can reserve your spot here.

  • Date: Wednesday, October 14
  • Start time: 9:00am San Francisco | 12:00pm New York | 5:00pm London | 6:00pm Berlin | 7:00pm Nairobi | 9:30pm Delhi
  • Duration: 90 minutes
  • Location: Online
  • Cost: Free to attend
  • Register:Reserve your spot
Reserve your spot

A recording will be made available to all registrants after the event, in case you're not able to attend live.

We hope to see you there,

Evan Nesterak, Editor-in-Chief

Background on the debate

In their 2022 article in Behavioral and Brain Sciences, psychologist Nick Chater and behavioral economist George Loewestein ignited the i-frame vs. s-frame debate within applied behavioral science. The two argued that, in the decade since the field burst on the scene, applied behavioral scientists, themselves included, had focused too much on trying to influence individual behavior (i-frame) and not enough on trying to influence the systems in which individuals behave (s-frame).

The result, they said, especially as it related to public policy, was that interventions were coming up short, attention was being directed away from system-level solutions that could have a tangible impact, and, perhaps most seriously, that applied behavioral scientists “may have unwittingly promoted the interests of the opponents of systemic change.”

Perhaps unsurprisingly, not everyone agreed. One focus of Chater and Loewenstein’s criticism was nudging, which for them epitomized the i-frame approach. The format of the journal Behavioral and Brain Sciences is to feature a target article (in this case Chater and Loewestein’s) and then invite other scholars to respond to that article. Both Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, authors of Nudge, issued a response. “Nudging is being framed,” Thaler wrote. Sunstein argued, “Their complaint is baseless. In the real world of policymaking, behavioral science is mostly being used to reform systems, not to alter individual behavior.”

And Michael Hallsworth, a leader of the Behavioural Insights Team, wrote:

“I greatly respect the authors of the target article. However, in contrast to the target article's assertion, practitioners of behavioral public policy are indeed involved in developing and promoting systemic solutions. Its ‘i-frame’/‘s-frame’ distinction is incoherent, unhelpful, and obscures promising future directions for behavioral public policy. Its content and presentation undermine its stated goals and encourage sweeping dismissals of the field.”

Chater, Loewenstein, Thaler, Sunstein, and Hallsworth all believe that applied behavioral science can be a positive force in improving people’s lives. The question is: How does the field get there?

Earlier this year, Chater and Loewenstein expanded their argument about the i-frame and s-frame in their book, It’s on You. And the question of how applied behavioral scientists should approach their work continues to bubble up in commentaries and conversations.

We wanted to use this moment to bring together diverging viewpoints about the i-frame vs. s-frame debate and how the field fulfills its promise. At the roundtable discussion, in addition to Nick Chater and George Loewestein, we’ll be joined by Crystal Hall (Professor, University of Washington and President, Behavioral Science & Policy Association), Michael Hallsworth (Chief Behavioral Scientist, BIT), and Chiara Varazzani (Lead Behavioral Scientist, OECD).

Reserve your spot

About the roundtable guests

Nick Chater is a professor of behavioral science at the Warwick Business School. In 2023, he was awarded the Rumelhart Prize for lifetime achievement in cognitive science. He has advised the UK Government and co-founded Decision Technology, a research consultancy. He is the coauthor of It’s on You (with George Loewenstein).

George Loewenstein is the Herbert A. Simon University Professor of Economics and Psychology at Carnegie Mellon University. He is one of the founders of behavioral economics, neuroeconomics, and behavioral public policy and has advised many leading companies and government bodies. He is the coauthor of It’s on You (with Nick Chater).

Crystal Hall is the John and Marguerite Walker Corbally Endowed Professor in Public Service at the University of Washington, as well as the president of the Behavioral Science & Policy Association. She has served as a fellow with the White House Social and Behavioral Sciences Team and the Federal Office of Evaluation Sciences at the General Services Administration, and has advised government agencies, nonprofits, and community organizations. She is the coauthor of Antiracist by Design (with Mindy Hernandez).

Michael Hallsworth is the chief behavioral scientist at BIT. He has two decades of experience in developing policy and designing services for national governments and international organizations. He is also a distinguished lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania, and was previously visiting lecturer at Princeton University and assistant professor (adjunct) at Columbia University. He is the author of TheHypocrisy Trap and coauthor of Behavioral Insights (with Elspeth Kirkman).

Chiara Varazzani is lead behavioral scientist at the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). She is also a senior visiting fellow at the London School of Economics and Political Science. Previously, she served as a member of the Technical Advisory Group on Behavioural Insights for the World Health Organization (WHO), advised the Australian government, and was an adjunct research fellow at Monash University.
