issues.title: Nomad Citizen: A New Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs
issues.summary: If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a... The post Nomad Citizen: A New Social Saf
issues.author: Matthew Kepnes
issues.content_html:
If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

So what do you do?

The travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just launched what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

What is Nomad Citizen?

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

Who can sign up?

Nomad Citizen covers people under 56 and earning at least $4,000 USD per month. You sign up online, choose your start date, declare that you’re in good health, and confirm you’ll be outside your passport country for more than half the year. You can also add your partner and any children under 18.

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really quickly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

How much does it cost?

For those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the plan can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

What’s Included?

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

If you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage : Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance, you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support : You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

Making claims

For health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

***

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

issues.content_html:

I’ve been writing about travel for nearly two decades and, in that time, I’ve watched the travel insurance industry change at roughly the speed of a glacier. For years, the pitch was always the same: buy a policy, hope you never need it, and if something goes wrong, prepare for a paperwork marathon and a check that arrives somewhere between “eventually” and “you’ve forgotten you ever filed.”

I’ve personally been on the receiving end of that runaround. So have most travelers I know. It’s just something you kind of deal with. After all, you should never, ever, ever, EVER travel without travel insurance. You don’t want to end up needing a GoFundMe to pay your bills and get home if something goes wrong. (You can’t predict the future!)

Now, there’s a lot of players in this space but one I want to highlight today is Faye Travel Insurance, which I think is doing something unique.

Faye is a digital-first travel insurance company that launched coverage in the U.S. in 2022 so it’s pretty new to the US market when you consider that brands like World Nomads or Allianz have been offering coverage for over twenty years.

Faye is based on a pretty simple idea: travel insurance shouldn’t just sit there waiting for things to go wrong. It should actively help things go right.

That means whole-trip protection (your trip, your health, your stuff, even your pet), an app that’s actually useful while you’re traveling, 24/7 access to real human customer support, claims that get processed in days instead of months, and a digital wallet that pays you back almost instantly instead of waiting around for a check in the mail, which some companies still do in this day and age.

It’s available in all 50 states.

One Plan, Done Right

Faye has one plan for domestic and international trips, which makes things super easy. A lot of travel insurance companies have lots of plans and you end up squinting at coverage tables trying to figure out which one isn’t going to leave you stranded and has the coverage minimums you need. Faye built a single comprehensive plan that covers most of what travelers actually need:

  • Trip cancellation and trip interruption
  • Emergency medical for non-U.S. travel (up to $250,000)
  • Emergency m edical evacuation (up to $500,000)
  • Trip cancellation (up to 100% of non-refundable trip costs)
  • Trip interruption (up to 150% of non-refundable trip costs)
  • Trip delay (up to $2,100/trip ($300/day) after a 6+ hour delay)
  • Missed connection (up to $200, after a 3+ hour covered delay)
  • Non-medical emergency evacuation (up to $100,000)
  • Lost, stolen, or damaged belongings (up to $2,000/trip (capped at $150/item))

These limits are pretty standard, especially on the medical coverage. If you want to add stuff on, they have a few optional addons that I think are really good and unique:

  • Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR) – up to 75% of nonrefundable trip costs reimbursed, if you buy it within 14 days of your initial trip deposit and cancel up to 48 hours prior to your departure date
  • Rental car damage – covers collision, theft, vandalism, natural disasters
  • Adventure and extreme sports – for the bungee jumpers, free divers, and skydivers
  • Vacation rental damage – for the inevitable spilled wine on someone’s Airbnb couch
  • Pet care – vet expenses up to $2K if your pet is traveling with you, kennel costs if you get delayed coming home

The CFAR insurance is really useful and I’ve rarely seen a company allow you to add it on to a policy. Usually, it’s already incorporated at a higher fee but this creates an affordable add on. I also love the pet care add on as more and more people travel with their pets.

All About the App

Here’s where Faye really separates itself. Faye built something completely different! Here’s what you can actually do inside the Faye app:

Buy a policy in as little as 60 seconds – Plug in your trip details, get a quote, get covered.

Get real-time flight tracking and alerts – You’ll get delay info, gate changes, or baggage carousel numbers when you land! A lot of apps do this but this is a nice add on.

Telemedicine – Faye gives you access to a network of 20,000 telemedicine doctors in 21 languages when you travel abroad. If you wake up with food poisoning in a town where you don’t speak the language and don’t trust the local hospital reviews, you can talk to a doctor from your hotel bed. (As someone who has had to find doctors in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Find a doctor, pharmacy, ER, or ATM nearby – The app does the work of figuring out where to go when you’re disoriented and just need to find the closest open pharmacy at 11 p.m. in a city you arrived in five hours ago. (As someone who has had to do this in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Get free airport lounge access – If your flight is delayed by three hours or more, Faye gets you into a lounge – and who wouldn’t want lounge access with free food and drinks for a long delay?

Store your documents in Safekeeping – Securely u pload your passport, visa, insurance card, vaccination records. If anything gets lost or stolen, you’ve got digital copies.

Check destination essentials before you go – Visa requirements, plug adapter types, local emergency numbers, weather, currency conversion, even local apps worth downloading.

Chat with real humans, 24/7 – Actual customer experience specialists, available every day of the year, including weekends and holidays.

Buy an eSIM – The app also enables you to purchase an eSIM meaning you can avoid pesky physical SIM swaps and get connected to the internet right when you land.

Filing a Claim

Here’s how Faye works: something bad happens. You open the app. You file a claim in a few minutes by uploading photos of your receipts. If it’s a qualifying issue like a baggage delay or flight delay, you may get reimbursed almost instantly. Funds go straight into Faye Wallet, a digital payment card built into the app that connects to Apple Pay or Google Pay. You tap and pay, right then and there, for whatever you actually need: a new outfit, toiletries, dinner, a hotel.

For larger or more complex claims, Faye aims to resolve them within 48 hours. of receiving the necessary documentation.

If you don’t want to use the digital wallet, you can transfer the funds to your bank account or get a paper check.

What It Costs

Pricing depends on your trip cost, destination, length, state of residence and age (same as every insurance product) but prices start at around $5.16 a day for international trips, which is a lot more competitive than other companies out there.

****

I’ve used a lot of travel insurance companies over the years. Most of them are fine. A few are awful. Faye is the first one that feels like it was designed by people who actually understand modern travel and get that we’re booking trips on our phones, communicating in apps, and expecting the same digital convenience from insurance that we get from everything else.

The combination of whole-trip protection, the app, Faye Wallet, real human support, and fast claims has genuinely changed how I think about this category. Travel insurance used to be the thing I bought and forgot.

If you’re heading out on a trip soon, check it out at withfaye.com, get a quote, and see for yourself.

issues.title: Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life
issues.summary: Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand... The post Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture,
issues.author: Matthew Kepnes
issues.content_html:
Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

Being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

Day 1: Immersion in the Art Walk


This first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

After a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

Day 2: The Grandeur of the Historic Center


The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

Nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

From here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Day 3: Culinary Discovery


Madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

For dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Day 4: UNESCO World Heritage Wonders


Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

Day 5: Off-the-Beaten-Path Treasures


On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

The Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial said to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

***

While Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

issues.title: Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard review: Can be worth it even if you don't fly Hawaiian often
issues.summary: The Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard may be worth it for you even if you rarely or never fly on Hawaiian. Here are all the reasons why.
issues.author: Olivia Mittak
issues.content_html:
I've never flown with Hawaiian Airlines, yet the Hawaiian Airlines® World Elite Mastercard® is the latest addition to my wallet. With Hawaiian and Alaska Airlines sharing the same loyalty program, Atmos Rewards, the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard is an attractive option for anyone who regularly flies with either airline.

This card offers common airline-associated perks, but like many cobranded airline cards, it will likely prove hard to justify if you aren't flying at least a couple of times each year with Alaska or Hawaiian. That said, if you're able to properly take advantage of its perks, it can offer a lot to boost your travels. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐

*Card ratingis based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The information for the Hawaiian Airlines World Elite Mastercard has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard: The basics

The $99-per-year Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard comes with some of the benefits you'd expect out of a mid-tier airline card, including:

  • Two free checked bags on eligible Hawaiian or Alaska flights (when you pay with your card)
  • $100 companion discount on Hawaiian or Alaska flights each year
  • Bonus points on Hawaiian and Alaska flights, plus other purchases

You won't find lounge access or statement credits on this card, but that simplicity may be welcome for those tired of needing a spreadsheet to help them justify a card's annual fee.

Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard pros and cons

ProsCons
  • Solid earning rates
  • Free checked bags
  • Companion discounts
  • No foreign transaction fees
  • Earns valuable Atmos Rewards points
  • Benefits shared between Hawaiian and Alaska Airlines
  • Points usable with Hawaiian and Alaska plus partner airlines
  • Has an annual fee
  • No lounge access
  • No priority boarding
  • No complimentary seat upgrades

Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard benefits

Living in the Pacific Northwest, I often fly Alaska Airlines domestically. As someone who unsuccessfully tried to get the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card earlier this year, I'm happy that my Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard offers perks on both Hawaiian and Alaska. They may not be as comprehensive as those offered by the Summit, but this card is substantially cheaper.

Receiving two free checked bags isn't too common for a mid-tier card, so I appreciate this perk. But it's important to note that free checked bags with this card are subject to a few restrictions:

  • With Hawaiian, you can only use this perk when flying between North America and Hawaii or between the Hawaiian Islands
  • International flights on both airlines do not qualify
  • Only the primary cardholder is eligible for this benefit
  • You must pay for your flight with your Hawaiian Airlines card to qualify

If you're traveling with a companion, you could check their bag as your own bag to navigate around this card only allowing the primary cardholder free checked bags.

I face a $45 checked bag fee for my first bag and a $55 fee for my second when flying Alaska within the continental U.S. and Alaska. Even as someone who usually only checks one bag, I just need to do so on one round-trip with Alaska to almost entirely cover this card's annual fee.

Aside from that, using the full $100 annual companion discount on a trip you'd otherwise book can offset the $99 annual fee. New cardholders also receive a one-time 50%-off companion discount. Both discounts can be used on eligible round-trip Main Cabin travel between Hawaii and North America on either airline.

I wish the Hawaiian Airlines card had priority boarding, since overhead bin space can be hard to come by and I'm not a fan of gate-checking my bag. Still, it isn't a deal-breaker for me given this card's annual fee is easy to at least break even on.

This card has no foreign transaction fees and offers standard travel protections like trip cancellation/interruption and travel accident insurance.

How to earn and use your rewards

Earning rewards

The Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard earns Atmos Rewards points, which is the loyalty currency both Hawaiian Airlines and Alaska Airlines use. It earns:

  • 3 points per dollar spent on Hawaiian and Alaska purchases
  • 2 points per dollar spent on dining, gas and groceries
  • 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases

Through Dec. 31, you'll earn 50% bonus points on every dollar spent if you're a resident of Hawaii (up to 5,000 points).

With this card, you'll also earn 1 Atmos Rewards status point per $3 spent, with no cap. You won't get an elite status boost at the start of the qualification year, but this card can help you close the gap to elite status if you're close.

Redeeming rewards

The best way to use your Atmos Rewards points is for flights on Hawaiian and Alaska or with partner airlines, such as American Airlines. Alaska Airlines in particular offers a lot of value for your points, especially on short-haul domestic flights.

Recently, I redeemed 5,000 Atmos Rewards points (plus $5.60 in taxes and fees) for a flight between Portland International Airport (PDX) and Spokane International Airport (GEG). Given the cash price was $184, I received over 3.5 cents per point in value (after taking taxes and fees into consideration). That's more than double TPG's November 2026 valuation of Atmos Rewards points at 1.6 cents per point.

It's this combined loyalty program that allows me to justify holding this card despite never setting foot on a Hawaiian flight and having no current plans to do so. It's hard to earn Atmos Rewards points, since they currently only partner with Bilt as a transfer partner. Without an Alaska Airlines-associated card, the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard is my best bet for earning points I can use with this program.

As an alternative to redeeming your points for flights, you can also use them for Alaska Vacations packages and Alaska Airlines-curated experiences.

Where the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard falls short

As I mentioned previously, the Hawaiian Airlines card lacks priority boarding and a comprehensive elite status boost at the start of the year. In ways like this, it's clear this card hasn't received a refresh recently, unlike many other popular airline cards.

That means this card may fall short of expectations if you're anticipating a card with well-rounded airline perks. The inability to use this card's free checked bag perk with companions is a non-issue if you're only traveling with one person and two bags, but it becomes a larger limitation if you're traveling with many bags or a group.

Is the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard worth it?

If you fly at least a couple of times each year with Hawaiian or Alaska and don't have a cobranded Atmos Rewards card, I believe this card is more than likely worth it. Despite lacking several perks we've come to expect from airline cards these days, it's still quite easy to get outsize value from the $99 annual fee.

When to apply for the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard

Currently, new Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard cardholders can earn up to 70,000 bonus points:

  • Earn 60,000 points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 90 days
  • Earn an additional 10,000 points after spending a total of $2,000 on purchases within the first 180 days

According to TPG's valuations, this welcome offer is worth up to $1,120. In an era when many welcome offers ask for thousands in spending, it's refreshing to see a valuable one that only requires $2,000 in total spending.

Even if you're on a limited budget, this should be an attainable welcome offer. I recommend applying now, given how much this bonus is worth and how easy it is to earn.

Just remember that Barclays can be inquiry-sensitive. If you've opened six or more cards in the past 24 months, you may have a hard time getting approved.

Other cards to consider if you don't want the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard

If this card isn't a good fit for you, consider one of these alternatives:

  • If you want more perks when flying Alaska: The Atmos Rewards Summit credit card offers an accelerated pathway to Alaska Airlines status, Alaska Lounge passes and preferred boarding. To learn more, check out our full review of the Atmos Summit.
  • If you want a card that earns rewards that can transfer to Atmos Rewards: The Bilt Palladium Card (see rates and fees) has a higher $495 annual fee (see rates and fees), but it's one of the few ways to earn points on your rent without incurring transaction fees (subject to terms; see rates and fees). The Bilt Points you earn with this card are transferable to Atmos Rewards. To learn more, check out our full review of the Bilt Palladium.
  • If you want more Alaska and Hawaiian benefits for a similar annual fee: The Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card carries a $95 annual fee — but its free checked bag perk extends to six companions on the same reservation. You'll also receive preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian flights. To learn more, check out our full review of the Atmos Ascent.

For additional options, check out our picks for the best airline cards.

Bottom line

I'm happy I chose to add the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard to my wallet. Between two free checked bags and the annual $100 companion discount, I expect I'll be able to easily get outsize value against the $99 annual fee each year.

While this card offers significant value to the right traveler, if you don't fly with either Alaska or Hawaiian at least a couple of times each year, you will likely struggle to find a lot of value in this card. If you're an Alaska Airlines loyalist and you qualify for a Bank of America card, I'd suggest the Atmos Rewards Summit instead.

That said, if you fly at least occasionally with Hawaiian or Alaska, or you want to earn Atmos Rewards points to use with partner airlines, I recommend giving this card serious consideration.

Related: How to pick the best Atmos Rewards accrual method for you

issues.title: The best holiday gifts for the outdoor enthusiast in your life
issues.summary: From hiking essentials to the perfect gift for the avid skier in your life, these are our favorite outdoor adventure gifts to give this holiday season.
issues.author: Ellie Nan Storck
issues.content_html:
Any time I get overwhelmed these days, the first thought I have is: I need to go touch grass. And I really mean it — the great outdoors is exactly where I go to unwind, relax, challenge myself and have a good think. In fact, for many of us at TPG, it's a big part of the reason we love to travel.

This holiday season, you might find yourself shopping for someone who plans their entire winter travel schedule around where to ski the best powder on the planet, or maybe for someone whose traveling around the world bagging peak after peak. Maybe you're close with a national park enthusiast, or you need a really good stocking stuffer for a dedicated marathon runner. Or maybe someone in your life loves nothing more than cozying up at the perfect camping spot for a long weekend.

No matter what type of outdoor adventure their passion might be, this gift guide (though non-exhaustive; I had to cut myself off at some point!) compiles some of my absolute favorite, go-to items for those who simply love to spend time outside. Have a scroll, and let us know in the comments what your dream outdoor gift would be.

Ikon pass

Best for: The powder chaser

It goes without saying that anyone who skis or snowboards throughout the winter season can benefit from a pass. My personal favorite in recent years has been the Ikon pass, which has taken me to mountains like Mammoth, Steamboat Springs and Killington. But the opportunity to get your turns in certainly doesn't stop at the U.S.; the Ikon pass famously gets passholders access to all four major ski resorts in Niseko, Japan, known for having some of the best (if not the best) powder in the world.

TPG tip: With a purchase as hefty as this one, you'll want to ensure you use a card that will maximize rewards. I'd recommend a card that earns an elevated, flat rate across all purchases — like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

Shop Ikon pass

Patagonia Provisions Tinned Fish Variety Pack

Best for: The sustainability-minded gourmand

While I've taken Pataognia Provisions tinned fish on the trail before, I have to admit I eat it at home all the time, too. Anyone with an affinity for tinned fish — and for sustainably sourced seafood — will love this variety pack that gives you a taste of everything from lemon herb mussels to sardines in coconut curry.

TPG tip: American Express often has valuable Patagonia deals for cardholders, so check your Amex offers during the holiday season to see if you'll get a statement credit for spending a certain amount at Patagonia.

Shop Patagonia Provisions Tinned Fish Variety Pack

Darn Tough Hiker Micro Crew Cushion Socks

Best for: The everyday hiker

Not all hiking socks are created equal, and after many a mile spent scrambling up the granite of the White Mountains, I've found that Darn Tough are true to their name in every sense. I'm partial to the micro crew cushion sock — they provide just enough cushion without taking up too much space in my boot, they're breathable and they hold up well on multi-day trips. But pick any Darn Tough style and it's pretty tough to go wrong.

TPG tip: Darn Tough is often eligible for Capital One Shopping Rewards via several online retailers like Cabela's and Shoebacca. If you're a cardholder, make sure you're shopping with the Capital One portal Chrome extension to make sure you're getting the best deal.

Shop Darn Tough socks

Outerknown Blanket Shirt

Buy here, $168

Best for: The cozy camper

Cozy is the primary concept with Outerknown's Blanket Shirt (available for men and women in a wide array of colors and patterns). The first time I put one of these on about a decade ago, I knew it would become a staple in my everyday wardrobe, but especially for shoulder season camping trips and cabin getaways, when evenings and early mornings are cold and crisp.

TPG tip: Outerknown is available at Nordstrom, so Nordstrom cardholders and Nordy Club members can consider cashing in their valuable awards for this item — or even earn cash back on top of your Nordy Club rewards by starting your online Nordstrom purchases via Rakuten.

Shop Outerknown's Blanket Shirt

Sawyer Squeeze

Best for: The one whose always prepared

Anyone who goes out into the backcountry regularly knows that having a plan for hydration is a necessity — and having a dependable, safe way to filter water is simply nonnegotiable. Sawyer makes some of the most popular and reliable water filtration systems for those hitting the trail — I recently used my Sawyer Squeeze on a four day backpacking and was blown away by how simple and functional it is. It removes 99.99999% of bacteria — that's a lot of nines. Whether its used while camping, hiking, backpacking, hunting, fishing or just packed for an outdoor-centric travel excursion, this is a valuable tool for any outdoor enthusiast to carry with them.

TPG tip: You can buy a Sawyer water filtration system on Amazon to get Amazon Prime benefits like free two-day shipping. Just make sure to use a card that's great for Amazon purchases.

Shop Sawyer Squeeze on Amazon

MSR Pocket Rocket 2 Stove

Best for: The backpacker

If you know someone who loves to backpack — or maybe they're a first timer and you're helping them round out their backpacking setup — the MSR Pocket Rocket is the camp stove I come back to again and again (and I think many, if not most, backpackers would say the same). It's famously lightweight and foldable, boils water very quickly, has a sturdy base for excellent pot support and is super easy to use and set up (this is coming from someone who lit a camp stove on fire once — I've never had that issue with this one).

TPG tip: If you carry The REI Co-op® Mastercard® you'll get 5% in rewards on REI Co-op purchases.

The information for the REI Co-op Mastercard has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Shop MSR Pocket Rocket at REI

Patagonia Nano-Air Light Hoody

Best for: The lightweight packer

One of the best things about this hoody is its versatility — I'd venture to guess that almost anyone on your holiday list could get good use out of Patagonia's Nano-Air Light Hoody. The idea behind it is that you don't have to take it off during start-and-stop activities; the brand's FullRange insulation technology, both warm and stretchy, ensures that you can release excess heat while exercising hard, but it keeps you toasty when you stop for a break. Whether worn during crisp autumn hikes, on the slopes while getting turns in or during a camping trip, it's sure to be a closet staple.

TPG tip: American Express often has valuable Patagonia deals for cardholders, so check your offers during the holiday season to see if you'll get a statement credit for spending a certain amount at Patagonia.

Shop Patagonia Nano-Air Light Hoody

Salomon ADV SKIN 5

Best for: The long distance runner

Seems like everyone is training for a marathon these days, doesn't it? If one of your nearest or dearest falls into that category, they're going to need a well-crafted, reliable hydration vest — and time and again, avid runners rave about this one. It can hold up to five liters of water (two 500-ml soft flasks are included) and features a sleek, adjustable design with plenty of pockets

TPG tip: Eligible Capital One cardholders can order via REI and get 10 percent back in Capital One Rewards, or use The REI Co-op® Mastercard® and get 5% in rewards on REI Co-op purchases.

Shop Salomon ADV SKIN 5 at REI

issues.title: 12 fabulous gifts inspired by some of my favorite destinations and hotels
issues.summary: My personal guide to the best holiday gifts for the travelers in your life, all inspired by incredible destinations and luxury hotels.
issues.author: Eric Rosen
issues.content_html:
I'm on the road about half the year on assignment for TPG and on any given week, you might find me browsing the jade market in Taipei, window-shopping through Galerie Vivienne in Paris or strolling through the San Telmo market in Buenos Aires on the hunt for collectibles.

I can't tell you how many times I've seen a souvenir, piece of art, sweet treat or other little curio and thought, "Wouldn't this make a great gift for so and so?"

The only trouble is, I travel light, so there's nary a nook or cranny in my carry-on to fit a gift, let alone several.

I do, however, make a mental inventory of potential gifts I see so that I can order them for friends and family later. Here are a few of my favorite recent finds that might be perfect for someone on your holiday gift list, all inspired by my travels.

1 Hotels hooded bathrobe

Best for: Armchair travelers who like to keep cozy

There's a lot I love about 1 Hotels — their sustainable ethos, the Bamford bath amenities, in-room filtered water taps, the smattering of hyperlocal, destination-specific activities on offer to guests, bustling public spaces with unique dining concepts and…the bathrobes. I'm not usually a bathrobe kind of guy, but I can't resist donning one of these ultracomfortable numbers anytime I'm a guest at one of these properties. Simple and soft, with a gray jersey-knit lining and a loose hoodie, they're perfect for lounging with a cappuccino while you try to stave off jet lag.

TPG tip: You might want to make this purchase at an actual 1 Hotel boutique so you can earn more points per dollar with a credit card that offers a travel or hotel category bonus.

Shop 1 Hotels

Gold-leaf lacquer boxes from Zohiko

Best for: The Japanophile you want to impress

Like an unstoppable force meeting an immovable object, my delight in purchasing travel souvenirs is only impeded by the limited space in my small city apartment. That's why I love the little lacquerware boxes and trays from Zohiko, a boutique in Kyoto's Nakagyo Ward that traces its history back to the 17th century. I especially love the finely filigreed Kirikane style, where patterns or shapes are cut out in gold or silver leaf and pressed into place. I purchased a glossy black box with gold inlay of cherry blossoms and autumn leaves on my last visit, and I keep it on my nightstand to hold my wedding ring and watch.

TPG tip: Make a trip to Japan out of it and browse the physical Zohiko boutique (you can also enjoy tax-free purchases if you're visiting) while checking out some of Kyoto's exciting new hotels.

Shop Zohiko

Handicrafts from Artesanías de Colombia

Best for: Folks who appreciate colorful, culturally significant crafts

Inevitably, every time I'm traipsing around Bogotá, I find myself drawn to this gorgeous little boutique in the city's upscale Chapinero neighborhood, which sources fair-trade handcrafted pieces of art and decor from small communities around the country, including woven baskets starting at just $18. I am personally drawn to carefully carved wooden Tamo bowls from the coastal Nariño region, decorated with brightly dyed strands of wheat or barley fiber, but you can find everything from woven baskets to hammocks, jewelry and even pieces of furniture.

TPG tip: While you can often haggle for handicrafts in Colombia, prices in this boutique are as marked, so save your negotiating skills for street vendors.

Shop Artesanías de Colombia

Luxurious Lao textiles from Ock Pop Tok

Best for: Helping a friend spruce up their interior decor game

Although long popular with backpackers and river cruisers, Luang Prabang still feels like an under-the-radar find in mountainous Laos, sitting on the confluence of the Mekong and Nam Khan Rivers. It's also a hotbed of fair-trade arts and crafts. A standout atelier in town is Ock Pop Tok, an art school, store and restaurant that aims to revive, support and teach traditional Lao artistic techniques. Visitors can take classes in silk-weaving, batik-dyeing and embroidery, among other offerings. I am always tempted to buy out the textile section of the boutique, but I usually limit myself to a vibrant wall hanging or two.

TPG tip: Don't just make a purchase; spend a few days as a student at Ock Pop Tok to pick up a new craft yourself.

Shop Ock Pop Tok

Officina Profumo Farmaceutica Santa Maria Novella

Best for: Travelers who like their perfumes with a hint of historical luxury

Of course, I'd suggest visiting the original Florence flagship of this bath and beauty purveyor, which dates back to 1221. It feels a little like visiting Ollivanders Wand Shop from "Harry Potter," with antique cases bursting with all-natural unguents and elixirs whose formulas were originally developed by Dominican friars. But if you can't get there, there are also locations around the U.S., including those in West Hollywood, California, Soho in New York City and Bal Harbour, Florida. I tend to keep it simple and go for the pure sweet almond oil, but you could also go regal and buy a bottle of the perfumery's citrusy Acqua della Regina, created for Catherine de' Medici as a gift for her husband, the future king of France, back in 1533.

TPG tip: It can sometimes be less expensive to purchase these products from the original store in Florence, so why not make a trip out of it?

Shop Santa Maria Novella

A gaucho belt from Arandu

Best for: The fashionable cowboys at your rodeo

I love an eye-catching accessory, and belts are my statement pieces of choice. So on my last visit to Buenos Aires, I stopped by Arandu Talabarteria's tony boutique in Recoleta. The whole store is inspired by a romanticized version of gaucho life on the pampas. You can find sturdy leather boots, billowy bombacha pants, cozy ponchos and my favorite: woven belts with intricate threadwork and high-quality leather. They start at $45 and can range into the hundreds of dollars, depending on the level of detail and craftsmanship. Best of all, you can ship to the U.S., so you don't have to cross the equator to stock up.

TPG tip: They also have dog collars for your faithful canine companion.

Shop Arandu

KLM's Delft houses

Best for: The high-flying #avgeek in your life

If you've followed me for the past few years, you know I'm pretty much obsessed with KLM's tile Delft houses, the little replicas of actual historical buildings around the Netherlands that the airline hands out to long-haul business-class passengers. I've attended the unveiling of each year's new house for several years now, and my own collection has grown into a veritable village. If you have an equally #avgeeky member of your gifting circle and are looking for the perfect present, then you might want to consider buying one of these beauties for them. Historian Mark Zegeling's "Little Kingdom by the Sea" book set, which delves into the history of all 107 of the houses, is a great accompanying gift as well.

TPG tip: Be sure to use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees so you don't get dinged with a 1-3% surcharge when buying your house.

Shop KLM Houses

Carlton Cannes beach bag

Best for: Swanky sunseekers who want to make a splash

How do you tell me you summer on the French Riviera without telling me you summer on the French Riviera? You simply tote around a sunshiney yellow-and-white-striped beach bag from the iconic Carlton Cannes, the first luxury hotel to open in the city, way back in 1911. A lot has changed since then, but the simple design is meant to evoke the Côte d'Azur of yore, when you might have found Cary Grant and Grace Kelly sunbathing on the plage between scenes of "To Catch a Thief."

TPG tip: Make your purchase in person and use an IHG One Rewards credit card to earn multiple points per dollar.

Shop Carlton Cannes

Singapore Sling glass from Raffles Singapore

Best for: International imbibers with a sweet tooth

You might find it hard to remember your visit to Singapore, let alone pick up some souvenirs as gifts for friends, after you've had a few Singapore Slings at the Raffles Hotel's iconic Long Bar. That's why it might come in handy to pick up a keepsake Singapore Sling glass for your friends from the hotel's online boutique. It's like taking a sip of history with you. The nation's signature drink was invented by Ngiam Tong Boon back in 1915 and is an intoxicating (and sweet!) mix of gin, grenadine, cherry liqueur, Benedictine, Curacao and both pineapple and lime juice. Even a sip can transport you back to a sultry Southeast Asian evening.

TPG tip: Pick a card that earns bonus rewards on everyday purchases, like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, so you're making the most of your spending.

Shop Raffles Boutique

Little Passports subscription

Best for: Your friends' (or your own) globe-trotting tots

We can't forget about the kids! In my experience, there are few better or more engaging (or educational) ways to get the tykes in your life interested in travel than Little Passports, a subscription membership where each month, your child is mailed a new box focusing on individual countries, animals, crafts and even DIY science experiments, depending on their specific subscription and age.

TPG tip: Don't forget to choose the subscription length you want from the start, otherwise, these charges might sneak up on you month after month if you don't cancel.

Shop Little Passports

Officine Universelle Buly combs and creams

Best for: Your favorite skincare aficionado

I first came across Officine Universelle Buly's sweet-smelling body products during a stay at the Rosewood Hotel de Crillon in Paris last year, and I promptly swiped several tubes of shampoo, conditioner and body lotion from my suite to use at home. On my next visit to the City of Light, though, I stopped by the enchanting store in the 6th arrondissement to sniff through various scents and balms tinged with exotic notes like Madagascar amber and Maltese iris. They also have fabulous tortoiseshell hair clips and combs that you can have monogrammed for even the most discerningly coiffed companions in your life.

TPG tip: If you're purchasing liquid products and not checking a bag, make sure they comply with carry-on limits.

Shop Officine Universelle Buly

Four Seasons bed

Best for: Yourself! This is the ultimate self-care splurge

In recent years, more and more hotel chains have started selling the mattresses they use directly to customers. And while you might be a Westin Heavenly Bed fan, or perhaps a devotee of DoubleTree's signature Sweet Dreams mattress, I personally recommend a Four Seasons mattress, which has the plushest pillowtop of any hotel bed I've experienced. After staying at dozens of Four Seasons over the years, I finally took the plunge and purchased one for myself about six years ago and I've never slept better. It's definitely a splurge, but you can't put a price tag on a great night's sleep. So make this one a gift for yourself.

issues.title: The Areni-1 Cave Shoe in Yerevan, Armenia
issues.summary: This leather shoe was discovered in Areni 1 cave during excavations in 2008. issues.content_html:
This leather shoe was discovered in Areni 1 cave during excavations in 2008.

Made from a single piece of cowhide leather, and still with its leather laces it has been measured as corresponding to a modern US size 7 / EU size 37 / UK size 6. It is stuffed with grass to either maintain its shape or keep the foot warm. It is unknown at this stage whether it was a man or woman's shoe.

Researchers have managed to date it back to 3600-3500 BC based on the radiocarbon dating.

The shoe managed to survive in near-perfect condition because of the cool, dry cave environment which was sealed off by several layers of sheep dung. The shoe was found upside down at the base of a shallow, rounded, and plastered pit, beneath an overturned broken Chalcolithic ceramic bowl.

The original skeleton now resides in Chicago's Field Museum. Faith p
issues.content_html:
At the edge of the South Dakota prairie, a scrap-metal Tyrannosaurus rex rises from the small town of Faith. A tribute to one of the most famous dinosaurs ever unearthed.

Built from recycled tractors and agricultural materials, this sculpture honors Sue, the largest and most complete T. rex fossil discovered in the United States. The original skeleton now resides in Chicago's Field Museum.

Faith proudly calls itself the "T. rex Capital of the World," a title rooted in the fossil-rich lands nearby. Sue was discovered on August 12, 1990, by fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson while working with the Black Hills Institute on the Cheyenne River Reservation. The skeleton, found in the Hell Creek Formation, was astonishingly complete, about 90 percent by bulk and 73 percent by bone count, missing only a few ribs, vertebrae, an arm, and a foot.

What followed was nearly as dramatic as the life of the dinosaur itself: a prolonged legal battle over ownership, then a Sotheby's auction in 1997 that fetched $8.36 million, and an eventual home at one of the nation's premier natural history museums.

Alongside the sculpture is a small museum dedicated to the history of Faith. Established by settlers who took advantage of the Homestead Act, the town's story is reflected in the museum's collection of early photographs and railroad artifacts. One of the museum's highlights is its display on the two other T. rex's found in the area. One other small building stands nearby, one of the last surviving ice houses in South Dakota.

This recycled-metal predator stands not only as a tribute to a remarkable fossil, but also as a reminder that one of paleontology's greatest discoveries come from this quiet stretch of prairie.

issues.title: Xuan Phong Church in Tuy Phuoc Dong, Vietnam
issues.summary: Rising out of the rural landscapes of Tuy Phuoc, Xuan Phong Church presents an intriguing architectural cross-pollination that defies conventional ecclesiastical design. Originally established as a modest thatched sanctuary in the late nineteenth century, the current structure was erected around 1890 using repurposed ancient Cham bricks salvaged from the nearby Binh Lam area, creating a tangible p
issues.content_html:
Rising out of the rural landscapes of Tuy Phuoc, Xuan Phong Church presents an intriguing architectural cross-pollination that defies conventional ecclesiastical design.

Originally established as a modest thatched sanctuary in the late nineteenth century, the current structure was erected around 1890 using repurposed ancient Cham bricks salvaged from the nearby Binh Lam area, creating a tangible physical bridge between Catholic history and the region's medieval Champa heritage.

Most striking is its facade, dominated by three towering spires whose tapered geometric profiles distinctly mirror the iconic silhouette of traditional Cham towers, while church archives have also drawn structural comparisons to Khmer temple architecture.

Recently restored in a vibrant white-and-purple palette, this enigmatic house of worship stands as a captivating anomaly: a active Christian church built from the literal stones and stylized form of a long-vanished empire.

issues.content_html:
Oklahoma is known for its oil production. Normally, oil is trapped underneath impermeable rock and must be pumped out of the ground. Sometimes there is a gap in the impermeable rock, and oil oozes out of the ground. As the gaseous part of oil evaporates, it leaves behind the solids, which become asphalt. This is the ‘tar’ found in tar pits.

There are few tar pits in the world, one of which is in southwest Oklahoma on the grounds of Fort Sill. The tar pits were noted by early explorers, and the local Native Americans used to put it on saddle sores of horses. It is not as grand as the tar pits of La Brea in Los Angeles, California, but it is a tar pit nonetheless. Actually it's more of a tar 'seep', as it is basically a stream of tar oozing from a pond with tar seepage at the bottom. There are no mammoths or saber-toothed tigers in the tar. Some tar in the pond runs down a nearby ditch, and some tar is naturally oozing out of the same ditch.

Parking is about 50 feet from the pond; the ditch is coming out of that. The ditch runs hundreds of feet. The exposed tar hardens over time, but just underneath the hardened crust is fresh tar and it is slippery, so care must be taken on hot days not to permanently damage items including cameras, clothes, etc.

Nearby sticks and rocks allow play with the tar. Some of the random tar seepage has a hardened crust, and broken slowly will look like a half-baked brownie, with fresh tar on the inside.

issues.title: Comrades No More: Thoughts on Russia’s Invasion of Ukraine
issues.summary: Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our … Continue reading "Comrades No More: Thoughts on Russia’s Invasion of Uk
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our world.

Our mission at RSE is to help Americans better know and understand our neighbors through travel. But when we bring travelers to another country, we also bring their dollars — dollars that would support Putin’s aggression. Therefore, as of today, we have canceled all 2022 tours that include a stop in Russia.

Of course, we will keep a close eye on unfolding events and monitor any travel impacts through the rest of Europe. But it is important to keep geographic realities in mind and remember that a war in Ukraine is as far from our European vacation dreams as a war in Guatemala would be from Texas or Florida. For 40 years now, we have lived, worked, and traveled through many periods of tragic warfare in lands far from where we lead our tours (and some closer). And at this time, we see no reason to change the rest of our travel and touring plans.

The tragic reality unfolding in Ukraine only reminds me how important it is for Americans to keep on traveling and to do so in a way that makes us better and more engaged citizens of our world. I’m flying to Europe next month for a 40-day trip through a dozen great cities from London to Athens — and I’m proud that thousands of my fellow travelers will experience the European trip of their dreams while having rich learning experiences far from home on a 2022 Rick Steves tour.

In the meantime, let’s be thankful for our blessings, support our nation’s leaders as they do their best to navigate this crisis, and keep the troubled corners of our world (Ukraine, Russia, Afghanistan, and more) in our thoughts and prayers.

—Rick

issues.title: The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way
issues.summary: At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me. For total novices like Shelley … Continue reading "The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me.

For total novices like Shelley and me, it’s wise to be proactive about health and safety. Here are some tips I learned along the way:

Good boots, liner socks, slippery powder, and moleskin for tender skin are essential. We kind of became gear geeks — investing in good day bags (Osprey), woolen clothes (socks, underwear, shirts), and great hiking shoes. I was never so thankful for a wool cap in Europe.

I was skeptical about a lot of “good ideas,” but two things I eventually appreciated were a daily baggie of trail mix and my metal water bottle. (I complained about its steep $40 price tag…but soon came to recognize it was a great value).

I must say, if the weather turned bad and it rained hard, I think much of the trail would become no fun at all. In fact, it would be dangerous. Hiking poles are essential, and even in perfect weather, I would have been worried about a stumble without my own trusty set.

Eat a solid breakfast. The one day we had breakfast with no protein, climbing was tougher.

Put on sunscreen, even if the weather’s bad.

After learning my lesson on other long hikes, I decided to be religious about stretching on the Tour du Mont Blanc from the start. I had a routine of six stretches and spent time throughout the day making sure I didn’t tighten up. Very important!

Don’t be a hero. If skin is getting hot, wrap it up. I did the entire TMB hike without a blister — and then just got one on purpose in the last two hours.

Good gear, smart and proactive ways to stay healthy, stretching, and taking it easy… it all worked just great.

issues.title: Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc
issues.summary: While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was … Continue reading "Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was the uphill part, and for others (with weak knees), it was going downhill. We just took it easy, with lots of little breaks.

For long climbs, steady, smaller steps are best. The trail could be really rocky, and I can’t imagine doing it without hiking poles. The trail signs were great, and apps made staying on the trail easy: Just follow the blue dot. And I got good use out of a top-quality printed map. (I’d spend time the night before reading up on the hike and familiarizing myself with the trail on the map.)

While the weather forecast looked threatening, we hiked six days (in September, during the last week of the season) and, thankfully, had only one hour of rain. Still, each day we’d pack rain gear, and we’d add on and take off layers as we gained and lost altitude. After four days, we had it sorted out, and it occurred to us rank beginners, “We’re getting good at this.”

As we were hiking in a big circle around a big clump of mountains and sleeping in charming towns each night, every day seemed to be up and over a daunting mountain pass. A nightly treat was a stroll under a milky blanket of stars.

I’ll be sharing more photos, stories, and tips from Mont Blanc on the Nov. 29 edition of Monday Night Travel. Want to come along? Register now for this fun — and free! — event.

As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends … Continue reading
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Hiking Europe’s Tour du Mont Blanc was a totally different slice of European culture for me: Coming upon a remote farmhouse-turned-thriving-cafe serving wonderful lunches…flowers and cows (with classic bells) scenically sprinkled throughout…and an esprit de corps where everyone is like family.

As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends with fellow hikers. It seemed like half the people on the trail were from the US, and I met lots of Seattleites.

And in the interest of hiking light, lunches were very simple — just a sandwich from the hotel, maybe a carrot, a piece of fruit, and water. But upon reaching the mid-day summit, lunch was a marmot’s banquet. (Speaking of marmots, we saw no wildlife except a couple of mice that had been squished under hiking boots on the trail.)

issues.title: We filmed our Sigma FP2 review with the Sigma FP2
issues.summary: Making the most of modularity.
issues.author: Mitchell Clark
issues.content_html:
Making the most of modularity.

While reviewing the Sigma FP2, a camera that splits its attention between the cine and stills worlds, we thought it would be a good idea to film a video with it to see how it handles and what its footage looks like. With new camera gear a bit thin on the ground at this time of year, we decided the subject of the video might as well be the FP2 itself.

The gear we use to shoot our videos often varies depending on which camera we’re using. Some we’ve done hyper-minimally before, using just the camera, a microphone and headphones, and others we’ve rigged up more gear around the camera. For this one, I went relatively far towards the latter end of that spectrum, powering the camera and an external monitor with a V-mount battery, using most of the camera’s ports, and mounting it all on rods attached to a fluid tripod head.

Unsurprisingly given its focus, it handled quite well in this configuration, and its small, boxy shape would’ve made it easy to throw on a gimbal, or attach a matte box to.

There were a few wrinkles we ran into along the way. Our Atomos recorder interpreted the camera’s Log footage as being substantially brighter than it actually was, and we found the LUTs for Leica’s L-Log required a bit more color grading than many of the ones we’ve used for other flavors of Log. However, those are mostly easy to work around once you’re familiar with the camera, and, if you don’t need the additional latitude that comes with shooting Log, the standard 10-bit footage looks quite beautiful, in my opinion.

Richard sums up most of his thoughts on the FP2 in the video, but if you want to go more in-depth, you can read our full review.
