issues.title: What you should know before using Adobe’s latest photo-editing tools
issues.summary: Demonstrations with Adobe’s product managers offered more insight into how the new features work. Trying them myself raised a few more questions.
issues.author: Abby Ferguson
issues.content_html:
Demonstrations with Adobe’s product managers offered more insight into how the new features work. Trying them myself raised a few more questions.

Disclosure: DPReview attended Adobe Max, with Adobe covering travel and lodging expenses.

This year at Max, Adobe’s annual conference, the company announced a handful of updates to both Photoshop and Lightroom. Some were featured in the larger keynote, while others flew under the radar. In both cases, though, details weren’t all that plentiful.

Thankfully, during the conference, I had the opportunity to get demonstrations from product managers for both programs, giving me a closer look at what’s new and how those features work.

Photoshop features

Relight

Relight is a tool that lets you change the apparent lighting in a photograph. It allows you to add up to three lights, with controls for location, depth, color, diffusion and more.

During my demonstration with Stephen Nielson, Adobe’s senior director of product management for Photoshop, he showed how you can control how much of the original lighting remains. You can retain some of the existing light for a more blended look, or replace it entirely for something dramatically different.

What stood out to me most, though, was that the changes also extend to reflections. Nielson said Relight can remove reflections associated with the original lighting or blend them with the new effect. The AI processing behind the tool is doing far more than adjusting brightness in different parts of the image.

One key point to keep in mind for those interested in using Relight: there’s a difference between your photograph’s resolution and the resolution of the generated content. According to Nielson, Relight generates its output at 2K, then upscales it to match the image’s resolution. Your document’s pixel dimensions remain unchanged, but that doesn’t mean all of the original detail survives. Nielson acknowledged that the process can lose some detail, as is typical of generative AI.

When I tried Relight myself, Photoshop also displayed a warning that hadn’t come up during the demonstration: ‘Relight operates on 8-bit image data; fine color detail may be lost.’ So resolution isn’t the only potential compromise; the tool also has a limitation on the color data it processes.

I was also curious what happens when you use Relight to reveal a subject in deep shadow, and whether the tool would generate facial details that weren’t visible in the original. Nielson said it probably wouldn’t completely make up a person, but he hadn’t tested that specific scenario, so it remains an open question.

As a highly generative feature, Relight does require Adobe’s generative credits. It costs 30 credits (the number you get varies by plan, but the Photography 1TB one comes with 1,000 per month), but Nielson specified that you can preview the lighting as long as you want and make as many changes as you want during that step without spending any credits. It’s only when you click “Done” in the Contextual Taskbar that you spend the credits.

Generative Restyle

Generative Restyle can also adjust lighting, but it goes far beyond that. It’s a multi-step process: start by writing a prompt in Photoshop’s Contextual Taskbar, then click the “Generative Restyle” button that appears in that taskbar once the image has been generated. Then, you’ll have access to a slider to adjust the effect. Lastly, you need to click “Capture as layer” to get a higher-resolution, final version.

Restyle can generate a completely new interpretation of photographs, whether that be changing the time of day, weather, season and more. Because of the reliance on generative AI, details can fall off when using Restyle. Faces can become distorted, while small people in the distance and text can also trip it up.

The adjustable strength gives you some control over the result, but it doesn’t solve the fact that it can change things you didn’t want changed. Nielson’s demo showed adjusting a wedding portrait, and the woman’s facial features were changed when asking for a different look for the background. After all, the tool is generating the image as a whole, not just parts. With one prompt, it also completely changed the forest the couple was in, so that it looked like a totally different location.

Nielson pointed out that you can mask out unwanted changes to preserve parts of the original, but that leaves you cleaning up after a tool that was supposed to make the edit easier. An adjustable effect amount is useful, but it isn’t the same as being able to tell Restyle which details it must leave alone.

It’s also important to know that the output resolution of Restyle is even lower than that of Relight. While Nielson didn’t know the exact resolution, he guessed it was around 1K, so there will be detail loss. Indeed, when I tested the tool on my own, I noticed a substantial loss of detail. For example, branches in the forest became just blobs of texture instead of being able to see each individual one.

There’s also the question of consistency across a series, as I could see situations where a photographer may want to use this on a set of images. Nielson suggested that results should be consistent, but the demo didn’t establish how reliably you could apply the same treatment to multiple photographs without introducing different changes in each. For now, I’d be more inclined to treat Restyle as a creative experiment than a dependable way to give a set of photographs a cohesive look.

All in all, if you’re hoping to change the mood of a photograph without altering its content, or need to retain fine detail and consistency, these could be deal-breaking limitations. And that’s not to mention other implications about changing the reality of the photograph, but that’s a subject for another day.

In terms of generative credits, Restyle is much more costly. It’s a very generation-heavy process and requires 80 credits to use.

Lightroom features

Blemish removal

One of the few Lightroom features that Adobe mentioned in press materials at Max was Blemish Removal. This tool was previously available in Lightroom Mobile, but it’s now available on the desktop version. During my demo, I was told that the initial mobile version was good enough for casual use, but it wasn’t at the level that professionals would need, which is why the team delayed its rollout to desktop.

Blemish Removal is an AI-based tool that can detect blemishes and automatically remove them. It retains natural skin texture, instead of just smoothing things over, and it can substantially speed up the retouching process. What’s nice about this feature, though, is that it allows you a fair amount of control over the results.

There’s a slider to adjust the intensity of the retouching, which, crucially, doesn’t just fade the edits across the entire face. It works by hiding the most prominent blemishes first, then removing progressively subtler marks as you move the slider. You can also manually go into the mask to remove things that were missed or add back in things you want to keep.

The tool also allows you to adjust how permanent marks, like birthmarks, piercings and scars, are handled. You can choose to retain them or have them edited out alongside the temporary blemishes. Lastly, it recognizes different people, so you can make per-person adjustments with the above controls.

Customizable UI

Finally, the cloud version of Lightroom now allows for quite a lot of customization of the UI. You can choose between a default view and one that’s meant for power users. Or, you can also choose the Classic UI, which may make it more enticing for those who have stuck with Classic to move over to the cloud application.

But perhaps more useful is the Favorites panel, which allows users to essentially create their own Edit panel. That means you can hide the adjustments and controls that you never find yourself using and make the ones that you use constantly more prominent.

While I use Adobe Camera Raw (and Photoshop), not Lightroom, I find myself constantly scrolling past things that I don’t use in ACR, which takes time and does get a bit annoying. I’d imagine there’s a similar situation in Lightroom, so having the option to set up a UI based on how I work is very enticing and would make the editing process a little less painful.

issues.title: The way I share photos has changed and I didn’t even notice
issues.summary: My social network has replaced social media.
issues.author: Mitchell Clark
issues.content_html:
My social network has replaced social media.

A picture of my friend’s camera from a photowalk we did together.

It was a stray comment from Eric Yang, founder and CEO of our parent company Gear Patrol, that made me realize that something has shifted in how I share my photography. “I bought this camera on a whim. Atrocious flash, terrible shooting speed, auto-focus is highly questionable… yet most liked photos in the WhatsApp friend group.”

It was that last part that stuck with me, because it reflects a behavior of mine that I’ve noticed recently. Whenever I take a picture that I’m really excited about, my thought isn’t “I can’t wait to share this on [insert social media platform here].” Instead, I’ll share it in a group chat, or in my local Discord server, where a handful of my real-life photographer friends hang out.

Of course, my best photos end up making it to the internet, since using cameras and talking about it is, you know, my job. But if it weren’t, I’m pretty sure it’d stop there; I’d share my photos with my literal social network, not with social media.

There are a few benefits to this approach. I won’t pretend to be some enlightened monk who isn’t swayed at all by photo trends; I’ve done a shutter drag shot or two in the past few months, after all. But since moving away from sharing to a broader audience, I’m much closer to my sources of inspiration, and there’s more of a give-and-take. If one of my friends posts a really cool photo, it’s easy to talk about how they took it. And while nothing I post on r/photography will make a dent in broader photo culture as a whole, I’ve absolutely seen some of my friends take influence from my style of photography, or that of others in the group.

I’m sure there are some of you thinking “wait, all those things you just mentioned are what we used to like about Instagram and Flickr.” And, indeed, it’s what I used to like about Instagram. But those sites have either changed dramatically or become substantially less relevant, and, while there have been a few attempts, nothing has really taken on the role they once held. With the state of the internet and culture these days, I’m not sure anything ever will.

My approach of mostly sharing my photos with friends and colleagues has some downsides. While there are benefits to not comparing yourself to every other photographer on the internet, the wider, more experienced and more diverse a community is, the easier it is to run into inspiration that you may never have otherwise. There will be useful critiques I just don’t get from the places I share my photos, and there’s obviously a much smaller potential audience.

For the most part, though, I think it’s worth it for one important reason: it makes sharing photos fun again. Instead of something that feels like an obligation, it’s something I spend the trip home from a shoot looking forward to. Until that’s no longer the case, it’s hard to imagine looking for alternatives.

I’m curious about how the members of our community feel, though. Are you in the same boat, and have found yourself moving away from sharing your work on social media? Are you the opposite, and still finding joy in Instagram? Or perhaps you mainly post to DPReview’s forums (thank you!). Let me know in the comments.

issues.title: How a retired Adobe employee photographs wild birds in West Virginia
issues.summary: DPReview community member RicohMatt shares his Nikon Z8 setup, the monopod he trusts in mud and rain, and the strategy behind every bird photo.
issues.author: Mathew Anderson
issues.content_html:
DPReview community member RicohMatt shares his Nikon Z8 setup, the monopod he trusts in mud and rain, and the strategy behind every bird photo.

Meet RicohMatt

Home base: West Virginia, United States

Some of the best photography advice has nothing to do with gear. RicohMatt, a retired Adobe employee in the West Virginia Panhandle, will arrive at a meadow just before sunrise and stand nearly motionless for an hour, waiting for a songbird to return to its favorite perch. Sometimes he goes home with nothing but a tick crawling up his leg. He still calls it “good morning.”

That mindset stood out to me when I read through RicohMatt’s answers for this installment of “What’s in your bag?” As he puts it: “My approach is rooted in patience, observation, and natural light. Rather than simply documenting the birds I encounter, I hope to create photographs that capture their beauty, character and connection to the environments they inhabit.”

Our ‘What’s in your bag?’ community spotlight series features readers sharing their favorite gear and photography, including from past DPReview collaborators. See below for what RicohMatt has to share about his unique bird photography.

Have your photography featured on the DPReview homepage! Find out how.

What’s in RicohMatt’s bag

Favorite cameras(s): Nikon Z8

Favorite lens(s):NIKKOR Z 180-600mm F/5.6-6.3 VR and a NIKKOR Z 24-120mm F4 S for general shooting.

Favorite gear: “I used to wait for songbirds to take flight and found I could only hold my rig steady for a couple of minutes. Fortunately, the LEOFOTO Carbon Fiber Camera Monopod gives me near-handheld flexibility, and I can now wait much longer for birds to take flight.”

Favorite bag: “Definitely the Think Tank BackLight 26L Camera Daypack Backpack. It’s rugged and gets the job done on those days when you’re crawling through dense woods.

Also with the bag, I carry a LEOFOTO Carbon Fiber Camera Monopod 65″ Tall 4-Section, LEOFOTO NFC-01 Lens Collar and a Wimberley MH-100 Wimberley MonoGimbal Head. The monopod fits my setup just right and is built tough as nails. I get it wet and muddy, and it looks like new when I clean it.”

Where do birds nest that allows for great photography?

“I love the West Virginia Panhandle. I’m within an hour’s drive of Washington, D.C., so there’s plenty to do beyond the nature West Virginia offers. I always know I’m within a 15-minute drive of home, where it’s silent except for the sounds of nature.

I spend early mornings exploring the Shenandoah Valley and surrounding countryside. My favorite locations are shooting by rivers, in meadows, by ponds and in marshlands. There’s something about sitting on a boulder with my feet dangling over the river in the early morning light. The sound of the river flowing beneath me as the sun rises over the mountains is peaceful, even therapeutic.

The river produces species such as Bald Eagles, Great Blue Herons, Spotted Sandpipers and many others. I also shoot in marshlands where I’ve successfully photographed Gray Catbirds. I try to make it to at least one large meadow a week to shoot songbirds, especially Northern Cardinals, Indigo Buntings, Bluebirds, American Goldfinches, Mockingbirds and the occasional Red-shouldered Hawk.

Photographing birds must take extraordinary patience. How long do you wait for them?

“Many times, I arrive at a location just before sunrise and stay for 3–4 hours. It’s not unusual for me to stand in a spot as motionless as possible for an hour as long as I see and hear bird activity. I enjoy watching the birds around me, how they frustratingly fly high above the meadow to reach the canopy of trees that make up its perimeter, how songbirds will often return to the same perch and how they can fidget endlessly and fly from perch to perch.

There are times when they find a perch and sit still for extended periods. Sometimes I come home with nothing but a tick crawling up my leg, but even those days are enjoyable because I’ve spent several hours in nature.”

How has your photography changed since you started?

“I’ve loved photography for many years. It began with taking photos of my family and evolved into becoming a part time portrait, and finally bird photography, which I find is my true passion. I photograph locally, mostly throughout the Panhandle of West Virginia and western Virginia. Sometimes I’ll go to the Shenandoah and Potomac rivers, as I talked about earlier. I would like to visit Cape May someday during bird migrations.

I almost always shoot in manual with auto ISO and use exposure compensation heavily. One minute I’m photographing a Great Blue Heron standing in a pool with a clear reflection, and then a Great Egret comes along in the morning sun. These two scenes are hugely different in how to take a shot, so the manual with auto ISO helps a lot.”

How can other photographers get a great bird shot?

“My approach is rooted in patience, observation and natural light. That’s crucial when shooting wildlife. Rather than simply documenting the birds I encounter, I hope to create photographs that capture their beauty, character and connection to the environments they inhabit. I believe that purpose elevates my photography.

I first let them get used to my presence, hoping they will come near me. Most of the time it works, but not always. I try to guess at the settings I’ll need for the current environment and the bird I hope to photograph, since there are often only seconds to react.”

RicohMatt really enjoyed participating in this spotlight article and would love to hear what you think of his photography and to answer any of your questions in the comments below.

You can check out RicohMatt’s other work and photography methods right here on DPReview in the community forums.

issues.summary: The post Is it still photography if you’re only using your phone? appeared first on Digital Photography School . It was authored by Sime . Yes. issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Is it still photography if you’re only using your phone? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

Yes.

That’s as simple as the answer need be, but that’s not the point of this article.

Another Godox press release (Those guys are busy!) and again, we’ve not had a chance to play with one of these so you’ll need to do your own research, but Godox have just announced the Smartphone Xenon Flash A2, and their tagline is “Your phone, now a pro camera” which isn’t exactly factual, but also, the definition of “pro camera” is very loose.

The thing to keep in mind with ANY small light source is that its going to be harsh – there’s stuff you can do about it, though. You can diffuse it, bounce it (though a small light like the A2 might not give quite enough output to do much there) but even things like bouncing it off a close wall or even a sheet of paper in a pinch – use what you have, experiment.

I love the idea of small portable lights, this one is certainly an interesting addition to your phone photography – maybe worth giving a try, it’s certainly a good starter to your photography lighting journey.

Here’s the Godox Press Release (With a little bit of my own ramble)

Smartphone Photography, Now With More Zap

Phone cameras keep getting better, but low light, backlighting and mixed lighting can still make them sweat. Enter the Godox A2: proper pro-style lighting for your phone, with more control over your light and a lot more room to play.

Its short, punchy burst of xenon light freezes motion in its tracks, which is great for action shots and stylized looks.

Xenon Flash: Bring Your Subject to Life

Go bold with direct flash, or add a subtle lift to a backlit portrait. With a guide number of roughly 15 (ISO 100, metres), the A2 has plenty of oomph for close-range shots. When flash is your main light, that quick burst also helps freeze movement. *For best results, keep the A2 within 2 m of your subject. Want more power or wider coverage? Pair Godox’s upcoming smartphone wireless flash trigger (sold separately) with Godox speedlights or outdoor flashes.

TTL and Manual Modes: Stay Spontaneous, Get Precise

Fast and flawless when the moment’s fleeting, or hands-on when you want to flex your creative muscles. TTL and Manual modes have you covered both ways.

High-Speed Sync: Find Your Balance

Why banish that bright background when it can star in the story? With high-speed sync up to 1/8000s, the A2 lets you control ambient exposure while lighting your subject. Balance a face against a sunlit scene, or go for a faster shutter speed to keep the action crisp.

Bi-Color LED: True Color for Everyday Stories

Truer colors and flattering skin tones make portrait videos look natural and beautifully textured. Low light or indoors, the results feel authentic and ready to share. Your content doesn’t just look good, it feels right, and it’s always social-media ready.

Godox Camera App: Your Look, at Your Fingertips

Find your look right on your screen. Built on Godox’s TTL know-how, the Godox Camera app keeps exposure simple in Auto (A) mode, with Natural, Even and Contrast flash effects to try out. Feeling fussy? Switch to Manual (M) mode and tweak shutter speed and flash output yourself. Bluetooth with NFC-assisted setup lets you adjust flash and LED settings wirelessly, on or off camera.

Dual-Side Magnetic Mounting: Snap On, Explore New Angles

The A2’s dual magnetic design isn’t just for the back of your phone. Snap it to any metal surface or pop it on a stand and you’re ready to roll. On the front, the magnetic ring lets you attach accessories to shape the light exactly how you like. Simple, flexible and always creative.

Magnetic Accessories: Change the Light, Set the Mood

Go moodier and more dramatic with optional extras like a honeycomb grid, barndoors or a snoot to aim your light and tame the spill. Add a touch of warmth with a full CTO magnetic filter. *For best results, use the A2 off-camera with light-shaping accessories.

Compact. Magnetic. More Ways to Light.

Pro flash power in a palm-sized body. Pocketable, portable and happy to go anywhere you do.

Four Colors, A Style of Your Own

The A2 brings pro lighting to your phone in four distinctive colors. Pick a finish that suits your everyday style, and make your kit as personal as the photos you take.

And it got me thinking, even at a simple, easy to use level of printing like this little guy, who is
issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Do people still print their photographs? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

The guys at Godox sent across a press release (A few weeks back now I’m sorry as I’ve been a little ‘offline’) for their then new Godox Portable Colour Photo Printer, the P100. And it got me thinking, even at a simple, easy to use level of printing like this little guy, who is still printing out their photographs?

We celebrated my dad’s life recently, and at the wake my brother had printed out a couple hundred photographs that showed the life and times of dad and those he cared about. There’s something very real about having a print you can hold in your hand, nothing to log in to, no computers to boot up, just a square of paper and your memories.

Before we share this press release, here’s a challenge: In the next couple of months, aim to have one of your photographs printed, and to take that one step further, I was just listening to a clip from a podcast (You can see it here) Print Swap, what a great idea, print one of your images and send it to someone – to have and to hold.

Right, the Godox P100, it’s not an A3 Epson printing onto some beautiful Canson Rag, but it’s WITH YOU, you can print images and have them. (I’ve been grabbing frames with the beautiful FujiFilm Instax Mini 99 which prints a little 45x62mm photo)

On with our press release, please keep in mind we have not tested the P100 ourselves.

Godox Introduces P100 Portable Color Photo Printer

Godox has announced the P100 Portable Color Photo Printer, a compact dye-sublimation printer designed to turn digital images into physical prints wherever you are.

The P100 uses 300 dpi high-precision dye-sublimation printing, with 1,256 printhead heating elements and support for 16.7 million colours. According to Godox, the combination is designed to produce smooth colour gradations, fine detail and vivid colour reproduction.

Each print also receives an automatic protective overcoat, helping protect the finished photo from dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion.

Print and personalise from your phone

The P100 connects to the Godox Cam APP via Bluetooth, while NFC tap-to-connect provides another quick way to pair the printer.

From within the app, users can capture and print photos directly, or work with images already on their device. Creative options include filters, frames, stickers and templates, along with tools for creating ID photos and collages.

The app also allows users to check remaining paper and battery levels, making it easier to keep track of the printer’s status.

Designed to travel

With its compact design and lightweight construction, the P100 is intended to be easy to take along to parties, family gatherings, housewarmings and other everyday occasions.

Rather than leaving photos sitting on a phone or buried in a cloud library, the P100 gives users a simple way to turn them into physical prints that can be displayed, collected, added to a scrapbook or shared with friends and family.

Automatic protection

The P100’s automatic lamination process adds a protective overcoat to every finished print. Godox says this helps protect prints against dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion, as well as humid conditions.

The process happens automatically after printing, so there is no additional lamination step for the user.

All-in-one cartridge

The P100 uses an all-in-one photo paper cartridge, designed to make replacing the printing supplies quick and straightforward.

Combined with wireless connectivity and the Godox Cam APP, the system is designed to keep the process from capturing a photo to holding the finished print as simple as possible.

A physical home for digital memories

The P100 is ultimately aimed at something increasingly familiar in photography: we take plenty of photos, but relatively few ever make it off our phones.

By combining portable dye-sublimation printing with a range of simple editing and personalisation tools, Godox says the P100 is designed to make printing those images easier, whether you’re sharing them with friends at a gathering or simply putting a favourite photograph somewhere you’ll actually see it.

The Godox P100 Portable Color Photo Printer is now part of Godox’s expanding range of photography accessories.

You can get them online for around $200 Aussie, do a Google and see what you can find!

Don’t forget, PRINT YOUR WORK.

issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post News: National Indigenous art prize puts Lismore on Australia’s cultural map appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

National Indigenous art prize puts Lismore on Australia’s cultural map

Some of Australia’s most exciting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander artists will compete for $23,000 in prize money in Lismore this year, as finalists are announced for the 2026 Koori Mail Indigenous Art Award.

Run nationally from Lismore Regional Gallery in partnership with the Koori Mail Newspaper, the biennial award has grown into a significant platform for contemporary Indigenous art, attracting artists from across Australia and spanning painting, sculpture, photography, ceramics, moving image and fibre art.

This year’s prize pool has expanded to $23,000, with the Major Award doubling from $10,000 in 2024 to $20,000 and a new $3,000 Youth Award for artists aged 18 to 25.

Lismore Regional Gallery Director Susi Muddiman OAM welcomed the announcement of this year’s finalists.

“This award demonstrates that nationally significant contemporary art does not have to be centred in a capital city. From Lismore, we are providing a national platform for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander artists and bringing extraordinary work from across Australia to audiences in regional NSW,” Ms Muddiman said.

“Combined with the Youth Award this year, the shortlist highlights incredible fresh talent alongside established artists whose work commands attention on the national stage. It promises to be an inspiring and powerful exhibition that we are honoured to present.”

The 2026 finalists are:

Major Award Finalists

Michelle Anderson, Kieron Anderson, Sonya Breckenridge, Luke Close, Ralph Close, Chris Curtis, Louise Daniels, Joe Dhamanydji, Jodie Dowd, Troy Firebrace, Margaret Rarru Garrawurra, Donna Gayford McLaren, Maddison Gibbs, Jodie Harris, Melinda Ingram, Clare Jaque Vasquez, Kieren Karritpul, Virginia Keft, Jaymi Lawrence, Tara Lloyd, Zali Morgan, Amber Morris, Kent Morris, Jodie Munday, Gail Naden, Ian Nicholas, Tracey Piccoli, Ross Potter, Brandi Salmon, Damien Shen, Kyle Slabb, Valerie Smith, Jasmin Stanford, Douglas Tamwoy, Anthony Walker and Jeremy Worrall.

Youth Award Finalists

Cameron Cooper, Keesia Close, Levi Roberts, Monique Vuong and Mayarr Yanner.
This year’s entries are being judged by Yorta Yorta curator, writer and academic Dr Kimberley Moulton, Senior Curator Exhibitions at Melbourne’s RISING festival and former Adjunct Curator of Indigenous Art at London’s Tate Modern.

Reflecting on the shortlisted works, Dr Moulton praised the remarkable breadth and strength of the entries.

“It’s an honour to judge this year’s Koori Mail Art Award. With a diverse combination of local and national works, city based and regional, it’s an incredibly strong year with artists sharing their stories, connections to country and culture,” Dr Moulton said.

Koori Mail Cultural Lead Trevor Kapeen said the award created opportunities for First Nations artists to share their work with a national audience.

“Every year this award brings a magnificent gathering of First Nations artistic talent into focus,” Mr Kapeen said.

“For the Koori Mail, supporting these artists is about creating tangible opportunities for national visibility and cultural exchange. We congratulate all the 2026 finalists and look forward to celebrating their achievements when the exhibition opens.”

Finalists will come together at Lismore Regional Gallery for a major exhibition opening on 7 November, putting regional NSW at the centre of a national showcase of established and emerging Indigenous artistic talent.

Council and the Lismore Regional Gallery are incredibly thankful to the generosity of the major sponsors, the Koori Mail Newspaper and Hurford Hardwood, and to the Friends of the Gallery for their contributions to the prize pool.

EVENT DETAILS

2026 Koori Mail Indigenous Art Award Exhibition

* Exhibition Dates: 7 November 2026 to 14 February 2027
* Official Opening and Winner Announcement: Saturday, 7 November 2026
* Location: Lismore Regional Gallery, 11 Rural Street, Lismore
* Entry: Free
* Full Finalist List & Exhibition Info: https://lismoregallery.org/exhibitions/koori-mail-indigenous-art-award-2026-0

issues.title: At NYC’s ADAA Art Fair, Unlimited Shrimp and $2K Diebenkorns
issues.summary: The Art Dealers Association of America’s chummy five-day show returns to the Upper East Side after quietly canceling last fall’s edition.
issues.author: Aaron Short
issues.content_html:
There are many art fairs in New York City, but perhaps none are friendlier than the one hosted by the chummy Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA).

“We all know each other very well,” Dorsey Waxter, former president of the ADAA and partner at Van Doren Waxter gallery, told Hyperallergic. “We’ve vetted each gallery that comes into the association for levels of excellence and standards. And it’s not so big you can’t have conversations with dealers and find out things about what you’re looking at.”

Jovial conversations about pathbreaking newcomers and long-dead modernists abounded inside the Park Avenue Armory, which provided a needed refuge from the cold nor’easter pummeling Manhattan for Thursday night’s VIP preview.

issues.title: 45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds
issues.summary: In addition to declining funding, the survey identified a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns and financial precarity.
issues.author: Valentina Di Liscia
issues.content_html:
Nearly half of independent publications covering arts and culture in the United States said their businessmodels will not be sustainable without “profound changes” to the current funding landscape, according to a report from Critical Minded and the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation released this week.

The new survey notably identifies a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns, including external pressure from advertisers and sponsors, and financial precarity. The 41% of respondents who said they faced free-speech pressures or threats in the last two years were more likely to report funding declines, throwing into stark relief how what outlets choose to cover — or not — may determine whether they can pay staff and contributors, or keep the lights on altogether.

“Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent outlets that cover the arts on issues impacting the field and strategies used to address them. The anonymizedrespondents are based in 34 states and the District of Columbia, with the highest concentration (38.2%) in the Northeast, and reach an average annual audience of about half a million.

issues.title: The Secret Life of Hockney's Beverly Hills Housewife
issues.summary: Taking David Hockney’s painting of arts patron Betty Freeman as his subject, James Cahill tells the engrossing story of two friends who shaped the cultural landscape of 1960s Los Angeles.
issues.author: Matt Stromberg
issues.content_html:
In the summer of 1966, David Hockney began work on one of his most iconic paintings: “Beverly Hills Housewife,” a portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman. She is depicted on her garden patio in front of her sleek, modernist house, which is framed by strips of blue sky and green lawn. A few status symbols surround her — a William Turnbull sculpture, a zebra-skin lounge designed by Le Corbusier, and a mounted antelope head— but the focal point is Freeman in her bright pink dress, gazing wistfully beyond the confines of the canvas.

Critic and novelist James Cahill uses the painting as a jumping off point to expound on the intertwined lives of both artist and muse, as well as to provide a fragmentary snapshot of Los Angeles in the 1960s, in his new book. With The Beverly Hills Housewife: Hockney’s Californian Muse and the World Beyond the Pool (2026), Cahill bounces between formal analysis of the painting, historical anecdotes, and inferences about the broader culture, zigzagging as if driving across LA without a map. Some of the detours prove less relevant to his central narrative than others, but they are nonetheless diverting pit stops on a thoroughly engrossing journey about the friendship between two complex individuals who played formative roles in shaping LA’s cultural landscape.

issues.title: ARTnews Awards 2026 Best Gallery Group Show: “Horror”
issues.summary: For an exhibition at Sprüth Magers in Los Angeles curated by Jill Mulleady.
issues.author: Alex Greenberger
issues.content_html:
“Horror”
At Sprüth Magers, Los Angeles (November 21, 2025–February 14, 2026)
Curator: Jill Mulleady

With her group show “Horror” at Sprüth Magers in Los Angeles, artist Jill Mulleady took an expansive view of its titular genre, viewing horror not from the perspective of a single iconography or set of concerns but rather as a catch-all for everything we fear. Mulleady, a figurative painter whose work invokes spectral figures and mystical phenomena, did not offer a thesis necessarily with this show. Instead, she evoked a vibe that played out across more than half a century of art. Bringing together paintings, sculptures, photographs, and films, Mulleady reached as far back as the days of Surrealism by featuring a recording by Antonin Artaud and extended through the present with recent works by Anne Imhof, Henry Taylor, and Jordan Wolfson. Along the way, the exhibition addressed body horror, fear of the other, abjection, and other resonant topics.

“Horror” cast its net widely, refusing to adhere to a specific style while also making a number of shrewd curatorial decisions. An Andra Ursuta painting showing a mysterious skeleton in a purplish void could be found next to a Bruce Conner sculpture that placed a skull in a shrine-like setting. A Pol Taburet painting of two brown figures in a bed was placed beside a Precious Okoyomon sculpture composed of a racist doll. Mike Kelley’s Odalisque, a hulking black mass on a divan, was set before Sondra Perry’s Flesh on Flesh (2021), a work based on a 3-D image of the artist’s own facial skin.

The exhibition’s lodestar was Kelley, a sculptor whose work frequently invoked grotesque imagery. Taking inspiration from Kelley’s 1993 exhibition “The Uncanny,” the show sought to explore “the unsettling psychological tension created when the familiar is revealed to be disturbingly strange—a repressed domesticity surfacing in unsettling form,” as she wrote in an accompanying essay. Mulleady’s show was not explicitly political, but that, in a way, was its point. Her interest in horror comes from the way it presents a “a controlled confrontation with chaos,” as she told Wallpaper. There’s a sense of catharsis that comes through viewing work of this kind, which she described as “a strategy to talk about real-life forces that are too hard to digest directly.”

Nominees:

“How Beautiful This Living Thing Is”
at Ortuzar, New York (April 22–May 30, 2026)
Curator:Andrew Durbin

“Snake, Turtle, Alligator”
at David Peter Francis, New York, co-organized with Interrobang (January 10–February 7, 2026)

“Statics of an Egg”
at David Zwirner, New York (May 8–June 27, 2026)
Curator: Martin Germann

“What We Hold On To”
at Black Cube Nomadic Art Museum, Englewood, Colorado (September 5—December 12, 2025)

issues.title: ARTnews Awards 2026 Lifetime Achievement: Maren Hassinger
issues.summary: For “Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing” at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive.
issues.author: Alex Greenberger
issues.content_html:
Recognizing an influential living artist having a retrospective or survey exhibition at a major US museum.

Maren Hassinger
for “Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing” at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (June 6–November 29, 2026)

For five decades, Maren Hassinger has been making elegant, spare sculptures that have enlisted a diverse array of materials, from wire rope to pink plastic bags to newspaper to rose leaves. The objects she incorporates in her art are the kind that could easily be bent, twisted, or broken. In another setting, they might even be seen as flimsy. But Hassinger sculpts them in a way where they appear firm, monumental, and alive. Across an oeuvre that has included installations, performances, films, drawings, and more, Hassinger has repeatedly returned to the concept of motion, imbuing static objects with a sense of movement, as if they are shifting before our eyes. Frequently, she does so by referring to the natural environment, invoking trees and water with works that appear to undulate because of the way they are installed.

Her retrospective at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, billed as the most expansive show of her art to date, positioned her as a key figure in the transition away from Minimalism. During the 1970s, Hassinger began working with wire rope that she partially pulled apart. The use of a material associated with industry synched with a tendency seen at the time in New York, where a range of sculptors transformed steel, firebricks, and fluorescent lights into large and often heavy artworks. Hassinger’s approach differed in its overt allusions to the human body and its intentionally light touch. While Hassinger’s collaborations with artists like Senga Nengudi and Ulysses Jenkins are now well-known, the BAMPFA show put forward Hassinger as a performance artist in her own right, noting that she sought to become a dancer before settling on sculpture during her education. Her sculptures would go on to translate those choreographies, which could not be permanently viewable within gallery spaces.

The concept of ephemerality has also been core to Hassinger’s body of work, and the BAMPFA show highlighted it prominently by featuring her works that make use of pink plastic bags or old newspapers, objects that might easily be thrown in the trash but that Hassinger sees as worthy art materials. Ranging from large-scale installations to intimate weavings, she always seeks to make beauty of what could easily be treated as refuse. In the BAMPFA catalog, speaking to curator Lowery Stokes Sims of the newspaper pieces, Hassinger says, “Well I don’t want to look at something ugly. I want things to be as finished and pleasant as possible. And why not?”

Nominees:

Coco Fusco
“Coco Fusco: Tomorrow, I Will Become an Island” at El Museo del Barrio, New York (September 18, 2025–March 1, 2026)

Suzanne Jackson
“Suzanne Jackson: What Is Love” at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (September 27, 2025–March 1, 2026); traveled to the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis (May 14–August 23, 2026) and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (September 26, 2026–January 18, 2027)

David Lamelas
“David Lamelas: The Machine” at Dia Chelsea, New York (March 6, 2026–January 16, 2027)

Martin Puryear

issues.title: ARTnews Awards 2026 Historical Artist of the Year: Theresa Hak Kyung Cha
issues.summary: For “Theresa Hak Kyung Cha: Multiple Offerings” at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive.
issues.author: Maximilíano Durón
issues.content_html:
Honoring a deceased artist who is the subject of a major museum survey that offers a new lens with which to examine their work.

Theresa Hak Kyung Cha
for “Theresa Hak Kyung Cha: Multiple Offerings” at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (January 24–April 19, 2026); traveled to Artists Space, New York (September 11–November 21, 2026)
Curators: Victoria Sung, with Tausif Noor

Since her untimely death in 1982, Theresa Hak Kyung Cha has been a touchstone for academics and artists alike. Best known for Dictée, a genre-defying book that combines fiction, memoir, hagiography, and more, Cha was this year the subject of a BAMPFA retrospective that offered a new lens from which to view the artist’s practice. It expanded the scope beyond Dictée and brought together early ceramics, documentation of her performances, text-based works, mail art, and video art, all of which was elegantly installed.

Cha’s experience of moving to the United States from Korea during her childhood animated her practice, giving her fertile ground to think through what it means to live in diaspora and be caught between two cultures. In this space, where words might fail to fully explain one’s experience, she found a place to make art. The exhibition’s title “Multiple Offerings” borrows its names from the phrase “Multiple Telling with Multiple Offerings,” a conceptual framework that guided Cha’s art-making, resulting in works that were not meant to be experienced in just one way. Instead of giving easy answers, or even a single answer, Cha’s practice starts a conversation. We are left to pick up the pieces and make meaning from them.

Curator Victoria Sung traced the important moments of Cha’s short yet productive career, focusing on the decade she spent as a student at the University of California, Berkeley, which houses BAMPFA, and periods spent in New York, France, and South Korea. At the time of her death, Cha was at work on a major film, White Dust From Mongolia, that she was never able to fully realize, despite having produced storyboards and shot footage for the work. Artists like Na Mira and Cici Wu have looked to White Dust From Mongolia and created work in response to it; those pieces were included in the BAMPFA exhibition. With their inclusion, Sung also made the case for Cha as an artist whose influence has recently come into focus.

Nominees:

Wifredo Lam
for “Wifredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream” at the Museum of Modern Art, New York (November 10, 2025–April 11, 2026)

Tom Lloyd
for “Tom Lloyd” at the Studio Museum in Harlem, New York (November 15, 2025–March 22, 2026); traveled to the Frye Art Museum, Seattle (May 16–September 20, 2026)

Ceija Stojka
for “Ceija Stojka: Making Visible” at The Drawing Center, New York (February 20–June 7, 2026)

Betty Parsons
for “Betty Parsons: An Expanded World” at CCS Bard’s Hessel Museum of Art, Annandale-on-Hudson, New York (June 27–October 18, 2026)

issues.title: ARTnews Awards 2026 Emerging Artist of the Year: Coco Klockner
issues.summary: For “In Practice: Coco Klockner” at SculptureCenter, New York.
issues.author: Alex Greenberger
issues.content_html:
Recognizing an artist who is having their first significant gallery or small nonprofit solo show or has made an important contribution to a biennial.

Coco Klockner
for “In Practice: Coco Klockner” at SculptureCenter, New York (October 18, 2025–December 22, 2025) and her contribution to “Greater New York 2026” at MoMA PS1, New York (April 16–August 17, 2026)

Coco Klockner has said she approaches making sculpture “as though it were in transition,” a turn of phrase that refers to the unknowable, shape-shifting quality that has characterized much of her work since her first gallery show in 2018. At New York’s SculptureCenter, she continued that line of thinking with her “In Practice” exhibition, which was largely composed of one ambitious installation: null dialogue (2025), a work that was composed of subwoofers, construction fill, and an amplifier, among other materials. An easily missed motion detector at the entrance set off the piece’s soundtrack, which Klockner has described as “an undisclosed conversation between lovers.” Yet the words of that conversation were heavily edited and therefore difficult to understand, and the show itself contained little information about the work. A machine emitted fog every three minutes, cloaking the space in a mysterious haze. Depending on when one encountered Klockner’s SculptureCenter show, null dialogue may have been heard before it was seen. Indeed, Klockner has described drawing influence from the notion of thinking of “sounds as objects.”

She gave that idea new form with her contribution to MoMA PS1’s 2026 edition of Greater New York, where she showed Glottoplasty (2026), an installation in which plastic storage drawers embedded with speakers play sliced and sutured excerpts from trans oral archives. As with null dialogue, the words emitted were nearly impossible to parse, even if they were played quite loudly. The work suggested an effort to simultaneously reveal and conceal. Implicit in both the SculptureCenter show and the PS1 work was an interest in the body. Glottoplasty took its name from a medical procedure that is used to raise the pitch of one’s voice; null dialogue was accompanied by an untitled work composed of a plastic mouth retractor, wood filler, and 935 silver. Notably, at both presentations, it was possible to feel the rumbling of Klockner’s art while standing before it.

Nominees:

Eric Gyamfi
for “Eric Gyamfi: Exposure: Black Queer Visual Constellations” at Brown Arts Institute, Providence, Rhode Island (April 16 – June 15, 2026) and contributions to “If the word we: 59th Carnegie International” (May 2, 2026–January 3, 2027)

Blas Isasi
for “Currents 125: Blas Isasi” at Saint Louis Art Museum (February 6–August 9, 2026)

Emma McCormick Goodhart
for “sottobosco (climate remix): CAVE 0 by Emma McCormick Goodhart” at SculptureCenter, New York (December 11–22, 2025)

Christelle Oyiri
for “Christelle Oyiri: Belief May Vary” at Amant, New York (March 19, 2026–August 19, 2026)

issues.title: ‘The Sacred Ordinary’ Shines a Light on Heritage in Birmingham’s Civil Rights District
issues.summary: The participatory public artwork includes a self-guided tour via text every night from 5 to 8 p.m. until December 13. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
In the second stanza of “How to Be a Poet,” Wendell Berry wrote: “There are no unsacred places; / there are only sacred places / and desecrated places.” When it comes to preserving important historical locations, such as monuments, parks, and buildings, a new interactive public art installation asks, “what happens when preservation itself is endangered?”

The Sacred Ordinary is an initiative organized by 1504, a production studio based in Birmingham that emphasizes in-depth storytelling to connect people with meaningful, human-focused services and experiences. The participatory artwork is presented in collaboration with the National Parks Conservation Association, which aims to protect U.S. national parks for future generations.

In early 2025, President Trump issued an executive order that mandated the removal of some National Park Service signage relating to slavery, the LGBTQ+ community, climate change, and more, a move that erases histories inextricable from the nation’s identity. (The current administration has also blocked millions in funding for numerous parks and disrupted services.)

In Birmingham, the Civil Rights District is formally designated a national monument, comprising neighborhoods that Black people historically called home and where Jim Crow laws authorized segregation until the 1960s. The Civil Rights Movement reached a nexus here when activists Fred Shuttlesworth, Martin Luther King, Jr., and Ralph Abernathy, among many others, organized nonviolent marches in 1963, known today as the Birmingham Campaign. Police turned their dogs on demonstrators and used fire hoses on children. A bombing at a Baptist church killed four young Black girls.

The Sacred Ordinary venerates access to things most of us take for granted: the ability to shop at any store, attend the nearest school, walk around any neighborhood, and sit at the front of the bus. The exhibition is installed around-the-clock, but by day, elements of the installation comprise vintage yet mundane objects that one typically walks by without giving a second thought.

A huge midcentury television rests on an open lawn, and a red newspaper vending box for The Birmingham News, which ceased its print publication in 2012, advertises 25 cents per copy. Additional sites include a characteristically blue U.S. Postal Service mailbox and a walk-in telephone booth. Sheets of paper with tear-off tabs posted around town invite participants to learn more by texting a phone number. If you text “HERE” to the number, you’ll be directed to a starting point and an otherwise nondescript yellow fire hydrant.

In scavenger-hunt style, visitors are prompted to enter the year stamped on the unit, and if it’s between 5 and 8 p.m., the sequence of texted prompts doubles as a multimedia self-guided tour of Birmingham’s Civil Rights District like you’ve never seen it: the television screen, mailbox, phone booth, and more begin to glow once the sun has set.

“Birmingham, Alabama, is known around the world for such places—sites of civil rights history that many regard as sacred and that connect us to something larger than ourselves. But today, that memory is endangered,” 1504 says in a statement. “Aging infrastructure, the passing of a generation of foot soldiers, and federal efforts to erase chapters of American history raise an urgent question: if institutions alone cannot sustain history, what role can the public play in caring for sacred sites?”

Rather than center primarily on signage, The Sacred Ordinary focuses on objects associated with civic life in the mid-20th century, evoking collective memories and providing touchpoints for younger generations for whom boxy televisions, printed newspapers, and telephone booths feel distant from today’s experiences. Emblematic of the way news and information spread before the internet and smartphones, the objects confront visitors with not only the realities of how people organized and communicated during that time but also how those memories are preserved today. Even without didactics, objects and places carry meaning that no one can simply delete.

The tour opens with a narration by actor André Holland, who played a fundamental role in preserving a historic theater in nearby Bessemer, Alabama, and 1504 has dedicated the installation to Birmingham-based artist Joe Minter. The Sacred Ordinary continues nightly through December 13, with accompanying guided walks and other programs scheduled in the meantime. Learn more on the project’s website, and explore the studio’s work on Instagram. You might also be interested in “The Praise House,” directed by 1504’s Tyler Jones.

issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
Celestial filmmaker Seán Doran is back with a new project that interprets stellar snapshots from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. The footage-like video tours the sun and reveals its fiery surface complete with brilliant solar flares, all depicted in a distinctive crimson.

To create the film, Doran attributed various pinks and reds to different wavelengths, creating an alluring interpretation of the fiery orb. Doran stitched together NASA’s captures, or more accurately, he says, the images were “conformed, repaired, graded, blended, rescaled and retimed” into a seamless film. “Crimson Star” is one of several astral projects he’s undertaken in recent years, and you can keep up with his latest works on YouTube. (via Kottke)

issues.title: How Sky Glabush Conjures Atmospheric Landscapes in Sand and Oil Paint
issues.summary: Sky Glabush identifies the feelings he associates with a particular place and translates that through color and intuitive interpretations of the terrain. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article How Sky Glabush Conjures Atmospheric Landscapes in Sand and Oil Paint appeared first
issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
Looking at the serene paintings that emerge from Sky Glabush’ s studio, it’s easy to feel a soft breeze sliding off bare summer shoulders or hear the crunch of leaves underfoot, their parched fibers reverberating across the autumn landscape. Transportive and atmospherically charged, the landscapes harness the allure of texture to draw the viewer in and invite them to stay a while.

Raised on the west coast of British Columbia and currently based in rural Ontario, Glabush has long been attuned to the natural world. He often identifies the feelings he associates with a particular place and translates that through color and intuitive interpretations of the terrain: the spindly, strangely straight tree trunks of a forest, for example, or the ways a sunflower echoes the radial form of the sun.

Glabush typically utilizes limited palettes that adhere to just one or two color families. He also mixes oil paint with granular particles, sand being the most common, although he’s used crushed quartz and raw pigment. Originally, the idea of combining materials emerged because the artist wanted, he says, to “obliterate the image… But I realized it didn’t destroy the image. It was still present and humming under that surface layer. So it gave me the freedom of deciding what I wanted to hold on to or what I wanted to erase.”

Adding and removing has since become integral to Glabush’s practice, which involves adding thin stains of paint and turpentine to the point of the painting becoming relief-like. He tends to begin with an architectural structure that anchors the work. Sometimes a grid and others a radial arrangement, the foundational patterns inform each resulting layer. Color, though, is always “the unifying principle, it is the energy and dynamism, it is the element of surprise. Each painting often goes through several iterations of colour before deciding on a direction.”

Although he’s worked with other materials in the past and has particularly enjoyed carving, the conventions and limitations of painting always drew him back. “That period of experimentation with sculpture allowed me to treat my paintings in a more physically robust and experimental way. But even during my most experimental period, I saw myself as a painter and wanted to find a way to express myself within that language,” he tells Colossal.

Some of the works here will be on view in Glabush’s solo exhibition, If the Wild Bird Could Speak, on view from November 20 to January 9 at Alison Jacques in London. Until then, explore more of his paintings on Instagram.

issues.summary: Ten years in the making, "The Cloud House" is a whimsical response to its eclectic neighboring architecture. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Peter Morris Architects’ Pastel Pink ‘Cloud House’ Billows in Northwest London appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
A confection of arches and windows has emerged in the Gospel Oak neighborhood of Camden in northwest London, thanks to Peter Morris Architects and a unique collaborative ownership approach. “The Cloud House,” which actually comprises two side-by-side townhomes, practically froths from its foundations. One side is occupied by the architect himself along with his partner, Emily, while the other half is owned by a resident who embraced the stylistic potential of the project and agreed to the exterior design and the same contractor.

Ten years in the making, “The Cloud House” is a playful response to its eclectic neighboring architecture, from the quirky Victorian church of St. Martin’s to a school next door that has a stone exterior mimicking a castle. Morris conceived of a bright, whimsical design with pink walls, robin’s egg-blue window frames and doors, and arched details in relief made from a dense recyclable polystyrene that mirrors the arches of the church across the street. See more on the firm’s Instagram.

issues.title: The 5 Best Booths at ADAA Fair 2026
issues.summary: The ADAA Fair has returned to New York with a new name, a reimagined format, and something to prove. Following a one-year hiatus, the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA)’s annual fair has been relaunched as the ADAA Fair, bringing 63 member galleries to the Park Avenue Armory from November 13 to 16, with a benefit preview supporting The Whitney Museum of American Art on the 12th. The edition
issues.author: Annabel Keenan
issues.content_html:
The ADAA Fair has returned to New York with a new name, a reimagined format, and something to prove. Following a one-year hiatus, the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA)’s annual fair has been relaunched as the ADAA Fair, bringing 63 member galleries to the Park Avenue Armory from November 13 to 16, with a benefit preview supporting The Whitney Museum of American Art on the 12th.

The edition marks the first organized by executive director Kinsey Robb, who has overseen a smaller, more focused roster. The fair’s roots stretch back to 1989, when the ADAA launched The Art Show at the Park Avenue Armory. Over its 36-year history, it grew into one of the country’s most respected gallery-led fairs, distinguished by its emphasis on scholarly presentations and its strong relationship with museums and nonprofits.

The ADAA’s decision to return with a smaller exhibitor pool—roughly a dozen fewer than its last edition in 2024—reflects a broader industry conversation about the saturation of the art fair schedule and the importance of more considered presentations. “The pause gave us the time to make deliberate decisions about the fair’s evolution while building on what has always distinguished it,” Robb told Artsy.

The fair’s timing places it just weeks before the art world descends upon Miami in early December, and within New York’s expanding art calendar. Attendees ebbed and flowed during the VIP preview evening, with the first hour noticeably quiet, a welcome opportunity to view the artworks with some breathing room before the crowds filled in.

For collectors, the ADAA Fair offers an opportunity to encounter an impressive selection of historical, modern, and contemporary art through dealers whose expertise and long-standing relationships with artists are central to their appeal.

Here are five booths that stand out at this year’s edition.


Roberts Projects

Booth B1

With works by Betye Saar

Journey to Zimbabwe, 1974
Betye Saar
Roberts Projects

Shaman, 1991
Betye Saar
Roberts Projects

Los Angeles’ Roberts Projects is presenting a timely tribute to the late Betye Saar, who passed away in July just four days before her 100th birthday. The gallery is staging a rich survey spanning more than six decades of Saar’s multidisciplinary practice. A pioneering figure in assemblage art, Saar was known for transforming found objects, family heirlooms, and vintage imagery into evocative works that confront America’s racial history.

Often incorporating elements of African American folklore and mysticism, her work is perhaps best known for its incisive use of symbolism and its reclamation of racist imagery.

“More than an influential figure in contemporary art, Saar has fundamentally redefined the possibilities of everyday objects, transforming them into powerful vehicles for examining complex historical and political narratives,” said gallery co-founder Julie Roberts.

The booth brings together rarely exhibited works priced between $20,000 and $650,000, including the wall assemblages Eternity (1974) and Journey to Zimbabwe (1974), both featured in her landmark 1975 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art.


Piero Atchugarry Gallery

Booth B9

Works by Túlio Pinto

Making its debut at the ADAA Fair following its recent admission to the association, the Uruguay- and Miami-based Piero Atchugarry Gallery is staging a solo booth devoted to Brazilian sculptor Túlio Pinto, whose work explores the precarious relationship between weight, balance, and resistance. A much-needed injection of sculpture in a fair dominated by two-dimensional works, the presentation includes Gravitas #3, a long U-shaped steel beam that appears to teeter on the brink of collapse, held upright by a delicate glass chain. Likewise, in Gravitas #01, a block of quartz sandstone is improbably supported by the same fragile material.

The booth reflects the gallery’s commitment to sculptural practices and artists from the Global South, as well as its minimalist sensibility. “Túlio Pinto builds sculpture from suspended tension,” said gallery founder Piero Atchugarry. “Glass, stone, and steel are materials with opposing natures: one fragile, one inert, one rigid. In his hands they come to depend on one another, held in an equilibrium so exact that each work exists in the threshold between stability and collapse.”

The works on view range in price from $10,000 to $30,000, and Atchugarry expressed optimism at the VIP opening, commenting on the enthusiasm of attendees who were equally excited to encounter sculpture at the fair.


Jessica Silverman

Booth B7

Works by Julie Buffalohead

In Jessica Silverman’s booth, the San Francisco–based gallery is presenting paintings and works on paper by Julie Buffalohead. A member of the Ponca Tribe of Oklahoma, Buffalohead creates richly imaginative compositions that weave Indigenous histories, personal experience, and contemporary social commentary into surreal, darkly humorous narratives. Her works often feature anthropomorphic animals—particularly coyotes, trickster figures, and other creatures drawn from Native storytelling—alongside human characters who inhabit worlds where folklore and everyday life collide.

Through these hybrid figures and unexpected encounters, Buffalohead explores questions of cultural identity, colonialism, and motherhood. She also uses irony and familiar visual stereotypes to expose the ways Native American culture has been misrepresented and commercialized. Buffalohead’s open-ended allegories invite viewers to reconsider whose stories are told, who gets to tell them, and what is passed down between generations.

“Despite the pouring rain outside, the Park Avenue Armory was packed with collectors and press thrilled to be back at ADAA tonight,” gallery founder Jessica Silverman said. “Our solo booth for Julie Buffalohead—a fresh, richly deserved platform for her work—was met with overwhelming enthusiasm, affirming just how powerful it is to experience her paintings in person.”

Indeed, during the preview evening, the gallery reported eight sales of Buffalohead’s works, ranging in price from $22,000 to $50,000.


Berry Campbell Gallery

Booth C6

Works by Elaine de Kooning, Janice Biala, Bernice Bing, Dorothy Dehner, Perle Fine, Mercedes Matter, Edith Schloss, Lynne Drexler, Judith Godwin, and Yvonne Thomas

At the center of Berry Campbell Gallery’s presentation is an important example of Elaine de Kooning’s portraiture, Gandy Brodie (1973), a lively, gestural depiction of the artist’s friend and fellow downtown New York fixture. Priced at $450,000, the painting combines the spontaneous energy of Abstract Expressionism with a clear sense of character, a reminder of de Kooning’s remarkable versatility beyond her better-known association with the movement’s abstract painters.

A founding member of the avant-garde Artists’ Club in Greenwich Village, de Kooning was also an influential critic, writing early essays on artists including Mark Rothko, Arshile Gorky, Hans Hofmann, and Franz Kline. Her renewed visibility comes amid a broader reassessment of women’s contributions to post-war abstraction, including Berry Campbell’s current exhibition of the artist, which brings her work into sharper focus and earned her a New York Times feature this fall.

In its booth, the New York gallery—whose program specializes in postwar American art and the women of Abstract Expressionism—places de Kooning in conversation with works by Janice Biala, Lynne Drexler, Judith Godwin, Dorothy Dehner, and others.


Yares Art

Booth A5

Works by Larry Poons

In another impressive solo presentation, Yares Art turns its spotlight on Larry Poons. The gallery, which has New York, Santa Fe, and Beverly Hills locations, is staging a focused survey of late abstract paintings by the artist spanning 2005 to 2026, including two works never before exhibited. A major figure in American abstraction for more than six decades and one of the last living protagonists of the Color Field movement, Poons has built a career on experimentation, continually pushing painting toward new forms of movement, texture, and chromatic intensity.

Remarkably ambitious in scale for the confines of the booth, the large paintings command attention with their riotous surfaces and kinetic energy. Thick, looping bands of paint twist and tumble across the canvases, colliding with broad, sweeping gestures and flashes of saturated color.

Some passages appear almost sculptural, with layers of pigment rising from the surface, while others dissolve into loose, rhythmic patterns that seem to vibrate and shift before the viewer's eyes. Prices range from $150,000 to $400,000.

The presentation also anticipates a significant moment in the artist’s career: a major 60-year retrospective at the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, opening March 2027.

issues.title: Aiza Ahmed wins the inaugural Artsy Vanguard Acquisition Prize with the Brooklyn Museum.
issues.summary: Artsy and the Brooklyn Museum announced Aiza Ahmed today as the winner of the inaugural Artsy Vanguard Acquisition Prize, selected from the 10 emerging artists featured in The Artsy Vanguard 2027 . A trio of her cut-out sculptures on wood— Ananta (2024), Ganguly (2024), and Lamaan (2026)—will enter the Brooklyn Museum’s permanent collection, marking her first acquisition by a New York museum. The
issues.author: Katie White
issues.content_html:
Artsy and the Brooklyn Museum announced Aiza Ahmed today as the winner of the inaugural Artsy Vanguard Acquisition Prize, selected from the 10 emerging artists featured in The Artsy Vanguard 2027. A trio of her cut-out sculptures on wood—Ananta (2024), Ganguly (2024), and Lamaan (2026)—will enter the Brooklyn Museum’s permanent collection, marking her first acquisition by a New York museum.

The prize, new this year, was made possible through the support of Sayoko and David Teitelbaum and judged by a four-person jury: Anne Pasternak, the director of the Brooklyn Museum; Adam D. Weinberg, director emeritus of the Whitney Museum of American Art; Glenn Fuhrman, founder of The FLAG Art Foundation; and producer and collector Kasseem “Swizz Beatz” Dean.

“Aiza Ahmed is an exciting and ambitious artistic voice whose originality and command of materials stood out to the jury,” Pasternak said. “We are thrilled to bring her work into the Brooklyn Museum collection, where it will inspire new conversations with audiences. This prize reflects our commitment to championing artists whose work is shaping the future of contemporary art.” Weinberg, in a statement, pointed to the range of Ahmed’s work. “Aiza Ahmed’s art moves with boundless, unruly freedom, yet every material and subject is handled with remarkable control. Rooted in history, tradition, personal memory, and the visual languages of drawing, theater, and film, her work builds a rich and layered world,” he said.

Ahmed said of the recognition, “To be included in The Artsy Vanguard 2027 alongside such extraordinary artists already felt like a gift, and to then be chosen for this prize is truly humbling.” She added: “The Brooklyn Museum is one of my favorite museums in the world, and to have my work enter its collection as my first New York acquisition is an absolute honor. I am so grateful to Artsy, the esteemed jury, the Brooklyn Museum, and Sayoko and David Teitelbaum for believing in my work. This recognition strengthens my confidence to keep making, growing, and pushing my practice further.”

How to build a man, 2026
Aiza Ahmed
Nature Morte

Born in Lahore, Pakistan, and based in New York, Ahmed works across painting, drawing, sculpture, installation, and video, tracing borders, migrations, and private and public histories of the Indian subcontinent. Her grandparents left Calcutta in India for Pakistan after the 1947 Partition, a history she has described as central to her practice. Her figures begin as blind-contour drawings, made without looking down at the page, before developing into paintings, carved wood sculptures, and textile installations.

Her work also probes ideas of masculinity, from men who project power to those compelled to perform it. During a recent residency at Doha’s Fire Station in Qatar, Ahmed found herself drawn to the men she encountered around the city’s waterfront, from boatmen to Uber drivers. “I was noticing a very different kind of masculinity that was more tender, that was soft, something that I hadn't experienced before,” she told Artsy.

Ahmed’s recent institutional recognition has moved quickly. Her work has been acquired by ICA Miami, Qatar Museums, and the Pérez Art Museum Miami, and in February 2026 she presented a solo booth at the inaugural Art Basel Qatar with Sargent's Daughters, where she was the fair’s youngest artist with a solo presentation. She also showed with Nature Morte at Frieze London 2026, in a presentation curated by Habda Rashid of the Fitzwilliam Museum, University of Cambridge.

Where's The Cake?, 2021
Aiza Ahmed
Aicon Contemporary

Ahmed made her New York solo debut in fall 2025 with “The Music Room” at Sargent’s Daughters, a show inspired by Satyajit Ray’s 1958 film of the same name. Upcoming projects include a solo exhibition at MASSIMODECARLO’s Pièce Unique space in Paris and a show in Doha as part of Fire Station’s inaugural Artists Intensive Study Program, curated by artist Wael Shawky.

Now in its ninth year, The Artsy Vanguard spotlights 10 artists defining what’s next in contemporary art, selected this year from more than 900 nominations. The 2027 artists also include Sammi Lynch, Donyel Ivy-Royal, Mmangaliso Nzuza, Danielle Fretwell, Diambe, Leon Xu, Maddy Inez, Xolo Cuintle, and Tania Franco Klein.
