issues.title: The scientists fighting to help Maui wildfire survivors heal
issues.summary: A wildfire exposure study in Hawaiʻi created a new blueprint for public health research and support after disasters — but funding was drying up. Could the organizers keep it afloat?
issues.author: Keerti Gopal
issues.content_html:
Early on a Saturday morning in May, Ruben Juarez took the 45-minute flight from Oʻahu to Maui, just like he’d done dozens of times over the past three years.

This one felt different.

Juarez landed in Kahului Airport with his partner, Alika Maunakea, and drove on a long winding highway beside the piercing blue ocean until they reached the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center.

A cool breeze wafted in from the Pacific less than half a mile below as they set up stations for blood collection, lung function tests, and mental health check-ins, directing a team of Ph.D. students and local healthcare providers. Then they waited for the fire survivors to arrive.

On August 8, 2023, Maui was hit with the deadliest wildfires the U.S. has seen in over a century. They killed at least 102 people, displaced nearly 13,000 residents, and destroyed more than 2,200 buildings. Three years later, just 15 percent have been rebuilt.

Juarez, an economist, and Maunakea, a biomedical scientist, never expected to focus on disaster recovery. But after the fires, they were thrust into the space by the overwhelming scale of need. The two University of Hawaiʻi professors dreamed up the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, as a form of rapid response: an effort to track the impacts of the fires on survivors’ health.

Three years and 2,500 participants later, the study has blossomed into a combination of research and intervention, a web of community organizations working together to give participants not just free testing but also therapy, food assistance, cash support, and help connecting with doctors and insurance. Some even say the study saved their lives.

The researchers hope MauiWES could become a national blueprint for public health response after disasters. Experts across the country are paying attention. One longtime disaster researcher, David Eisenman at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the study’s holistic approach is “singular.”

But critical federal support to keep the effort going for at least a decade was running out, and its renewal was uncertain — grant applications had been met with silence for months. And just two weeks before Juarez and Maunakea landed on Maui, state funding they were counting on fell through.

Now, here they were at what might be their last big event to understand how survivors were doing and what help they needed.

Juarez was distraught: It felt like the end. But Maunakea, usually the pessimist of the pair, refused to believe it. He felt the study had to continue. The need was too great. They would find a way.

At the health center that Saturday morning, Maunakea greeted Lisa and Nilsson Panis, a pair of siblings born and raised in Lahaina. As he checked them into the study, he explained what they’d do that day. Urine samples to track environmental exposures. Saliva collection for biomarkers of stress and aging. Blood tests for metabolic function. Two assessments of lung health. Recordings of blood pressure, height, and weight. A mental health screener.

At the end of it all, they’d meet with a volunteer physician who would help them understand their test results, and they’d each walk away with $100, compensation for their time.

“We’re trying to do this every year,” Maunakea told the Panises.

He was determined to make that happen.

The lobby of the health center had a dark stain on its ceiling where water had leaked in just a month before.

The building — run by the state’s Department of Health and loaned to MauiWES for the weekend — sits near the base of the sprawling West Maui mountains. That weekend, the foothills above the center were covered in dry, yellowing grass that was nonetheless much greener than usual, courtesy of recent Kona low storms.

The storms swept water damage into construction sites and homes that had just been rebuilt. They busted up highways and caused torrential flooding, triggering millions of dollars in damage across the county. They also kicked off an unusually verdant spring, with flowers blooming on the trees outside the center and along the highway below. Wetness that early can heighten the fire risk later in the year, fueling grass and brush growth that dries out and becomes plentiful tinder, susceptible to heat and strong winds.

Lisa Panis had an appointment with MauiWES that day, but she was hoping they’d have room for her older brother, too. In a fluorescently lit room just beside the center’s main lobby, she introduced Nilsson to Maunakea and explained that he had been a first responder after the wildfires, cleaning up debris in the burn zone. Maunakea immediately instructed the Ph.D. students working the check-in desk to sign him up, along with Nilsson’s girlfriend, another survivor.

MauiWES had limited resources, especially with funding so up in the air. But on an island already suffering from a severe healthcare provider shortage, Maunakea and Juarez didn’t like turning anyone away.

Maunakea listened to Nilsson explain what his life looked like in the months after the fires:12-hour days, seven days a week, clearing the burn zone for a construction company. He wore full-body gear to keep as much of the dust out as possible, but he still ended each day coated in grime. Though he’d never been tested, Nilsson felt confident the constant inhalation of ash and the debris that covered his body as he worked had impacted his health.

“We tried to push all the dust down with water,” Nilsson said to Maunakea, describing the cleanup. “But you cannot get everything.”

“Are you still doing that, or pau?” Maunakea asked.

“Pau,” Nilsson replied. Finished. Now he was working as a mason, bringing his sister on whenever he could. It wasn’t steady. He hoped jobs would pick up in the summer.

The Panis siblings’ father is descended from Filipino immigrants who came to the island to work on the sugar plantations more than a century ago, during a period when American and European companies brought indentured laborers from the Philippines to work under brutal conditions for extremely low pay. The plantations, established before Hawaiʻi’s illegal annexation by the United States and continuing another century after, sucked water out of Lahaina’s once green and fertile hills.

That set the stage for modern-day wildfire risks, now worsened by climate change, and cemented a pattern of local disenfranchisement that continued as the tourism industry took hold.

For years, the Panises had experienced the harder realities of life in Lahaina, like gentrification and unstable housing and employment. On the day of the fires, Nilsson was meant to fly back from Las Vegas to spread the ashes of two siblings who had passed away just weeks apart that spring. Lisa was living with an aunt whose home would not survive. She remembers standing on the field next to the post office where she and her brothers played football as kids, watching as flames engulfed the town above and below her.

After they finished checking into the study, the Panis siblings moved through the stations, a sort of medical assembly line: urine samples, then blood tests, then blood pressure, then spitting into a tube. A few feet away, Juarez coached another participant on how to blow into a spirometer to test lung function.

“Sigue, sigue, sigue,” he said, reminding the man to keep breathing out. Throughout the day Juarez greeted Spanish-speaking participants, acting as one of a handful of interpreters who walked people through the study’s tests in English, Spanish, and Tagalog.

Juarez was pulled into Maui’s recovery because of his connections to Lahaina’s abundant immigrant community. One-third of Lahaina residents were born outside the U.S., many in Asia or Latin America. Juarez moved from Mexico to Houston for a doctorate at Rice University, then to Oʻahu for a job at the University of Hawaiʻi. There, he met Maunakea, and as neighbors in the university’s faculty housing, they fell in love.

When they met, Juarez’s research was focused on social networks and Maunakea’s on health disparities in disease. After the fires, Maunakea was drawn to Maui by his connections with people working to address the disproportionate public health burdens faced by Native Hawaiians across the islands. Although he lives on Oʻahu, his great-grandmother, a Native Hawaiian healer, was born in Kula, an upcountry Maui community that was also badly impacted by the 2023 fires.

He and Juarez met with community leaders and healthcare workers on Maui soon after the fires. They became part of the MauiWES advisory board, consulting on design and implementation. For many study participants, that grounding made a big difference.

Mikey Burke, a Native Hawaiian mother of four who grew up in West Maui, remembers an influx of mental health practitioners from the continent who swarmed to Maui after the fires. They roamed the lobbies of hotels where she and other displaced families were sheltered. But though they were well-intentioned, they felt largely unapproachable. She gravitated toward local organizations like Maui Medic Healers Hui, which was working with MauiWES. It was something in their mannerisms, the way they spoke to her, the normalcy and familiarity they offered.

In the months after they lost their home, Burke, her husband Rob, and their four young sons were shuttled between temporary shelters, family homes, and rental properties. She could see that her twin boys, just 8 years old when the fires hit, were struggling. But it wasn’t until they got screened by MauiWES that addressing their mental health shot to the top of her lengthy to-do list. The study team told her that both boys were showing serious signs of post-traumatic stress disorder, and got them connected with a free therapist right away.

The Burkes aren’t an anomaly. The study found widespread emotional distress and trauma in adults and children, and connected many with therapists.

On an island with a severe shortage of physicians, MauiWES was also most early participants’ first time seeing a doctor after the fires. Over the past three years, the team made some big saves.

In August 2024, one year after the fires, a former trauma nurse named Amy Jackson had such a low hemoglobin count that it wasn’t registering on MauiWES’ testing system. The team urged her to go to the emergency room immediately. Jackson had signed up for the study because the cash would be a good birthday present for her daughter. If it wasn’t for that, she wouldn’t have gotten checked out at all.

At the hospital, she remembers a doctor telling her he was amazed she was still alive. She was admitted and treated, and she credits MauiWES with saving her life.

In February 2024, another participant presented with symptoms suggesting a serious lung infection. Volunteer physicians were concerned and said she needed medical attention right away. But she was an undocumented immigrant and one of the 10 percent of study participants who had both lost their jobs in the fire and weren’t eligible for state insurance.

Juarez coordinated with Roots Reborn — a local organization supporting Maui’s immigrant community — and reached out the next day to ask an insurer with a charitable health coverage program to consider an emergency enrollment.

She got the insurance and then the treatment she needed. She’s one of more than 200 participants Juarez estimates have been connected with private insurance via Kaiser Permanente because of interventions from MauiWES and Roots Reborn. He was happy to see her now, in good spirits and good health, coming in for her follow-up at the May collection event. He thought the immigrant population had the most to lose from the study ending.

The team still had so much to do.

After her lung test, Lisa Panis stood underneath the stain on the lobby’s ceiling and waited for her brother. The Panis siblings stay strong for one another. But she’s experienced depression since the fires, like many other survivors, and her tests revealed elevated levels of several toxic metals in her body.

In their first, smallest cohort, about six months after the fires, Juarez, Maunakea, and their colleagues found that about half of study participants were experiencing breathing problems that suggested ongoing, residual impacts from wildfire smoke. They’ve also found that poor lung function was linked to elevated levels of heavy metals in participants’ urine, including some of the same metals the health department found in the burn zone.

After looking at so many test results, Maunakea can guess with considerable accuracy what neighborhood a participant lives in just by seeing the distribution of metals in their body. Some of that contamination may predate the fires. But the health implications are the same.

Before Nilsson Panis left for the day, Juarez gave him a T-shirt with the MauiWES logo — a sun rising behind the island — and a hundred-dollar bill. Then he ushered him over to the front desk, where a case manager who works for the Department of Health was waiting.

She asked Nilsson if there was anything he might need help with.

He paused for a moment before answering. Maybe some assistance with food, he said. He also asked about opportunities to volunteer and help other survivors.

The case manager took down his email.

The next day Maunakea supervised a group of staff and volunteers administering lung function tests. A participant wearing a neon-yellow baseball hat and flower-patterned shorts walked in and took a seat.

“It’s unfortunate that you guys didn’t get more additional funding from the legislative session this time,” Ekolu Lindsey said to Maunakea as he took a break from breathing hard into a plastic mouthpiece.

It had been MauiWES’ most recent funding attempt: A bill sponsored by the state senator for West Maui, Angus McKelvey, would have allotted $3 million to keep the study going and expand the number of children it could serve. But at the last minute, the bill failed to make it through.

“I get it, they went for the bigger-ticket items, but the health part is also a big-ticket item that didn’t take precedence,” continued Lindsey, who is the president of a grassroots land trust organization on Maui. “I don’t think they understood, because probably none of them went through it.”

Maunakea agreed. He had thought that public health would be more of a priority in the wildfire recovery, especially in a state with a doctor as a governor. But funding MauiWES has been an ongoing challenge.

The study’s first cohort, in early 2024, began with charitable funding from the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation and Kaiser Permanente, while the researchers pursued government support. That summer, they got $2.3 million from the state. And almost one year after the fires, they received a $1.4 million grant from the National Institutes of Health’s minority health disparities program.

That support quickly turned precarious after Donald Trump retook office and slashed funding for programs focused on diversity or health disparities, along with a wide swath of academic research.

The MauiWES researchers hoped to renew their federal funding and keep the study going for at least a decade. But heading into the May event, applications they submitted to the agency had been languishing without a decision for more than a year. By that time, the NIH had lost 23 percent of its staff under the Trump administration, almost double the reduction across the entire federal government, according to an analysis by Inside Climate News.

The MauiWES researchers started getting national recognition in the disaster recovery space, speaking on panels and presenting at conferences on the mainland, hoping that might drum up more cash. But private funding wasn’t enough to keep the study going, and the speaking engagements had yet to pay off. More state funding seemed like Juarez and Maunakea’s best hope.

Initially, the team had strong backing from the state’s Department of Health, which wrote enthusiastic letters of support for federal grants. But as the study progressed and the researchers began publicizing their results, the agency pushed back.

The Department of Health had earlier screened 557 West Maui residents for lead in their blood, saying in May 2024 that so few had elevated levels that it was not necessary to screen the general population for toxic substances identified in the burn zone.

“On the basis of these results with lead as an indicator of exposure, we do not expect to find health impacts caused by toxins in the wildfire ash,” agency director Kenneth Fink said in a statement at the time.

But lead is just one of the toxic substances the department found at elevated levels in burn zone ash, and it’s undetectable in people’s blood relatively quickly after exposure, unlike some other substances found in the burn zone. Environmental health experts questioned why the department used a limited sampling of lead to draw broad conclusions about the burn zone as a whole.

Then MauiWES found elevated levels of heavy metals associated with heart and lung issues and cancer risks in a cohort of more than 1,200 fire survivors.

The findings seemed to contradict the Department of Health’s assertion that the burn zone was safe. Emails and letters Inside Climate News obtained through public records requests suggest that agency staff quickly moved into damage-control mode.

The day after Honolulu Civil Beat published a story about the preliminary findings last year, a naturopathic doctor on Maui emailed state toxicologist John Jacob for information about the effects of heavy metals like arsenic, nickel , cadmium, mercury, and lead on psychological function. Her clients had been tested by MauiWES and registered high levels of those metals, she wrote.

Jacob forwarded the email to colleagues at the Department of Health.

“I don’t want to affirm what UH is stating,” he wrote, referring to the University of Hawaiʻi. “The panic has begun!”

A few days later, agency staff discussed whether to stop assisting MauiWES with data collection. Fink, the director, said staff could continue for now, but he felt the department’s recommendations on study design had been either inadequate or disregarded. “If the latter, I would need to reevaluate our involvement,” Fink wrote to colleagues.

In October, the Department of Health sent a letter to the University of Hawaiʻi, criticizing MauiWES’ reliance on sampling survivors who showed up — as opposed to a randomized cohort — and its findings of elevated heavy metals in their urine.

Read Next Long after the Maui fires, toxic metals linger in residents’ bodies Joseph Lee

The university defended the research in its response and explained that MauiWES was not claiming a definitively causal relationship between the fires and the heavy metals.

Although the team remained committed to working with the state, Juarez said he saw the Department of Health’s letter as an attempt to censor their research. Academics not involved with MauiWES told Inside Climate News the exchange seemed unusual for a university and a state agency, and they did not think the health department’s dismissal of burn-zone dangers was warranted based on the limited information it had collected.

The agency’s director said in a statement to Inside Climate News that discussions about the best way to approach research “are a normal and healthy — and often essential — aspect of scientific collaboration.”

“While our perspectives may differ, both DOH and UH remain committed to respectful dialogue and evidence‑based inquiry,” Fink wrote in his statement. “Most importantly, the public needs clear, accurate, and consistent information about how the wildfires may have affected their health. Residents deserve timely communication they can trust — free of speculation and grounded in the best available data.”

In an emailed statement to Inside Climate News, Jacob acknowledged that the researchers’ approach was acceptable but said that not disclosing limitations could “result in confusion among the general public.”

In defense of the agency’s own approach to quantifying post-wildfire health risks, a department spokesperson said in an email that a structured soil sampling technique allowed staff to use the lead screening as a “reasonable indicator for population exposure.”

In internal emails in January, agency staff discussed a bill with funds earmarked to keep MauiWES alive. They agreed to keep a close watch on the effort. “Especially since we are not satisfied with their science,” wrote Jacob, the toxicologist.

In the end, a department subagency was among those submitting testimony in support of the funding. But that wasn’t enough to push it through. When the bill fell short with still no word on federal money, it looked like the end of MauiWES.

At nearly 5 p.m. on Sunday, the team packed up while finishing tests for the last few stragglers. Most of the staff and volunteers had to catch a flight back to Oʻahu in a couple of hours, but Christopher Knightsbridge, a therapist working on the study’s research team, would stay on Maui a few more days to see patients in person.

Knightsbridge was overcome with pure frustration. All weekend, he’d done mental health check-ins with participants still focused on getting by, day by day. He felt certain the study was having an impact. He saw it every week. And he was still concerned about what he’d been hearing in his sessions. He wanted his patients to wake up and feel like they were living, not simply fighting to survive. For that, they needed more support, not less.

Knightsbridge poured everything he had into supporting survivors’ mental health in recovery. He spent half of most weeks away from his wife and young children on Oʻahu to see patients still dealing with ongoing crises: survivors in temporary housing and unstable employment, people with cancer diagnoses, young children whose lives were turned upside down by the fires. He’s seen serious PTSD symptoms, depression, and even suicidal ideation from kids as young as 6.

That same week, he sat in his video gaming group for kids at the health center with two of Mikey and Rob Burke’s sons, the twins dealing with PTSD. Knightsbridge was seeing both boys for therapy and organized the gaming group as another form of support, a low-stakes place for kids to open up. But the federal emergency grant supporting his position — separate from MauiWES’s funding — was also about to run out.

Read Next First came the wildfire. Then came the scams. Naveena Sadasivam

On the other side of the lobby, Juarez stood in a doorway, gutted. The study had made painfully apparent the gaps in healthcare access on the island, and it felt like their work was just beginning. The thought brought him to the brink of tears. Throughout the weekend, he heard from worried participants who asked if the study was going away. He didn’t want to let them down.

Near the entrance to the courtyard, Maunakea carried a table from the hallway back into one of the offices, tired but heartened by how many people had come through. Sitting with returning participants, learning about their recovery journeys and watching how they were putting the pieces back together was energizing for him. Healing is a communal task in Lahaina. The study leaned into that.

Maunakea knew the next disaster was just around the corner. He believed Maui could adapt and offer a model to the rest of the world for building resilience to the steep challenges climate change brings.

Maybe, he thought, that would be the ultimate lesson from the study: that documenting and addressing health inequities in the wake of a disaster helps communities withstand what they cannot escape.

Toward the end of the day, more survivors arrived without appointments after hearing about the study from family and friends. By closing, he estimated the team had turned away more than a dozen new people, taking down their names in case funding came through. Maunakea met people that weekend who said they’d known about the study for several years but hadn’t felt ready to participate until now. It hammered home to him how crucial it was for their work to go on.

The team would find a way to continue the study, Maunakea felt certain. He didn’t know how, but he saw no other choice. If his great-grandmother was alive, she would have said: ‘O ka pono ke hana ‘ia a iho mai nā lani. Continue to do good until the heavens come down to you.

He believed that this study is pono, and that the community wanted and needed this service. So, somehow, iho mai nā lani. The heavens would come down.

Inside Climate News’ Peter Aldhous contributed to this story.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline The scientists fighting to help Maui wildfire survivors heal on Nov 14, 2026.

issues.title: Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action
issues.summary: As climate disasters mount, Indigenous advocates are pushing governments to follow through on commitments made at previous global climate summits.
issues.author: Joseph Lee
issues.content_html:
The annual United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change gathering drew historic levels of Indigenous attendance in Belém, Brazil last year, leading some to dub it “the Indigenous COP.” But the event was marked by frustration and protest, with many Indigenous leaders calling it little more than a continuation of a longstanding pattern of exclusion from international negotiations.

This year’s gathering in Antalya, Turkey, is billed as an “implementation” conference focused less on sweeping new pledges than on the procedural work of turning previous agreements into action. For Indigenous advocates, that makes COP31, which started November 9, a test of whether the promises made last year translate into tangible changes, including greater authority over climate action.

“It is still a struggle,” said Edward Porokwa, who is Maasai and a member of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. “I’m yet to really determine whether there will be any more progress that is made in terms of realization of the rights of Indigenous people.”

Indigenous advocates are pressing governments to follow through on their commitments to secure and strengthen Indigenous land rights on 400 million acres in tropical forest countries, provide $1.8 billion in funding, and respect rights to free, prior, and informed consent in the energy transition.

Despite those pledges, funds have been slow to reach affected communities and Indigenous land defenders say their rights and lives remain under constant threat. Porokwa said that he feels that responsibility to address climate change continues to fall on smaller countries and Indigenous peoples.

The stakes have been particularly stark over the last year. In Nepal, massive floods and landslides in August killed more than 1,500 people and destroyed entire villages. In Canada, a historic wildfire season saw millions of acres burned, causing thousands of evacuations. And in Indonesia, wildfire smoke alone has caused thousands of deaths and led to school closures and other emergency measures across Southeast Asia.

“The recent large-scale mountainside collapse on the border of Nepal and Tibet should serve as a wake-up call to the global community,” said Biswash Chepang, who is a founder of the Institute for Indigenous Affairs and Development in Nepal.

Climate-driven threats to Indigenous peoples and their lands continue to mount as a historically powerful El Niño threatens to drive famine, heat-related deaths, and other catastrophes across the globe.

Read Next DOGE cuts cost tribes $470M, gutting funding for climate projects Joseph Lee

The conference comes in the wake of a recent United Nations report that said it will be virtually impossible to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees, the goal set under the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement. Indigenous delegates find that reality particularly frustrating because they see it as a direct result of decision makers ignoring their knowledge and all the ways their stewardship has been proven to benefit the environment and climate.

“For over 30 years we have brought Indigenous knowledges and sciences to these negotiations,” Māori activist Quack Pirihi said in an opening statement on behalf of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. “Yet emissions continue to rise, putting 1.5 degrees C beyond reach.”

While the work of reducing emissions and protecting Indigenous rights in the energy transition continues, securing funding for nations and communities most impacted by climate disasters is also a priority. In October, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage approved $21.6 million for Nepal — its first disbursement and less than 1 percent of the nearly $5 billion in damage the country sustained. But the process to receive and administer those funds is ongoing, and Indigenous leaders say the fund must work faster. Their push comes as wealthy countries face renewed scrutiny over climate-finance pledges they have failed to deliver.

“Loss and damage is not simply a question of humanitarian assistance,” Chepang said. “It is also a question of climate responsibility, historical emissions, equity, and the right of affected communities to recover with dignity.”

Indigenous peoples also hope to hold polluters to account. Bianca Ranson, who is Māori and a board member of the Aotearoa Climate Action Network, is attending COP31 in part to highlight the landmark climate case her father Mike Smith led against major emitters in New Zealand. The case, which uses Māori customary law, has been blocked by the national government.

Despite the logistical, financial, and political hurdles of attending an event like COP, Ranson said there is value in global spaces. “I think that with the geopolitical moment that we’re in, with the rise of the far right and fascism and war, and the struggles that Indigenous peoples are facing across the globe, it’s a really important place for us to be able to come together to connect, to strengthen our solidarity,” Ranson said.

As negotiations continue through November 20, Indigenous advocates will continue their push for all the discussions to lead to tangible actions. “Now I think it is not time only to talk about the commitment,” Porokwa said. “It is time to change the commitment into practice.”

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action on Nov 13, 2026.

issues.title: The affordability election delivered billions for public transit
issues.summary: For a wide swath of voters, transit funding doesn’t compete with affordability concerns. It’s part of the answer.
issues.author: Benton Graham
issues.content_html:
In an election dominated by concerns about affordability, voters across the country overwhelmingly agreed to raise taxes to preserve or expand public transit.

Out of 27 ballot measures supporting transit, 22 passed on November 3, representing $27.4 billion in funding to rescue faltering systems and expand or build new ones. Some of the biggest wins of the night included voters in the San Francisco Bay Area staving off enormous cuts to Bay Area Rapid Transit and other regional systems, Coloradans backing new regional rail, and residents of Seattle and nearby Pierce County favoring expanded bus service.

“It’s an indication that the public is willing to pay for these public transit improvements,” said Sohail Husain, a policy analyst at the Eno Center for Transportation. “That’s very telling –– especially in a world like today where people are concerned about affordability. I think people are still also concerned about mobility and having options to move.”

Public transit has now fared well in the red wave of 2024 — when 19 out of 25 measures supporting transit passed — and this year’s blue wave. Although few candidates campaigned on the issue, the results could significantly alter policy. At the state level, transit advocates see opportunities to advance projects or simply get the government out of the way. Meanwhile, a Democratic majority in Congress will shape a major transportation infrastructure law that is up for renewal. Together, the results could remake how Americans get around.

States have broad discretion to fund transportation as they see fit, which is why Democratic wins in red states and Democratic control of the governorship and both legislative chambers in 22 states have many public transit advocates excited about what comes next.

Pennsylvania is one of those states. It has endured a bitter battle over the finances of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, which serves the Philadelphia area. When the agency faced 45 percent service cuts last year, Governor Josh Shapiro directed the state Department of Transportation to allow the agency to shift nearly $400 million from its capital to operational budget. He also made another $220 million available to the system.

Now, with Democrats taking control of both chambers of the state legislature, transit advocates say SEPTA can look beyond self-preservation. Stephen Bronskill of Transit Forward Philadelphia pointed to projects including trolley modernization, new fleets to replace vehicles from the 1970s, more frequent regional rail service, and fully accessible stations.

“This is a once-in-a-generation moment to invest in public transit –– safe, reliable, accessible transit that Philly needs, but all of Pennsylvania deserves,” he said.

The prospects are less straightforward in Texas, where Republicans still control the Senate. Jay Blazek Crossley, executive director of Farm&City, a nonprofit focused in part on road safety, has spent more than a decade trying to nudge GOP lawmakers toward less violent and less polluting transportation options. Every legislative session has seen him unsuccessfully push legislation that would make it easier for cities to reduce speed limits on residential streets. He sees new hope for that measure and, more broadly, a future that might include additional public transit funding, which accounts for just 0.72 percent of the transportation department’s budget. State Republicans have generally been more interested in moving more cars more quickly, primarily by building bigger highways, while pushing back against some city-led public transit efforts.

“At the very least, the state, I believe, will get out of the way on things like building good light rail and transit,” he said.

There’s hope for bigger projects too. State Representative John Bucy III has again filed legislation directing the Texas Department of Transportation to find a public-private partnership for a high-speed rail line linking Dallas and San Antonio. He believes the bill will appeal to lawmakers whose constituents would benefit from an alternative to driving on the heavily congested Interstate 35 corridor.

“I think the voters spoke loud and clear that they want a Texas government that is going to work on kitchen table issues,” he said. “I think that’s healthcare, education. It’s also mobility and transit, and how do we get around this big, vast state?”

Read Next Brightline shows people want more trains. But who will pay for them? Benton Graham

Georgia is another state where Democrats took the governorship and flipped the House, but Republicans still control the Senate. That could be a challenge for Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who has called for dedicated state funding for the Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority and other systems that have historically relied heavily on local and federal support.

The election could have even greater implications at the federal level, where Congress must soon decide how much spending to allocate to transit and passenger rail. The BUILD America 250 Act passed out of a key House commitee with bipartisan support in May, but left public transit advocates concerned about funding cuts. With Democrats taking control of Congress, the legislation is likely to look different. Representative Jerry Nadler of New York, the lone Democrat on the committee to oppose advancing the legislation, sees an opportunity to change its direction.

“Unlike the current Republican proposal, next year’s bill should not prioritize one mode of transportation at the expense of others. This bill must make robust investments in rail and public transit, to connect communities, create good-paying jobs, lower transportation costs for families, and reduce the cost of moving goods across the country,” he said in a statement.

But rewriting the bill won’t necessarily happen quickly. Rebecca Higgins, the Eno Center for Transportation’s vice president of policy, said lawmakers will face some urgency because Congress is already relying on an extension to fund transportation. At the same time, she expects lawmakers to give their newly elected colleagues a chance to weigh in. One major question is what happens to money for intercity passenger rail that was included in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act but dropped from BUILD America 250.

Whatever happens in Washington, the local and regional measures voters approved will have a more immediate impact. In the Bay Area, a 14-year regional sales tax is expected to raise about $1 billion annually to preserve service on BART and other systems that had been facing steep budget shortfalls. Colorado voters approved a 0.333 percent sales tax to build, operate, and maintain passenger rail connecting Pueblo and Colorado Springs with Denver and Fort Collins.

In Seattle, voters doubled an existing sales tax over the next decade, generating an additional $138 million per year largely for transit service. In nearby Pierce County, voters also approved a sales tax increase to expand bus service.

The Pierce County win is particularly notable because voters there hadn’t increased public transit investment since 2002, said Kirk Hovenkotter, the executive director of the Transportation Choices Coalition. The fast-growing region also faces an affordability crisis. The American Public Transportation Association estimates that relying on public transit rather than owning a car can save a household more than $14,000 annually.

Hovenkotter makes a similar argument about the costs facing residents of the Pacific Northweest. “The average cost of car ownership in Washington state is about $12,000,” he said. “The fastest way we can put $12,000 back in someone’s pocket is making it easier for them to live without a car or with one fewer car.”

The election results suggest that, for a wide swath of voters, transit funding isn’t competing with affordability concerns. It’s an answer to them.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline The affordability election delivered billions for public transit on Nov 13, 2026.

issues.title: The cozy radicalism of repair cafés
issues.summary: In church basements and warehouses, Americans are mounting a quiet resistance to throwaway culture.
issues.author: Johnny Kauffman
issues.content_html:
On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with tool boxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.

That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.

“This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus said, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”

This is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café, one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies selling everything from hiking boots, smartphones, and hot water boilers, that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throw-away economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change.

Yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés as more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy.

At the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through.

Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus said. “We are a big family.”

The newlyweds settled on a simple table and six chairs — two “host style” with arms, four without — from the local Ethan Allen store. The furniture came to feel more like home than the many houses where Pettus, her husband, and their children lived. They moved the table and chairs with them from Florida to Connecticut, then to Indiana, Michigan, Texas, and finally to Georgia. “ I don’t know anyone’s chairs that I like more than my own,” Pettus said.

But after absorbing shakes of laughter during countless games of Hearts, and fidgets of anxiety at family meetings about upcoming moves, one of the chair’s joints finally cracked. “We had the chair just sitting in the corner,” Pettus said, “but no one actually sat in it.” She didn’t know how to fix the chair, but if she sent it to a landfill that would mean trashing a reminder of her fondest memories from the last 30 years.

Pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house, Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair, and decided to give it a second chance.

“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely,” said Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a new item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.”

Postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future. “Markets are flooded with trash — with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma said. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.”

Repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste — the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft — according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families.

Postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair.

Read Next Discarded toys are creating an e-waste disaster. Here’s how to stop it. Maddie Stone

In 2023, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and New York passed “right to repair” legislation meant to encourage repair over replacement. A year later the European Union passed a similar directive. Postma and other organizers consider the cafés a natural place for activism to push for right-to-repair measures, although Postma hopes for more sweeping changes in Europe, like a tax on raw materials. She argued it would limit emissions and bolster repair shops, even if it increases the cost of products.

“ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken,” she said.“I want to make repairing a normal thing in everyday life once more.”

According to Postma, repairing goods is more common in relatively poor countries where replacing them can be especially difficult and expensive. It’s in wealthy countries that repair cafés are thriving, but they’re not at all uniform. Each reflects the surrounding area and its socioeconomics.

On a Sunday afternoon in the Collier Heights neighborhood of Atlanta, volunteers brought most of their own tools to the basement of a building owned by a Seventh Day Adventist Church, setting them on white plastic folding tables atop a light pink carpet. The café looked much different from the one a 30-minute drive across the city in Decatur. The median annual household income in the mostly Black Collier Heights neighborhood is roughly $40,000 lower than in Decatur. Many people who brought items wanted them fixed less for sentimental reasons, and more so they could keep using them.

Gale Pines walked in with a red air fryer that stopped working after they used it to dehydrate ginger. When their oven ran, Pines said, it heated the entire kitchen. So, while in nursing school, they cooked many of their evening meals in the air fryer, most often chicken nuggets and fries.

Pines recently graduated, but had trouble finding a job and couldn’t afford to buy a new $100 air fryer. “It’s just hard to exist,” Pines said. “I don’t really have a very big support network outside of my friends.”

One of Pines’ housemates told them about Collier Heights’ repair café. They keep a bag of broken electronics in the garage that they’d prefer not to send to a landfill. “Being in the height of climate collapse we can’t just keep buying new stuff all the time, both for the economy and for our material scarcity,” Pines said.

When a volunteer at the Collier Heights repair café opened up the airfryer, they quickly discovered the problem: a bad capacitor. Another volunteer had brought a replacement part, and the two of them made the fix as Pines watched, impressed, but unable to follow the relatively complex repair. Pines felt OK that they hadn’t learned how to fix the air fryer themself.

“ To just be around people that want to help other people with the skills that they have, that’s value that is really important to me, and something that I try to do as well,” Pines said. “If somebody in my community has a question about their medication or something and can’t afford to go to the doctor, I’m happy to answer any questions that people have.”

Another volunteer, Lew Lefton, said he thought that the satisfaction humans draw from making and fixing things has largely been lost, but apocalyptic threats like climate change and artificial intelligence have driven many people toward rediscovering more basic, human skills that are key to survival. People who come to a repair café have a different way to view the future, according to Lefton, especially if they learn something or volunteer themselves. “If the world ends” he said, “at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.”

Back in Decatur, Pettus left the repair café with a newly sturdy chair. A screw and some glue fixed the crack around the joint, but the chair still needed upholstery work. Someone Pettus met at the café, who had provided one of the sets of hands that held her chair together as the glue set, advised her on where to buy fabric. Pettus thought she might bring the chair back to the repair café for help reupholstering its seat cushion.

“The beauty of it,” Pettus said, “was that I actually was able to learn more about the chair. It was a great experience to know that — I’m not gonna say I birthed it, I of course did not — but I actually had something to do with helping to get it put back together.”

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline The cozy radicalism of repair cafés on Nov 13, 2026.

issues.title: Targeted by al-Shabaab for defending Kenya’s ecosystems: Foundation founder gets award
issues.summary: Conservation is rarely conflict-free. On Kenya’s northern coastline, in Lamu and Tana River counties — a biodiversity hotspot where the nation’s longest river meets the Indian Ocean — the work of protecting marine and terrestrial habitats often takes a willingness to challenge industrial fishing and extractive industries. For Raabia Hawa, defending nature against these activities […]
issues.author: Anita Makri
issues.content_html: Conservation is rarely conflict-free. On Kenya’s northern coastline, in Lamu and Tana River counties — a biodiversity hotspot where the nation’s longest river meets the Indian Ocean — the work of protecting marine and terrestrial habitats often takes a willingness to challenge industrial fishing and extractive industries. For Raabia Hawa, defending nature against these activities has meant operating in areas largely neglected by official conservation bodies. A former broadcast journalist and Montessori teacher turned environmental defender, Hawa founded the Ulinzi Africa Foundation (“Ulinzi” means the defenders in Swahili) in 2014 to provide frontline ranger patrols against elephant poaching and wildlife crime. Her work has since expanded beyond anti-poaching to combat illegal industrial bottom-trawling and empower local communities resisting extractive mining concessions. Operating near the Somali border comes with high political insecurity. Hawa’s vocal stance against environmental destruction has come at a personal risk, including death threats and being designated a target by the militant group al-Shabaab. Despite these perils, Ulinzi has continued to operate on a shoestring, powered by volunteer family support. In London to receive the 2026 Tusk Award for Conservation in Africa — which provides Ulinzi with three years of critical funding — Hawa spoke with Mongabay about the realities of countering industrial fishing and mobilizing rural women against mining giants, highlighting the disconnect between global biodiversity targets and the daily battles frontline nature defenders fight on the ground. issues.author: Sandy Watt
issues.content_html: On the front line of the human-elephant conflict, coming up with non-lethal methods of protecting crops means getting creative. In one village in Zimbabwe, a multilayered approach is taken – first a fence covered in chili infused rags and chili powder traps, if that fails elephant dung covered in chili oil is set alight, finally as a last resort a makeshift bazooka (powered by a deodorant) fires chili-oil filled ping-pong balls at persistent elephants. The last elephant who took a pingpong ball to the face did not return to the village for over a year.This article was originally published on Mongabay

issues.title: South African court dismisses appeal over planned coal-fired power plants
issues.summary: The South African Supreme Court of Appeal recently dismissed the government’s appeal against a ruling that struck down plans for 1,500 megawatts of new coal-fired power. The so-called #CancelCoal case was brought by a coalition of environmental NGOs that argued the new planned coal capacity violates children’s constitutional rights to a healthy environment. Already, air […]
issues.author: David Brown
issues.content_html: The South African Supreme Court of Appeal recently dismissed the government’s appeal against a ruling that struck down plans for 1,500 megawatts of new coal-fired power. The so-called #CancelCoal case was brought by a coalition of environmental NGOs that argued the new planned coal capacity violates children’s constitutional rights to a healthy environment. Already, air pollution from coal-fired power plants kills more than 2,200 South Africans each year and “causes thousands of cases of bronchitis and asthma,” according to a statement from the Centre for Environmental Rights. The Minister of Electricity and Energy argued that additional coal capacity is necessary for energy security. A previous High Court judgment ruled against the plan “on the basis that it violates the right to an environment not harmful to health and well-being,” per the statement. “The High Court further found that government’s arguments about grid stability offered by coal, was not sufficient justification for the violation of constitutional rights,” said Michelle Sithole in an email to Mongabay. Sithole is senior associate in the pollution and climate change program at the Centre for Environmental Rights, the group that represented the plaintiffs in the court case. The Minister appealed the High Court decision. The recent Court of Appeal’s decision dismissed the Minister’s appeal, meaning the previous High Court decision stands. “While this does not mean a definitive end to the development of new coal-fired power as part of the energy security policy, it does mean that government has a higher onus/standard to justify choosing coal…This article was originally published on Mongabay

issues.title: Honduras declares ‘environmental emergency’ in Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve
issues.summary: Deforestation, organized crime and the expansion of cattle ranching have led the government in Honduras to announce an “environmental emergency” in the Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve, the largest protected area in the country. The 36-month emergency, issued as a presidential decree on Nov. 10, will devote 1.5 billion Honduran lempiras (more than $55 million) over […]
issues.author: Maxwell Radwin
issues.content_html: Deforestation, organized crime and the expansion of cattle ranching have led the government in Honduras to announce an “environmental emergency” in the Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve, the largest protected area in the country. The 36-month emergency, issued as a presidential decree on Nov. 10, will devote 1.5 billion Honduran lempiras (more than $55 million) over the next three years to halt “environmental deterioration,” according to an official statement. “The initiative represents a commitment by the government to move from addressing threats to sustained intervention, with defined resources and institutional responsibilities,” presidential legal advisor Roberto Zacapa said in the statement. The more than 832,000-hectare (2 million-acre) reserve stretches across the departments of Gracias a Dios, Colón and Olancho, and includes numerous Indigenous Miskito, Pech and Garífuna communities. In 1982, a section of it was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The reserve’s remote location along the Nicaraguan border has made it vulnerable to deforestation, drug trafficking, cattle ranching, gold mining, wildlife trafficking, roadbuilding and other illegal activities. At least 6,691 hectares (16,533 acres) of forest were cut down between 2023 and 2025, according to the Forest Conservation Institute (ICF), the agency managing the country’s forests. Since 2011, the reserve has been on UNESCO’s List of World Heritage in Danger, a list of sites facing serious threats to their environmental or cultural heritage. “It’s like the wild west, where there’s no law and people come in and do whatever they want, and the rights of Indigenous communities are violated,” Wildlife Conservation…This article was originally published on Mongabay

issues.title: Texas A&M stock report, from Saturday's loss to Tennessee
issues.summary: Texas A&M's Week 11 Stock Report: After a 22-7 loss to Tennessee, who's rising and who's slipping?
issues.content_html:
Texas A&M suffered another disappointing SEC loss Saturday, falling 22-7 to No. 8 Tennessee at Kyle Field despite a defensive effort that kept the Aggies within striking distance for most of the afternoon.

The Aggies (4-6, 1-6 SEC) entered halftime leading 7-6 after KJ Edwards broke free for a 25-yard touchdown run in the second quarter. However, Texas A&M failed to score again as Tennessee took control in the second half, scoring 16 unanswered points to secure the victory.

Unlike last week's loss to South Carolina, when the Aggies moved the ball but couldn't finish drives, offensive production was a problem from start to finish. Texas A&M struggled to sustain possessions, leaving its defense on the field for extended stretches.

The Volunteers managed just one touchdown, but five field goals were enough to overcome an Aggie offense that never found its rhythm. Several defensive performances and another strong running game offered some encouragement. However, the passing attack continued to struggle, and two late interceptions ended any chance of a comeback.

With two games remaining, Texas A&M's hopes of reaching a bowl game are dwindling away, leaving head coach Mike Elko with difficult decisions about the direction of his offense.

Here is whose stock rose and fell against Tennessee.

Stock up: KJ Edwards

Edwards provided the Aggies' biggest offensive highlight, breaking free for a 25-yard touchdown run that gave Texas A&M a 7-3 lead in the second quarter. The freshman showed his explosiveness when given an opportunity, but the Aggies couldn't consistently get him involved as the offense struggled to sustain drives.

Stats: Seven carries, 44 rushing yards, one touchdown.

Stock up: Tyler White

White continued to be one of Texas A&M's most reliable contributors, helping the Aggies win the field-position battle at times despite their offensive struggles. His punting was particularly valuable in the first half, including a 62-yard kick that pinned Tennessee at its own 4-yard line. With the offense repeatedly going three-and-out, White was once again asked to do more than his share of the work.

Stats: Highlighted by a 62-yard punt that pinned Tennessee inside its own 5-yard line.

Stock up: Texas A&M defense

The defense deserved a better outcome after holding one of the nation's top-ranked teams to a single touchdown. Tennessee repeatedly reached scoring position but struggled to finish drives, settling for five field goals. The Aggies also held the Volunteers to nine points through three quarters, giving the offense several opportunities to take control of the game.

Stats: One touchdown allowed, five Tennessee field goals, nine points allowed through three quarters.

Stock down: Marcel Reed

Reed's struggles continued against Tennessee, as the sophomore quarterback failed to generate much through the air. The passing attack rarely threatened the Volunteers' defense, and Reed couldn't establish any consistency when Texas A&M needed to move the chains.

His fourth-quarter interception was particularly costly, giving Tennessee possession deep in Aggie territory and setting up another field goal that effectively ended the game.

Stats: 9-of-22 passing, 71 yards, zero touchdowns, one interception.

Stock down: Mike Elko

At some point, the responsibility falls on the head coach, and Mike Elko deserves his share of the criticism after another disappointing SEC loss. Texas A&M's offense has struggled for most of the season, and Saturday's performance against Tennessee was another example of a team that has failed to find answers.

Elko has continued to stand behind offensive coordinator Holmon Wiggins, but the results haven't changed. The Aggies managed just seven points despite a defensive effort that kept them in the game for most of the afternoon.

With Texas A&M now sitting at 4-6 and officially out of bowl contention, questions about the direction of the program are only going to get louder. Elko has two games remaining to show fans something different, but the bigger concern is what changes he's willing to make once the season ends.

Stats: 4-6 overall, 1-6 SEC, five consecutive conference losses.

Stock down: Second-half offense

Texas A&M entered halftime with a one-point lead and an opportunity to pull off an upset in front of more than 108,000 fans. Instead, the Aggies failed to score a single point after halftime.

The offense repeatedly put the defense back on the field, struggled to pick up first downs and failed to respond when Tennessee took the lead. At this point, the offensive struggles are no longer isolated performances. They have become a consistent problem, and with two games remaining, something needs to change.

Stats: Zero second-half points, two late interceptions, one touchdown for the game.

Contact/Follow us @AggiesWire on X and like our page on Facebook to follow ongoing coverage of Texas A&M news, notes, and opinions. Follow Jarrett Johnson on X: @whosnextsports1.

issues.title: College Football game between Louisville and UNC ends in heated on-field brawl
issues.summary: A tense finish in Chapel Hill sparks heated reactions after the final whistle.
issues.content_html:
Louisville Cardinals‘ 16-14 victory over North Carolina Tar Heels ended with a heated on-field brawl as players from both college football teams clashed after the final whistle on Saturday night.

The incident happened in Chapel Hill after the Cardinals secured their fifth consecutive win. Players began exchanging words during Louisville’s victory formation before pushing escalated into several physical confrontations.

The tension followed a crucial defensive play by Louisville. With 58 seconds remaining, defensive back Jabari Mack intercepted a fourth-down pass from North Carolina quarterback Travis Burgess.

Mack returned the ball 32 yards before sliding to secure possession. Louisville then ran out the clock to claim the two-point victory.

MORE: Landry Kiffin turns heads in stunning yellow minidress for final LSU home game

However, the postgame celebration soon turned into chaos. North Carolina defensive tackle Xavier Lewis and Louisville offensive lineman Johnnie Brown III continued jostling after the final kneel-down.

Other players soon joined the confrontation. Several pushed and grabbed opponents, while apparent punches were thrown during multiple skirmishes across the field.

We got a brawl at the end of the Louisville vs UNC game pic.twitter.com/nIeyCwJuOc

— gmannVOLS (@gmannVOLS) November 15, 2026

Louisville and UNC coaches react to the brawl

North Carolina head coach Bill Belichick stepped onto the field to help separate players. One confrontation also spilled into the end zone, where another group became involved.

Belichick addressed the incident after the game, making his position clear.

“You play the game between the whistles, that’s not what we’re here for,” Belichick said. “We got out there and got everybody out as quickly as possible.”

Louisville coach Jeff Brohm also expressed disappointment about the incident.

“It’s obviously unfortunate,” Brohm said. “You try to get things broken up as fast as you can. It didn’t get broken up too fast, and you never want to see that happen.

“I’d have to see what really started it. Hopefully we can correct that and not do that again.”

MORE: When will college football AP Top 25 rankings release for Week 12? Poll delayed after FAA ground stop

The Cardinals improved to 7-3 overall and 6-2 in the ACC. North Carolina dropped to 5-5 and remains one victory away from bowl eligibility.

Louisville will host Pittsburgh next Saturday, while North Carolina travels to Virginia. Neither team nor the ACC has announced disciplinary action.

issues.title: Wizards vs. Rockets Prediction: Preview, Injury Report, Advantages, X-Factors
issues.summary: Kevin Durant and Alperen Sengun lead the Rockets into Washington seeking their fourth consecutive victory against the Wizards.
issues.content_html:
The Washington Wizards welcome the Houston Rockets to Capital One Arena on Sunday, Nov. 15, with tipoff scheduled for 7:00 p.m. ET.

The Wizards are 12th in the Eastern Conference at 4–9 and have lost six straight games. They came close to ending that streak against the Detroit Pistons on Thursday but fell 144–140 in double overtime.

The Rockets are third in the Western Conference at 10–3 and have won three in a row. They are coming off a 125–118 victory over the Utah Jazz in NBA Cup play, with Alperen Sengun putting up 43 points, 12 rebounds, and five assists on 17-of-24 shooting. Washington has the size to make things harder on Sengun, but it will need to defend the players around him just as well.

Injury Report

Wizards

Alex Sarr: Questionable (Illness)

Tre Johnson: Questionable (Lower Back Soreness)

Bub Carrington: Questionable (Chest Contusion)

Tristan Vukcevic: Out (Hip)

Reece Beekman: Out (AC Joint)

Justin Champagnie: Out (Foot)

Jamir Watkins: Out (ACL)

Rockets

Steven Adams: Probable (Calf)

Clint Capela: Out (Ankle)

Fred VanVleet: Out (Knee Injury Management)

Marcus Smart: Out (League Suspension)

Why The Wizards Have The Advantage?

The Wizards rank 26th in offensive rating at 108.7, 19th in defensive rating at 114.3, and 23rd in net rating at minus-5.5. They average 110.0 points per game, but they do have a way to score when their jumpers aren’t falling. Washington makes 20.4 free throws per game, good for 10th in the league.

Attacking the paint early could get the Wizards into the bonus and test Houston’s center depth with Capela out.

Anthony Davis has been Washington’s most reliable player, averaging 25.6 points, 10.5 rebounds, and 2.0 assists while shooting 52.4% from the field. Trae Young is averaging 19.7 points and 8.8 assists, although he’s shooting just 39.3% from the field and 31.5% from three.

The Wizards should put those two in the pick-and-roll and make Houston decide how much help to send. Young can hit Davis on the roll, and if a defender rotates over early, he can find Kyshawn George on the perimeter.

Washington also ranks 10th in defensive rebounds at 32.4 per game and ninth in blocks at 5.3. If Sarr plays, the Wizards can put Davis on Sengun and still have another big near the rim to contest cutters and clean up misses. That gives them a better chance of defending Houston without pulling a wing away from one of its shooters.

Why The Rockets Have The Advantage?

Houston ranks third in offensive rating at 119.3, eighth in defensive rating at 110.2, and fourth in net rating at +9.1. The Rockets shoot 47.8% from the field and 37.2% from three, and their 13.2 offensive rebounds per game give them another way to score when the first shot doesn’t fall. Washington can defend well for most of a possession and still give up points if it doesn’t finish with a rebound.

Sengun is averaging 23.1 points, 9.6 rebounds, and 7.6 assists while shooting 54.4% from the floor and 45.8% from three. Davis can make him work for his points, but Sengun can also run the offense from the elbow. If the Wizards stay home on Houston’s shooters, he can give the ball to a cutter or back his defender down. If they help, he can make the pass before they recover.

Kevin Durant is averaging 21.0 points, 5.8 rebounds, and 3.8 assists while shooting 48.3% from the field and 36.0% from three. Jabari Smith Jr. adds 15.9 points and 6.3 rebounds on 40.7% shooting from deep.

Smith gives Sengun a dependable outlet, and Durant gives Houston someone who can get a shot late in the clock if Washington takes away the first option.

X-Factors

Kyshawn George is averaging 18.2 points, 4.5 rebounds, and 4.8 assists while shooting 42.1% from three. He can punish Houston for helping on Davis and handle the ball when Young sits. AJ Dybantsa is averaging 15.0 points and 6.1 rebounds, but shooting 23.3% from three gives Houston a reason to sag off him. He can use that space to cut behind defenders instead of settling for jumpers.

Sarr averages 11.2 points and 7.4 rebounds on 53.0% shooting. If he’s out, Deandre Ayton’s minutes become more significant, particularly when Davis rests. Bilal Coulibaly can also help by taking some of the defensive possessions against Durant.

Amen Thompson is averaging 15.0 points and 7.0 rebounds while shooting 51.4% from the field. With VanVleet and Smart out, he can take on more of the ball-handling and pressure Young on defense.

Tari Eason adds 9.7 points and 6.2 rebounds, and his work on the offensive glass could be especially valuable if Washington goes smaller. Reed Sheppard, who averages 9.1 points and 2.6 assists, will need to keep the offense organized when Sengun sits.

Prediction

Davis and Young can keep Washington competitive, especially if Sarr plays and helps finish possessions on the glass. Houston has more ways to get a good shot over four quarters. Şengün can run the offense without VanVleet, Durant can take over when Washington breaks up the first action, and Smith and Thompson can punish the help in different ways.

I expect the Rockets to pull away in the second half and extend their winning streak to four.

Prediction: Wizards vs. Rockets 115-121

issues.title: Boulder Cup cyclo-cross: Sidney McGill and Eric Brunner take the honours in the Elite races
issues.summary: Both riders continue their hugely successful seasons
issues.author: Owen Rogers
issues.content_html:
Former Canadian champion Sidney McGill continued her excellent start to the 2026/27 cyclo-cross season by winning the Boulder Cup on Saturday, while Eric Brunner was completely dominant in the men’s race.

Riding for the Materiaal-Lastig team, McGill bounced back from her third place at the Pan-American Championships last week, winning a two-up sprint to take the sixth win of her season. Kaya Musgrave (Competitive Edge Racing) was edged into second place, while Lauren Zoerner (Corner Racing p/b Beyond Horizon Media) finished alone in third place, some 30 seconds back.

Brunner (Competitive Edge Racing) has had a dream start to the year, winning all five races he’s started, including a fifth Pan-Am title last week, and continued his stranglehold on the North American Elite scene by winning alone, with the biggest winning margin of his year to date.

Garrett Beshore (Colorado Mesa UNiversity)led the chasers home, finishing second, some 1:08 behind, while his teammate Ivan Sippy was third, a further 53 seconds down.

Both races are run at UCI C1 level and are equivalent to the Superprestige and X2O Trofee series in Europe.

issues.title: Paul Seixas chases down World Champion Brandon McNulty at Tour de France Saitama Criterium to close out 2026 season with a win
issues.summary: French superstar goes solo in final lap of exhibition event to delight fans in Japan on Sunday
issues.author: James Moultrie
issues.content_html:
Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM) put on a show for the fan-lined streets in Japan as he reeled in a late attack from World Champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) to win the Tour de France Saitama Criterium on Sunday.

After 14 of the 17 laps of action at the off-season exhibition event were completed, the big-name riders moved away from the peloton: Seixas, McNulty, former yellow jersey wearer Torstein Træen (Uno-X Mobility), and former Tour fourth-place finisher Oscar Onley (Ineos Grenadiers).

McNulty made his move on the penultimate lap around the 3.7km city circuit, centred around the Shintoshin train station and the Saitama Super Arena, with Seixas slowly clawing him back before going solo and celebrating over the line.

A week after finishing second behind McNulty's teammate Isaac del Toro in the equivalent exhibition event in Singapore, Il Lombardia winner Seixas was able to close out his 2026 racing fully with a "win" that delighted the local fans.

"It was quite a good race. With three laps to go, we started to attack, and we got the breakaway to four, and then we rode well together for one lap," said Seixas.

"After that, Brandon attacked; it was really strong. I tried to follow and quickly saw I was alone in the pursuit. I started to come back – I tried and tried, and with one lap to go, I found a moment that I think I was a bit stronger, and I counter-attacked, and then it was the right move. I finished it in the TT way, like I like.

"It's a great finish for me after the disappointing second place last week, so I'm happy to finish like this, and it was nice to see a new country for me in Japan and to race here."

Seixas succeeded Jonas Vingegaard as the champion in Saitama, joining a list of winners that also includes Tadej Pogačar, and the 2026 race ambassador, Mark Cavendish.

To keep the action exciting for the 100s who showed up in the grey and rainy conditions, the likes of Michael Matthews (Jayco AlUla), Davide Ballerini (XDS Astana), and Valentin Paret-Peintre (Soudal-QuickStep) made sure to keep the points and King of the Mountains classification sprints close.

Matthews took home the former at his first time doing the Saitama Criterium, with Paret-Peintre winning the KOM classification, and Mauro Schmid (Jayco AlUla) taking the combativity prize

With several Japanese riders also joining the WorldTour stars on the start line for the 62km race, the locals had plenty to cheer for, including some early moves from long-term pro Yukiya Arashiro (Solution Tech NIPPO Rali) and current national champion Yuhi Todome (Aisan Racing Team).

issues.title: Reports suggest XDS may withdraw sponsorship of the XDS-Astana team before the scheduled 2029 date
issues.summary: The Chinese bike manufacturer joined the team in 2025
issues.author: Owen Rogers
issues.content_html:
Reports in the French sports paper L'Equipe have emerged questioning the future of bike manufacturer XDS as a name sponsor of the XDS-Astana team.

Escaping what was, at one stage, almost certain relegation from the WorldTour at the end of 2025, the Kazakh squad have been one of the revelations of the men’s peloton in the last two years since the Chinese bike manufacturer came on board.

In 2025, XDS’s first year as a title sponsor, the team cleverly targeted UCI points at races all over the World, closing the year as the fourth-ranked team and escaping the drop to ProTeam level. While they slipped to sixth place in 2026, they still finished ahead of the vast bulk of WorldTour teams, with Netcompany-Ineos and Soudal-QuickStep among the outfits trailing in their wake.

Now that progression could be under threat, with L'Equipe reporting the Chinese company is unhappy with some of the changes at the top of the team, their departure allegedly possible as soon as next year, despite having committed until the end of 2029.

XDS’s issues with the team are not known, but have emerged in the wake of the appointment of Yana Seel as General Manager. Belgian with some Kazakh heritage, Seel was Chief Executive Officer of the team between 2018 and 2021 and rejoined in a similar job in early October. Her new role at the team is mainly financial and commercial, though some responsibilities are sporting, influencing rider transfers and race schedules.

However, when she initially left the team in 2021, there were rumours of a clash with General Manager Alexandr Vinokurov, something Seel denied in an interview with Het Laatste Nieuws.

"I left the team at the time because the team wanted to focus exclusively on the Kazakh market and Kazakh sponsors. They didn't need me for that, and they could work perfectly well with another general manager. My added value lay precisely in developing international partnerships and attracting foreign sponsors."

It is this historic, though rumoured, clash that might have unsettled XDS, who, according to L’Equipe, are apparently considering joining forces with another top team.

Seel has a rich history in team governance, working at Lotto-Dstny as Chief Business Officer for two years, before moving to the UAE ADQ Women’s WorldTour team, first as Head of Business and Communications, then as Team Principal, leaving in summer 2026.

As well as working with Astana, XDS provided bikes for the Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskadi team in 2025, though they have been replaced by BMC for next year and beyond.

issues.title: Michael Vanthourenhout back on rollers after crashing out of Superprestige Merksplas
issues.summary: Belgian dropped to sixth overall and ‘can now forget the classification’ - video
issues.author: Lyne Lamoureux
issues.content_html:
Michael Vanthourenhout seemed to be in prime position at Aardbeiencross, the fourth round of the Superprestige Series in Merksplas, Belgium, on Saturday. On a dry and fast course, the Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw rider had moved to the front of the pack, leading into the decisive sand section by the end of the second of 11 laps. He then spoke to his teammate Yordi Corsus, who immediately went to the front to put pressure on the group and cause a first split of around 25 riders.

The next time around on the sand, Vanthourenhout once again came to the front, riding smoothly and staying out of trouble. But that would all change on the fourth lap.

As Wout Janssen increased the pace at the front, a crash brought down Vanthourenhout after his teammate Gerben Kuypers, riding close by, hit a post. While the other riders involved quickly remounted, Vanthourenhout remained on the ground, slapping it in pain and frustration. After receiving assistance from the medical team, he eventually managed to get to his feet and gingerly walk off the course before remounting his bike to return to the team camper. His ripped skinsuit showed a bloodied left hip.

The 32-year-old rider was on the rollers when Belgian media caught up with him

"I only have problems with my hip. The movement on the bike works, but clicking out is difficult. Maybe have it examined anyway, but at first glance it's not too bad," Vanthourenhout told VTM Nieuws.

"Before I knew it, I was on the ground. A corner where we sat next to each other with four to five riders, and there I was…," he added. "Too bad, because I had set my sights on it and I can now forget the classification"

Vanthourenhout dropped from third overall, only two points from the leader, to sixth place, 15 points down from new leader Joran Wyseure.

"Hopefully we can start tomorrow,” he added, “if it really doesn't get any better, then yes, have further tests done in the hospital."
