issues.title: How Kelly Rowland Keeps Her Eczema Flare-Ups Under Control During Winter
issues.summary: BURBANK, CALIFORNIA – November 2, 2026: Actress and singer Kelly Rowland appears on “The Jennifer Hudson Show” airing November 12, 2026, in Burbank, California. (Photo by Chris Haston/WBTV via Getty Images). Grammy-winning singer Kelly Rowland shares her experience living with moderate-to-severe eczema and how she manages flare-ups, particularly during the winter months. Cold weather, dry air, and
issues.content_html:
• Grammy-winning singer Kelly Rowland shares her experience living with moderate-to-severe eczema and how she manages flare-ups, particularly during the winter months.
  • Cold weather, dry air, and indoor heating can worsen eczema symptoms by drying out the skin and weakening its protective barrier.
  • Managing stress, avoiding hot showers, moisturizing regularly, and talking with a dermatologist about treatment options can help people manage eczema flare-ups.

Wintertime can bring everyone down with its colder weather and less sunlight. But for those with eczema, this time of year can wreak havoc on their skin, too.

That’s the case for Grammy-winning singer, actress, and Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who has been living with eczema since her 20s. During the winter months, she often dreads the cold.

“[You] don’t know what the environment is going to give you—because mine is also environmental—or what the weather is going to give you,” Rowland told Healthline.

Cold weather and indoor heating can reduce humidity, drying out the skin and triggering or worsening eczema flare-ups.

“[What we know] about the skin barrier is that it really is like a gate or wall against the outside world,” Camille Howard-Verovic, MD, a dermatologist at Active Dermatology, told Healthline.

In healthy skin, the barrier controls what enters and leaves the skin. However, for people with eczema, Howard-Verovic said they have skin barrier dysfunction, which allows substances such as allergens and irritants to penetrate the skin.

Cold weather can increase transepidermal water loss, a process in which moisture escapes through the skin’s outer barrier and evaporates into the surrounding air.

“People with eczema have a tremendous amount of transepidermal water loss, so you’re just drier,” said Howard-Verovic. “[You’re] not holding onto the water as well, so that causes the itching and the rash that we feel when we have eczema.”

Kelly Rowland’s journey to an eczema diagnosis

Rowland first noticed eczema flares behind her ears as well as on her elbows, arms, and the back of her knees.

“[It] looked like a rash, so that’s what I thought it was all this time, and I dealt with it for so long until after I had my son and then it started to get worse on my face,” she said.

She eventually went to a dermatologist who diagnosed her with moderate-to-severe eczema, a chronic inflammatory skin condition that can cause intense itching, painful skin cracking, thickened skin, and redness or swelling.

When Rowland learned that eczema can be genetic, it made sense to her.

“I remember seeing big rashes on [my mom’s] neck and her arms…so she had it, and I guess I was the lucky one,” said Rowland.

How Kelly Rowland found relief from eczema symptoms

At first, she tried eliminating foods that she thought might be triggers. She also bathed in oatmeal.

“[I] literally have had a tub full of oatmeal, like literally went to the store to get store-bought fresh oats,” she said. “I tried everything, and it doesn’t help until you go talk to a doctor about it.”

At first, she tried prescription topical medications but found them cumbersome.

“I don’t have the time, if I’m being honest, and we live in a world that is moving so fast…I started buying like three tubes of whatever it was I was using and losing it; it was just too much for me,” Rowland said.

Rowland said she found relief with Ebglyss, a prescription injectable medication for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. She has also partnered with Eli Lilly and Company, its manufacturer, to raise awareness about eczema.

Rowland said she’s sharing her experience to help others living with eczema, including people she’s met who have experienced greater challenges managing the condition.

“One lady was telling me about how she’s having a tough time [looking] in the mirror cause she doesn’t know who’s looking back at her, and she saw her skin before eczema and after,” said Rowland.

When she first had symptoms, she said she felt embarrassed, too.

“[Because] it was just in the middle of my arm space and…[if I] put out my hand to shake someone’s hand, you don’t know if somebody’s judgy,” she said.

Rowland hopes being open about her condition will encourage others to advocate for themselves and talk with their doctor about treatment options.

Because eczema can look different on deeper skin tones, Howard-Verovic noted that a dermatologist can help make the correct diagnosis.

“Some people may not even know that they have eczema,” she said. “We know that eczema is a rash; it can appear red on certain skin tones, and it can be grey or white on certain skin tones, so it can look a little different.”

Tips to help manage eczema flare-ups during winter

In addition to medication, Rowland said managing stress helps reduce her eczema flare-ups.

“Before [when] I went on tour, because I was under so much stress, it flared up like crazy, like you wouldn’t believe,” she said. “We were in the back trying to figure out how to cover certain things up, and we figured some of it out, and some of it was really tricky, but what helped was when I actually just calmed down…not that it helped overnight, but it did just kind of bring the flare down.”

She said red light therapy, feeling grounded outside without her shoes on, getting vitamin D from natural sunlight, and cooking are ways she reduces ongoing stress.

“Cooking calms me when my kids aren’t here, and I have a really good [Zen] playlist on,” said Rowland. “[If] you ask me a question [in those moments], I might give you my heart; I’m just so happy.”

She also tries to cut back on sugar, which she believes triggers flares.

“I do enjoy chocolate chip cookies and chocolate cake…and the holidays are coming up. I usually [indulge] around the holidays,” Rowland said.

Another way to reduce flares, according to Howard-Verovic, is to avoid hot showers, especially in the winter.

“[We] know eczematous skin likes lukewarm water,” she said.

Because Howard-Verovic and her daughter both live with eczema, she set a rule about when it’s time to get out of the shower.

“[If] you see condensation on the bathroom mirror, you’ve spent too much time in the shower,” said Howard-Verovic. “[That] really hot, hot water feels really good in that moment…but when you get out all that water evaporates, and there’s no moisture in the atmosphere, and it dries your skin out, and now your skin is unhappy again.”

If you prefer to take baths, she said use gentle cleansers.

“[There] are bleach baths for really, really bad flare-ups,” she noted.

Diluted bleach baths are sometimes recommended for people with eczema, but they should only be used according to a healthcare professional’s instructions.

As soon as you get out of the shower or bath, Howard-Verovic said to apply a quality moisturizer to your damp skin. According to the National Eczema Association (NEA), lotions containing the following ingredients can help ease dry skin associated with eczema.

  • Aloe
  • Glycerin
  • Niacinamide
  • Oat butter
  • Petrolatum
  • Shea butter
  • Vitamin E

To help identify appropriate products, look for ones that have the NEA’s Seal of Acceptance.

issues.title: Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What a Missed Deadline Taught Me About Switching Off
issues.summary: Healthline Editor-in-Chief Robin Hough and his wife enjoy time outdoors during a weekend getaway. Photo by Robin Hough Switching off from work is hard for many of us, but research suggests vacation has a strong effect on well-being, and that genuinely not thinking about work while you’re away may be among the healthiest things you can do. With Thanksgiving and the holidays approaching, the column
issues.content_html:
• Switching off from work is hard for many of us, but research suggests vacation has a strong effect on well-being, and that genuinely not thinking about work while you’re away may be among the healthiest things you can do.
  • With Thanksgiving and the holidays approaching, the column offers practical tips for leaving work at work and carving out moments for yourself, whether you’re working through the break, don’t have help on hand, or your time off looks very different.
  • Healthline’s Editor-in-Chief, Robin Hough, reflects on what a missed deadline and a long weekend in Italy revealed about disconnecting from the desk, and why doing just that matters so much.

I missed a deadline last week. The piece you’re reading was supposed to be filed before I headed out on a long weekend to Italy for my wife’s birthday.

It’s a trip we try to take every November, one where we leave the kids behind with their Granny for a few days of relaxation and indulgence – for all of us. The kids and Granny get cookies, ice cream, and bedtime stories on tap. We get spritzes, pasta, and an all-too-rare chance to sleep in.

The main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece. An urgent stakeholder ask out of the blue, a couple of unanticipated work fire drills, and a long-standing evening social commitment earlier in the week made for a perfect storm, and something had to give.

The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.

It caught up with me at 6 am on the first morning, when I found myself drafting this column in my head. I should have been dozing peacefully. I continued to ruminate on my lengthy to-do list at work deep into day one as we headed from Venice into the Dolomites. My body was in Italy, but my brain was clearly still at my desk.

Why switching off from work is so hard

Switching off, particularly from work, is hard for most of us, and especially in an age of ubiquitous screens and wall-to-wall information competing for our attention. For me, that always-on reality plays a major role in the difficulties I have disconnecting from the daily grind.

Practical tips for leaving work at work:

  • Set your own rules for when you’re reachable. Decide when you’ll check email and when you won’t, and tell your manager what’s realistic outside working hours.
  • Swap some passive screen time for something purposeful. A book, time outdoors, a hobby. There’s nothing wrong with a bit of binge-watching, but something creative can feel more restorative.
  • Write down what’s stressing you. A quick log of triggers and how you reacted can show you patterns you’d otherwise miss.
  • Ask for help, and lean on your people. Reassign, delegate, or let family and friends cover something. Feeling supported can make it easier to detach when the day is done.
  • If exhaustion lingers, talk with a professional. Persistent fatigue, or changes in mood, appetite or sleep, are worth raising with a doctor or therapist.

I’m fortunate to love my job, and if I’m candid, I probably take a little too much of my identity from it. I hold on tight, and the phone in my pocket is an ever-present enabler.

A meme that has stuck with me over the years goes something along the lines of being an adult is staring at medium screens all day only to come home and stare at a little screen while a big screen is on in the background. The irony is not lost on me that I came across this rather withering take on modern life while scrolling on said little screen.

What the science says about detaching from work

Regardless of the role the screen plays, psychologists who study employee well-being describe what I was missing for the early part of the weekend as “psychological detachment.” A state where you are genuinely able to not think about work while away from it. The science suggests it’s an important thing to work on.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 32 studies found that vacationing has a strong effect on well-being, and that the effect lasts longer than earlier research suggested. A second, smaller analysis of eight studies points to detaching from work, along with physical activity, as among the most helpful things to do while you’re off. In another study that tracked teachers during a two-week break, exhaustion, anxiety, and low mood all declined, while those who kept ruminating about work recovered less.

Whatever the science says, I know that for me the act of stepping away from work and being disciplined about not checking back in while I’m away is critical for my mental health and for staving off burnout. Getting out in nature and hiking or cycling or swimming keeps me present. It resets and recharges my batteries, and it tops up my creativity in a way that I find benefits what I am then able to bring back to the office.

Sure enough, as we drove deeper into the mountains on a crisp, blue-sky day, I could feel the golden autumnal hues and majestic rock formations drawing me in, closer to an elemental feeling of calm and happiness. That sense of equilibrium stayed with me all weekend, and while I’d be lying if I said my mind didn’t occasionally drift to my desk, it was fleeting, with the knowledge that all the things would be waiting for me when I got back. Just like this piece was.

How to take a break this holiday season, whatever it looks like

With Thanksgiving on the horizon, and the holidays coming thick and fast thereafter, I’ll leave you with this bit of hard-earned advice: if your job is deeply entwined with your life and part of who you are, as mine is, time away can sometimes feel like a small act of disloyalty. It isn’t. In fact, it’s probably the most important thing you can do to remain faithful to your work ethic, and to yourself.

And if you’ll be working over the holidays, or you’re not working right now, or you don’t have the benefit of someone on hand to carry some of the load for you (shout out to all the Grannies out there), or your vacation looks very different from mine, that’s all okay. Find the pockets where and when you can: an evening, a walk, an hour in front of a screen, or better yet a book, and let work wait. Above all else, be kind to yourself. That’s how you really give yourself a break.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our HealthlineWellness Wire newsletter.

issues.title: Hailey Bieber Says She's Been Diagnosed With PMDD: What Are the Signs, Symptoms?
issues.summary: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 17: Hailey Bieber attends the 6th Annual Academy Museum Gala at Academy Museum of Motion Pictures on October 17, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Kevin Winter/GA/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images) Hailey Bieber is sharing her experience with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) and how her diagnosis inspired her growing involvement in women’s hea
issues.content_html:
• Hailey Bieber is sharing her experience with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) and how her diagnosis inspired her growing involvement in women’s health research.
  • PMDD is a severe form of premenstrual disorder that can cause debilitating physical and psychological symptoms that interfere with daily life.
  • An estimated 1.6% of women and girls worldwide meet the strict diagnostic criteria for PMDD, affecting approximately 31 million people.
  • Treatment options include certain FDA-approved antidepressants and birth control pills, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), and lifestyle changes such as stress management and maintaining a consistent sleep schedule.

Hailey Bieber is sharing her experience with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a condition she says has fueled her growing interest in women’s health research.

The Rhode Beauty founder recently announced a $5 million, three-year partnership with the Foundation for Women’s Health in an interview with Women’s Wear Daily (WWD).

“As a woman, I feel frustrated by the lack of research, the lack of awareness, the lack of certain conversation around it,” Bieber told WWD.

Motherhood has also shaped her perspective. Bieber welcomed her son, Jack Blues, with her husband, Justin Bieber, in 2024, describing the experience as a “really intense and special journey.”

She also shared that she “struggled” with PMDD after giving birth, noting that there’s “not a lot of conversation or research around it.”

“When we can identify with each other and have conversations relating to each other and talking about the things we’re dealing with and struggling with, I do think it makes it feel like less of a lonely journey,” Bieber said.

PMDD Affects an Estimated 31 Million Women and Girls Worldwide

PMDD is a complexcondition that causes severe physical and psychological symptoms that typically occur in the days or weeks leading up to menstruation.

“What distinguishes PMDD from the more common PMS (premenstrual syndrome) is the severity of the symptoms and how significantly they can interfere with daily functioning,” Sari Eitches, MD, dual board certified physician and medical advisor to Terra Mare, told Healthline.

“Another defining feature is the timing: symptoms typically worsen in the week or two before a period, resolve within a few days after menstruation begins, and are minimal or absent during the rest of the cycle,” she said.

Eitches also noted that PMDD is a chronic condition that can affect women at any stage of their reproductive lives, from adolescence through perimenopause, as long as they are having menstrual cycles.

“It is caused by a sensitivity to cyclic hormonal and neurotransmitter fluctuations, so [it] can occur in anyone with a menstrual cycle, though stages of hormonal fluctuation- including postpartum, weaning breastfeeding, and perimenopause- can be a trigger,” she added.

According to research published in 2024, approximately 1.6% of women and girls meet the strict diagnostic criteria for PMDD, equivalent to an estimated 31 million people worldwide.

A higher percentage of 3.2% have a provisional diagnosis, meaning a healthcare professional may believe a person has PMDD, but symptoms have not been measured for a sustained amount of time to meet the criteria for a confirmed diagnosis.

Eitches said that women with a personal or family history of depression or anxiety may be more prone to developing PMDD, as are women with a family history of PMDD itself.

“PMDD is understood to be caused by a combination of heritable biological sensitivities and environmental triggers. These can include a history of trauma, chronic stress, and other chronic medical conditions,” she noted.

Eitches also said that you should consider seeing a doctor if your symptoms are severe enough that they’re interfering with your ability to go to work or school, maintain your relationships, or participate in your life in the same way that you do during the other weeks of the month.

Signs and symptoms of PMDD

To diagnose PMDD, a healthcare professional will review your medical history and symptoms and may perform a physical exam. They will typically ask you to track your symptoms over at least two menstrual cycles.

A PMDD diagnosis generally requires at least five symptoms, including at least one mood-related symptom, that occur before menstruation, improve shortly after a period begins, and significantly interfere with daily life.

The symptoms of PMDD may include:

  • feelings of sadness or despair
  • lasting feelings of irritability or anger that may affect people around you
  • feelings of tension or anxiety
  • panic attacks
  • mood changes or crying often
  • lack of interest in relationships or daily activities
  • difficulty thinking or concentrating
  • tiredness or low energy
  • food cravings or binge eating
  • difficulty sleeping
  • feeling out of control

Physical symptoms may include:

  • cramps
  • bloating
  • breast tenderness
  • joint or muscle pain
  • headaches

Medications and lifestyle changes can help manage PMDD

Treatment options for PMDD include prescription medications and over-the-counter treatments that may help relieve certain symptoms, such as:

  • Antidepressants: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved three serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for PMDD: sertraline (Zoloft), fluoxetine (Prozac), and paroxetine (Paxil) HCI.
  • Birth control pills: The FDA has approved a birth control pill that contains drospirenone and ethinyl estradiol (Yaz).
  • Over-the-counter (OTC) pain relievers: OTC pain relievers like ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin may help with physical symptoms like cramps and muscle aches.

Eitches noted that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can also help manage symptoms.

Lifestyle changes may also help manage PMDD symptoms, including practicing relaxation techniques, eating a balanced diet, limiting sugary and salty foods, and getting regular physical activity.

Eitches noted that getting enough high quality sleep and resting on a consistent schedule is also important.

“I also recommend focusing on a whole-foods-based diet, limiting added sugar and caffeine, and avoiding cigarette smoking,” she said.

issues.title: Does Menopausal Hormone Therapy Lower Dementia Risk? Timing and Genetics May Hold the Answer
issues.summary: Recent research shows that MHT may be associated with better brain health later in life. SDI Productions · E+/Getty A longer reproductive life span, particularly later menopause, was associated with fewer signs of small-vessel disease in the brain, including approximately 8% lower odds of having multiple disease markers. Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) was associated with fewer signs of small-ves
issues.content_html:
• A longer reproductive life span, particularly later menopause, was associated with fewer signs of small-vessel disease in the brain, including approximately 8% lower odds of having multiple disease markers.
  • Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) was associated with fewer signs of small-vessel disease and better white matter integrity, although these associations may vary depending on genetic and individual health factors.
  • While MHT may offer potential brain health benefits when started around menopause, it has not been proven to prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a new study.

The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.

The findings could offer new insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.

Researchers also found that certain associations between hormone therapy and brain health differed depending on whether women carried a genetic variant associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

However, the relationship between estrogen and brain health is complex. While the findings suggest that longer estrogen exposure may be associated with healthier brain aging, they do not establish that hormone therapy can prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

Longer estrogen exposure linked to better brain blood vessel health

The researchers drew data from the Gothenburg H70-1944 Birth Cohort, a longitudinal study of 1,203 individuals born in 1944 who resided in Gothenburg, Sweden.

The final cohort included 352 cisgender women, with an average age of 70, who had no neurological disorders and reliable self-reported data on their estrogen exposure.

Individual estrogen exposure was measured through structured interviews. It included:

  • age of first menstruation
  • age of menopause
  • type of menopause (surgical or natural)
  • use of oral contraceptives
  • use of MHT

The researchers used this information as a proxy for lifetime estrogen exposure, though the study didn’t measure actual hormone levels.

Participants were also given a brain MRI at baseline and then again at a 5-year follow-up.

The researchers found that those with a longer reproductive span had a lower risk of small vessel disease (SVD). Participants with a longer reproductive life span had an 8% lower risk of having two or more signs of SVD. However, later menopause, rather than earlier menstruation, appeared to be the main driver of this association.

Those who used MHT also tended to have fewer signs of SVD and better microstructural integrity in the white matter.

In individuals who carried the APOE-ε4 variant, which increases a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s disease, MHT was associated with greater cortical thickness in brain regions vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease. However, there was no association for those without this variant.

The researchers noted that longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and white matter trajectories over time.

Dung Trinh, MD, internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that estrogen has several important effects on the brain that may help support cognitive health.

It influences communication between brain cells, supports the brain’s ability to use glucose for energy, helps regulate neurotransmitters, and plays a role in maintaining healthy blood vessels and reducing inflammation and oxidative stress.

“As estrogen levels decline during menopause, some of these protective effects may diminish. Replacing estrogen closer to the menopause transition could potentially help preserve some of these functions during a vulnerable period for brain health,” he said. “While these findings are encouraging, MHT has not been proven to prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.”

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed and noted, “Starting menopausal hormone therapy earlier in the menopause transition may help minimize some changes by supporting the brain during this period of hormonal fluctuation.”

“There is growing interest in whether early estrogen therapy may also help reduce the long-term risk of Alzheimer’s disease, although more research is needed before we can establish that benefit,” she added.

Why menopause hormone therapy should be individualized

Ross told Healthline that this research reinforces the importance of recognizing menopause as more than a reproductive or hormonal transition.

“We know that women are disproportionately affected by dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, and some women experience noticeable cognitive changes beginning in perimenopause,” she said. “If future research confirms that starting hormone therapy earlier can help protect long-term cognitive health, it could influence how we approach menopause treatment and encourage more proactive conversations between women and their healthcare providers.”

“The goal should be to individualize treatment based on a woman’s symptoms, medical history, and overall health rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach,” Ross added.

Trinh agreed that an individualized approach to menopause management is important.

“This does not mean that every woman should start hormone therapy to prevent dementia. Instead, it highlights the importance of understanding which women might benefit, when treatment should begin, and which formulations are most appropriate,” he said. “Factors such as age, time since menopause, cardiovascular risk, metabolic health, family history, and potentially genetic factors may all help guide future recommendations.”

“We still need stronger clinical evidence before changing current prescribing guidelines specifically for dementia prevention,” Trinh added.

issues.title: Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apnea?
issues.summary: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) like Ozempic can help with weight loss, which may assist with sleep apnea symptoms. If your sleep apnea has worsened with weight gain or you have other medical conditions that warrant the use of GLP-1s, your healthcare provider may prescribe one, but they can be pricey. Monthly out of pocket […] The post Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apne
issues.author: melissa
issues.content_html:
• How Does Ozempic Work for Sleep Apnea?
  • Is Ozempic Approved for Sleep Apnea?
  • Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apnea?
  • How to Check Your Insurance Coverage
  • Alternatives if Insurance Won’t Cover Ozempic
  • Frequently Asked Questions
Key Takeaways
  • Most insurance plans don’t cover Ozempic for sleep apnea, but some partially cover costs of another GLP-1, Zepbound, that’s prescribed for sleep apnea.
  • In 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Zepbound for the treatment of moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity. Currently, Ozempic is only approved to treat type 2 diabetes.
  • You can find out if your insurance covers weight loss medications for sleep apnea by checking their online directory or calling your insurer directly.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) like Ozempic can help with weight loss, which may assist with sleep apnea symptoms. If your sleep apnea has worsened with weight gain or you have other medical conditions that warrant the use of GLP-1s, your healthcare provider may prescribe one, Trusted Source National Association of Insurance Commissioners View Source but they can be pricey. Monthly out of pocket costs often reach several hundred dollars, and some plans require you to try CPAP or a weight-loss program before approving the medication.

So, will insurance cover Ozempic for sleep apnea? The short answer is no, but some insurance plans may cover other GLP-1s for sleep apnea, especially if you also have other health conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes.

Even if your insurance won’t cover a GLP-1, you still have options. Your provider can document medical necessity, which strengthens insurance approval attempts for weight loss medications. Below, learn how weight loss drugs may improve sleep apnea, how to check your insurance coverage, and what other options exist.

Get a Home Sleep Study for as Low as $0

Based on claims data, eligible insured patients may pay as little as $0 for the home sleep study and related consultations. Actual out-of-pocket costs vary by insurance plan, deductible, coinsurance, and coverage. We will provide your out-of-pocket cost prior to your first consultation. Cost does not include any post-diagnosis medication or treatment, if and when prescribed.

Take a one-night sleep study in your own bed, review results with a certified sleep expert, and get a personalized treatment plan for as low $0 with most major insurance plans.

Check Your Coverage 4.8 60,000+ patients

How Does Ozempic Work for Sleep Apnea?

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) happens when your airway gets blocked during sleep, causing a pause in breathing. These episodes can happen many times throughout the night and last anywhere from 10 to 30 seconds.

Carrying extra weight around the neck is a major risk factor for OSA, as excess tissue can crowd your airway while you sleep Trusted Source MSD Manuals First published in 1899 as a small reference book for physicians and pharmacists, the Manual grew in size and scope to become one of the most widely used comprehensive medical resources for professionals and consumers. View Source . About 31% of people with obstructive sleep apnea have obesity while 44% are overweight Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source . Because of this connection, experts have started researching to see if GLP-1s like Ozempic can also improve symptoms of OSA Trusted Source Journal of Translational Medicine View Source .

A clear relationship exists between weight loss and better sleep apnea outcomes. A study review found that a 20% decrease in BMI led to a 57% reduction in sleep apnea symptoms Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source .

Other research confirms GLP-1s may improve sleep apnea symptoms through weight loss, a lower BMI (body mass index), and a smaller waist size. But not all GLP-1s offer the same benefits. For example, another study review found that tirzepatide (Zepbound) improved OSA symptoms more than liraglutide (Saxenda). Trials also show that tirzepatide improves daytime sleepiness and blood pressure, two issues that often accompany sleep apnea.

Is Ozempic Approved for Sleep Apnea?

Currently, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved Ozempic to treat sleep apnea or weight loss. Ozempic is only approved by the FDA to treat type 2 diabetes. The only FDA-approved GLP-1s for weight loss are semaglutide (Wegovy), liraglutide (Saxenda), and tirzepatide (Zepbound).

Among these, only Zepbound has FDA approval for sleep apnea. In 2024, the FDA approved Zepbound for the treatment of moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity Trusted Source U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) The FDA is responsible for protecting the public health by ensuring the safety, efficacy, and security of human and veterinary drugs, biological products, and medical devices; and by ensuring the safety of our nation's food supply, cosmetics, and products that emit radiation. View Source . This approval was based on a large clinical trial showing significant reductions in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) or sleep apnea severity after weight loss.

Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apnea?

Insurance typically won’t cover Ozempic for sleep apnea since the FDA hasn’t approved its use for that condition. Sometimes, providers will prescribe medications “off-label,” meaning they offer them because they may help with a condition not listed in the approved indications. But insurers typically won’t cover a drug for off-label use.

However, if you have another health condition alongside OSA, you may still be eligible for GLP-1 coverage. For example, Ozempic is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes, so if you have this condition, your insurance may pay for it. Weight loss and improved sleep apnea become added benefits. Trusted Source National Association of Insurance Commissioners View Source .

Some insurance plans also cover GLP-1s for obesity-related health conditions like high cholesterol or high blood pressure, but each company sets its own criteria. If you have one of these health conditions plus a high BMI and obstructive sleep apnea, you may get insurance coverage for GLP-1s.

Now that Zepbound has been approved to treat OSA, more insurers may cover this medication. Many payers are adding Zepbound to formularies, although prior authorization is common. Requirements often include a BMI threshold, documentation of CPAP intolerance or failure, and proof of structured weight loss attempts.

How to Check Your Insurance Coverage

Every insurance company has a range of coverage plans and each covers different drugs. The first place you can look is your insurance provider’s website. Most insurers have a formulary listed under each of their plans, so you can see exactly what’s covered and how much you can expect to pay.

Medicare and Medicaid have a similar list available online. If your insurance company’s online formulary is confusing or difficult to use, you can call the customer service number on the back of your insurance card to ask for copay information on any medication.

You can also submit an appeal if your provider submits a GLP-1 request for approval and insurance says they won’t pay. Appeals can push insurers a little harder if they have denied payment for your weight loss drug or if it’s not on their list of approved medications. You may be able to get it covered with an appeal if your provider can prove it’s medically necessary.

For most plans, you have six months to file an internal appeal with your insurer. If that appeal is denied, you can request an external review for a third-party to weigh in. Typically, appeals are submitted through your insurer’s website, but you may also request more information through their customer service.

Alternatives if Insurance Won’t Cover Ozempic

If your insurance plan won’t pay for Ozempic, you can ask about Zepbound or another GLP-1 medication. If no weight loss medication is covered, you still have options. Exercise and diet changes are encouraged for people on GLP-1s, and these changes improve sleep apnea symptoms on their own Trusted Source UpToDate More than 2 million healthcare providers around the world choose UpToDate to help make appropriate care decisions and drive better health outcomes. UpToDate delivers evidence-based clinical decision support that is clear, actionable, and rich with real-world insights. View Source .

To lose weight through diet, create a calorie deficit: take in fewer calories than you use daily. Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source .

Cutting foods like sweet and alcoholic beverages, may also help you lose weight faster. However, everyone responds differently to diets, so you may need to try more than one approach. Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source . You should also talk to your doctor before making any big lifestyle changes, especially because they may be able to make medically-sound suggestions based on your history or refer you to a nutritionist.

You can also boost your calorie deficit by exercising.. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services recommends getting 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous exercise each week. They also suggest you include muscle strengthening exercises at least two days per week . Adding resistance training is especially helpful because increased muscle mass improves metabolic rate.

Beyond lifestyle changes, your provider can recommend sleep apnea treatments like Trusted Source MSD Manuals First published in 1899 as a small reference book for physicians and pharmacists, the Manual grew in size and scope to become one of the most widely used comprehensive medical resources for professionals and consumers. View Source :

  • CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) therapy, which keeps your airways open while you sleep.
  • Oral appliances that reposition or retrain your tongue to stay clear of your airway and prevent blockage.
  • Surgical options like nerve stimulation, tonsil removal, and excess tissue removal to improve OSA symptoms through a variety of methods.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Medicare cover Ozempic for sleep apnea?

Medicare does not cover Ozempic for sleep apnea, but partially covers another GLP-1, Zepbound, for this diagnosis. Under Medicare, patients are expected to pay $50 per month for Zepbound.

How much is Ozempic without insurance?

Ozempic costs $499 per month without insurance. Some pharmacies offer discount programs, but costs still remain high.

How much is Ozempic with insurance?

The cost of Ozempic with insurance depends on your plan, but you may pay as little as $25 per month on some plans. To get a better idea of how much Ozempic can cost with your insurance plan, you can contact a representative from your insurance network to talk through any out-of-pocket costs.

How long will insurance cover Ozempic for sleep apnea?

The length of Ozempic coverage depends on your plan and health history. Typically, an initial authorization lasts for six months, but some plans cover this medication for 12 months at a time [/ocm_reference] . Renewals often require documented weight loss progress or updated provider notes.

Medical Disclaimer: The content on this page should not be taken as medical advice or used as a recommendation for any specific treatment or medication. Always consult your doctor before taking a new medication or changing your current treatment.

issues.title: Confusion about causation
issues.summary: It’s not difficult to develop an incorrect theory. Ice cream and spaghetti have more letters than tofu and celery, so therefore, foods with long names are more fattening than those with short ones. If you start moving forward with this theory, you’ll soon find outliers. Sugar only has five letters, and watercress has ten. If […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
It’s not difficult to develop an incorrect theory. Ice cream and spaghetti have more letters than tofu and celery, so therefore, foods with long names are more fattening than those with short ones.

If you start moving forward with this theory, you’ll soon find outliers. Sugar only has five letters, and watercress has ten. If we want to stick with our theory, we’ll have to come up with more and more complex reasons why we ignore some of the data and embrace the rest.

Of course, this is absurd.

And yet we do it all the time. Ornate explanations about the stock market, SEO or politics. Charts and graphs where we spend most of our time fitting a plot to a few dots, or amplifying the obscure to justify the theory.

A simple theory that matches the data is much more likely to accurately explain causation. It might not be a comfortable theory, or one that matches our trajectory, but it’s a better theory.

It turns out that the number of letters is completely irrelevant to how fattening a food is. I’m sorry you spent all this time on research, but you’re on the wrong path.

If you want to know why your marketing, your investments or your arguments are floundering, it might pay to reconsider the theory, not look for more data to justify the current one.

issues.title: Have your AI call my AI
issues.summary: Sharp lawyers have often used the fine print to win an advantage in a contract. It’s called the fine print for a reason–you’re not supposed to read it. But you should. Now, armed with AI, it’s significantly easier to bury arcane, unfair or unanticipated clauses in agreements, even (and especially) if we don’t expect it. […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
Sharp lawyers have often used the fine print to win an advantage in a contract. It’s called the fine print for a reason–you’re not supposed to read it. But you should.

Now, armed with AI, it’s significantly easier to bury arcane, unfair or unanticipated clauses in agreements, even (and especially) if we don’t expect it.

You shouldn’t sign anything until you’ve had your AI read it. And if it’s important, have your lawyer and her AI read it too.

The next step seems reasonable to me: You and I describe our agreement in plain English and then our mutual AI’s work out a written agreement that actually captures what we’ve agreed on. And for the avoidance of doubt, append each AI’s interpretation to the contract itself.

It shouldn’t be confrontational or adversarial. After all, it’s an agreement.

On the other hand, here are a dozen things many of us can do (or do better) if we stick with it: Three-ball jugglingTouch typingRubik’s CubeDrawingMental mathMemorizing a deck of cards or people’s namesMeditatingHistory or geographyFinding […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
You can’t become fluent in a foreign language in ten minutes a day, even if you try for months.

On the other hand, here are a dozen things many of us can do (or do better) if we stick with it:

Three-ball juggling
Touch typing
Rubik’s Cube
Drawing
Mental math
Memorizing a deck of cards or people’s names
Meditating
History or geography
Finding joy in small things
Typography
Ukulele
Italic handwriting
Morse code
Excel and HTML

There are two hard parts:

  1. The seven minutes after minute three
  2. Doing it again tomorrow

“I can’t do that,” might often be more honestly reported as, “I haven’t chosen to be able to do that.”

I hope it gives small businesses a bit of a boost.

issues.title: Come Meet Us Live at Granola HQ in SF: Granola’s VP of Sales and I Will Be There to Talk Agents for GTM, What’s Working and What Isn’t
issues.summary: We’re doing something a bit different. No stage, no 5,000 people, no badge line. Just a room at Granola’s HQ in San Francisco on December 8, a real conversation about agents for GTM, and time to hang out after. I’ll be there in person with Bardia Shahali, VP of Sales at Granola, for GTM Series... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
We’re doing something a bit different. No stage, no 5,000 people, no badge line. Just a room at Granola’s HQ in San Francisco on December 8, a real conversation about agents for GTM, and time to hang out after.

I’ll be there in person with Bardia Shahali, VP of Sales at Granola, for GTM Series #05. It’s part of Granola’s ongoing series where GTM leaders sit down with Bardia and get into the details of how they’re actually selling today.

Request to join here: luma.com/gtm-series-jason-lemkin

What We’ll Cover: 10 SDRs and AEs Down to 1 AE and 20 Agents

Not long ago, SaaStr had a pretty normal B2B sales team. About 10 SDRs and AEs, the usual tools, the usual ramp times, the usual turnover.

Today it’s 1 AE and 20+ AI agents running in production. That’s how we sell sponsorships, work inbound, run outbound, and follow up on the long tail of leads that no human team ever gets to.

Bardia and I are going to get into all of it:

  • Which agents are actually doing the work. Outbound, inbound, follow-up, qualification. Which ones we’d rebuild the same way, and which we’d do differently.
  • What broke. Plenty did. Agents need a ton of training and daily management. “Set it and forget it” doesn’t exist yet, and anyone telling you otherwise hasn’t deployed one at scale.
  • What the one human AE does now. The job changed a lot. Less prospecting, a lot more closing and orchestrating.
  • Who manages the agents. Running 20 agents is real, daily work for the humans on the team. That’s the part nobody talks about, and it’s where most deployments fall apart.
  • What this means for your sales team in 2027. Headcount plans, quota, comp, and which roles get rebuilt first.

Why Granola’s VP of Sales Is the Right Person to Push on This

Granola is one of the fastest-growing AI apps in B2B right now, and Bardia is building a sales org in the middle of all this change. He’s hiring humans, deploying AI, and figuring out the mix in real time, same as most of you.

That makes this a working session between two people with very different answers to the same question. Granola is scaling a sales team up. We scaled ours down and rebuilt it around agents. Both can be right depending on stage, ACV, and motion, and that’s what we’ll dig into.

Who Should Come

  • CROs, VPs of Sales, and sales leaders deciding how much of their 2027 plan runs on agents
  • Founders and CEOs who are still doing a lot of the selling themselves
  • RevOps and GTM ops leaders who’ll end up owning the agents either way
  • Anyone who has deployed an AI SDR, wasn’t happy with it, and wants to talk about why

The Details

  • What: GTM Series #05: Jason Lemkin, SaaStr AI, in conversation with Bardia Shahali, VP of Sales at Granola
  • Where: Granola HQ, San Francisco (exact address shared after you’re approved)
  • When: December 8, 2026, 6:00 to 8:30 PM. Please arrive by 6:30 PM
  • How: Registration requires host approval, and space is limited. Request to join at luma.com/gtm-series-jason-lemkin

Bring your hardest questions about agents in sales. The best part of these smaller sessions is always the Q&A and the conversations after, and we’ll both be sticking around for them.

See you there.

issues.title: Our AI VP of Revenue Can’t Close a Deal Yet. But It Co-Closed Two Six-Figure Deals in One Week.
issues.summary: In September I wrote that there still isn’t a good AI account executive. Agents had taken over most of our SDR work, much of first-line support and a lot of CSM work, but none of them could close. We Run 21 AI Agents and They’ve Closed Millions. But There Still Isn’t a Good AI Account... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
In September I wrote that there still isn’t a good AI account executive. Agents had taken over most of our SDR work, much of first-line support and a lot of CSM work, but none of them could close.

We Run 21 AI Agents and They’ve Closed Millions. But There Still Isn’t a Good AI Account Executive. Yet

That’s still true. 10K, our AI VP of Marketing and Revenue, can’t run a deal on its own. It isn’t on live calls yet, it doesn’t negotiate, and it doesn’t sign anything.

It can co-sell, though, and it’s very good at it. In a single week in November, it co-closed two six-figure sponsorship deals with us. One was Base44, Wix’s AI app builder. The other was a well-known B2B company we’ll leave unnamed. A third sponsor deal closed the same week.

"Our AI VP Revenue can't close a deal on its own yet. But it can come close.

It can co-sell.

And it does a really, really good job of it. It just co-closed two six figure deals this week." https://t.co/lYyPsqjrkhpic.twitter.com/RPsjpwPlvV

— Jason ✨👾SaaStr.Ai✨ Lemkin (@jasonlk) November 13, 2026

Top takeaways:

  • 10K handled the research, deck building, pricing, procurement prep, CRM updates and paperwork. Amelia ran the calls and the relationship.
  • The work 10K took over is what usually slows deals down: custom pricing, procurement questions, vendor forms and follow-up.
  • Renewal rates for our $100K+ sponsors went from the 20s to the 70s this year. 10K describes its contribution as “operational support.”
  • Every write 10K makes to Salesforce still needs approval, and we set it up that way on purpose.

1. Base44 Came in Inbound, and 10K Built the Deck During the Session

Base44 reached out after seeing our work with Replit, Lovable and Vercel at SaaStr AI Annual.

While the session was still underway, 10K built a deck showing how those direct competitors performed at our show: Replit first, Vercel around fifth, Lovable around tenth. It then laid out how Base44 could benchmark itself against them and why it would likely perform well too.

Someone on our team could have built that given a few days, but none of us has a few days. Most reps also wouldn’t know how each of those sponsors performed, and one three months into the job would have gotten it wrong. 10K had the numbers immediately because it’s connected to every system we use.

2. Pricing the Custom Work From 13 Years of Invoices

Base44 wanted something outside our standard packages, which meant third-party vendors for custom booths and other build-outs.

That usually takes a week of digging through old quotes. 10K went through 13 years of SaaStr Annual emails and paid invoices, estimated the cost of each custom item, added it to the Gamma deck and sent it.

A lot of deals stall at this step. The buyer is excited, the seller says “let me get back to you on pricing,” and two weeks go by. 10K had it done the same afternoon.

3. Procurement Prep: Wix as the Parent, Payment Terms and Collections

Before the procurement call, 10K flagged that Wix is Base44’s parent company and listed what we needed to settle: payment terms, T’s and C’s, the main points of contact, and who we’d collect from and how.

10K brings up collections on every deal, before the contract is signed.

4. After the Call: Commit in Salesforce, Revised Terms, Vendor Paperwork

By the time Amelia got off the procurement call, 10K had processed the transcript. It said it heard a verbal commit and asked to move the deal to Commit in Salesforce.

It then revised the T’s and C’s to match what Wix asked for, updated billing with the right addresses, and filled out Wix’s vendor paperwork.

The deal closed in November. Base44 is now listed on the site as a SaaStr AI Annual sponsor for next year.

5. What 10K Did and What Amelia Did

10K:

  • Competitive research and the deck, during the session
  • Pricing the custom work from historical invoices
  • Procurement prep: parent company, terms, contacts, collections
  • Reading every call transcript and flagging what the buyer wanted
  • Moving the deal stage, updating the opportunity, revising terms
  • Vendor paperwork and billing details

Amelia:

  • Every live call
  • The relationship and the judgment calls in the room
  • Final approval on anything 10K wanted to write to Salesforce or send

10K covers everything around the conversation, and Amelia covers the conversation. Right now 10K gets call transcripts through a third-party recorder. It’s close to joining calls live as an avatar, possibly within weeks. Until then, a human runs the meeting.

Amelia describes it as having a great CRO, finance lead and procurement person co-selling with you, with no commission.

6. Renewal Rates for $100K+ Sponsors Went From the 20s to the 70s

Events struggle with retention. Even the top B2B events have trouble keeping 50% of sponsors year over year. When the old B2B world cut marketing budgets to zero, renewal rates for our $100K+ sponsors fell into the 20s.

This year they’re in the 70s, roughly triple.

When we asked 10K how much credit it deserves, it called its contribution “operational support” and said it couldn’t split the dollars between itself and the humans. When pushed, it named three things:

  1. Making sponsor value easy to show. It builds renewal, outbound and inbound decks from every data point we have on an account, benchmarks the account against unnamed competitors, writes a narrative, and publishes it in Gamma. That used to take weeks. 10K regularly finds data Amelia had forgotten we had.
  2. Taking admin off the humans. It reads every call’s notes, updates opportunities, drafts contracts, reminds us about media upsells, and tracks everything daily.
  3. Making renewals and expansions visible. Meeting prep goes to Amelia’s Muse during the call, with competitive analysis and signals from Coresignal, Exa and others, including the person’s buying authority.

We can’t put a precise number on 10K’s share. Renewal rates tripled in the 11 months since it started.

7. Why Every Salesforce Write Still Needs Approval

10K can read Salesforce on its own. A human approves every write and anything sent to a customer.

Agents with too much autonomy do unexpected things. The same week, Amelia’s Muse ordered $138 of flowers for her on its own after a deal closed, and we didn’t know which card it would use. Another agent’s top idea was emailing every past SaaStr Annual speaker. With a base of about 400,000 B2B execs, an agent sending the wrong email to the wrong list would take months to clean up. Approvals take a few seconds each.

What Changed Since September

In September, agents could fill the top of the funnel and handle what happens after the sale, and the middle of the deal was still all human. Three months later, 10K covers most of the middle. The live conversation is what’s left.

10K started in January as a dashboard. Eleven months later, running 12 to 18 hours a day, it co-sells six-figure deals.

To test this on your own team this quarter: pick your next five deals that need custom pricing or procurement. Connect an agent to your CRM, call transcripts, email and invoice history, and have it do everything except the calls. Then measure how many days it takes off each deal.

issues.title: SaaStr AI App of the Week: SciFin. The Nutanix and Cohesity Founder Raised $44 Million to Build AI for Sales Teams.
issues.summary: SciFin is a sales tool. Let us start there, because its own marketing sometimes buries it under a bigger idea. Every sales organization runs on a picture of the pipeline that nobody fully trusts. The forecast call runs on rep opinion. Reps spend their week updating deals instead of selling. Managers collect updates instead of... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
SciFin is a sales tool. Let us start there, because its own marketing sometimes buries it under a bigger idea.

Every sales organization runs on a picture of the pipeline that nobody fully trusts. The forecast call runs on rep opinion. Reps spend their week updating deals instead of selling. Managers collect updates instead of coaching. RevOps rebuilds the same reports every week and still cannot tell leadership how much of the pipeline is real. And churn risk shows up a quarter after anyone could have acted on it.

Mohit Aron has run revenue organizations at serious scale: he co-founded Nutanix and founded Cohesity. His diagnosis is that the data is not missing. It is fragmented across the CRM, call recordings, Slack, and a dozen other tools, and it goes stale the moment it is entered. He calls that the Revenue Context Gap.

SciFin, which emerged from stealth in September 2026 with $44 million in seed funding, is his fix: one continually maintained picture of the revenue business, with an AI companion on top of it.

What SciFin Does

SciFin connects the tools your GTM team already uses and pulls the revenue context together: accounts, deals, forecasts, reps, territories, customer conversations, and operating workflows. It does not just aggregate the records. It unifies them, corrects them, and keeps them current as work happens. The company calls the approach Context Convergence, and the pitch underneath it is simple: replace your system of record with a system of reality.

On top of that picture sits Pixie, SciFin’s AI companion. Pixie is not a chatbot bolted onto the CRM. A set of agents runs continuously behind it: tracking deal metrics, processing meeting transcripts as they land, updating account context when new information arrives, and flagging risk before a manager has to ask.

So a sales leader can ask: which Q4 deals have had no contact in 14 days? Why is the East region forecast down from last week? And get an answer grounded in the current state of the business, not whatever was typed into Salesforce three weeks ago.

The value is spelled out seat by seat. Sales leaders see which deals and accounts need attention, and where reps need coaching before deals slip. RevOps can test targets against pipeline health, capacity, and coverage, and stops rebuilding the same answers every week. Reps walk into every meeting with the full deal picture, know what to ask and what to do next, and let Pixie draft the follow-ups and deal updates for their review. Teams can also build their own skills on Pixie and run them on demand, on triggers, or on a schedule.

And Pixie meets sellers where they already work: chat, voice, email, Slack, Microsoft Teams, and WhatsApp.

The Story, In Numbers

  • $44 million in seed funding, announced September 1, 2026, co-led by Altimeter and Madrona, with Foundation Capital, S32, and Zetta Ventures participating.
  • 2024: founded by Mohit Aron, co-founder of Nutanix and founder of Cohesity.
  • September 2026: emerged from stealth, focused first on revenue organizations.
  • One continually maintained operating picture across accounts, deals, forecasts, reps, territories, and customer conversations, instead of a dozen partial ones.

Why It Works

Revenue intelligence is a crowded graveyard of good demos. The pattern is always the same: a tool reads your CRM and your calls, produces confident answers, and the answers are only as good as the data hygiene of your least disciplined rep. Which is to say, not good.

SciFin’s ordering is different, and it is the whole bet. Maintain the context first, continuously, with software. Then put the AI on top of a picture that is actually current. Aron says it plainly: revenue teams do their best work when everyone shares the same current understanding of the business.

There is a second, quieter pitch in here for RevOps and finance: tool consolidation. SciFin’s line is keep the tools you value, consolidate the rest. If it retires two or three point tools in the GTM stack, the ROI conversation gets much easier.

And the founder matters. Aron did not discover the forecast problem in user interviews. He lived it running sales organizations at Nutanix and Cohesity, and he has the credibility with CROs that a first-time founder in this category simply does not.

Who It Is For, And The Honest Limits

SciFin is for mid-market and enterprise GTM teams: CROs and sales leaders who do not trust the forecast until they have interrogated five people, front-line managers who want coaching priorities instead of status meetings, RevOps teams drowning in manual reporting, and reps losing selling hours to admin. If your pipeline fits on one screen, you do not need it yet.

The honest limits. SciFin came out of stealth in September 2026. It has disclosed no customers, no pricing, and no performance benchmarks, so every product claim above is the company’s own until deployments speak for themselves.

The category is also a knife fight. Gong, Clari, and Avoma own pieces of this picture, Salesforce and HubSpot are building agents into the CRM itself, and every revenue leader has been burned by a tool that promised one true view before. SciFin’s distinction, maintained context versus aggregated records, has to survive contact with genuinely messy enterprise data.

And $44 million of seed capital cuts both ways. It buys time and talent. It also sets expectations very few seed companies ever meet.

The SaaStr AI Take

This is the problem we hit ourselves building agents at SaaStr. Our agents read every inbound lead, every reply, every renewal, and the model was never the hard part. The hard part was giving the agent a picture of the business that was complete and current enough to act on.

SciFin is aimed squarely at that layer, for the exact teams SaaStr serves: sales leaders, RevOps, and reps. That focus is why it makes sense as an App of the Week, and frankly why its sponsorship of SaaStr Annual makes sense too: this is a GTM product, sold to GTM leaders, in a room full of them.

The proof will be in the first named deployments. If the picture stays true inside a messy enterprise pipeline, SciFin will not stay a seed story for long.

You can find SciFin at scifin.ai.

issues.title: Dear SaaStr: How Do VCs Mitigate Investment Risks?
issues.summary: Q: How Do VCs Mitigate Investment Risks? For a while in the peak craziness of late 2020-early 2022, VCs in many cases … stopped mitigating risk. The upside seemed just so high when public SaaS companies were trading as high as 50x ARR or sometimes more. But now we’re back. To every VC taking risk,... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Q: How Do VCs Mitigate Investment Risks?

For a while in the peak craziness of late 2020-early 2022, VCs in many cases … stopped mitigating risk. The upside seemed just so high when public SaaS companies were trading as high as 50x ARR or sometimes more.

But now we’re back. To every VC taking risk, yes, that’s the job. But also mitigating it where practical.

There are a number of slightly subtle things the best VCs do, and the rest often don’t, to mitigate risk:

  • Getting other investors to carry their “Yellow Lights” . You’ll end up with investments sort of doing OK, with customers, but really burning too much cash to justify another check. The best VCs find Another VC to put in 90% of the Next Check here. You don’t have to write off the investment, but you don’t have to throw much more questionable money into the deal, either.
  • Selling their underperformers for more than they are worth . The best firms somehow sell their worst deals for $0.50 on the dollar, or $1 on the dollar, or even $1.50 on the dollar … when, really, they are write-offs. This helps a lot. I don’t know how they do it. But they do. They get acquirers to buy startups that others can’t engineer.
  • Minimizing fund politics. Politics can wreck returns . Yes, every partner needs to deploy $X per fund. But returns are rarely consistent across partners. By making sure investment decisions are as free of politics as possible, fewer “Almost” deals get done, and fewer second and third checks are wasted on the wrong portfolio companies. The Almost deals never return much, if any, capital. Partners with little deal flow, or poor deal flow, or fewer relationships, should be doing fewer deals, or playing other roles.
  • Building the right syndicates for capital-intensive deals . The wrong syndicate can wreck a capital-intensive start-up. No one wants to write the next check until there is a lead and FOMO. Lack of support in the syndicate, or a tapped-out syndicate, dramatically impacts growth and returns.
  • Getting really good at pricing. This is different than low-balling founders and deals . The best deals are always expensive, so this is hard. Even more so today, in the Best of Times in SaaS and Cloud. So it’s not as simple as being “disciplined” on price. Then you would have missed Slack at $250m. Or passed on Facebook’s Series B — Peter Thiel’s #1 investing regret. It’s especially important at medium and later stages, and there are many ways to do this. You can take a little more stage risk. You can build an epic brand. You can be an amazing partner to the VCs in the round before. You can pass when you can’t make enough money on a great one. It’s nuanced. But the best firms are really, really good at this.
  • Moving on with their time . Top VCs will often support the best founders even through tougher times. But mediocre founders? Or founders not giving it 100%? You sort of need to step off the board and step out of engagement if possible.

A related post here:

Need a Second Check From Your VCs? Here’s How “Reserves” Work

(note: an updated SaaStr Classic answer)

issues.title: AI influencers: What consumer sentiment data tells brands
issues.summary: As you scroll through your TikTok or Instagram feed, you’ll no doubt come across at least a handful of influencers trying to sell you something by wearing the latest viral lip gloss, hopping into luxury cars, and taste-testing popular treats. But what if I told you that while these content creators may look like real people, they’re actually AI influencers?
issues.author: esantiago@hubspot.com (Erica Santiago)
issues.content_html:
As you scroll through your TikTok or Instagram feed, you’ll no doubt come across at least a handful of influencers trying to sell you something by wearing the latest viral lip gloss, hopping into luxury cars, and taste-testing popular treats. But what if I told you that while these content creators may look like real people, they’re actually AI influencers?

If you’re a marketer or business owner who is already fully using AI in your digital marketing strategy, then you’re likely already familiar with the concept. You may even be curious about leveraging AI influencers in your influencer marketing strategy.

But how will your target consumers feel about the use of AI influencers? Will they be receptive, or can AI influencers erode the trust you’ve built with your audience? Can AI influencers really save you money compared to working with human influencers? And are all virtual influencers AI? Keep reading for answers to these questions and more.

Table of Contents

  • What are AI influencers, and why are brands considering them?
  • What do consumers think about AI influencers and AI models?
  • Do AI influencers build or erode brand trust?
  • Notable Virtual Influencers + Brand Examples to Learn From
  • Do AI influencers save brands money?
  • How to Use AI-Assisted Content Workflows Without Losing Authenticity
  • Common Pitfalls With AI Influencers and How to Avoid Backlash
  • What’s Next for AI Influencers
  • Frequently Asked Questions About AI Influencers

What are AI influencers, and why are brands considering them?

AI influencers are virtual personas whose appearance, voice, behaviors, or content are created or assisted by generative AI. An example of an AI influencer is Aitana Lopez, who has over 400,000 followers on Instagram. She’s marketed as a virtual fitness and lifestyle influencer and has promoted brands such as Amazon, Victoria’s Secret, Olaplex, and Razer.

Her work as an influencer has reportedly earned her and The Clueless, the Barcelona-based tech company that created her, over $11,000 per month.

          View this post on Instagram                      

A post shared by Aitana Lopez (@fit_aitana)

AI influencers fall under the umbrella of “virtual influencers,” but make no mistake — while every AI influencer is a virtual influencer, not all virtual influencers are AI-generated. For example, the virtual influencer, singer, and model Miquela Sousa (formerly known as Lil Miquela) was created in 2016 using artist-driven CGI, and her music is created by a collective of singers, songwriters, and instrumentalists—not generative AI.

Over the last decade, Miquela Sousa has worked with brands like Gucci, Prada, and Calvin Klein. She’s also the first virtual avatar to sign with a model agency, having signed to CAA in 2020 and previously being represented by WME.

          View this post on Instagram                      

A post shared by Miquela (@lilmiquela)

Why are brands interested in AI Influencers?

Brands are dabbling with using AI influencers and virtual models like Aitana Lopez and Miquela Sousa for three reasons — creative control, reduced costs, and scalable content.

Creative Control

Ruben Cruz, founder of The Clueless, says Aitana Lopez was created so the company could make a “better living and not be dependent on other people who have egos” or “who just want to make a lot of money by posing.”

In other words, Cruz wanted to avoid working with influencers whose personalities, creative processes, and work styles clash with his company’s creative vision—a sentiment brands wanting to leverage AI influencers can relate to.

AI and virtual creators will recite a script, deliver a video, or conform to a brand’s aesthetic exactly as agreed upon. Companies never have to worry about unwanted input or script changes that could slow production.

Reduced Costs

The initial creation of an AI influencer or virtual internet personality can cost anywhere from a few hundred dollars to a few hundred thousand. However, once out of the initial setup phase, AI influencers can save companies money on lighting, production, and paid partnerships.

Scalable Content

Human influencers need to sleep, eat, take breaks, pick up their kids from school, or walk the dog — they can’t make content 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. But AI influencers can. Though AI influencers like Aitana Lopez may look super busy doing their makeup, traveling, and hopping into luxury cars, it’s all fake— so they always have time to make content.

What do consumers think about AI influencers and AI models?

Many consumers feel that AI influencers corrode trust, with one Reddit user saying, “If I see something that is AI but tries to appear real, it’s an instant turn-off and trust killer. It’s enough for me to see it once for a brand, and the trust is gone forever.”

The skepticism toward AI influencers shows up in surveys, too. According to a study published via ResearchGate, 45.3% of consumers would view an ad with an AI influencer without taking action, 28.3% would ignore the ad completely, and only 26.4% would actively engage with the ad, such as by clicking or searching.

Do AI influencers build or erode brand trust?

AI influencers pose a high risk of eroding trust between brands and consumers because using a fake person to promote a brand’s goods or services doesn’t read as authentic. The appeal of human influencers and content creators is that they’re real people who cultivated a consistent following by being their genuine selves.

Influencers and content creators bond with their followers over shared interests, hobbies, and beliefs, and they often get their audience interested in a product or service by using it themselves.

In fact, a survey by Clutch shows that if a human influencer is found to use AI-generated content, 71% of consumers say they would question the recommendation, and 53% are less likely to buy from a brand known for using AI in social content.

An AI or virtual influencer can’t use a product or service, can’t have a genuine interest, nor a human experience to connect with human followers.

That said, the trust risk is not equal in every situation. It concentrates where audiences are skeptical, where safeguards are missing, where disclosure is weak, and where nobody is measuring the effect. Score each area below before you decide to leverage AI influencers.

How to score it:

  • Any No-go: Don’t launch. Fix the issue or choose a different approach.
  • All Go: Proceed to a limited pilot.
  • Mix of Go and Conditional: Launch only if each Conditional item has an owner and a fix date before the first post.

Why these four areas matter: Consumers aren’t rejecting AI across the board. That same Clutch survey also found that 42% view AI positively when it’s used for educational content, but 64% would trust a brand or creator less if AI were used to misrepresent products. Nearly 90% say it’s important to disclose AI-generated content.

Disclosure is also becoming a legal matter. For example, as of June 9, 2026, New York requires certain ads featuring AI-generated human performers to include a disclosure, and the EU’s Article 50 transparency obligations have applied since August 2, 2026. Always double-check to confirm what applies to your markets.

Notable Virtual Influencers + Brand Examples to Learn From

Virtual influencers have been working with brands for years, so their campaigns show what works and what doesn’t. Each example below is broken down by what it teaches about creativity, community, transparency, representation, and governance.

1. Miquela x PAC SUN Back-To-School Campaign

PacSun teamed up with Miquela for its back-to-school and holiday 2022 campaigns, and said the deal marked the start of a broader push into virtual influencers. The two collaborated on social content to amplify those seasonal campaigns after both had taken part in the ComplexLand digital event.

Source

Creative

The partnership was built around a persona who already lived online, with roughly 3 million Instagram followers at the time. Choosing a virtual star with an existing audience meant the brand didn’t have to build one from scratch.

Community

The fit rested on shared audience territory. PacSun framed the move as a way to strengthen its connection with a core demographic exploring the digital space. Takeaway: pick a persona whose community already overlaps with yours.

Transparency

Miquela is open about being a virtual influencer, describing herself as a “Robot living in LA,” so there was no deception to manage. The audience was in on it from the start.

Representation

PacSun’s president pointed to Miquela’s involvement in the Black Lives Matter movement and the Rally the Vote campaign as aligned with the brand’s values. That raises a fair question for any brand: a persona’s advocacy is authored by its creators, so scrutinize whose voice is really speaking.

Governance

A virtual star never ages, clothes always fit perfectly, and she does what you ask, but that control is also a responsibility. Set clear approval processes for any social or political messaging attached to a persona, since you are effectively the speaker.

2. Samsung and Sam

Sam is Samsung’s own virtual influencer, created in collaboration with Cheil and the Brazilian design firm Lightfarm. She is used mainly in Latin America, and in July 2023, she connected to the regional launch events from Seoul, where she covered the global Galaxy Unpacked event.

In January 2024, she was named Samsung’s AI ambassador ahead of Galaxy Unpacked 2024, where she was set to present products and interview five live influencers from Latin America.

Source

Creative

Sam works because she’s integrated into real brand moments rather than confined to social posts. She has blogged, made tutorials, released a music video promoting the Galaxy Z Flip 5, and helped sell devices at Unpacked events.

Giving a persona several jobs, from host to educator to performer, builds her into the brand’s story rather than treating her as a one-off stunt.

Community

Samsung paired Sam with real people. At Unpacked 2024, she interviewed Latin American creators live, bridging the virtual and human sides of the community. Her role was also regionally focused, which suggests a persona can work better as a local community figure than as a global one.

Transparency

Sam is openly presented as a virtual influencer, and Samsung’s own newsroom calls her one. Her role is also clear (host, guide, ambassador), so audiences aren’t asked to believe she personally uses Samsung products.

Representation

As a brand-owned character, Sam’s look, voice, and personality are entirely Samsung’s choices. Treat that as a casting decision: involve regional teams and creators in shaping a persona who will speak to their audience, rather than designing her centrally and exporting her.

Governance

Samsung reported that Sam helped boost early sales of its new devices in Latin America, including a 30% increase in sales on its Mexico live-shopping portal.

Set measurable goals and a content plan before launch, attribute any performance claims to their sources, and decide in advance who will maintain the persona, since a neglected virtual influencer can quickly feel stale.

3. Amazon Prime, boAt & Kyra

Kyra was launched by FUTR Studios in January 2022 as a virtual influencer that is both CGI and AI-powered. Her first brand partner was boAt for the #FutureOfAudio campaign, which launched its Rockerz 330 and 333 ANC neckbands.

Amazon Prime Video followed, integrating Kyra into the promotion for its sci-fi series “The Peripheral,” with her creator noting that the team recreated the show’s VR headset and transported her to its setting.

Source

Creative

Both campaigns leaned into science fiction, which is where a virtual persona excels. boAt said the collaboration enabled a sci-fi-like audio-visual experience that wouldn’t be possible with any other influencer. Choose briefs a human can’t easily deliver.

Community

The boAt launch reached beyond social posts. Kyra appeared at an in-person boAt party through a 3D projection installation, alongside human creators. Bridging virtual and live moments helps a persona feel part of a scene rather than an ad.

Transparency

The pairing with Prime Video worked partly because it was an obvious fiction-meets-fiction match. When the story is openly synthetic, disclosure becomes part of the creative rather than a caveat.

Representation

Kyra was positioned as India’s first virtual influencer, and her creators said they planned a new model with a South Indian focus. That’s a useful prompt for brands: local relevance matters, and a single persona rarely represents an entire market.

Governance
