Early results were strong, but they come from launch-novelty periods. Judge a persona on sustained performance, not a debut.

4. Dior & Noonoouri

In 2018, Dior’s beauty team had Noonoouri recreate its Rouge Dior Ultra Rouge launch film. The original starred Natalie Portman; the tribute was nearly a shot-for-shot reenactment, down to the Dior ring. Noonoouri also took over the Maison’s Instagram during the Dior Cruise show.

Source

Creative

Rebuilding a famous campaign with a stylized animated character created instant buzz. The contrast between the original and the tribute did most of the work.

Community

Dior used the persona to reach younger Instagram audiences interested in high-end beauty. The takeaway is to match a persona to an audience you’re trying to grow, not just one you already have.

Transparency

Noonoouri’s doll-like proportions make her unmistakably an animation, so nobody is misled about what they’re seeing. A clearly stylized persona carries less deception risk than a photorealistic one.

Representation

Her exaggerated features reflect a stylized ideal, not a real body. Brands should consider what beauty standard a digital character promotes, especially in cosmetics.

Governance

Stepping into a role originally played by a real actress raises questions about likeness, permission, and optics. Clear agreements around any reference to a real person’s work are essential.

Do AI influencers save brands money?

AI can save brands money, but it depends on what you count. AI influencers can cut the most visible line item, production, while adding costs elsewhere: oversight, disclosure, rework, reputation, and measurement. A fair comparison looks at the total cost of the program, rather than the cost of a single post.

You can look up costs online but be aware that cost claims are mostly published by vendors and agencies that sell AI content, and they vary widely. Some guides puts AI influencer creation at $15,000 to $100,000+ upfront, with monthly costs of $500 to $15,000+. But other sources claim 80-95% savings on large volumes of video. Treat all of these numbers as starting points for your own testing, not benchmarks.

Taking a Total-Cost View

1. Production. This is where savings are most credible. Once a persona exists, the marginal cost of producing one more piece of content approaches zero, and there are no talent fees, travel, or scheduling.

The catch is the upfront build and the ongoing work of generating, editing, and approving content. A persona that looks effortless usually still has a team behind it.

2. Risk management. Brands often cite reduced risk of scandal as a draw. In a World Federation of Advertisers finding reported by Favikon, 58% of brands interested in AI influencers named reduced risk of influencer scandals as a top draw. But the risk doesn’t disappear completely; it only changes shape.

You swap the risk of a creator’s behavior for the risk of your own content errors, off-brand outputs, or a backlash against the concept itself. Budget for review and an escalation plan.

3. Disclosure compliance. This cost is growing. Platforms like Instagram and TikTok have their own AI labeling rules and protocols. And other countries and regions have legal requirements regarding AI disclosure. In the EU, for example, transparency obligations for AI-generated content began to apply in August 2026.

The direct cost is modest, covering labels, templates, and legal review. The hidden cost is audience trust: consumer distrust is a recognized downside when disclosure is unclear.

4. Rework. Generated content needs corrections: anatomical glitches, inconsistent facial expressions, misreading cultural cues, tone issues. Rework hours rarely appear in a vendor’s cost comparison, so track them in your own use case.

5. PR and reputation. As I said earlier, public perception of AI influencers or synthetic personas ranges from curiosity to hostility, and it varies by category and audience. Set aside time and budget for a communications plan, including how you’ll respond if people accuse you of replacing real creators.

6. Community impact. Human creators bring a ready audience and a relationship with it. A new AI persona has to build both. The savings can also be offset on the other side: some AI adopters found that when creators use AI to cut their own costs, those savings haven’t led to lower fees, because brands pay for influence and credibility.

And partnerships with AI accounts aren’t a sure thing; Data shows that brand deals with AI social accounts fell by about 30% in the first eight months of 2025 compared with the same period in 2024.

7. Measurement. Fairly comparing AI and human influencers takes planning. You need matched campaigns, consistent metrics, and enough time to see past the novelty effect. Some of this has a real cost in analyst hours and tooling, and without it, you’re making decisions based on anecdotes.

As one analysis puts it, the honest comparison isn’t a cost debate but a question of what a campaign asks the influencer to do.

Where AI Influencers Tend to Save Money (and Where They Don’t)

They tend to help when you need high volumes of content, many variations to test, a tightly controlled brand look, or multilingual output. They tend to be a poor fit when the sale depends on lived experience or personal credibility, such as skincare results, health claims, parenting, or financial advice.

There, the cheaper post can cost you in conversion and trust.

A Qualitative Worksheet to Complete Before You Model Any Finances

Before you build a spreadsheet, answer these in plain language. If your team can’t answer them, then you’ll already know you need to reevaluate your strategy.

Then add two summary questions: What is the strongest reason this would save us money, and what is the strongest reason it wouldn’t? Count the “High” ratings. A cluster of them in risk, disclosure, or community impact is a signal to slow down, no matter how good the production savings look.

Then, build the model.

Once you’ve done the worksheet, a simple model has four parts: one-time setup costs, recurring monthly costs, the hidden costs from your worksheet (rework hours, legal review, monitoring, crisis reserve), and the performance side (conversions, engagement, or sales per dollar spent). Run it against a human-creator pilot of similar scope, and revisit it after a quarter, not a week.

The Bottom Line

AI influencers can lower the cost of making content. Whether they lower the cost of the program depends on your category, your audience, your compliance exposure, and how honestly you count what’s outside the production line. The brands most likely to come out ahead are the ones that measure the whole picture and start small.

How to Use AI-Assisted Content Workflows Without Losing Authenticity

Audiences forgive AI-assisted content that’s honest and consistent. They don’t forgive content that feels off-brand, evasive, or unreviewed. Build the workflow around human judgment, and aim for consistency over perfection.

Codify your brand voice.

Write the voice down in a form both people and AI tools can use.

  • Voice guide: Tone, vocabulary, phrases to use and avoid, and a few on-brand and off-brand examples.
  • Persona sheet (if you use a virtual influencer): Backstory, values, topics they will and won’t discuss, and visual style.
  • Standing prompts: Turn the guide into reusable instructions so every draft starts from the same baseline.

Set clear approvals.

Not every asset needs the same scrutiny. Tier them by risk:

  • Low risk (routine posts, repurposed content): Social lead approves.
  • Medium risk (sponsored content, product claims): Brand and social approve.
  • High risk (health, finance, political or social topics, anything involving a real person’s likeness): Brand, legal, and social all approve.

Name one person who can pull a post immediately.

Standardize disclosure.

Create templates in advance so disclosure is never improvised. Cover three cases: AI-generated persona, AI-assisted content from a human creator, and paid partnerships. Each should state who made it and whether it’s an ad, in plain language. Have legal review the templates once, then reuse them.

Check requirements for each platform and market, since they differ and are changing.

Govern your assets.

Keep one source of truth for approved content.

  • Store approved images, prompts, character references, and disclosure templates in a single library with version history.
  • Log which tool and prompt produced each asset.
  • Record usage rights, especially for any real person’s likeness or voice.
  • Retire outdated assets so they can’t be reused by accident.

A content management system, such as HubSpot Content Hub, can serve as a shared home for assets and approval steps, but the process matters more than the tool.

Run review loops.

  • Before publishing: Check voice, accuracy, cultural fit, and disclosure. Reject anything that looks polished but feels hollow.
  • After publishing: Review comments and sentiment weekly in the early weeks.
  • Monthly: Compare a sample of recent posts against the voice guide to catch drift, and update the guide with what you learn.

Establish who owns what.

Escalate questions on tone to brand, questions on claims or rights to legal, and questions on audience reaction to social. One person should own the overall workflow so nothing falls between teams.

Favor consistency over realism.

Hyper-realistic output isn’t the goal. A persona that stays recognizable, sounds like your brand, and is clearly labeled will earn more trust than one that’s flawlessly lifelike but inconsistent. When in doubt, a human decides.

Common Pitfalls With AI Influencers and How to Avoid Backlash

Most backlash comes from a few repeatable mistakes, but each one is avoidable.

Weak Disclosure

The problem: Audiences feel tricked when they discover a persona is AI after the fact, and regulators and platforms increasingly expect clear labeling.

How to avoid it: Say it upfront. Put the AI label in the bio and on sponsored posts, and use plain language rather than burying it in hashtags.

Uncanny Visuals

The problem: Almost-human faces, odd hands, and inconsistent features break trust fast and invite mockery.

How to avoid it: Choose a stylization you can execute well and keep it consistent. A clearly stylized character often lands better than a flawed attempt at photorealism. Have a human review every image before it goes live.

Values Misalignment

The problem: A persona that comments on social issues or endorses products it can’t plausibly use will seem opportunistic, because a company is writing every word.

How to avoid it: Define what the persona will and won’t talk about. Skip causes you aren’t prepared to support with real action, and avoid testimonials that depend on personal experience.

Poor Representation

The problem: Using AI to depict diverse identities without involving those communities can read as tokenism, and generative models can reproduce stereotypes.

How to avoid it: Involve people from the communities being portrayed in development and review. Use AI personas alongside human creators rather than as a replacement for them.

Over-Automation

The problem: Fully automated posting and replies produce tone-deaf responses, repeated phrasing, and errors nobody catches in time.

How to avoid it: Keep a human in the approval loop for anything public, especially replies, sensitive topics, and sponsored content. Automate drafting and scheduling, not judgment.

Unclear Ownership

The problem: If it’s unclear who owns the persona, the underlying model outputs, or any real person’s likeness or voice involved, disputes can surface at the worst moment.

How to avoid it: Document ownership and usage rights in contracts from the start, including agency and vendor agreements. Record which tools and training materials were used.

Mitigation Checklist

Disclosure

  • AI label appears in the bio and on every relevant post
  • Sponsored content is marked as an ad
  • Disclosure wording is approved by legal and checked for each platform and market.

Visual Authenticity

  • Style is consistent and deliberate, not a half-realistic compromise
  • A human has checked every asset for glitches and artifacts
  • A reference sheet defines the persona’s look

Voice Consistency

  • A written voice guide and persona sheet exist
  • Off-limits topics are defined
  • Posts are sampled monthly against the guide

Cultural Review

  • Content is reviewed by people familiar with the target market
  • Imagery and language are checked for stereotypes
  • Community members are consulted where the persona represents them

Consent

  • Written consent covers any real person’s likeness or voice
  • Contracts specify permitted uses, duration, and compensation
  • Rights to the persona and its assets are documented

Privacy

  • Follower data and DMs are handled under your privacy policy
  • No personal data is entered into AI tools without approval
  • Data practices comply with the rules in each market you serve

Crisis Response

  • One person has authority to pause or remove content immediately
  • A holding statement is drafted in advance
  • Roles for brand, legal, and social are assigned
  • A plan exists for retiring or pausing the persona if trust breaks down

What’s Next for AI Influencers

I can absolutely see both virtual and AI influencers becoming more common as businesses further integrate AI into their digital marketing strategy, but three shifts are worth planning around: more interactivity, more personalization, and tighter regulation. The regulatory evidence is much stronger than the evidence on the other two, so plan accordingly.

Near-term Shifts

Interactivity: expect more, with thin evidence so far. Industry commentary points to AI influencers paired with chatbots to offer 24/7 personalized engagement. Marketers also describe tracking conversation depth and return engagement as AI-driven interactions grow. Most of this is vendor and agency commentary rather than measured results, so treat it as direction, rather than proof. One practical point is firm, though: if a persona chats with people, EU rules now require that they be told they’re interacting with AI (see below).

Personalization: promised, not yet proven. Brands can use AI personas to give customers more personalized attention without expanding costly support teams. I found no independent data showing this works better than human-led engagement, so test it before building a strategy on it.

Regulation: the clearest shift. Governments are starting to set rules for AI-generated content in advertising, particularly around disclosure. For example, the EU’s AI Act includes transparency requirements for AI-generated content and for AI systems that interact with people.

In the US, New York has passed a law requiring disclosure of AI-generated “synthetic performers” in ads, and the FTC has indicated that its endorsement guidance applies to virtual endorsers as well as human ones. Other jurisdictions are considering similar measures.

Now, I’m not a lawyer and this isn’t legal advice, but I can tell you these rules differ by region and platform, and they change frequently. So, before running a campaign with an AI persona, check the current requirements for each market you’re targeting with qualified counsel.

Review quarterly.

Rules, platforms, and tools are changing quickly enough that annual reviews will lag. Each quarter, review four things:

  • Policies: Check disclosure language and templates against current EU, US federal, and state requirements. Update anything that changed.
  • Voice standards: Compare a sample of recent posts against your voice guide and persona sheet. Fix drift and add new examples of on-brand and off-brand content.
  • Vendors: Reconfirm contracts, usage rights, data handling, and AI-labeling features. Ask what changed in their tools and terms.
  • Pilot results: Review performance against your human-creator benchmark, plus sentiment, rework time, and incidents. Decide to continue, adjust, or stop.

Assign one owner to run the review, with brand, legal, and social each contributing.

Start with a phased pilot.

The timeframes below are suggestions, so adjust them to your campaign cycle.

Phase 1: Limit channels (weeks 1-4). Launch on one or two channels and in a limited set of markets. Start with the markets where disclosure rules are clearest. Write starter creative guardrails before the first post, covering topics to avoid, tone, and approval steps.

Phase 2: Test messages (weeks 4-8). Run small A/B tests comparing AI-persona content with a human-creator benchmark on the same message. Change one variable at a time and measure conversion, not only engagement.

Phase 3: Monitor sentiment (ongoing from launch). Review comments, mentions, and shares weekly. Track whether audience reaction is curious, neutral, or hostile, and flag any confusion about whether the persona is AI. Set a threshold in advance for when you pause.

Phase 4: Codify guardrails and decide (weeks 8-12). Turn what you learned into written rules for visuals, voice, topics, disclosure, and escalation. Then make an explicit scale, hold, or stop decision based on results and sentiment, not momentum.

Expand only after a pilot passes your own criteria. Keeping it small is what lets you change course cheaply.

Frequently Asked Questions About AI Influencers

Do AI influencers need to disclose that they are AI?

In practice, yes, and the rules are tightening. Platforms like Meta, TikTok, and YouTube have their own AI labeling requirements. On the legal side, the EU’s AI Act transparency obligations (Article 50) began to apply from 2 August 2026, and they cover content generated or modified with AI.

In the US, the FTC still expects a clear “this is paid” disclosure on sponsored posts. Some sources also report that the FTC treats presenting an AI-generated persona as a real human without disclosure as potentially deceptive, and that several states are moving toward requiring a synthetic-performer disclosure.

Treat the legal details as a moving target and have counsel review any paid campaign, especially if it reaches EU audiences. Beyond compliance, disclosure is also good brand hygiene: audiences tend to react worse to a reveal than to an upfront label.

How should brands measure AI influencer success?

Use the same core metrics you’d apply to any creator: reach, engagement rate, click-through, conversions, and cost per acquisition. Then add a few that are specific to synthetic personas.

Track audience sentiment (are comments curious, indifferent, or hostile?), brand-lift or recall in the persona’s target segment, and content production efficiency, since one of the main advantages is speed and cost.

Be cautious with headline numbers. Some analyses suggest AI personas can be cheaper than human creators. In contrast, others find human influencers drive higher engagement, so run your own test against a human-creator benchmark rather than trusting industry averages.

When should brands avoid AI influencers?

Avoid them wherever personal credibility is the product. That includes skincare or supplement claims that rely on real results, health and wellness advice, parenting, financial guidance, and any category where followers expect lived experience.

An AI persona can’t truthfully say “I tried this and it worked for me.” They tend to fit better into visual, aspirational, or entertainment-led categories such as fashion, gaming, and lifestyle.

Also steer clear if your audience is hostile to synthetic content, if you can’t commit to clear disclosure, or if your team lacks the capacity to manage the persona consistently over time. Public backlash against AI-generated models in fashion advertising shows the reputational risk is real.

Can AI influencers fit DEI and representation priorities?

They can broaden the range of faces and identities a brand shows, but they come with real trade-offs. A brand can create personas across ages, body types, ethnicities, and abilities without a casting budget.

The risk is that this substitutes for hiring and paying real people from those communities, and it can read as tokenism or “representation without the representatives.” Generative models also carry biases from their training data, so outputs often skew toward narrow beauty standards unless you actively guide them.

A sensible approach is to use AI personas alongside human creators rather than instead of them, involve people from the communities being depicted in the creative process, and review outputs for stereotypes before publishing.

How do we keep brand voice consistent with AI-assisted content?

Start with a documented voice guide: tone, vocabulary, words to avoid, and example posts that are on-brand and off-brand.

Feed that guide into your prompts or tooling as a standing reference, and keep a fixed character sheet for the persona (backstory, values, visual style) so the look and personality don’t drift between posts. Keep a human editor in the approval loop, especially for anything customer-facing or sponsored.

Finally, audit regularly by comparing a sample of recent posts against your guide, since drift tends to creep in gradually.

issues.title: AEO benchmarking: What market data reveals about AI search
issues.summary: AEO benchmarking measures your brand’s AI search visibility against competitors and market trends. It tells you whether a change in your visibility comes from the market or from your own brand, so you can prove performance to leadership before you change tactics.
issues.author: ttaylor@hubspot.com (Tristen Taylor)
issues.content_html:
AEO benchmarking measures your brand’s AI search visibility against competitors and market trends. It tells you whether a change in your visibility comes from the market or from your own brand, so you can prove performance to leadership before you change tactics.

Here’s the problem it solves.

Your AI visibility drops this week, and you can’t tell whether ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity changed how they answer or your content slipped. Without a benchmark, every dip looks like your fault — and every spike looks like your win.

Table of Contents

  • What is AEO benchmarking, and why does it matter now?
  • AEO Benchmarking With a Two-Tier Model: Market Benchmarks Plus Brand Performance
  • What to Measure in AEO Benchmarking: Citations, Share of Voice, and Sentiment
  • How AEO Benchmarking Datasets Work: Prompt Cohorts, Cadence, and Coverage
  • AEO Benchmarking Tools You Can Try Now with AI Search Sensor
  • AEO Benchmarking to Diagnose Market Shifts vs. Brand Issues
  • Turn AEO benchmarking into an action plan.
  • Best AEO Benchmarking Practices for Teams
  • Frequently Asked Questions About AEO Benchmarking

What is AEO benchmarking, and why does it matter now?

AEO benchmarking is the practice of comparing your brand’s visibility in answer engines against a reference point: competitors, an industry baseline, or your own history. If you’ve done competitive benchmarking in other channels, the logic is the same. You measure against peers on consistent metrics so a number like “38% visibility” carries meaning. The channel is what changes. Instead of rankings and clicks, you measure how often ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity mention and cite your brand.

It matters now for two reasons.

  • Buyers research in AI search.HubSpot’s 2026 survey of more than 3,000 CRM purchase decision-makers worldwide found that 42% used AI search during their evaluation, and those buyers were 36% more likely to purchase than those who didn’t.
  • Clicks are shrinking. Pew Research Center tracked 900 U.S. adults’ browsing in March 2025. Users clicked a traditional result in 8% of visits when a Google AI summary appeared, versus 15% when it didn’t, and clicked a link inside the summary in 1% of visits (Pew, July 22, 2025).

Together, these create an accountability gap. Organic traffic can fall while rankings hold, because the answer appears above the links. Leadership asks what changed, and without a benchmark you can’t separate a market shift from a brand-specific issue.

Pro tip: Treat every unexplained change as two questions. What happened to the market? What happened to us? Benchmarking answers the first so you can focus on the second.

AEO Benchmarking With a Two-Tier Model: Market Benchmarks Plus Brand Performance

The two-tier model pairs market-wide benchmarks with brand-level performance data. It’s how you benchmark your AI search performance against your industry: read the external trend first, then your internal KPIs.

AI Search Sensor provides market-wide AEO benchmarks. It’s a free dashboard (currently in beta) covering ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. HubSpot AEO measures brand-level AI visibility performance, and teams on Marketing Hub Pro or Enterprise get AEO included. AI Search Sensor pairs with HubSpot AEO for two-tier AEO measurement.

A single tier misleads in both directions. Brand-only data can’t show whether a drop is yours or everyone’s. Market-only data can’t show whether you’re keeping pace. Comparing the two before you change tactics prevents the most expensive AEO mistake: fixing a problem that isn’t yours.

HubSpot’s AEO case study shows benchmarking first in practice. Benchmark data revealed significant Reddit citation growth in German and French markets with zero HubSpot mentions. After a localized campaign, HubSpot’s mention rate rose from 0% to 33.5% in France and 17.1% in Germany within one month.

What to Measure in AEO Benchmarking: Citations, Share of Voice, and Sentiment

AEO benchmarking measures four things across AI engines: citation rate, share of voice, sentiment, and citation/source attribution. Each answers a different diagnostic question.

The citation rate formula comes from Stackmatix’s September 2026 measurement guide. AI Search Sensor reports two related market benchmarks: visibility score (how often a brand is mentioned relative to other tracked brands, 0 to 100%) and citation share (how often a brand’s domain appears among all citations analyzed).

Share of Voice vs. Competitors

Share of voice shows how prominent you are relative to competitors. If 100 brand mentions appear across you and your competitors and 25 are yours, your share of voice is 25%. It’s the metric most likely to explain why a competitor gets named in buying conversations, and you don’t.

Sentiment

Sentiment shows whether engines describe your brand favorably, and it connects directly to your brand health. If sentiment falls while visibility holds, you have a perception problem rather than a discovery problem, and the fix differs.

Citation and Source Attribution

Source attribution shows where engines get their information about you, and it often points off your own site. In AI Search Sensor’s Top Citation Domain Analysis, NerdWallet and Bankrate out-cite Bank of America and JPMorgan combined in Financial Services (HubSpot, updated October 2026, based on 50 representative HubSpot AEO portals). When third parties shape your category’s answers, your own blog can’t move the number alone.

Brand-Level Companions: Topic Coverage and Entity Alignment

Topic coverage is the share of your priority topics where your brand appears at all. Entity alignment is whether engines describe your brand, products, and pricing accurately, which Stackmatix tracks as brand mention accuracy. Market benchmarks don’t show either one, so they belong in your internal tier.

How AEO Benchmarking Datasets Work: Prompt Cohorts, Cadence, and Coverage

A reliable AEO benchmark depends on three design choices: which prompts you track, how often you run them, and which engines you cover.

Prompt Cohorts

A prompt cohort is a fixed set of prompts that you run the same way over time. Prompt cohorts improve benchmark reliability through consistent coverage. An ad hoc query set, where you test whatever question comes to mind, can’t show trends because week-to-week results aren’t comparable.

Build the cohort around intent. Stackmatix recommends 50 to 100 prompts organized by topic cluster and intent type, covering category, brand-adjacent, and direct brand questions.

Pro tip: Check out more market research tools and resources that can help you source category questions and competitive context.

Cadence and Consistent Sampling

Run the same cohort on the same schedule. Weekly is a practical default and matches the weekly rhythm of AI Search Sensor’s traffic and citation data. Keep engines, prompt wording, and settings fixed, and label any change so a method shift doesn’t look like a market shift.

Confidence and Limitations

AI answers vary from run to run, so one sample can mislead. A 2026 paper by Ronald Sielinski sampled Perplexity, OpenAI’s SearchGPT, and Google Gemini repeatedly. It found unstable citation rankings and many apparent domain differences inside the noise floor, and it recommends reporting uncertainty estimates.

If you’re new to the concept, this guide to statistical significance explains why small gaps often mean nothing. Stackmatix reaches a similar conclusion and recommends 30 to 60 day trend windows over point-in-time snapshots.

AEO Benchmarking Tools You Can Try Now With AI Search Sensor

AI Search Sensor is a free tool that benchmarks AI visibility, citations, and traffic by industry, and you can test it below. Paid options exist too. Stackmatix’s guide compares platforms such as Scrunch AI, Otterly AI, Semrush’s AI Toolkit, and Ahrefs Brand Radar. For market context, start with the widget.

How to Test Category Questions in the Widget

Work through the dashboard in this order:

  1. Answer Engine Volatility Tracker. The daily 0 to 100 score reads Calm (0 to 29), Moderate (30 to 59), Elevated (60 to 89), or Extreme (90+). It shows whether engines changed recently.
  2. AI Visibility Benchmarks by Industry. Toggle between visibility score and citation share, and note where recognizable brands in your industry sit.
  3. Citation Share Trends. See which content types and source channels engines favor right now.
  4. Your own numbers. Check these last.

That order applies the two-tier model: external market signal first, then internal brand performance.

What we like: AI Search Sensor publishes its methodology. Industry benchmarks use four representative companies per industry, built from public information. Traffic, citation, and volatility charts use anonymized HubSpot customer data.

To see your brand’s numbers, use HubSpot AEO.

AEO Benchmarking to Diagnose Market Shifts vs. Brand Issues

To tell whether answer engine behavior is shifting across the market right now, check the volatility score, then compare it with your own metrics. The AI Search Sensor compares daily mention rate, citation rate, citation type, and AI-referred traffic against rolling averages. A spike means the engines changed. Market-wide benchmark changes help diagnose external AI shifts versus brand-specific performance issues.

Two hypothetical scenarios show the logic.

In the first, your visibility falls during a week when volatility reads Elevated. Wait a week, gather more data, and report it as a market event.

In the second, your visibility falls during a Calm week while a competitor’s share of voice climbs. That points to your brand, and a content audit is justified.

Both scenarios prevent the same false alarm: rewriting content to fix a change that content didn’t cause.

Turn AEO benchmarking into an action plan.

An AEO benchmarking action plan sorts findings into two buckets: actions the evidence supports and hypotheses that need testing.

Actions Supported by Evidence

  • Answer-first content updates. If citation share shows engines favoring a content type you under-publish, such as comparison pages or guides, prioritize it. HubSpot’s case study reports a 56% increase in AI citations after it updated product pages with FAQs, question-based headlines, tables, and structured data.
  • Structured data and entity checks. If accuracy or sentiment data shows engines misdescribing you, audit schema markup and the pages engines pull from.
  • Off-site gaps. If review sites, earned media, or forums gain share, add off-site work to the plan.
  • Competitor gaps. Pull prompts where a competitor is named and you aren’t. A competitive analysis kit gives you a structure for comparing positioning and content side by side.

Hypotheses That Need Testing

Conclusions from a single week of data, and explanations for why an engine favors a format, are hypotheses. Test them on a limited set of pages, then watch your cohort for several weeks before scaling.

Reporting to Stakeholders

Lead with the two-tier comparison: what the market did, what you did, and the gap. Label which conclusions are evidence and which are hypotheses. Leadership trusts a team that states its uncertainty.

Best AEO Benchmarking Practices for Teams

Comparable AEO benchmarks require governance. The practical version is a short checklist:

  • Assign cohort ownership. One person owns the prompt list and approves changes.
  • Version the cohort. Keep a dated log of added, removed, or reworded prompts.
  • Fix engine coverage. Start with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, and add engines deliberately.
  • Label everything. Every chart carries its window, engine set, cohort version, and sample size.
  • QA before reporting. Spot-check raw answers against your tool’s scores.
  • Set a reporting cadence. Weekly for the team, monthly for leadership.
  • Baseline before targets. Collect four to six weeks of data before setting goals.

Frequently Asked Questions About AEO Benchmarking

How many prompts should I include in an AEO benchmarking cohort?

Start with 50 to 100 prompts organized by topic cluster and intent. That range, recommended by Stackmatix, covers category, comparison, and brand questions. Smaller cohorts work for pilots but produce noisier results, so keep the set stable and trend it over several weeks.

Which AI engines should I track first for AEO benchmarking?

Track ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity first. AI Search Sensor and HubSpot AEO both cover these three, so your brand data and market data line up on the same engines. Add Google AI Overviews and others once your core workflow is steady.

How often should I run my benchmark tracking?

Run it weekly. Weekly cadence matches the rhythm of AI Search Sensor’s market data and gives you enough points to see a trend. Review monthly for strategy, and judge change over 30 to 60 day windows rather than single days.

How do I connect AEO benchmarking to my content roadmap?

Map each finding to a content decision. Citation share by content type shows which formats to publish, competitor prompt gaps show which topics to cover, and channel data shows where off-site work belongs. Rank the list by evidence strength and put hypotheses behind a test.

How do I report AEO benchmark changes to leadership without over-attributing the cause?

Show the market trend and your trend side by side, then state what you know and what you’re testing. If volatility was Elevated or Extreme when your numbers moved, say so, and hold off on claiming credit or blame until you have several weeks of data.

Ready to see where the market stands? Get the data behind these benchmarks in the State of AEO report.

issues.title: How to use AI to write a blog post (that isn’t slop)
issues.summary: Like a hammer or even a hair dryer, AI is just a tool. It needs to be wielded skillfully by an expert to achieve greatness. And in a world increasingly full of “AI slop,” this is especially true when exploring how to use AI to write a blog post.
issues.author: rsukhraj@hubspot.com (Ramona Sukhraj)
issues.content_html:
Like a hammer or even a hair dryer, AI is just a tool. It needs to be wielded skillfully by an expert to achieve greatness. And in a world increasingly full of “AI slop,” this is especially true when exploring how to use AI to write a blog post.

When using AI to write blog posts, you can’t just sit back and click copy-paste and publish. You need to create a thorough brief, build an outline, draft one section at a time, and then edit with the emotion, lived experience, and discernment only a human can.

Despite the popularity of AI-assisted content creation, 62.7% of marketers admit brands need more unique, human-centered content to compete. Google agrees, saying AI can help with research and structure, but you should fact-check and review everything by hand before you publish, as it can get facts wrong.

AI can produce quantity, no doubt, but its quality is up for debate — at least without your guidance. AI is wonderful for structure and first drafts, but only you can bring the expertise, voice, and final quality assurance that produces great content. And this guide will show you how.

You’ll get a five-step process for creating blog posts with AI, human-review checkpoints, prompt templates, and tips for keeping your voice and avoiding the “slop” label.

Table of Contents

  • What is AI slop? (And why you want to avoid it)
  • How to Use AI to Write a Blog Post in 5 Steps
  • AI Prompts for Blog Posts You Can Copy
  • Frequently Asked Questions About Using AI to Write a Blog Post
  • Great content needs human and machine.

What is AI slop? (And why you want to avoid it)

Generative AI is powerful and useful. It can analyze information and produce materials faster than any human could by hand, which is likely why 80% of marketers now use AI for content creation in some form.

But I’d argue we’re crossing into “too much of a good thing” territory when it comes to generative AI, and I’m not alone. Our research shows that more than half of marketers say AI has made content creation so easy that they are now struggling to stand out in a heavily saturated market.

AI has also faced concerns around plagiarism, bias, data privacy, and inaccuracy for several years. Add its now-mainstream accessibility, and the formulaic output has earned an unsavory nickname, “AI slop.”

AI slop is low-quality, mass-produced digital content created using generative AI with little to no human input or creative thought. (I’m sure you’ve seen the fliers.)

          View this post on Instagram                      

A post shared by @sandsvisual

Users and businesses sharing it have been ridiculed as low-effort, unoriginal, or even “fake.” Harsh, yes, but also easy to avoid.

Solution: A Blend of Man and Machine

Listen: It’s easy to get caught up in the speed and “polished” finished products that AI generates in seconds; I don’t blame anyone. But at this point, we, as marketers and consumers, have seen enough of its generic output to know we need to do better.

AI is a collaborator, not a replacement for your judgment, creativity, experience, or effort.

Now, I know what many of you are thinking: “Why would I do all that work when AI can do it for me?” And I get it. You want to save time and labor, but to quote former Director of the HubSpot Blog Karla Hesterberg: “The only truly effortless [AI] process produces slop.”

Producing high-quality content with AI — content that delivers real value, builds trust with your audience, ranks well in search engines and answer engines, and closes qualified buyers — requires human effort and insight. It requires human knowledge and input to produce something new and extraordinary.

I’m not saying don’t use AI. I’m saying use your skill with it.

This is something we learned firsthand by adopting AI into our editorial process at HubSpot, and it heavily influenced the steps in this guide. Tools like HubSpot’s brand voice and AI content writer were built with this all in mind.

How to Use AI to Write a Blog Post in 5 Steps

AI is like an eager new intern. It’s fast and takes direction, but it doesn’t have your lived expertise or knowledge of your customer, data, and standards. The steps we share in this guide are designed to compensate for that and ensure you maintain your brand voice.

Each step has something you give AI, a choice you make, something you get back, and a moment when a human steps in, based on my decade as a content editor and strategist.

You can follow these steps in common tools like Claude or ChatGPT, or in HubSpot, which offers multiple options.

HubSpot’s free AI Content Writer can draft blog posts, outlines, and more inside the tools you already use. For a full blog workflow, Content Agent builds blog posts, social content, and landing pages in your brand voice. It lives in Agent Hub, which is included in Starter, Professional, and Enterprise editions.

Now that you know what you need, let’s break down our five steps.

1. Gather your input.

Before you turn to an AI content creation tool, you need the right input. Think of these as the creative brief you send an intern.

What inputs does AI need to perform well?

  • Audience: Who is reading, and what do they already know? HubSpot’s 2026 State of Marketing report found that only 65% of marketers report having high-quality audience data. If you’re in the other 35%, start small. HubSpot’s free Make My Persona tool can help you sketch a reader profile in minutes.
  • Goal: What should the reader learn or do next?
  • Primary keyword & search intent: What are people really asking when they search it?
  • Angle: What’s your take? What makes your post different?
  • Approved sources: The facts, data, and links the AI may use.
  • Examples: Two or three samples of writing that sound like you.
  • Format: Word count, headings, and any must-have sections.
  • The point of view. AI can summarize what’s out there. Only you know what you believe and have seen.
  • Which claims can you back up. If you can’t source it, don’t ask AI to write it.
  • Data privacy: What data stays out. Don’t paste customer details, private financials, or unreleased plans into a tool your company hasn’t approved.
  • A “do not use” list. Add outdated stats, competitor claims you can’t support, and any topic your legal team wants to review.

The “data privacy” point is worth calling out. The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology lists data privacy as one of 12 risks that are unique to or worse with generative AI. The risk includes leaks of personal or sensitive data. Check your company’s AI policy first.

If you use HubSpot, Agent Hub runs on your CRM data. HubSpot says its third-party AI providers are contractually barred from training on your data. You also control what AI can access. You can read how it works in the HubSpot Trust Center.

Pro tip: Put all your consistent inputs (e.g., brand voice, company history) on a one-pager and save it as a template you can reuse for every post. This saves you time and maintains consistency across different editors.

Need a blog topic? Try HubSpot’s free Blog Idea Generator to spark ideas, then pick the one that fits your goal.

2. Create an outline.

An outline is the heading and talking points plan that AI follows. Skip it, and drafts wander. Start with your brief of inputs. Then ask AI to turn it into an outline. Pair each heading with the reader’s question it answers and the source that supports it.

Outline Prompt for a Blog Article

To get an outline you can actually use, get specific. The more ambiguity you leave, the more likely the finished product will miss the mark.

Look at the difference between a vague prompt and a specific prompt.

The specific prompt:

  1. Asks for three options.
  2. Outlines what it expects from headers. Each H2 should answer a real question. This makes it easier for answer and search engines, as well as readers, to find what they need.
  3. Attaches a source to each section. Tell AI which approved source supports which heading.
  4. Emphasizes answers. HubSpot’s 2026 State of Marketing report advises answering users’ questions directly, in conversational language, with structured, scannable content. That said, ask AI for a direct answer to every question in the first two sentences of the section.

Try entering your topic in HubSpot’s free AI Content Writer and asking for an outline. Then edit the headings to match your brief.

Want more prompt ideas? Our guide to writing AI prompts shows how specific details lead to better results.

3. Draft in sections.

Once you have a solid outline, you can work with AI to generate the main sections of your article.

Generate section by section for higher quality.

You wouldn’t just give a new intern a brief and say “go,” right? You’d likely have them complete the assignment in small chunks to make sure they’re on the right track. Approach A the same way.

Draft sections one by one to increase focus and maintain quality, or even better, draft select sections rather than all of them. Review each one in depth (more on that in the next section). Then move on to the next.

Try this flow:

  1. Paste your approved brief and outline. Tell AI to follow it.
  2. Draft the intro first. Ask for a direct answer in the first two sentences. Edit and provide feedback.
  3. Draft one H2 at a time. Include the sources for that section only.
  4. Review and edit. Fix voice, facts, and flow while the section is small.
  5. Ask for a tighter version. Short sentences read better. So do plain words.

With challenges like plagiarism and inaccuracy, this chunked approach to writing a blog post with AI is worth the effort.

Personally, I prefer to use AI-generated copy simply as a very rough example that gets my creative juices flowing. I edit and revise to fit my own voice, adding my original thoughts, knowledge, and examples, among other things.

You can follow this drafting workflow in Content Hub, HubSpot’s content marketing software. The free AI Content Writer lets you enter a prompt or use slash commands to generate text on demand. Highlight a paragraph, and you can ask it to edit or rephrase the copy.

Pro tip:Content Agent, currently in beta, builds blog posts, LinkedIn content, and landing pages from a single starting point. It researches competitors, pulls keyword data, and loads your brand voice before it writes. For more on where AI helps most in blogging, see our guide to AI writing tools for blogging.

But remember: Drafts written in chunks still need human editing.

4. Edit like a human.

Even your best human-written draft shouldn’t be published without thorough editing. Trust, quality, and originality are ensured in the edit, and that goes double for AI-assisted blog posts.

Before anything goes live, have a human team member check four key things:

  • Facts and sources
  • Originality and clarity
  • Unique data and examples
  • Brand voice

Fact-check and cite sources.

AI has a way of sounding extra confident, even when it’s wrong.

Heck — Most tools even come with a disclaimer like this one from ChatGPT admitting it “can make mistakes.”

Google says this is because generative models predict a likely sequence of words instead of retrieving facts. So, the output can contain errors, or what we call “hallucinations.” NIST, the U.S. standards agency, lists this risk (it calls it “confabulation”) among the 12 risks associated with generative AI.

So what should you do?

Fact-check and review all AI-generated content before you publish. Here’s a routine you can use for every draft:

  1. Highlight every claim. Facts, stats, names, dates, quotes, and product features all count as claims.
  2. Ensure they’re linked to a current, primary source. That’s the original study, the official page, or the company itself. If they’re not linked to a primary source, ask the AI to find the sources and add them. Remove or replace anything from a secondary roundup or summary.
  3. Open the link yourself. AI can make up URLs. Confirm the page is live and includes the information shared.
  4. Check the date. Prioritize sources from the last two years. This helps ensure the information you’re sharing is current and accurate.
  5. Cut what you can’t verify. If you can’t back it up, take it out.

For high-stakes topics (i.e., legal, medical, financial, or anything that names a specific person or company), add a second reviewer. People can slip up, too, and when it comes to risky subject matter, it’s wise to double-check.

Ensure originality and clarity.

Original means more than not copied. It means your content adds something new. AI-generated content, by its very nature, is derivative, so editing is a must to deliver fresh value.

Edits can be important for ownership, too. In January 2025, the U.S. Copyright Office said that AI-generated output can be protected by copyright only if a human author contributed enough of the expressive elements. Writing prompts doesn’t count. Creative arrangement and modification can, but “enough” leaves a lot of ambiguity. Ask your legal team about your specific situation.

Before you publish any AI-assisted content, run through these checks:

  • Plagiarism: Run a plagiarism check. Compare key passages with your sources, and rewrite anything that is too close. Tools like Grammarly and Scribbr offer free plagiarism tools to flag suspicious passages.
  • Clarity: Cut long sentences. Define jargon the first time it appears. Read it aloud. If it doesn’t sound like something your brand would say, chop it.
  • Privacy: Make sure no confidential information slips into the draft (e.g., customer details, private numbers, or other sensitive data).
  • Accessibility: Add descriptive alt text to images, use clear headings, and write link text that makes sense out of context.

Also, eliminate common AI writing patterns by:

  • Cutting the fluff. Delete extra words or generic sentences that don’t add value to the article. Keep an eye out for redundancy as well. (I’ve definitely noticed AI tends to say the same thing repeatedly using different words.)
  • Adding specifics. For instance, replace “many companies” with a named company, a number, or a story.
  • Taking a stand. Add your own opinions. AI won’t do this for you.
  • Varying the rhythm. Change up the sentence structure to keep things interesting and flowing naturally.
  • Banning the clichés. Add a short “never use” list to every prompt. Some common phrases can help make an article easier to digest, but too many are a trademark of AI.

Add original data and examples.

AI doesn’t know your customers, numbers, or stories. You do. That’s why adding first-hand research, case studies, or examples to support AI-assisted blog posts is a powerful way to make them more original.

Enhance AI content with:

  • Your own data. A survey result, a customer count, a before-and-after metric. This not only gives readers something they can’t get anywhere else, but it also gives people a reason to link back to your website as a source.
  • In-house case studies and examples. A campaign you ran, a mistake you fixed, a result you saw.
  • Quotes from experts. Use real people, with their permission and their title.
  • Screenshots. Show the tool or the steps as they appear today.
  • First-hand or personal anecdotes. Like in-house examples, relevant personal experiences give your content lived proof that readers can’t find elsewhere.

This matters for search, too. Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines flag main content made with little effort, originality, or added value. Your data and examples are the added value.

Including unexpected examples is one of my favorite ways to add originality and personality to my articles. I mean, come on: how often do you see Bollywood mentioned in marketing blogs?

Source

(You’re welcome, readers.)

For more edits that make AI drafts sound human, see our guide to humanizing AI content.

Edit for brand voice and perspective.

More than anything, make sure that your AI-assisted content is true and consistent with your brand voice and perspective.

Using language or sharing opinions that contradict what your brand has already established can cause confusion, and any confusion about your brand’s beliefs can lead to distrust.

To help maintain your brand when using AI to write a blog post, create a voice profile. A voice profile is a short description of how you write and what you sound like. Think of it as a style guide you include in every prompt.

Example:

Voice: Friendly, expert, plain-spoken.

Sentences: Under 20 words. Mix short and medium.

Address the reader as “you.”

Explain industry jargon or acronyms the first time they appear.

Avoid: “game-changer,” “unlock,” “in today’s fast-paced world.”

Here’s how to build one:

  1. Share 2-3 examples that show your brand. Choose posts that sound like you at your best and represent a variety of formats. Skip anything another editor heavily rewrote.
  2. Name three to five traits that describe your brand. Then say what each looks like on the page. For example, “friendly” might mean using “you” and a little humor.
  3. Set simple style rules. Cover sentence length, words you love, and words you avoid. Add how you handle jargon, humor, and calls to action.
  4. Document and save it. Store it where your team can find it, and update it whenever you make the same edit.

HubSpot’s Brand Voice learns your style from your writing samples and generates this guide for you. After that, you can export it to share with AI tools or have it automatically apply your style in supported tools, such as Marketing Hub. You can also set up a brand voice using AI, then fine-tune its personality and tone. Features can vary by plan, so check what your subscription includes.

Source

Need a deeper dive? See our guide on AI brand voice training.

5. Optimize for search and AI answers.

Whether you’re writing by hand or by AI, write for readers first, then polish for search and answer engines. Thankfully, they aren’t dramatically different. Google’s guide to AI search features says AI features are built on the same core ranking and quality systems as traditional search. So, you just need a clear, useful, well-organized post. Here’s how that looks tactically.

Structure for skimmability.

People skim; so do search and AI systems. Make your post easy to scan by:

  • Putting answers first. Include clear, direct answers in the opening lines of a section.
  • Using clear headings. Google says readers generally prefer pages organized into sections with clear headings.
  • Incorporating structured data and schema.
  • Keeping paragraphs short. Two or three sentences are easier on the eyes, especially when reading on mobile.
  • Using lists and tables when the content has steps or comparisons.
  • Adding helpful visuals. High-quality images, videos, charts, and other visual aids can help drive home your messages and also add variety to your content.

Litmus is a great example of skimmable formatting in action.

On-Page SEO Prompts

AI is a handy assistant for small, repetitive SEO tasks. Ask it for options to edit for:

For a deeper walkthrough of search intent, structure, internal links, and measurement, see our guide to blogging for SEO.

Publish.

You’ve drafted, edited, and optimized for getting found. Now it’s time to publish. Check your final boxes in four main steps.

1. Do a final check. Read the whole post once, start to finish, as a reader would. Look for voice slips, vague claims, and broken links, and edit as needed. Then confirm the basics:

  • The post opens with a direct answer.
  • The title, meta description, and URL match your primary keyword.
  • Every stat links to a reputable, primary source.
  • Images have accurate captions and alt text.

2. Decide on disclosure. Some teams add a short note on how AI was used in their writing process. Google says sharing how content was created can give readers helpful context and set expectations. Check your company policy and local rules first. (See the FAQ below.)

3. Publish & measure what matters. In HubSpot’s 2026 State of Marketing report, measuring ROI was the top challenge, cited by 33% of respondents. So, keep it simple. Pick three numbers that reflect your goals. A good baseline to consider:

  • Search visibility: impressions and clicks in Google Search Console. Google also offers a generative AI performance report there that shows how your content appears in AI features.
  • Engagement: Time on page, scroll depth, and hovering.
  • Conversions: clicks on your call to action and the leads that follow.

HubSpot can show many of these in one place with its marketing analytics. To see how your brand shows up in AI answers, try the free AEO Grader or HubSpot AEO, currently in beta.

4. Learn from every post. Keep a short prompt log:

  • Which prompts gave you usable drafts?
  • Which edits did you make again and again?
  • What did your reviewer catch?

Turn those repeat edits into new rules in your voice profile. Your next draft will start closer to being done.

Ready to put this process into action? Try HubSpot’s AI Content Writer to draft your next post, then follow the five steps above to make it yours.

AI Prompts for Blog Posts You Can Copy

Below is a series of prompts that work with HubSpot’s AI Content Writer and most other AI tools. Replace everything in [brackets] before you send, but remember that whatever you get back is just a starting point.

All AI-generated content needs to be reviewed with a human touch to deliver unique value and achieve your long-term search and sales goals. This is especially true when using public prompt templates, as AI tools generally produce the same results for the same inputs.

Every prompt needs your audience, your goal, your approved sources, and your voice profile. Without them, you’ll get generic results. So, include this block before you start drafting anything:

Audience: [who they are and what they already know]

Goal: [what the reader should learn or do]

Approved sources: [paste links or notes. Use only these.]

Voice profile: [paste your voice profile]

1. Brief Creation

Using the details above, create a one-page brief for a blog post about [topic]. Include the reader’s main question, the angle, a two-sentence direct answer, an outline with H2s and H3s, and the approved source that supports each section. Flag anything the sources don’t support.

2. Outline

Give me three outline options for a [word count] blog post about [topic]. Each H2 must answer one reader question. Put the direct answer first. Don’t add sections that the approved sources can’t support.

3. Section Drafting

Write the section titled “[H2 heading]” in [150-250] words. Use short sentences. Use only the approved sources. Mark any claim that needs a source check with [CHECK].

4. Voice Rewriting

Rewrite the paragraph below in my voice profile. Keep every fact the same. Don’t add new claims. Cut filler and cliché phrases.

[paste paragraph]

5. Fact-Check Planning

List every factual claim in the draft below: stats, names, dates, quotes, and product features. For each one, tell me what kind of primary source would confirm it. Don’t confirm anything yourself.

[paste draft]

6. Meta Descriptions

Write five meta descriptions of around 150 characters for a post titled “[title]”. Use the primary keyword “[keyword]” once. Promise only what the post delivers.

7. Internal Links

Below are my draft and a list of related posts with URLs. Suggest up to five places to add internal links. For each, give the sentence, the post, and descriptive anchor text. Only suggest links that truly help the reader.

[paste draft]

[paste related posts and URLs]

Use these prompts strategically and flesh them out with your own original thoughts. For more on writing prompts that work, see our guide on how to write AI prompts.

Pro tip: Save your best prompts in a shared doc. Add notes on what each one is good for. Your whole team will get better results, faster.

Frequently Asked Questions About Using AI to Write a Blog Post

Will Google penalize AI-written blog posts?

Google hasn’t explicitly said that it penalizes AI-written content, but its quality standards and spam policy on content abuse at scale target mass-produced pages that add little value for users, regardless of how they’re made. Using AI to generate many pages without adding value is one of its named examples. Publish helpful, accurate, edited posts, and you’re on the right side of that line. For more, see Google’s guidance on generative AI content.

How should I disclose AI assistance?

Start with what readers would find useful. Google says sharing how a piece of content was created can give readers helpful context and establish expectations. For example, take “We used AI to help draft this post. Our editors reviewed and fact-checked it.”

Laws are also changing. The EU AI Act’s transparency rules under Article 50 took effect on August 2, 2026, and cover AI-generated text published on matters of public interest, with an exception for text that receives human review or editorial control and is attributed to a person or organization. Whether these rules apply to you depends on your content and audience. Ask your legal team.

Which parts should humans always review?

All of it. But these parts need extra care:

  • Facts and stats: Trace each one to a primary source.
  • Quotes and names: Confirm who said what, and their title.
  • Product and pricing claims: Check them against the official page.
  • Voice and tone: Does it sound like you?
  • Data privacy: Remove any customer or confidential details.
  • Metadata: Title tags, meta descriptions, structured data, and alt text. Google says to review these, too.
  • Final approval: One named person signs off.

How do I stop AI hallucinations?

Unfortunately, you can’t eliminate AI hallucinations, but you can reduce the risk. Give AI approved sources and tell it to use only those. It may not always listen, but do your due diligence. Draft in small sections. Ask it to mark any claim that needs checking. Then verify every fact yourself.

Hallucinations occur because generative models predict likely words rather than retrieve facts, as Google explains. NIST lists confabulation among the key risks of generative AI. Human review is the safeguard.

Can AI create images or charts for the blog?

Yes, AI can help generate visuals, suggest layouts, or turn your own data into a chart. But never ask it to invent numbers. Build charts from data you can document, and note the source in the caption.

For AI-generated images, add accurate alt text and check the tool’s usage terms. Google also recommends adding image metadata when generating content with automation. Then review every visual the way you’d review any other part of the post.

Great content needs human and machine.

I can’t say it enough: AI is a tool. It’s a powerful tool, but a tool nevertheless. A hammer can’t build the house, and AI can’t write a great blog post on its own.

Use AI for monotonous things like general info, structuring, outlining, and small repetitive tasks. And save the work that matters most for your people: unique expertise, lived experience, and discernment. That’s what readers want more of, and it’s what AI can’t fake.

Ready to try it? Start drafting with HubSpot’s AI Content Writer, then make every word your own.

issues.title: Branded vs. unbranded queries in AI search — and how to track them
issues.summary: Picture two shoppers. One asks ChatGPT, “Are Nikes good shoes for marathon runners?” The other asks, “What’s the best running shoe?” Both want top-notch athletic shoes. Only one specifically wants to know about Nikes. That’s the idea behind branded vs. unbranded queries in AI search.
issues.author: rsukhraj@hubspot.com (Ramona Sukhraj)
issues.content_html:
Picture two shoppers. One asks ChatGPT, “Are Nikes good shoes for marathon runners?” The other asks, “What’s the best running shoe?” Both want top-notch athletic shoes. Only one specifically wants to know about Nikes. That’s the idea behind branded vs. unbranded queries in AI search.

But why does this small difference matter for your brand? A branded query comes from someone who already knows you. They’re checking you out, comparing you with a rival, or even confirming a choice. AI’s answer can shape how someone sees you right before they decide.

An unbranded query comes from someone who’s still shopping. They haven’t picked a brand yet, so if the AI names you, you’re in the running. But if it doesn’t, you may never get a shot. In AI search, unbranded queries are where new buyers meet you, or don’t if you don’t play your cards right.

Each type reaches a different audience and tells you something different about your performance. Optimize for and track only one, and you reach half the audience and get half the story.

Don’t believe me? In November 2025, Google added a branded queries filter to Search Console that automatically separates branded and unbranded search queries and keywords. AI search needs the same split. It also needs a plan to track both.

In this guide, you’ll learn how to:

  • Tell branded and unbranded prompts apart.
  • Run a simple tracking routine each week.
  • Read your results without fooling yourself.

Let’s start with the basics.

Table of Contents

  • What are branded vs. unbranded queries in AI search?
  • Why Branded vs. Unbranded Queries Change How You Measure AEO
  • How to Run Prompt Tracking & Measure for Branded vs. Unbranded Queries
  • How to Interpret Branded vs. Unbranded Results and Share of Visibility
  • How HubSpot AEO Scales Prompt Tracking for Branded vs. Unbranded Queries
  • Frequently Asked Questions About Branded vs. Unbranded Queries
  • Keep track of both shoppers and queries.

What are branded vs. unbranded queries in AI search?

A branded query names a brand. That can be your company name, a close variation, a common misspelling, or one of your product names. For example, “Are Nikes good shoes for marathon runners?” is a branded query.

So is “Are Air Force 1s good running shoes?” as they include a Nike product. Branded queries are valuable because they indicate that users are aware of your brand and are using AI to research it specifically.

An unbranded query, on the other hand, names no brand. It describes a category, a problem, or a use case. “What’s the best shoe for marathon runners?” is unbranded. Unbranded queries are valuable in their own right, as appearing in them can expose you to a new audience of potential customers.

These types of queries aren’t new to AI or answer engines. Branded search has always meant people looking for you by name. Google even built the idea into Search Console, where a filter now sorts the two for you.

Source

Queries vs. prompts: What’s the difference?

You’ll notice two words throughout this guide: queries and prompts. They sound alike, but they’re not quite the same.

In traditional search, people type short queries, like “best running shoes” or “Nike shoes.” In AI search, they write longer, chattier prompts, like “Which brand makes the best shoes for running a marathon?”

Here’s how we’ll use them. “Query” is the general idea. “Prompt” is the exact question you track in an answer engine like ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity.

There are also three types of unbranded prompts.

Three Kinds of Unbranded Prompts

A branded prompt is easy to spot. It names a brand. Unbranded prompts take a little more care, because they come in three flavors. Each one matches a different moment in the buying process. The table below puts them next to a branded prompt so you can see the contrast.

Pro tip: Watch out for prompts that name only a competitor, like “Mailchimp alternatives.” They’re not unbranded, because they name a brand. They’re not yours either. Give them their own label so they don’t skew your numbers later.

If you can sort a prompt into one of these four rows in five seconds, you’re ready for the rest of this guide.

Note: One more bit of vocabulary. We use “AI search” and answer engine optimization (AEO) to mean the same thing as you adapt to this new era of search. And the goal with both is to show up inside AI-written answers.

So, why does this sorting matter so much? Because branded and unbranded prompts behave very differently in AI answers. Mix them, and your results get misleading. Let’s look at why.

Why Branded vs. Unbranded Queries Change How You Measure AEO

Branded and unbranded prompts measure two different aspects of your AEO.

  • They answer different questions. Branded prompts show how AI describes you and reveal user intent, while unbranded prompts show whether AI brings you up at all.
  • They produce very different results. A brand name in the prompt makes a mention far more likely. Without one, you have to earn it.

They also need different fixes. A weak branded result usually points to messaging or facts. A weak, unbranded result usually indicates how much the rest of the web talks about you. Because of this, branded and unbranded prompts also require different measurement. This is where many teams go wrong.

The Blended-Score Trap

The most common mistake teams make when measuring branded and unbranded queries in AEO is combining both types into a single score. Combining makes your AI visibility look better than it really is, leading to skewed strategy and missed goals.

A branded prompt names you, so the answer almost always mentions you. An unbranded prompt doesn’t, so the engine has to decide whether you belong in the answer. If it does, that’s discovery — the part of AI search that brings in new buyers.

If you combine your branded and unbranded scores, you can end up thinking more new people are discovering your brand than actually are.

Think of a restaurant to illustrate. Regulars walk in and ask what your specials are. New diners ask, “Where should we eat?” If you count both groups in one number, you can’t tell whether new customers are finding you or if regulars are coming in more frequently. AI answers work the same way.

Here’s how that can look with numbers. Say you track 500 answers.

The blended 34% visibility looks fine, but separately, you see buyers who don’t know you only 20% of the time. Now add 50 more branded prompts. Your blended score climbs. Your discovery doesn’t move at all.

So what should you do instead? To avoid the blended trap, the fix is simple: report the two groups separately, then read them side by side.

It all starts with prompt tracking.

How to Run Prompt Tracking & Measure for Branded vs. Unbranded Queries

So far, we’ve covered what to compare: branded and unbranded results, kept apart. But a score has to come from somewhere. That’s where prompt tracking comes in.

Tracking works best as a routine. We recommend weekly, as AI answers are probabilistic. Ask the same question twice, and you may get two different answers.

SparkToro and Gumshoe.ai tested this and found there was less than a 1-in-100 chance of getting the same list of brands twice on ChatGPT, while getting the same list in the same order was closer to 1-in-1,000.

HubSpot’s own guidance says the same. HubSpot AEO runs tracked prompts daily, and because responses change, you should review multiple days or weeks before judging a trend. Also expect gaps. An engine may not return a usable answer for every prompt on every day.

All that said, think of tracking as two layers: the tool runs prompts daily, and you review the results weekly.

Step-by-Step: Running a Weekly Prompt Tracking Cadence

First, set up your tracking.

  1. Build and deduplicate your library. Merge prompts that ask the same thing in different words.
  2. Label every prompt. Record its status (active, paused, or retired), buyer stage, branded or unbranded, and whether it names a competitor.
  3. Assign an ICP and geography. Each prompt should point to one buyer and one market.
  4. Start tracking. Let at least a couple of weeks of data build up before you draw conclusions.

Next, establish your weekly tracking cadence.

  1. Check for gaps. Did any prompts or engines come back empty? Note them so they don’t skew your rates.
  2. Pull your two visibility rates. Read your results in two separate piles every week. Branded results tell you about positioning. Unbranded results tell you about discovery.

To get your visibility rate, divide the answers that mention you by all the answers in that group.

Visibility Rate = mentions of your brand / total number of answers tracked

In our earlier example, that’s 90/100 = 90% for branded and 80/400 = 20% for unbranded. Compare these rates with the last four weeks, not yesterday.

How to Interpret Branded vs. Unbranded Results and Share of Visibility

With your numbers recorded, it’s time to understand what those numbers are telling you and turn their insights into actionable takeaways.

First, let’s go through some core terms and concepts as defined by HubSpot AEO.

  • Brand Visibility: How often your brand is mentioned in answers to the prompts you track. If you’re named in 70 of 100 answers, that’s 70%.
  • Prompt coverage: The share of tracked prompts where your brand appears at least once.
  • Competitor mentions and share of voice: Your mentions divided by all brand mentions, yours and your rivals’, across the same prompts.
  • Citations: The pages and domains engines point to. A source can be cited without naming you, so citations and mentions are separate.

These four numbers will show up in almost every report you write. The trick is comparing them fairly over time.

Raw Counts vs. Comparable Rates

A raw count is a number with no context. “We appeared in 12 prompts” sounds fine. But 12 out of 15 is great, and 12 out of 60 is not. A comparable rate always has a denominator. Use “12 of 60 prompts (20%).” Then you can compare this month with last month, even if your library grew.

Also, don’t fixate on where you appear in a list. The SparkToro study we covered earlier found that order was far less stable than the frequency with which a brand showed up.

Unbranded vs. Branded Ratio

Now let’s put it all together. The table below shows what each side of your data is really telling you.

Compare the two types with the branded-to-unbranded ratio.

Ratio = branded visibility rate / unbranded visibility rate

In our example, that’s 90/20 or 4.5 to 1. A high ratio means people find you mostly after they already know you. A falling ratio means discovery is improving.

If someone asks for one headline number, lead with the unbranded rate. It’s the harder one to move, and the better sign that new buyers are finding you. For our example, the blended 34% says, “We’re doing fine.” The split says, “People who know us find us. Strangers find us 2 times in 10.” That second version shows you where to focus.

Here’s a real example from our own work. HubSpot’s team found its awareness-stage visibility was weak. So it launched an FAQ glossary of top-of-funnel terms. When the glossary was cited, brand visibility for awareness-stage prompts rose 35 percentage points. That’s HubSpot’s own result, not a promise. But it shows how unbranded gaps point to specific content to build.

Findings like this only help if they reach the right people in a clear format. That’s what the checklist below is for.

Reporting Checklist: Branded-to-Unbranded Ratio

When analyzing your results every week, do the following:

  1. Read a sample of answers. Open five to ten captured answers. Who gets named? How are you described? Inspect whether AI describes you accurately and favorably.
  2. Inspect the citations. Which sites do engines lean on? Do you see third-party pages, such as reviews or listicles? Inspect whether AI brings you up when no one names you, and which sources it relies on.
  3. Check competitors. Note who shows up where you don’t.
  4. Record decisions. Write down what you’ll change, who owns it, and when you’ll look again.

Keep your labels in a simple tracking sheet. In HubSpot AEO, you can use prompt groups to organize prompts by topic or brand, and filters to slice the results.

Pro tip: Keep a short “what we changed” log next to your weekly numbers. When visibility moves, you’ll know what to credit.

Use this before you share any report:

  • State the date range, engines, and number of answers behind each rate.
  • Name the denominator for every percentage (answers or prompts).
  • Report branded and unbranded rates separately.
  • Show the branded-to-unbranded ratio and its trend over four or more weeks.
  • Flag any change to the prompt library since the last report.
  • Show competitor share of voice for unbranded prompts.
  • List top cited domains and mark which are third-party.
  • Note the limits: answers vary, and some runs come back empty.
  • End with one decision or action per finding.

How HubSpot AEO Scales Prompt Tracking for Branded vs. Unbranded Queries

A spreadsheet works for 20 prompts. It gets painful when engines return hundreds of answers a month. This is where having an AEO tool comes in handy.

HubSpot AEO tracks the prompts you choose across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity.

Here’s how it lines up with the workflow in this guide:

All of this comes from HubSpot’s own setup and analysis documentation and product page.

In short, HubSpot AEO handles your routine tasks like running daily prompts. That leaves you free to focus on the decisions: which prompts to add, which gaps to close, and what to report.

What we like: You can see the score and the answer behind it, side by side. That makes it easy to double-check a number before you share it.

Pro tip: Branded vs. unbranded isn’t a built-in label in the tool. Put it in your prompt-naming convention and use prompt groups to keep the two sets apart. Then pull your two rates and compare them yourself.

If you use Marketing Hub Professional or Enterprise, you also get CRM-based prompt suggestions, so your starter list reflects your real customers. HubSpot AEO is still in beta, so check the knowledge base for current features and limits.

Ready to see where you stand? Start tracking your branded and unbranded prompts with theHubSpot AEO tool.

Frequently Asked Questions About Branded vs. Unbranded Queries

Still have questions? Here are the ones teams ask most when they start tracking.

How many prompts do I need per buyer-journey stage?

There’s no official number. Start with a handful per stage, enough to see a pattern but few enough to review by hand. Tool limits shape this too. HubSpot AEO’s standard limit is 25 prompts, and Marketing Hub Enterprise allows 50. With 25, you could assign about six to each of the four stages, then split each stage between branded and unbranded.

How often should I refresh my prompt library?

Review results weekly. QA the library monthly. Refresh it each quarter, or sooner if your products, audiences, or competitors change. For ideas on what’s shifting, see our roundup of SEO and AI trends.

Should I include product names in unbranded prompts?

No. In this guide, a product name counts as a brand variation. If a prompt includes one, it’s branded. The same goes for competitor names. Keep unbranded prompts to category, problem, and use-case words only.

How do I handle geography or segment differences?

Write separate prompts for each market or segment, and label each one. Don’t blend them. A buyer in Toronto and a buyer in Texas may get different answers. HubSpot AEO builds prompts from the product and ICP you select, so set those first. Then compare each segment only against its own history.

What if AI engines refuse to answer certain prompts?

Log it as a gap, not a zero. Runs repeat daily, so check whether the problem persists across several days. If an engine keeps refusing, the prompt may be too sensitive or too vague.
