Rewrite it neutrally, or retire it. In your report, count refused or empty runs separately, and say whether they’re excluded from the denominator. For more on how answers behave in practice, see our AI search experiments.

Keep track of both shoppers and queries.

Let’s jump back to our two shoppers. One asked about Nikes. The other asked for the best running shoe. But both were ready to buy. That’s why your business needs to stay on top of both branded and unbranded queries in AI search.

Now you have what you need to track both. You can tell the two prompt types apart. You know why blending them into one score hides your gaps. And you have a simple routine to follow. So don’t wait.

Start small. Pick a handful of prompts of each type, record your two rates, and watch the branded-to-unbranded ratio over time. Remember that AI answers vary, so look for trends across weeks rather than a single day.

Your regulars already know where to find you. The next customer is still asking questions. Make sure the answer includes you. HubSpot AEO is here to help keep you on track.

issues.title: Decision theatre or decision design?
issues.summary: AI has made information easy, but it has not made decisions simple. As machines produce more than we can read, our job is shifting from building knowledge to owning decisions. Are we ready? In a 2025 survey by BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab, 40% of US desk workers said they had received workslop in the previous month: AI-generated work that looks polished but does not move the tas
issues.author: Patrizia Bertini
issues.content_html:
AI has made information easy, but it has not made decisions simple. As machines produce more than we can read, our job is shifting from building knowledge to owning decisions. Are we ready?

In a 2025 survey by BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab, 40% of US desk workers said they had received workslop in the previous month: AI-generated work that looks polished but does not move the task forward. Respondents reported spending nearly two hours, on average, dealing with each incident.

Imagine a team of ten, each receiving one piece of workslop a month. That is roughly 20 hours, more than two working days, spent cleaning up someone else’s shortcut.

We have never produced so much data, so many documents, decks and summaries. And we have never produced so much digital waste.

This is a productivity problem, but it is also a symptom.

The question is not how much faster we can produce something. It is how much extra work that production creates for everyone else, and who is left to decide what any of it means.

How did we get here?

For most of human history, change moved slowly. Roughly ten thousand years separated the birth of farming from industrialisation. Evolution had time to move from one stage to the next, across centuries and generations.

Then the interval shrank. Only about two centuries separated the first factories from the rise of service and knowledge economies.

And then it shrank again. In 1969, ARPANET connected its first computers: the beginning of the information society. Less than sixty years later, AI agents use the knowledge we put online to make recommendations and, more and more… decisions.

Think about what we did in those sixty years. We created the bits. We built digital worlds and a digital culture. We ran digitalisation programmes. We put books online with Project Gutenberg, information online with Wikipedia. We worked hard to make information accessible and ubiquitous, on every channel, for everyone.

Without knowing it, we were laying the foundation for an artificial form of intelligence to learn from our human-built infrastructure, and to work on top of it.

The information society was basically the training ground for AI. Our knowledge is now the bridge between the old, human-driven world and a new, AI-empowered one.

This compression raises a pressing question.
How quickly can people, organisations and institutions adapt?

Does more information make us wiser?

Not on its own. And we have known that for a long time.

In information management, one of the best-known frameworks is the DIKW pyramid: Data, Information, Knowledge, Wisdom. It is usually credited to Russell Ackoff, who formalised it at the end of the 1980s.

The logic is simple:

  • Data: the raw elements. Facts and signals with no context.
  • Information: data that has been processed and organised.
  • Knowledge: information that has been interpreted and put to use.
  • Wisdom: knowledge that allows judgement.

Each level is built on the one below, but the relationship only works one way. As Steyn puts it, wisdom is always knowledge, but knowledge is not always wisdom. Every level is a subset of the one beneath it.

In 1987, Milan Zeleny proposed the same four levels in a language that organisations understand much better:

  • Know-nothing: data
  • Know-what: information
  • Know-how: knowledge
  • Know-why: wisdom

Read it from the bottom up: each level is built on the one below, but no amount of data adds up to wisdom on its own.

For Zeleny, managing efficiently means knowing how to do things. Managing effectively means knowing what to do. Managing wisely means knowing why. And wisdom goes one step further: it is what lets us compare and judge our know-how and our know-what.

I first wrote about this back in 2013, on LegoViews. Back then, the challenge was getting organisations to make time for that reflection.
Today it is harder. AI hands us endless know-what and know-how in seconds, and reflection, the step that turns them into a shared know-why, is exactly the one we are tempted to skip.

Here is the point that matters most today. Wisdom comes from knowledge, but it is not a sum of knowledge.

Adding knowledge to knowledge does not make wisdom. Processing more information does not make us wiser.

What does AI know, and what doesn’t it?

AI is extraordinary at the bottom of the pyramid. It processes data at a scale no team could match, and it turns that data into know-how: summaries, drafts, analyses, code.

What it cannot settle for us is which problem deserves attention, whose interests should count, and whether we should act on its answer.

These questions depend on context. They put the output into a broader frame: what we are trying to achieve, under which constraints, and why it matters. That frame is where knowledge gets judged.

The worrying part is how many people now trust good-looking information, mistake it for wisdom, and pass it on. Especially in the domains where critical thinking is the whole job.

And even the know-how needs checking. Large language models still add unsupported claims when they summarise a document they were given. On Vectara’s hallucination leaderboard, which tests this, rates in 2026 run from 1.8% to 24.2% of summaries, depending on the model. These are task-specific figures, not universal error rates. But they show how hard it is to rely on AI output that nobody reads closely.

So we have a base of data and good-looking information, produced at a volume that no human can manage.

What are we losing?

For most of my career, the journey from data to judgement had its own pace. And it was work, real work.

We collected an adequate amount of data. We prioritised. We designed studies around sampling and around the constraints we had: time, resources, our ability to analyse, the tools at hand. The constraints forced us to choose, and choosing forced us to think.

Today we are in the middle of a data feast. We access more and more data not because we need it, but because we can.

Slowly, we are creating working conditions in which there is less room to think, prioritise, sequence and distil. Less room for intentionality.

The philosopher John Searle described intentionality as the mind’s capacity to be about something (Intentionality, 1983). In organisations, it takes a more practical shape: the deliberate decision to focus attention and action on a clearly defined purpose. What we are trying to achieve, why it matters, and how our choices serve it.

It is made of a few simple things:

  • Awareness: knowing where we are and what we are looking at.
  • Context: understanding the situation and its variables.
  • Prioritisation: directing attention to what has the most impact.
  • Distillation: separating value from noise.

Without it, we stay in the noise. We consume data because we do not know where we are going, or where we should focus.

All the narratives are about speed. We are omitting the craft.

We stopped trusting the process because we only look at the output. But an output without a process is a simulacrum: something that looks good and has no substance.

What gives value to data and knowledge is not the shape of the output. It is the process that generated it and gave it substance.

Who decides?

AI can do a lot, and it does some things better than we do. But there is one thing it cannot do: be held accountable.

The idea is much older than generative AI. A slide said to come from a 1979 IBM internal training warned that “a computer can never be held accountable”, and concluded that a computer should therefore never make a management decision. The original has never been found in IBM’s archives, but the principle has aged remarkably well (more here).

Nearly fifty years later, regulation gives human oversight a concrete organisational form. Article 26(2) of the EU AI Act asks deployers of high-risk AI systems to assign human oversight to people with the necessary competence, training and authority, and to give them the support they need.

So let’s be clear.

An insurance claim. A loan. A place at a school. Access to benefits.

AI can support every one of these decisions. It can sort the files, flag the risks, summarise the evidence. But these decisions must not become a way for organisations to hide responsibility behind a system.

These decisions affect people’s fundamental rights. Behind each one there must be a human with a name, a role, the responsibility, the authority and the skills to make the decision, stand by it, defend it, and answer for the consequences.

That does not relieve the organisation of responsibility for the system, the workflow or the conditions in which that person is expected to decide.

AI can inform. It cannot own.

This is where the paradox emerges: we have the illusion that we are outsourcing more and more work. In reality, our job is becoming that of the AI supervisor: the person in charge of making AI-enabled decisions.

In one sentence: after we digitalised knowledge and built all the infrastructure, our role is no longer only to build knowledge. It is also to take responsibility for how that knowledge informs decisions.

We are moving from the information society to an age of accountability, where we need to embrace our humanity to make decisions about other humans.

Decision theatre or decision design?

Responsible AI needs humans in the loop. That much is agreed. But a human in the loop is not enough on their own.

Put a disengaged, overloaded or alienated person in front of an AI output and you get decision theatre: the illusion that a decision happened when it did not. Someone clicked “approve”. Nobody decided.

We have a decision-making crisis, and more AI output will deepen it unless something changes. Most organisations lack a decision-making operational layer to support the people who must make the decisions.

A real decision needs three conditions:

  • Skills: the competence and training to read the context, the variables and the pre-digested input, and to tell a valid answer from a well-formatted one.
  • Authority: a name, a role and a position that allow the person to override the AI, and the responsibility to own the result.
  • Process: workflows designed to empower decision makers, with the right information, tools and time, and without drowning them in decision fatigue.

Take one away and the decision collapses into theatre.

Who holds the judgement?

It is tempting to map Zeleny’s forms of knowing onto an organisational chart: leadership decides why, management decides what, operations deliver how. But Zeleny was describing forms of knowing, not ranks of people.

The mistake is to confuse the authority to make a decision with the knowledge needed to make it well. A frontline worker may have no say in strategy, yet can be the first to notice when a process is failing or a case does not fit the rules. Research on digitalised frontline work shows that this tacit knowledge and discretion still matter, even where systems automate parts of the process.

Automate that work without asking what judgement it holds, and the organisation loses more than a task.

Imagine a caseworker reviewing benefit claims flagged by an AI system.

In the theatre version, they get hundreds of cases a day. They see a risk score and two buttons. They have no time to open the file, and overriding the system needs their manager’s sign-off. They approve what the machine suggests. On paper, a human was in the loop.

In the designed version, they get fewer cases, prioritised by uncertainty. They see the sources behind each score and the points where the system is least confident. They can override it, and they record why. Their overrides go back to the team that runs the system, so recurring problems can be investigated and corrected.

Same person. Same AI. A completely different decision.

This is where design enters the scene. Somebody has to design these decision-making workflows: to enable, and indeed empower, humans to decide, and to avoid both decision fatigue and decision theatre.

What skills will the human in the loop need?

If humans are expected to own AI-supported decisions, we need to be clear about what that responsibility requires. We need humans who think as humans, not as machines.

What does that mean?

It means humans who understand the problem, the context and the domain. It means humans who understand the AI output and the process that produced it. It means humans who can separate the validity of the content from the polish of the form.

Three families of skills will matter most.

  • Critical judgement: being sceptical, spotting errors, asking where a claim comes from, and noticing what is missing as well as what is there.
  • Sense-making: taking the knowledge we have built and organising it into structures that increase accuracy, logic, relationships and reliability.
  • Human skills: the so-called soft skills, and the hardest to delegate. Empathy for the person on the other side of the decision. The courage to disagree with the machine. The integrity to sign your name under the result.

None of these is new. What is new is that they are no longer a nice-to-have on top of the “real” work.

They are the work.

How do we teach people to decide?

If these skills are the work, we need to teach them differently. People reviewing AI-supported decisions need practice in judging incomplete evidence, recognising exceptions, understanding the context and rules that apply, and explaining what they decided and why. Without that preparation, we risk creating a new assembly line: people processing recommendations and carrying responsibility for decisions they barely have time to examine.

This means rethinking curricula, in schools, universities and workplaces, around a few plain questions:

  • How do we analyse data to tell the what from the why?
  • How do we read a situation as a system, with its relationships, feedback loops and unintended consequences?
  • How do we decide under uncertainty, and how do we stand by that decision?
  • How do we notice when we are being asked to perform a decision rather than make one?

This is why we need much more teaching in complexity theory and systems thinking. Not as niche electives for a few specialists, but as the foundation for anyone who will sign their name under an AI-enabled decision.

In one word: we need to teach judgement.

What’s next

For years, many of us watched design thinking turn into design doing: more output, faster, with less and less time to think. AI can now do the doing faster than any of us.

This is the crossroads.

One road leads to more of the same. More outputs, more workslop, more decisions that only look like decisions.

The other road brings thinking back to the centre. Framing the problem. Understanding the context. Prioritising. Designing the process that turns AI output into a decision a human can own. This is design thinking applied to the most human act of all: deciding about other humans.

References

  • Ackoff, R. L. (1989). From data to wisdom. Journal of Applied Systems Analysis, 16, 3–9.
  • Searle, J. (1983). Intentionality: An Essay in the Philosophy of Mind. Cambridge University Press.
  • Zeleny, M. (1987). Management support systems: towards integrated knowledge management. Human Systems Management, 7(1), 59–70.

Thank you for reading. I write about design, systems and the human side of AI, and I work with organisations that want to get it right. You’ll find more of my work at PatriziaBertini.com.

Author’s Note: The ideas, the research and the arguments in this piece are human — mine. I used AI to help shape the form and structure, then went through every line myself. The images are AI-generated.

Decision theatre or decision design? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

issues.title: AI is the new old design material
issues.summary: A long workbench where hand tools, a stack of paper, and an open laptop share the same surface. Creative makers and builders have always learned their medium by working with it, from grinding pigments to HTML. Models are the next material, and you need to learn them by building. The field keeps arguing about whether designers should code, as if that question were new. It’s not new. Art and design
issues.author: Patrick Neeman
issues.content_html:
Creative makers and builders have always learned their medium by working with it, from grinding pigments to HTML. Models are the next material, and you need to learn them by building.

The field keeps arguing about whether designers should code, as if that question were new.

It’s not new.

Art and design have always been taught through materials, going back centuries.

In the 1390s, the painter Cennino Cennini wrote a handbook that’s still translated today on grinding pigments, and that history still runs through my own family as builders and creators. My mother, Jean Neeman, ground her own pigments as a conservator for the Los Angeles Museum of Art, the Getty and Hearst Castle, and I watched her repair Chinese statues that were over 600 years old with original materials to restore history.

She lived that craft, as I wrote in Everything I Know About UX I Learned From My Parents. I learned print through paste up, developing film for prints, and running film output.

I understand that knowing the material is a timeless need, and most designers I meet don’t understand it, because their tools hide it. We need to respect it as part of the craft.

The reality is that visual tools like Figma and Sketch are an abstraction, and real craft happens in the final mile, working with the material. Great designers have always used the materials they had, and I’ve always written code as part of the job to understand mine.

On the web, that meant HTML, CSS, Javascript and whatever else that made it work. Artificial intelligence is the new material, teaching the same lesson faster.

The designers doing the strongest work with models run them and read the output. That takes sampling code: a loop asking one question over and over until the model’s habits show.

Study the Bauhaus Workshops

In April 1919, Walter Gropius published the founding manifesto of the Bauhaus, and its demand was direct.

As art historian Magdalena Droste explains in The Bauhaus Manifesto, Gropius told architects, sculptors, and painters to turn to the crafts. The curriculum ended in a list of workshops. Students learned wood, metal, glass, and weaving by cutting, bending, and threading them.

Josef Albers made the point with almost nothing. In his preliminary course, Droste notes, students had to make a flat sheet of paper stand on its own, or bend a straight wire until it held its shape.

A drawing can suggest a chair, but only the wood can tell you where it will split.

That habit produced the school’s best-known work. Marcel Breuer headed the carpentry workshop and bent tubular steel into chairs, and Herbert Bayer went on to run the printing and advertising workshop.

They knew their materials because they had worked them. Every new medium since has sent designers back to a bench of some kind, and the last two benches have been made of code.

Hand-Code 1990s Web Pages

The web forced the same return, and it started with a blank file.

In the mid-1990s, the design tool for the web was a text editor: Notepad on Windows, SimpleText on the Mac. You typed tags, saved the file, and reloaded the browser to see what you’d made. My earliest web credit, the Oliver North home page, came out of that era.

Dedicated tools followed quickly, and each one moved the designer a step further from the markup:

  • BBEdit (1992), a Mac text editor that added HTML tools in 1994.
  • HoTMetaL (1994), an early HTML editor that showed where each tag began and ended.
  • PageMill (1995), Adobe’s visual editor for print designers.
  • FrontPage (1995), a visual editor that Microsoft bought in early 1996.
  • HomeSite (1996), a Windows editor built for people who wanted to write the HTML themselves.
  • Dreamweaver (1997), Macromedia’s visual editor.

The designers who got the most out of the visual editors still opened the code underneath. They trusted the canvas only after checking the page in more than one browser.

A visual editor showed one browser’s best case, and the markup showed the rest.

In 2000, John Allsopp wrote A Dao of Web Design for A List Apart, arguing that the control designers knew in print was a product of the printed page’s limits.

Ten years later, ethan marcotte opened Responsive Web Design with a quote from Allsopp. He built a sample page on a fluid grid with flexible images and media queries, then showed the layout changing shape as the window narrowed.

Responsive design came out of a designer’s style sheet, and no mockup would have found it.

Five years later, Frank Chimero gave the idea a name in The Web’s Grain, writing that “every material has a grain, including the web.” He argued that the field’s best techniques grew out of that grain, and that sites built against it come out fragile and awkward.

Test Model Output Variation

Models break the mockup in a new way. A static screen shows one answer, chosen by the designer and usually the good one. A model returns a different answer each time, and that spread is the thing you’re designing for. Call the chosen answer the one-sample mockup: a screen built around the output the model gives on its best day.

In legal tech, where we designed search and summarization, every summary in a mockup was correct, because a designer wrote it.

  • In 2017, Lars Erik Holmquist argued in Intelligence on Tap: Artificial Intelligence as a New Design Material that designers should treat the technology as a material with its own limits.
  • In UX Design Innovation: Challenges for Working with Machine Learning as a Design Material (2017), Graham Dove and colleagues surveyed UX practitioners. They suggested that machine learning had seen little design innovation, possibly because it was a new and difficult material.
  • Qian Yang’s 2020 dissertation at Carnegie Mellon University, Profiling Artificial Intelligence as a Material for User Experience Design, went further. It traced those difficulties to two roots: uncertainty about what a system can do, and the complexity of what it might output.
A mockup is one sample, and the product is the distribution.

The Doherty Threshold entry on UX Guidelines, my own reference site, puts the point where software starts to feel conversational under 400 milliseconds. A static frame can’t show a four-second wait.

Bret Victor built a whole talk, Inventing on Principle (2012), around the idea that creators need an immediate connection to what they create. You find the spread, the misses, and the delays only by running the model again and again.

Code Prototypes Against Models

Josh Clark tied the two eras together in his 2018 talk The New Design Material, calling machine learning “a design material in the same way that HTML and CSS is.”

In Addressing UX Practitioners’ Challenges in Designing ML Applications (2023), K. J. Kevin Feng and David W. McDonald of the University of Washington ran a study with 27 UX practitioners. Each got a tool to build and test simple models while designing an app.

Hands-on experimentation helped them match model behavior to user goals, invent interface features for correcting the model, and spot ethical risks. One participant explained that without testing, you don’t know “how often or in what ways it’s going to error.”

The authors located the bottleneck in fabrication, the stage where models get made, because designers are usually kept away from it. Their tool needed no code at all.

Today, for language models, a few lines of code are the shortest route to the same hands-on access. Geoffrey Litt saw it coming in Malleable software in the age of LLMs (2023), arguing that language models would let ordinary users build small tools from scratch.

Designers have kept themselves at arm’s length from the material, and that distance is the bottleneck they can no longer ignore.

That distance is closing. Figma’s 2026 AI report found that the share of designers participating in development doubled in a year, from 21% to 41%.

Tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Figma Make let a designer describe a prototype, wire it to a live model, and watch what breaks in a single sitting.

Not every designer agrees that code belongs in the job. Alan Cooper wrote in Should Designers Code? (2017) that “coding is not a skill necessary to be a top notch interaction designer.”

Karri Saarinen of Linear warned in Design Is More Than Code (2025) that production-first habits can erode the thinking behind a design. Both warnings are about code that ships.

Sampling code gets thrown away the same afternoon, and its only job is to show you the material.

Write AI Evaluation Sets

Sampling code doesn’t need to ship. It works like a test bench, and its most valuable output is a record of every case where the model broke the design. Wood doesn’t change its grain overnight, but a model can change with a single provider update.

Engineers already have a name for this file: an evaluation set. Designers are well placed to write it. They know which failures users notice first, like the answer that runs past the edge of its card or the wrong date stated with total confidence.

A design tuned to last month’s model can fail without a single pixel moving.

Four habits turn the record into working practice:

  • Call the model directly. Ask Claude Code or Cursor for a script that sends real product inputs to the model and prints the answers, and read them before you draw a screen.
  • Run each prompt 50 times. Sort the answers by length, tone, and accuracy, then design for the longest and the most wrong rather than the typical one.
  • Bring the spread to review. Put the two worst of the 50 answers beside the mockup in design review, and decide together which ones the screen must survive.
  • Save failures as test cases. Keep every output that broke a layout or misled a user in a shared file, so engineering reruns it whenever the model or prompt changes.

Run the Model First

Gropius moved students out of drawing rooms because drawings hid what materials would do.

Designers on the early web learned the same thing in a text editor, and Marcotte proved it with a working page. The debate over whether designers should code has always been a debate about the material and how close designers can get to it.

For artificial intelligence products, the material is the model’s behavior across thousands of inputs. You won’t find it in a frame on a canvas. You find it by running the model, reading everything that comes back, and keeping the failures somewhere the team can see them.

These days I describe my job as building, and that’s the reason: I can’t design how a model-backed product works until I’ve watched the model work.

Next time your team reviews an artificial intelligence feature, skip the one-sample mockup. Run the prompt 50 times, bring the worst answer to the review, and design the screen that survives it. Notice which answers the whole room argues about, because those are the cases a static mockup was hiding.

That’s the workshop now, and the door is open to anyone willing to write a few lines of sampling code.

AI is the new old design material was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

issues.content_html:
#​497 — November 13, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

Declarative Dragging — Rather than designing drag and drop interactions as needed, what if you could declare the possible outcomes and let a library work out the interaction? Dragology is an experimental React library for SVG interfaces that does just that. There are lots of demos to try.

Horowitz, Blinn, and Heer

Debug Errors and Agents Faster: Sentry Changelog Live — A walkthrough of what’s new for debugging errors and performance issues, including fixing production bugs with Seer and tracing the agents you build. Live Q&A. Nov 18, 10am PT. Save your spot.

Sentry sponsor

📊 e18e's Ongoing Benchmarks for JavaScript Meta-Frameworks — e18e is now benchmarking meta-frameworks like Next.js, Nuxt, and Astro on everything from install and build costs to SSR throughput, alongside Core Web Vitals data. Built with input from maintainers, the results can be tracked release by release and have already led to fixes in Nuxt, React, and Solid.

e18e Project

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Using Vite? A critical flaw allows remote code execution on dev servers exposed to the network with --host or server.host. Update to 8.3.7, 8.2.5, 8.1.7, 7.3.8 or 6.4.6.

  • Storybook 11 beta now has an official post. React projects get faster, more accurate component metadata, and there are type-safe stories and official skills for agents. The final release is due in December.

  • React's <form> docs now explain how to keep field values after an Action, and requestFormReset gets a reference page of its own.

UI SDK: Vercel and shadcn's Headless UI Behaviors Library — A low-level library of behaviors, like keyboard navigation, popups, drag and drop, that you compose into your own components. A core idea is to give a solid base for agents to build full components from. In beta, but you can get started now.

shadcn (Vercel)

How X is Rebuilding Its Web App with React, Relay and Vite — X/Twitter is replacing its decade-old client-rendered React app with a stack built around streaming SSR and Suspense. Lab tests show profiles displaying posts much sooner, and the hydration and chunking fixes make this an interesting case study.

Yagiz Nizipli (X)

📊 Six React Chart Libraries vs Hand-Written SVG – The results are close at native speed but with large gaps under CPU throttling or with large datasets. Pavel Gusev

📊 Remix v3 vs TanStack Start: Fast Pages, Thin Ecosystem – Comparing the same site built in React-free Remix v3 and TanStack Start. Jonathan Arnault (Marmelab)

📱 How Five Web Developers Built an iOS Keyboard Extension with Expo Anirudh Coontoor (Supernova)

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Text.js: React Apps That Render in the DevTools Console — Continuing the trend of rendering React apps everywhere, this new framework heads to DevTools as a host environment, supporting App Router-style routing, Suspense, keyboard input and ASCII fonts. Open the console on the page to see it in action!

Anomaly

Exact: A New Rust-Powered App Framework from Expo's Co-Founder — It isn't React as the UI is written in a small, constrained language called Contract that's designed specifically for agents to write and test, but 𝕏 Andrew Clark says it's "eerily similar" to what he thinks React 20 is shaping up to be.

Charlie Cheever

React Shepherd 8.0: Guided Tours for Apps, Now with a Leaner Engine — The React wrapper (React docs here) for Shepherd, a popular library for building step-based on-page tours. Note that it's AGPL, with a paid license for commercial use.

Ship Shape

  • EmbedPDF 3.0 – Powerful PDF viewer with a drop-in React component and a headless library for adding your own UI. (Demo.)

  • react-virtualized 10.0 – The original list and grid virtualization library, modernized. Now in TypeScript, built on function components, and requires React 18+.

  • 📱 React Native Audio API 1.0 – Software Mansion's Web Audio API for React Native goes stable. Adds spatial audio, and FFmpeg is now opt-in.

  • Mantine 9.8 – Adds an emoji picker package, plus new Diff, PhoneInput and week and quarter picker components.

  • BagUI – A shadcn/ui registry of blocks and templates for SaaS landing pages, like pricing and hero sections.

📰 Classifieds

🔍 Can ChatGPT and Claude read your React site? Run a free SEO and GEO scan with Fimo and see what they miss. By the Strapi team.

🎬 Stop approving mobile PRs nobody ran. An agent tests each one on Expo Simulators and puts the recording in the PR.

Build durable AI agents & workflows in TypeScript with Trigger.dev. If steps fail or code deploys, tasks pick up right where they left off.

📢 Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • Vectoys is a set of React components that render phones, laptops and other small 3D objects as SVG, with interactive HTML inside their screens. Could be handy for mockups or 'in-situ' teasers on your homepage.

  • 🤖 Chrome's Modern Web Guidance 1.0 is a set of skills that steer coding agents toward modern, Baseline-aware HTML and CSS. The team has also listed the 'top 10 things AI gets wrong' when building for the Web.

  • Need a clip of a component or animation for a PR or README? Paul Irish's chrome-capture tool can record a Chrome tab to an MP4 at 60fps with a single npx command.

  • 📊 The State of JavaScript 2026 survey is now open if you want to get involved.

issues.content_html:
#​496 — November 6, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

Discord Dropping Electron and React Native for a Rust Rewrite — Discord, one of React Native's best-known users, is moving away, with its CTO 𝕏 showing off a Rust desktop client built on GPUI using 290MB of RAM, with mobile keeping native UI over Rust code shared with the desktop client.

Tom Warren (The Verge)

▶️ Just prior to this reveal, Software Mansion interviewed Discord's Chas Jhin about how React Native development works at Discord's scale, in the ominously titled 'Maybe React Native Is Impossible'.

Run AI Coding Models on Your Own Machine — Local models are now good enough for everyday coding. Learn to run them on your own Mac or GPU, wire them into your editor and terminal agents, and keep your code private with no per-token bill.

Master.dev sponsor

A Roadmap for Redux Toolkit v2.x and 3.0 — Mark Erikson has laid out the roadmap for Redux (complete with a neat history lesson) with RTK 3.0 expected in six to eight months, going ESM-only with 'React 19-scale' breaking changes. But a run of 2.x releases will ship the groundwork first, starting with 2.14 this week.

Mark Erikson

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Update to Next.js 16.4.5 or 15.5.29, as appropriate: the November security release fixes seven advisories. Most are Cache Components bugs, so the post is worth reading.

  • 🤖 TanStack Query maintainer Dominik Dorfmeister says work on Query v6 can start once 'slop PRs' stop coming in and taking up his time, leading to a thread on the effects of AI-made contributions on maintainers.

  • Vercel is folding Next.js's Data Cache into Runtime Cache with bigger allocations but… new per-read and per-write pricing. Hobby teams migrate on November 29, but check the dates and prices for your use case.

  • Vercel builds also now block known-malicious npm package versions before and during install, on all plans and with no configuration needed.

Next.js is Prototyping Go(lang) Route Handlers — A merged experimental PR lets an App Router route be a route.go file exporting GET and friends, compiled by Turbopack and run in supervised Go-powered workers. Tim says Rust could follow along the same path.

Tim Neutkens (Vercel)

Understanding React Internals: A Deep Dive — A seven-part, source-grounded tour of React's internals that, unusually, starts from the server end before getting to fibers, lanes and the commit phase.

Alexandre Trotel

Amazon's React Native-Based Vega OS Hits 2.0 — Vega, the React Native-based OS behind newer Fire TV devices, is out of beta. SDK 2.0 takes apps from RN 0.72 to 0.83, bringing the React Compiler and Hermes v1 into play. The release notes go into more detail than the post.

Barak Schlosser (Amazon)

📄 Why We Finally Left Next.js for TanStack Start – Production memory leaks in two Next.js 16.3 releases were the last straw. Harrison Milbradt

📄 Writable Derived State: Stop Synchronizing State – Using clientData ?? serverData instead of a useEffect that wipes user edits on refetch. Corbin Crutchley

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Skullet: Skeleton Loading States Measured from Your Components — Hand it sample data and it renders your real component invisibly, measures everything, and draws a matching skeleton to reduce layout shifts when data arrives. The docs have a neat How it Works section explaining the technique.

Lochie Axon

Parcel 3 Alpha: A Rust Rewrite with React Compiler, Tailwind and RSC — Parcel's core is now a Rust binary with no Node dependency, and the team reports cold builds up to 100x faster than v2. React Compiler (opt-in), Tailwind and MDX are built in, with RSC support in beta.

Devon Govett (Parcel)

🤖 Reticle: Let Coding Agents Verify Their Changes Against Your Running App — A dev-only SDK and MCP server so coding agents can drive your running app, inspect network requests, application state, and console activity, and return a pass, fail or 'can't tell' verdict with what needs fixing.

Reticle Labs

react-resizable-panels Gets a VS Code-Style Workspace Component — Brian Vaughn's popular panel library now does dockable tabs you can drag to split or merge panes, and moved tabs keep their state rather than remounting. There's a live demo here.

Brian Vaughn

  • Preact 11.2 – Now has a runtime for React Compiler output via preact/compat, plus scoped custom element registries in shadow roots.

  • XState 6.0 Beta – "No further breaking changes are planned" for public APIs, and @xstate/react 7 is in beta alongside.

  • TanStack Redact 0.3 – The lightweight, synchronous-only React / React DOM replacement adds browser SPA plugins for Webpack and Rspack.

  • React Native 0.89 RC – Faster text layout and native module calls, legacy bridge APIs gone. Stable expected in December.

  • Storybook 11.0 Beta

📰 Classifieds

🤖 Fimo gives your marketers a visual editor and AI agents for SEO and GEO. No more tickets for your React devs. By the Strapi team.

QVAC allows you to run any AI capabilities for free, on your phone or laptop, privately. Try the QVAC SDK now on GitHub.

📢 Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • James Long has been reviving Prepack, Facebook's abandoned JavaScript partial evaluator. There's a React demo where a pretend site is server rendered three ways, by React, by Prepack's output (which essentially 'compiles' React away), and a hybrid, with the render times to compare.

  • Node.js 27 Alpha has landed, the first version using Node's new release process (where a release will spend six months in 'alpha' before going Current), while Node 26 is now the new LTS line.

  • Chrome 157 rolled out this week with HTML-in-Canvas now stable. It provides a way to draw real DOM elements into 2D, WebGL and WebGPU canvases. The demos are striking.

  • Vercel has released Geist Serif, a new serif font that shares metrics with Geist Sans so the two can mix cleanly. It's not on Google Fonts yet, but the geist npm package includes it.

issues.content_html:
#​495 — October 30, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

Putting MUI, Mantine, Ant Design
and React Spectrum Under Load

Den Odell wanted to see how popular design systems cope when you give them real work, so he timed ten of them, including MUI, Mantine, Ant Design and React Spectrum, and profiled the slowest cases. "Performance belongs on the design system team's priority list, next to accessibility," he says. Some highlights:

  • 📊 With the CPU slowed 4x, opening a 249-country dropdown took 84ms in Mantine and 134ms in Ant Design, but over 200ms in MUI and React Spectrum, both of which froze the UI past his 100ms budget.

  • 🔍 React Spectrum's problem was React Aria measuring options one at a time and forcing layout for each. Den filed an issue and a fix is in review.

  • ⚖️ Framework alone didn't decide the results as non-React Ionic was by far the slowest to open (1,266ms) yet was quick at checking 100 checkboxes, while MUI handled them in 70ms compared to Ant Design's 421ms.

  • 🧪 Want to try this on your own components? Den's Playwright tests are available on GitHub.

Agentic Mobile Development Needs Mobile AI Infrastructure — Your agent writes mobile screens fast. Getting them built and into the App Store is where it stalls. Expo is mobile AI infrastructure: native builds, store submits, over-the-air updates and workflows your agent can run. Start free.

Expo sponsor

TanStack Redact: A Smaller React for the Browser — A drop-in replacement for React/React DOM in the browser. Add it to your build config (Start, Vite, Vinext and Next.js are supported) and ship less JavaScript. But it renders synchronously, with no time slicing, so the compatibility guide is handy.

Tanner Linsley

💬 Does Redact pay off? On r/reactjs, commenters pondered who needs it and how it differs from Preact, while one tester found re-renders cost about twice the CPU across two production sites.

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Next.js has a security release scheduled for November 3, fixing seven medium-severity vulnerabilities. Advisories will be published with the patches.

  • Dan Abramov is fuzzing React's Flight protocol, the format behind Server Components, by streaming random value graphs through the real server and client. It's turned up six stream bugs and three writer bugs so far.

  • TanStack AI 1.0 is stable: a vendor-neutral AI toolkit with React hooks like useChat(), 23 provider adapters and MCP support.

  • 📱 React Native Windows 0.85 completes its move to the New Architecture, and there's more React Native on the desktop with Expo Desktop (an independent project – not by Expo) and Legend Spark for macOS.

React.lazy, Suspense and the Hidden 300ms Startup Delay — A lazy component can suspend on its first render even when its code is already loaded, and React can throttle reveals of suspended content to once every 300ms. Here's how one team traced the delay, and what fixed it.

Matthew Wong (Tab Widgets)

TanStack DB 1.0 RC1, and How 'Oracles' Found Its Bugs — The reactive client data layer is now API stable, but check the migration guide, as mutation handlers, hooks and errors have changed. Kyle explains how agents, checked against simple reference models, found many of the bugs fixed.

Kyle Mathews (TanStack)

🤖 Ship Less JavaScript in Next.js with Your AI Agent – A new skill hunts bundle bloat using Turbopack's module graph. Will Binns-Smith (Vercel)

📄 Porting 287,000 Lines of React to Foldkit in 3 Days – Focuses on how they built a harness to ensure visual and behavioral parity. David Granzin (Maple)

📄 Async React and Progressive Server Actions – How to keep server action forms working before hydration, even with optimistic UI. Jacob Ebey

📊 React Compiler in Next.js 16.4: Babel vs Rust, Benchmarked Waseem Anjum

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Puck 0.24: The Visual Page Editor for React — A drag-and-drop page editor you embed in your own app, using your own components. 0.24 lets you lay out a component's settings panel as you wish, improves drag and drop, and more. GitHub repo.

Fede Bonel Tozzi

react-window 2.5: Virtualized Lists That Scroll with the Page — Brian's long-standing virtualization library adds a scrollElement prop, so lists/grids can scroll along with the page or an ancestor, plus a headless useVirtualizer() for building your own virtualized layouts. Docs and demos.

Brian Vaughn

Vinext 1.4: The Vite-Powered Next.js Reimplementation Gets Faster — A Vite plugin that reimplements the Next.js API so you can deploy anywhere. 1.4 focuses on performance, with a Hacker News clone example now using 43% less server CPU per request vs 1.3, putting it slightly ahead of Next.js in that test.

James Anderson

  • OpenTUI 0.8 – Terminal UI library with React bindings that powers OpenCode. Now repaints only what changed each frame.

  • React Hook Form 7.91 – Lots of useFieldArray and async validation fixes, plus fewer re-renders. v8 is also now at beta 5.

  • React-Toastify 11.2 – Popular toast notification library. Now with theme="auto" to follow the OS color scheme.

  • emoji-picker-react 5.1 – Full-featured customizable emoji picker. Live demo.

🎃 And finally…

Halloween is almost upon us, so how about a round of Graveyard Pinball? It's built with React Three Fiber, with skulls, cauldrons and a skeleton mage. Its creator explains more about how it works here, including how the 3D table actually uses 2D physics.

issues.content_html:
#​494 — October 23, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

TanStack Start Reaches 1.0

After a year as a release candidate, TanStack Start 1.0 is officially stable. Tanner Linsley explains how it grew out of TanStack Router, and is candid about RSC, which felt like "this box we had to check to be taken seriously as a React framework", and which tanstack.com itself no longer uses. Plus:

  • 📊 The same app in Start and Next.js 16.4, benchmarked – Start handled 2.9x-8.6x more dynamic requests and built ~1.7x faster with type-checking included.

  • 🚚 Moving over? There are official guides for migrating from Next.js and from the RC. Sarthak Mishra moved his site over from Astro (and explains why) and Lovable offers older projects a migration option (here's how one went).

  • 💬 Ryan Carniato called it "a React metaframework with an architecture I can get behind", while in the r/reactjs thread Tanner explained why '1.0' is listed as 1.169 on npm.

TypeScript in the Age of AI — Knowing TypeScript deeply is how you get better code out of AI. Adam Rackis of Spotify shows you how to steer AI toward simpler, correct types and catch the mistakes it slips in.

Master.dev sponsor

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Last week, Next.js patched two critical RCEs, one rooted in React Server Components, and a public PoC is now out. Update Next.js to 16.4.1 or 15.5.28; for other RSC setups, update the react-server-dom-* packages to 19.3.1 (or 19.2.9/19.1.10/19.0.9).

  • React DevTools for agents now has official docs, covering how it exposes profiling and component data to coding agents through Chrome DevTools MCP.

  • 📱 Expo SDK 58 is out, using the new React Native 0.88, targeting iOS 27 and ready for the iPhone Duo on day one.

  • React Native for Web has active maintainers again and is moving to the React Foundation's GitHub org.

  • TypeScript 7.1 is now in beta, adding a programmatic API and more speed. Type-checking MUI's docs is 1.9x faster and uses half the memory.

Improving Navigation Experience in v0 with Next.js 16.4 — How the Next.js team used Partial Prefetching, intent-based prefetching and the new navigation() API to cut loading skeletons across its v0 AI app builder.

Aurora Scharff (Vercel)

React Only Where Needed: Owner's Next.js to Astro Move — Owner's 10,000+ restaurant sites now run on Astro and Cloudflare Workers, keeping React for interactive islands. Menu-page p75 LCP went from 5.4s to 0.7s.

Selden and Hanford (Owner)

Dead Code Shouldn't Exist — The slides and transcript from a popular talk Dominik has given at several conferences this year on how Sentry removed 28K lines of unused code with Knip.

Dominik Dorfmeister

🤖 Testing AI-Generated Code: Lint the Pattern, Test the Decision – Structural lint rules and shared harnesses beat a test beside every component. Robin Wieruch

📱 Apple Didn't Invent the Foldable. It Might Make You Support One. – Getting a React Native app ready for the iPhone Duo's three compatibility tiers. Sean Barker (Infinite Red)

📄 Loading a 9MB WebAssembly Module Earlier Made Recraft's Editor 17% Faster – Suspending components left the module's download waiting its turn in the React tree. Sergey Patrakeev (Recraft)

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Pixel: Build Graphical Applications in the Terminal — Like Ink, but with "pixel perfect" graphics. It's a React renderer that draws rounded corners, gradients and proper fonts in terminals that support the Kitty graphics protocol, and that can even embed Chromium WebViews to run web apps in a pane(!)

Rob Pruzan (Zenbu Labs)

TanStack Hotkeys Beta: A Type-Safe Library for Keyboard Shortcuts — Hotkeys takes care of the fiddly, cross-platform edge cases of keyboard shortcuts, sequences, and user-recorded hotkeys. The beta adds scopes, so that, say, a dialog's Escape doesn't close the panel behind it. Try the demo on the homepage.

TanStack

React Router 8.5 Hands View Transitions Over to React — Its own view transition APIs are deprecated in favor of React 19.3's <ViewTransition>. Migrating starts with wrapping an <Outlet> and removing the old props and state styling. There's also an unstable 'API-only' mode that serves static HTML but keeps a server for loaders and actions.

Remix Team

issues.title: Embrace Your Obsessions: Susan Orlean on the Antidote to the Meaninglessness of Life

issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
Every great book, whatever its subject or genre or style, is about one thing only: the eternal question of what gives meaning to our tiny, transient lives. And every answer given, however faintly whispered, points to one thing only: the quality of attention we pay to those lives.

If attention is the lever of love, the particular — the sacred specificity of something small and singular, something easy to overlook — is its fulcrum. “Love quells fear,” Octavia Butler wrote in contemplating creativity, “and a sweet and powerful positive obsession blunts pain, diverts rage, and engages each of us in the greatest, the most intense of our chosen struggles.” Our highly clinical culture, with its tendency to pathologize the tendrils of personality that make us who we are, regards obsession as unambiguously negative — something that kidnaps us from the actuality of life. And yet all the creative energy that has given us our greatest works of art and most revolutionary breakthroughs in science has sprung from such a “powerful positive obsession.”

Susan Orlean takes up this question in her 1994 classic The Orchid Thief: A True Story of Beauty and Obsession (public library). One answer to what we long for in our existential longing, she posits, may be “to know what it feels like to care about something passionately” — to have an obsession, something very particular to which you pay rigorous and rapturous attention.

When she asks her protagonist what it is about orchids he finds so irresistible, how it is they are the animating passion of his life, he shrugs:

Oh, mystery, beauty, unknowability, I suppose… I think the real reason is that life has no meaning. I mean, no obvious meaning. You wake up, you go to work, you do stuff. I think everybody’s always looking for something a little unusual that can preoccupy them and help pass the time.

Often, it is not we who find that unusual something but it that finds us, jolts us awake from the stupor of near-living. Considering her own obsession with telling the story of the orchid thief, which had begun with a random article she read in a newspaper on a random day and ended up consuming years of her life, she observes how these obsessions take hold of us:

[It begins with] some glimpse of life that expands like those Japanese paper balls you drop in water and then after a moment they bloom into flowers, and the flower is so marvelous that you can’t believe there was a time when all you saw in front of you was a paper ball and a glass of water.

As Susan finds herself traveling through the vastness of Florida in the footsteps of the orchid thief, she comes to see these obsessions as our most powerful antidote to the hollow feeling of meaninglessness that visits upon every life — against the overwhelming bigness of life, we have the saving grace of smallness:

The land was marble-smooth and it rolled without a pucker to the horizon. My eyes grazed across the green band of ground and the blue bowl of sky and then lingered on a dead tire, a bird in flight, an old fence, a rusted barrel. Hardly any cars came toward me, and I saw no one in the rearview mirror the entire time. I passed so many vacant acres and looked past them to so many more vacant acres and looked ahead and behind at the empty road and up at the empty sky; the sheer bigness of the world made me feel lonely to the bone. The world is so huge that people are always getting lost in it. There are too many ideas and things and people, too many directions to go. I was starting to believe that the reason it matters to care passionately about something is that it whittles the world down to a more manageable size. It makes the world seem not huge and empty but full of possibility.

Nothing counterbalances our helpless givens and shapes our lives more powerfully than our relationship to possibility. To be overwhelmed is to be paralyzed by possibility. To be obsessed it to be catalyzed by it. Whatever the obsession is one of collecting or creating, whatever form it takes — orchids or oboe, birds or baking, writing or trapeze — it is a way of centering into our only task here: to fill our allotted days with maximum aliveness.

issues.title: Yes to Life, in Spite of Everything: Viktor Frankl’s Lost Lectures on Moving Beyond Optimism and Pessimism to Find the Deepest Source of Meaning
issues.summary: "Everything depends on the individual human being, regardless of how small a number of like-minded people there is... on each person... creatively making the meaning of life a reality in his or her own being."
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
“Everything depends on the individual human being, regardless of how small a number of like-minded people there is… on each person… creatively making the meaning of life a reality in his or her own being.”

“To decide whether life is worth living is to answer the fundamental question of philosophy,” Albert Camus wrote in his classic 119-page essay The Myth of Sisyphus in 1942. “Everything else… is child’s play; we must first of all answer the question.”

Sometimes, life asks this question not as a thought experiment but as a gauntlet hurled with the raw brutality of living.

That selfsame year, the young Viennese neurologist and psychiatrist Viktor Frankl (March 26, 1905–September 2, 1997) was taken to Auschwitz along with more than a million human beings robbed of the basic right to answer this question for themselves, instead deemed unworthy of living. Some survived by reading. Some through humor. Some by pure chance. Most did not. Frankl lost his mother, his father, and his brother to the mass murder in the concentration camps. His own life was spared by the tightly braided lifeline of chance, choice, and character.

A mere eleven months after surviving the unsurvivable, Frankl took up the elemental question at the heart of Camus’s philosophical parable in a set of lectures, which he himself edited into a slim, potent book published in Germany in 1946, just as he was completing Man’s Search for Meaning.

As our collective memory always tends toward amnesia and erasure — especially of periods scarred by civilizational shame — these existential infusions of sanity and lucid buoyancy fell out of print and were soon forgotten. Eventually rediscovered — as is also the tendency of our collective memory when the present fails us and we must lean for succor on the life-tested wisdom of the past — they are now published in English for the first time as Yes to Life: In Spite of Everything (public library).

Frankl begins by considering the question of whether life is worth living through the central fact of human dignity. Noting how gravely the Holocaust disillusioned humanity with itself, he cautions against the defeatist “end-of-the-world” mindset with which many responded to this disillusionment, but cautions equally against the “blithe optimism” of previous, more naïve eras that had not yet faced this gruesome civilizational mirror reflecting what human beings are capable of doing to one another. Both dispositions, he argues, stem from nihilism. In consonance with his colleague and contemporary Erich Fromm’s insistence that we can only transcend the shared laziness of optimism and pessimism through rational faith in the human spirit, Frankl writes:

We cannot move toward any spiritual reconstruction with a sense of fatalism such as this.

Generations and myriad cultural upheavals before Zadie Smith observed that “progress is never permanent, will always be threatened, must be redoubled, restated and reimagined if it is to survive,” Frankl considers what “progress” even means, emphasizing the centrality of our individual choices in its constant revision:

Today every impulse for action is generated by the knowledge that there is no form of progress on which we can trustingly rely. If today we cannot sit idly by, it is precisely because each and every one of us determines what and how far something “progresses.” In this, we are aware that inner progress is only actually possible for each individual, while mass progress at most consists of technical progress, which only impresses us because we live in a technical age.

Insisting that it takes a measure of moral strength not to succumb to nihilism, be it that of the pessimist or of the optimist, he exclaims:

Give me a sober activism anytime, rather than that rose-tinted fatalism!

How steadfast would a person’s belief in the meaningfulness of life have to be, so as not to be shattered by such skepticism. How unconditionally do we have to believe in the meaning and value of human existence, if this belief is able to take up and bear this skepticism and pessimism?

[…]

Through this nihilism, through the pessimism and skepticism, through the soberness of a “new objectivity” that is no longer that “new” but has grown old, we must strive toward a new humanity.

Sophie Scholl, upon whom chance did not smile as favorably as it did upon Frankl, affirmed this notion with her insistence that living with integrity and belief in human goodness is the wellspring of courage as she courageously faced her own untimely death in the hands of the Nazis. But while the Holocaust indisputably disenchanted humanity, Frankl argues, it also indisputably demonstrated “that what is human is still valid… that it is all a question of the individual human being.” Looking back on the brutality of the camps, he reflects:

What remained was the individual person, the human being — and nothing else. Everything had fallen away from him during those years: money, power, fame; nothing was certain for him anymore: not life, not health, not happiness; all had been called into question for him: vanity, ambition, relationships. Everything was reduced to bare existence. Burnt through with pain, everything that was not essential was melted down — the human being reduced to what he was in the last analysis: either a member of the masses, therefore no one real, so really no one — the anonymous one, a nameless thing (!), that “he” had now become, just a prisoner number; or else he melted right down to his essential self.

In a sentiment that bellows from the hallways of history into the great vaulted temple of timeless truth, he adds:

Everything depends on the individual human being, regardless of how small a number of like-minded people there is, and everything depends on each person, through action and not mere words, creatively making the meaning of life a reality in his or her own being.

Frankl then turns to the question of finding a sense of meaning when the world gives us ample reasons to view life as meaningless — the question of “continuing to live despite persistent world-weariness.” Writing in the post-war pre-dawn of the golden age of consumerism, which has built a global economy by continually robbing us of the sense of meaning and selling it back to us at the price of the product, Frankl first dismantles the notion that meaning is to be found in the pursuit and acquisition of various pleasures:

Let us imagine a man who has been sentenced to death and, a few hours before his execution, has been told he is free to decide on the menu for his last meal. The guard comes into his cell and asks him what he wants to eat, offers him all kinds of delicacies; but the man rejects all his suggestions. He thinks to himself that it is quite irrelevant whether he stuffs good food into the stomach of his organism or not, as in a few hours it will be a corpse. And even the feelings of pleasure that could still be felt in the organism’s cerebral ganglia seem pointless in view of the fact that in two hours they will be destroyed forever. But the whole of life stands in the face of death, and if this man had been right, then our whole lives would also be meaningless, were we only to strive for pleasure and nothing else — preferably the most pleasure and the highest degree of pleasure possible. Pleasure in itself cannot give our existence meaning; thus the lack of pleasure cannot take away meaning from life, which now seems obvious to us.

He quotes a short verse by the great Indian poet and philosopher Rabindranath Tagore — the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize, Einstein’s onetime conversation partner in contemplating science and spirituality, and a man who thought deeply about human nature:

I slept and dreamt
that life was joy.
I awoke and saw
that life was duty.
I worked — and behold,
duty was joy.

In consonance with Camus’s view of happiness as a moral obligation — an outcome to be attained not through direct pursuit but as a byproduct of living with authenticity and integrity — Frankl reflects on Tagore’s poetic point:

So, life is somehow duty, a single, huge obligation. And there is certainly joy in life too, but it cannot be pursued, cannot be “willed into being” as joy; rather, it must arise spontaneously, and in fact, it does arise spontaneously, just as an outcome may arise: Happiness should not, must not, and can never be a goal, but only an outcome; the outcome of the fulfillment of that which in Tagore’s poem is called duty… All human striving for happiness, in this sense, is doomed to failure as luck can only fall into one’s lap but can never be hunted down.

In a sentiment James Baldwin would echo two decades later in his superb forgotten essay on the antidote to the hour of despair and life as a moral obligation to the universe, Frankl turns the question unto itself:

At this point it would be helpful [to perform] a conceptual turn through 180 degrees, after which the question can no longer be “What can I expect from life?” but can now only be “What does life expect of me?” What task in life is waiting for me?

Now we also understand how, in the final analysis, the question of the meaning of life is not asked in the right way, if asked in the way it is generally asked: it is not we who are permitted to ask about the meaning of life — it is life that asks the questions, directs questions at us… We are the ones who must answer, must give answers to the constant, hourly question of life, to the essential “life questions.” Living itself means nothing other than being questioned; our whole act of being is nothing more than responding to — of being responsible toward — life. With this mental standpoint nothing can scare us anymore, no future, no apparent lack of a future. Because now the present is everything as it holds the eternally new question of life for us.

Frankl adds a caveat of tremendous importance — triply so in our present culture of self-appointed gurus, self-help demagogues, and endless podcast feeds of interviews with accomplished individuals attempting to distill a universal recipe for self-actualization:

The question life asks us, and in answering which we can realize the meaning of the present moment, does not only change from hour to hour but also changes from person to person: the question is entirely different in each moment for every individual.

We can, therefore, see how the question as to the meaning of life is posed too simply, unless it is posed with complete specificity, in the concreteness of the here and now. To ask about “the meaning of life” in this way seems just as naive to us as the question of a reporter interviewing a world chess champion and asking, “And now, Master, please tell me: which chess move do you think is the best?” Is there a move, a particular move, that could be good, or even the best, beyond a very specific, concrete game situation, a specific configuration of the pieces?

What emerges from Frankl’s inversion of the question is the sense that, just as learning to die is learning to meet the universe on its own terms, learning to live is learning to meet the universe on its own terms — terms that change daily, hourly, by the moment:

One way or another, there can only be one alternative at a time to give meaning to life, meaning to the moment — so at any time we only need to make one decision about how we must answer, but, each time, a very specific question is being asked of us by life. From all this follows that life always offers us a possibility for the fulfillment of meaning, therefore there is always the option that it has a meaning. One could also say that our human existence can be made meaningful “to the very last breath”; as long as we have breath, as long as we are still conscious, we are each responsible for answering life’s questions.

With this symphonic prelude, Frankl arrives at the essence of what he discovered about the meaning of life in his confrontation with death — a central fact of being at which a great many of humanity’s deepest seers have arrived via one path or another: from Rilke, who so passionately insisted that “death is our friend precisely because it brings us into absolute and passionate presence with all that is here, that is natural, that is love,” to physicist Brian Greene, who so poetically nested our search for meaning into our mortality into the most elemental fact of the universe. Frankl writes:

The fact, and only the fact, that we are mortal, that our lives are finite, that our time is restricted and our possibilities are limited, this fact is what makes it meaningful to do something, to exploit a possibility and make it become a reality, to fulfill it, to use our time and occupy it. Death gives us a compulsion to do so. Therefore, death forms the background against which our act of being becomes a responsibility.

[…]

Death is a meaningful part of life, just like human suffering. Both do not rob the existence of human beings of meaning but make it meaningful in the first place. Thus, it is precisely the uniqueness of our existence in the world, the irretrievability of our lifetime, the irrevocability of everything with which we fill it — or leave unfulfilled — that gives our existence significance. But it is not only the uniqueness of an individual life as a whole that gives it importance, it is also the uniqueness of every day, every hour, every moment that represents something that loads our existence with the weight of a terrible and yet so beautiful responsibility! Any hour whose demands we do not fulfill, or fulfill halfheartedly, this hour is forfeited, forfeited “for all eternity.” Conversely, what we achieve by seizing the moment is, once and for all, rescued into reality, into a reality in which it is only apparently “canceled out” by becoming the past. In truth, it has actually been preserved, in the sense of being kept safe. Having been is in this sense perhaps even the safest form of being. The “being,” the reality that we have rescued into the past in this way, can no longer be harmed by transitoriness.

In the remainder of the slender and splendid Yes to Life, Frankl goes on to explore how the imperfections of human nature add to, rather than subtract from, the meaningfulness of our lives and what it means for us to be responsible for our own existence. Complement it with Mary Shelley, writing two centuries ago about a pandemic-savaged world, on what makes life worth living, Walt Whitman contemplating this question after surviving a paralytic stroke, and a vitalizing cosmic antidote to the fear of death from astrophysicist and poet Rebecca Elson, then revisit Frankl on humor as lifeline to sanity and survival.

issues.title: How to Hear the Song of Life
issues.summary: “When we have learned how to listen to trees,” Hermann Hesse wrote in one of his least known, most beautiful essays, “then the brevity and the quickness and the childlike hastiness of our thoughts achieve an incomparable joy. issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
“When we have learned how to listen to trees,” Hermann Hesse wrote in one of his least known, most beautiful essays, “then the brevity and the quickness and the childlike hastiness of our thoughts achieve an incomparable joy. Whoever has learned how to listen to trees no longer wants to be a tree. He wants to be nothing except what he is. That is home. That is happiness.”

To be ourselves is rooted in the recognition that, rather than a tree, a self is a forest; to be at home in the world is rooted in the recognition that a forest is a self. While indigenous cultures have known this since the dawn of knowledge, we are only just beginning to unlearn everything we have been taught by the erasure of our creaturely belonging that we call civilization in order to remember what we were born knowing: Life and its rights are not something we can claim for ourselves unless we accord them to everything else that exists, bound to us by the mesh of mutuality that makes this drifting rock a living world.

In 2021, Ecuador led the way in this great unlearning by granting the Los Cedros Cloud Forest legal rights of personhood: the right to exist and flourish in the future.

Five years later, four pioneers of the rippling rights-of-nature movement have joined forces with the forest itself to celebrate the landmark decision, as Copernican in the history of our civilization as the Cambridge Declaration of Consciousness: Robert Macfarlane (who has asked the urgent, self-answering question “Is a river alive?” and who remains the closest thing to a Rachel Carson of our time), Giuliana Furci (who has changed not only how we think about nature with her Fungi Foundation work but the very container of our thoughts, language, coining the word funga, now inducted into the Cambridge Dictionary, to stand alongside flora and fauna in our classification of the living world), César Rodríguez-Garavito (whose legal scholarship and activism have anchored the rights-of-nature movement), and Cosmo Sheldrake (who has devoted his life to turning the soundscapes of the living world into music). That they have named the Los Cedros Cloud Forest itself as co-author is both a radical gesture — a first in the history of literature — and a kind of homecoming to an elemental reality our sciences are only just beginning to confirm: that we think not with the brain but with the world, that place and personhood are indelibly entwined, that life is a song singing us back to ourselves so that when we die we may be sung across the threshold into the rhizomatic everythingness of everything.

Illustrated by Ecuadorian artist Paula Terán Ospina, Song of the Cedars is a painted serenade to what the cloud forest can teach us about the song of life: about the time of stones, about the wisdom of rivers, about the creative tenacity of fungi.

It is a project breathtakingly beautiful in spirit and in matter, the song sung along the river that carries the ecosystem and unfolds like a paper harmonica to carry the words that break the civilizational spell of indifference with enchantment.

Trees speak in your leaves please
And streams tell me your dreams

Birds sing me your rhymes please
And stones teach me your times

Earth cover my limbs now
And mold thrive on my skin

Clouds deepen my sight please
And storms lend me your light

The back matter, following five short essays by the different contributors, is a painted encounter with the cloud forest’s wonderland of flora, fauna, and funga — 81 creatures each identified by their common and Linnaean names, occupying every niche and scale of existence, from the fierce ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) to the tender rosy flannel moth (Trosia neigropunetigera), from the air plant hovering ethereal midway between the canopy and the ground to the lichen clinging to the rocks more tenaciously than gravity itself.

Beholding this loving song of life, I am struck by what a rare achievement it is in this culture to teach without preaching, to protest not with militancy but with tenacious tenderness, to remember that care is a stronger and longer lever of change than complaint, that how we show up for the summons of conscience, as individuals and as a civilization, is the deepest measure of who and what we are.

issues.title: 🔮 The $22 billion question about AI self-improvement #610
issues.summary: Plus: Cheap solar, who pays for Claude & DNA immunotherapy++
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
It’s simply the best, data-rich source for the money on how AI is reshaping the economy. — Matt G., a paying member

Subscribe now

My AI agent bought an iPhone for me this week. For an Uber, I’d still reach for the app.

That’s where we start today – I look at which jobs are worth handing over to AI, and why more Brits are paying for Claude. We’ll also look at what cheaper renewable power still needs and whether AI self-improvement owes more to intelligence or a massive research budget.

If you’re a member of Exponential View, join me in the subscriber chat:

Claude Britannia

Brits are spending more and more on AI. One in twenty adults in the UK pays for AI, spending more than $1.3 billion a year. Five percent is early days, but it is a fast ramp – it was 1% two years ago, and 2.5% a year ago. London is the hotspot; the professional skew is predictable, with those involved in tech, finance, education, and PR. And we are increasingly falling for Claude. Its share has quadrupled in a year.1 Was the trigger the improved harness on Claude Cowork?

Separately, made his first purchase using his Instinct agent, sweaters for winter. My Instinct agent secured my iPhone Duo for me on Tuesday. ’s agent booked a squash court for a showdown with . We’re playing around with them and finding them quite useful.

But in general, agent-based shopping is still early. Uber says four rides out of 320 million during Halloween week were booked by agents. I’m not sure I’d use an agent to book an Uber yet; hitting the app is easier. But getting an iPhone Duo, which involved checking Apple’s website every few minutes from 7 am, is a perfect job for them. So is finding finicky, complicated products like surge-protected power extensions, medicine pouches, or, in Will’s case, woolly jumpers.

Subscribe now

Fair-weather friends

The technology is doing its bit. Adding wind to solar and batteries cuts the median cost from $105 to $86 per MWh. North of Milan and Montreal (yes, they are on the same latitude), it falls from $164 to $99. Based on hourly modeling over ten years, and reckon that sun and wind mostly cover for each other – except for a difficult combined lull for about a week every four.

Ember also finds that 83% of the 750GW of fossil plants being planned sit where reliable renewables (with a bit of gas backup) cost under $100/MWh (which is roughly implied with oil at $60 a barrel).

My take is that technology costs will keep falling, and those that haven’t yet benefited from reductions (like panel installations) will start to yield as robotics improve. But redesigning the grid into a largely renewable-based one also requires more than better technology. It’ll need both a better cost of capital (gas plants still find capital cheaper than solar) and financial instruments that match energy prices to the volatility renewable-based energy brings.

issues.title: 🔮 What does it cost to make a worker?
issues.summary: Some early sketches of the economics of manufactured intelligence
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Azeem’s sketchbook is an experimental format we’re trialing for paying members, where we share raw research notes, early frameworks, and unfinished ideas that haven’t been fully polished. They are the earliest indication of what I’m thinking through.

Here is another peek into my sketchbook. I’m trying to understand the economic trade-off between getting work done by an AI or a human. One way of doing this is to look at tasks in the economy and see how much it costs a human to do them compared to a machine.

Another way is to view the worker as an entity the economy needs, and to consider the minimum cost of creating one. (Of course, humans are much more than that, but I’m limiting the frame purely to economics here.) Those costs include the parenting, educating, and feeding from bairn to adult. We can then compare that to the cost of bringing in a machine capable of doing the same types of work using AI.

AI is manufactured intelligence. That is not the same intelligence that we humans have, but it’s clearly something that looks like intelligence.

While it is being manufactured, it’s highly replicable and follows the classic learning curve I described in my first book. And in my forthcoming second book, I extend these ideas.

Economically useful human intelligence is created very differently. It takes much longer than making a chip, and you don’t know the outcome for a long time.
